#5597. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5596. Anthropic Claude AI Predicts an Unbelievable XRP Q4 Move

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts a frankly insane XRP price target by January 1, 2027. Somewhere in its notes, there’s a number. It’s a market cap in the trillions, contingent on a hypothetical catalyst for Ripple that could see it flip Ethereum as the market’s second-largest digital asset.

XRP price is sitting around $1.29, after drifting down from a roughly $1.50 open. Spot ETF inflows have dried up, sentiment is sleepy, and the next support level is $1.25. That’s what makes it the perfect time for an out-there prediction.

It’s the first week of December. After a closed-door summit, a coalition of G20 central banks announces in a joint communiqué that its cross-border CBDC settlement network will use the XRP Ledger as its neutral bridge layer.

XRP is named the default bridge asset for settling between currencies without a direct corridor. Think of it as the “SWIFT moment” XRP maximalists have dreamed about for a decade, except it happens in public, with official signatures, and with no hedge language.

How likely is it? Very unlikely. Central banks move at the speed of committees, and sovereigns dislike depending on assets they don’t control. But it’s not physically impossible, which is the whole game here.

Then the dominoes fall. Treasury desks scramble for liquidity, sovereign wealth funds ask their prime brokers an awkward question about “operational inventory,” and a market with roughly 62 billion tokens in circulation meets demand it has never seen.

On the weekly chart, XRP has spent months coiling between $1.25 support and a $1.57–$1.70 supply zone, which is a textbook compression pattern. Right now, the 50-day EMA sits below the 200-day, so the chart looks bearish.

In this scenario, that death cross turns into the most-hated bull trap in history. A weekly close above $1.70 would trigger stop-loss cascades from shorts, and reclaiming the $3.65 all-time high would leave the chart with no overhead resistance and no historical sellers to absorb the move.

Measuring the height of the multi-year base and projecting it upward gives a first target near $9. Fibonacci extensions from the 2025 cycle high, stretched into price discovery, put the 1.618 and 2.618 levels in double digits.

Momentum indicators would sit pinned in “overbought” for weeks, which is exactly how parabolic markets behave. Meanwhile, volume would explode, and the usual rule that overbought means sell would stop working.

#5595. Project-by-project security reviews can’t keep pace with enterprise AI agents

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are finding that tokenization and other data protection methods now decide how fast those projects move.

But sensitive data fed into models is hard to pull back — and security reviews built for a slower era are stalling deployments. The challenge is shifting from locking data down to keeping it usable once it is protected. That tension is playing out across Cloudera Inc.’s partner ecosystem, where security is becoming a prerequisite for AI value rather than a final gate, according to Diego Loureda (pictured), vice president of customer success and presales at Protegrity USA Inc.

“Data leaks are still a thing. If you put sensitive data on a model, if you put sensitive data on a vector store or in the memory of an agent that is going to propagate to other agents, good luck removing that sensitive data,” Loureda said. “There’s no way you’re going to be able to do that.”

Loureda spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed data security along with Protegrity being named Cloudera’s Emerging Technology Partner of the Year. (* Disclosure below.)

Traditional encryption can lock data so tightly that analysts and models can no longer use it. Protegrity centers its approach on tokenization, which swaps sensitive values for substitutes instead of relying on a mathematical algorithm, Loureda explained. That design also matters as quantum computing threatens today’s cryptography.

“Our main method of protection, that is tokenization, it’s already quantum ready,” Loureda said. “The reason behind that is because there is no mathematical algorithm behind it. It’s all based on replacement in memory.”

Protection alone doesn’t solve the speed problem, however. In research Protegrity commissioned from Enterprise Management Associates Inc., 83% of leaders reported project delays, Loureda noted.

“The main problem with governance is that companies are approving projects and that will not scale in the age of AI,” Loureda said. “They have to approve patterns.”

The same study found 82% of leaders push agents into production in a diminished state, stripped of the tools and data that would make them useful, he added. Controls such as tokenization let security teams clear the way for those agents instead, according to Loureda.

“Security has always been the business of no, the department of no. That changes now,” he said. “These days security is the team that can enable AI to give you value.”

#5594. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5593. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5592. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5590. Court Report: NAR Fires Back in Compass Subpoena Spat; Keller Williams Sued for ‘Junk Fees’

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

NAR defends Compass subpoena in private listing lawsuit

The latest dust-up in the battle between now defunct PLS.com and the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) continues, as both parties await a judge’s decision on whether Compass can be compelled to provide witness and other evidence in the case.

Last week, a filing from NAR’s attorneys outlines the association’s opposition to a motion—by Compass, which is a non-party in the case—to quash subpoenas issued by NAR.

Within the memorandum, NAR argues that “Compass wants to supply PLS a friendly Compass witness while simultaneously, and blanketly, refusing to produce any documents for fair cross-examination. That hand-picked witness is Compass’s Chief Strategy Officer, Ashton Alexander.”

After significant back-and-forth, it appeared that NAR had dropped its demand to depose Compass CEO Robert Reffkin, but the two sides continue to wrangle over other witnesses—including rank-and-file Compass agents—as well as document requests that Compass has described as overly broad and “burdensome.”

“As outlined in our court filing, the petitioners cannot provide a witness to testify in support of PLS while simultaneously refusing to produce documents necessary for NAR to fairly cross-examine its witness,” an NAR spokesperson told RISMedia.

The association also argues that through various email threads, Reffkin and Alexander coordinated with PLS co-founder Mauricio Umansky in a “quest” against NAR’s Clear Cooperation Policy (CCP). PLS first sued NAR (and big MLSs) way back in 2020, settling with the MLSs and temporarily dropping the case against NAR before reviving it last year.

NAR’s court filings included emailed exchanges between Compass executives and Umansky over the last two years, including Reffkin sharing an op-ed slamming Clear Cooperation ahead of publication, and talking points on the policy ahead of both men attending an industry conference in early 2025.

In a joint filing from Compass and NAR, the brokerage argued that subpoenaing six non-party witnesses—including Reffkin, Alexander and Compass President of Integrated Services Cory Perkins—is “unduly burdensome on its face.”

NAR’s subpoenas focus on communications with clients and how those clients want to list their homes for sale, documents about membership in real estate trade association and other communications that Compass argues NAR should also possess.

So far, Compass stated that NAR is retaliating against Compass because one executive agreed to provide a deposition testimony for PLS.

NAR, on the other hand, argues that Alexander’s deposition and the documents it requested could implicate the testimony or documents of the other Compass-affiliated agents.

“The stakes are high,” NAR’s argument states.

The association’s explanations for the subpoenas also touch upon requests for further information from Compass, specifically information that PLS cannot provide.

“(The documents the parties themselves have produced) do not entail the Compass-affiliated agents’ listing agreements, which would reflect seller opt-outs of the MLS, or show whether off-MLS marketing was driven by seller preference or the agent’s business objectives. The bare listing information that PLS produced does not absolve Compass of its duties; PLS, for example, never tracked sales data,” NAR’s argument states.

Both parties, and Compass as a non-party, await a judge’s decision on whether the brokerage will have to provide the subpoenaed documents and communications.

Another player enters Compass MLS lawsuits

The Northern California-based MLS, MLSListings, announced that it has joined six MLSs in their federal lawsuit against Compass.

The six other MLSs in the lawsuit alongside MLSListings are Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service (ARMLS), BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS and REcolorado.

Two other MLSs—OneKey and CRMLS—are suing Compass in a separate but largely identical lawsuit. All of the MLS’ appeared to have received legal threats from Compass back in September, focused on listing restrictions.

According to the amended complaint, the lawsuit arises from a “campaign by Compass to pressure MLSs into changing cooperation rules in a way that would favor Compass but would make the market for residential real estate less transparent and less competitive, ultimately hurting consumers.”

“In Silicon Valley and throughout Northern California, buyers, sellers and real estate professionals depend on timely, accurate information to make important financial decisions,” MLSListings President and CEO Dave Wetzel said. “When publicly marketed homes are withheld from the shared marketplace, buyers lose access to opportunities, sellers may miss potential offers, and smaller brokerages are placed at a disadvantage. We are joining this lawsuit to defend the cooperation that gives everyone a fair opportunity to compete and helps consumers make informed decisions.”

Although the case is still ongoing and has just begun, the results of the lawsuit could change how brokerages list their properties on MLS databases. The amended complaint argues that Compass “wants to have its cake and eat it too,” where the brokerage may benefit from listings provided by other brokerages onto each MLS, without having to add their own listings into the database.

Initially, ARMLS and its fellow organizations filed the lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 21, after California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS) filed its initial complaint against the brokerage a few weeks prior.

MLSListing’s participation in the lawsuit adds another name to Compass’s list of disgruntled MLSs. The New York-based MLS, OneKey® MLS, had also joined CRMLS as a plaintiff in its federal lawsuit against Compass last week.

Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison

The affluential luxury real estate brokers, Tal and Oren Alexander, along with their brother Alon were sentenced to 30 years in federal prison last week.

Earlier in March, the brothers were found guilty on all charges of rape and sex-trafficking, after several named and unnamed women came forward and shared their stories.

One victim, under the pseudonym Isa Brooks, stated that she was just 16 years old when two of the brothers and their friend had raped her.

“I cry for the innocence of that terrified 16-year-old and stand for her today,” Brooks said, reported by CNN. “Their eyes went black. As if I was being mauled by animals.”

“I grieve the girl that I was,” she said.

The case began toward the end of 2024, where the brothers were arrested on charges of operating “a long-running sex trafficking scheme, as part of which they raped and sexually assaulted women to whom they had provided ‘material benefits,’ including domestic and international travel to vacation destinations, luxury accommodations at high-end hotels and vacation properties, and access to other luxury experiences and events,” according to a filed indictment.

Within the court proceedings, Judge Valerie Caproni showed little mercy for the brothers, who continued to claim their innocence to the charges throughout the sentencing process.

“Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives. It has caused long lasting damage to them. Many have significant problems trusting people,” Caproni said, reported by CNN.

Despite several letters written to Caproni by friends and family of the Alexander brothers, Caproni once again reprimanded the trio for their crimes and their conduct.

“You did not have to stand up and say you’ve never raped anyone,” Caproni said, according to ABC News. “That’s a lie and you know it.”

Zillow pays out over $210 million to settle shareholders

After nearly five years of court proceedings, a settlement was reached in Jaeger v. Zillow Group litigation, in which shareholders argued that the portal did not adequately disclose its struggles to ramp up its now-defunct iBuying business, and misled investors.

Last Wednesday, Zillow announced that it would pay out over $212.5 million to the shareholders, who claimed that the portal had misrepresented the success of “Zillow Offers,” and failed to accurately disclose struggles it faced in flipping homes.

Both Zillow and Hagens Berman—the plaintiff’s attorneys for the case—have stated that they are satisfied with the settlement and await a judge’s approval.

“We are incredibly pleased to obtain this result for investors,” said Steve Berman, managing partner of Hagens Berman.

In a statement shared with RISMedia, a Zillow spokesperson commented, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

According to a regulatory filing from Zillow, about $48 million of the settlement will be paid through insurance proceeds. Hagens Berman said in a statement the settlement was “potentially the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington federal court.”

Prior to the settlement, the case was slated to reach trial in September 2027.

The case began with Zillow’s iBuying business, also known as Zillow Offers, which was launched in spring 2018. Zillow Offers was a house flipping initiative, where the company promised that it could scale the business model of buying and quickly flipping homes using technology to predict short-term market fluctuations and patterns.

Zillow Offers was shut down later in 2021, and sold a backlog of nearly 18,000 homes at a loss of about $550 million. Within the original complaint, Hagens Berman argued that several statements and communications from Zillow were “materially false and/or misleading” and had failed to disclose “material adverse facts” about Zillow’s business, operations and prospects.

Homebuyer sues Keller Williams over $650 “junk fee”

Broker fees are once again on the receiving end of litigation, as one homebuyer in Pennsylvania filed a complaint—consisting of over 30 pages—against Keller Williams Elite in Lancaster County’s Court of Common Pleas.

According to the complaint, Gregory Deivert, a recent buyer client, is suing the franchise over a $650 fee that he claims is essentially for nothing.

“The fee had no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it. It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for him,” the complaint states.

A final settlement statement was included in the filing, and the complaint references the breakdown of fees within the statement. Deivert’s attorney argues that the $650 broker fee is a prototypical “junk fee,” and that Keller Williams Elite was fully compensated for its services by the $14,700 commission it received from the seller.

The issue of “junk fees” is nothing new to the real estate industry. In 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) launched a formal inquiry into the issue of extra fees tacked onto home mortgage costs.

Generally, the complaint argues that customarily, broker fees are paid for by the seller and are included in the broker’s commission. Within the lawsuit, Deivert is suing the brokerage for a breach of fiduciary duty and a violation of the Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law.

As for relief, Deivert is asking for $50,000 from the brokerage, along with a declaration that Keller Williams Elite will be prohibited from charging the $650 fee again, and labeling it as a fixed fee for broker compensation without disclosing what it entails.

#5589. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5587. With Agentic Studio, LinearB provides the critical context needed to accelerate software delivery

Application development intelligence startup LinearB Inc. said today it’s trying to ease the growing congestion in organization’s software delivery pipelines that has arisen with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence coding tools.

It’s doing so with Agentic Studio, a new offering announced today that’s focused on providing more actionable context for human engineers and autonomous coding agents alike.

The startup says the emergence of generative AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex has led to new headaches for enterprise software development teams. Though writing software code now can be basically effortless, shipping that code into production is still as painful as it has always been, and now they have much more of it to ship.

In its recent Software Engineering Benchmarks report, the company analyzed more than 2.7 million pull requests across 250 organizations and found that those who rely on AI coding tools have almost doubled their merged code changes year-over-year. But the problem is that AI-assisted pull requests are nearly 2.6 times larger, and consequently they’re waiting more than five times longer to be reviewed.

That has led to significant backlogs. And it’s compounded by the fact that AI agent’s proposed code changes are merged just 79% of the time at “elite organizations,” compared with 92% for human-authored code.

LinearB says that human software engineers struggle to clear this backlog because the traditional dashboards they’re forced to work with only provide metrics, rather than the context needed to resolve those pull requests. With Agentic Studio, it’s trying to address this by normalizing the data and insights generated by Git repositories and project tracking tools into a unified context layer. It means that instead of muddling through various charts to try and understand why release velocity has stalled, software engineers can ask questions in plain language to understand the root cause and receive recommendations on how to speed things up.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Ori Keren said context has become the new king, not only for AI tools but also for humans. “We realized we hold a knowledge graph that nobody else has of everything that is happening across the software delivery lifecycle,” he said. “That’s exactly what agents and teams need to deliver high quality software faster, so we rebuilt LinearB around it.”

What’s different about Agentic Studio is that it’s designed to help autonomous coding agents just as much as human software engineers, Keren said. By integrating through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, it feeds historical context such as rework rates, past production incidents and code ownership to AI agents, preventing them from making blind modifications to pull requests.

Early adopters have benefited from dramatically increased productivity with Agentic Studio. A case in point is the cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, which used LinearB’s MCP integration to pinpoint why its code reviews were lagging. It discovered that timezone misalignments were the main culprit rather than pull request sizes, and subsequently reorganized its workflows to cut its review times by more than half within just four months.

“For years, engineering leaders told us the same thing: metrics are useful, but they don’t tell you what to do,” said LinearB’s chief operating officer Dan Lines. “A dashboard says your cycle time is two days, but so what? Now [with Agentic Studio] a leader can ask what to improve in their engineering organization and get a clear answer. When that same context goes to coding agents, the platform is not just reporting, it’s acting.”

To help AI agents operationalize the context it provides, LinearB is developing a bunch of new agent skills. The first one, an “effort skill,” is available in early access now and analyzes the complexity of a pull request and its proposed code changes, its rework history and risk to calibrate dynamically how much computational effort a coding agent needs to expend as it works on it.

Simple, low-risk changes are done faster with minimal tokens. More sensitive, high-priority modifications will be implemented with deeper reasoning and more exhaustive testing to ensure nothing goes wrong.

LinearB said it’s planning to expand its agent skills library in the coming months with additional skills focused on automated code review, merge governance and token cost optimization.

#5586. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5585. Exclusive: Guardz brings Palo Alto Networks browser protection to MSPs serving small businesses

Cybersecurity startup Guardz Cyber Ltd. today added browser protection from Palo Alto Networks Inc.’s Prisma Browser for Business to its security platform for managed service providers that protect small businesses.

The integration is aimed at phishing attacks that slip between separate security tools. A typical one starts with an email that lures an employee to a counterfeit login page, and the credentials typed there can put connected accounts at risk. “For most small businesses, the browser is now the office,” said Shivam Srivastava, vice president of product at Palo Alto Networks.

Prisma Browser for Business can block the page when the link is clicked. Guardz then matches that browser event to the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity and endpoint telemetry for the same user identity. From there, the provider and Guardz’s 24/7 managed detection and response team can work the whole chain as a single incident.

The browser-side detection comes from Palo Alto Networks. Inline machine-learning models screen pages for phishing, and Advanced URL Filtering helps block malicious sites, including fake sign-in pages and attacks built to steal live session tokens. The company’s WildFire service analyzes suspect files. Uploads and downloads are scanned as they pass through the browser, which also picks out risky extensions.

Guardz Co-founder and Chief Executive Dor Eisner called the browser “the primary gateway to the modern workspace.” Traditional security tools work in silos that leave gaps in visibility and response, he said, and the agents running on Guardz’s platform are meant to let providers investigate threats autonomously anywhere in that workspace.

Setup falls to Guardz, which handles provisioning and default configuration. Kevin Kehoe of early-access provider Datawise Networks Inc. said the rollout through his firm’s remote monitoring and management software was “super smooth.” Within minutes, he said, the browser extension was “on every Chrome and Edge profile.”

For generative artificial intelligence services used in the browser, Guardz’s AI Usage and Control features let technicians set a separate policy for each client. Those policies can restrict copying, pasting and file transfers by website or by category. Guardz has also introduced a report that gives providers a per-client view of AI tool usage.

Palo Alto Networks moved into enterprise browsers with its 2023 acquisition of Israeli startup Talon Cyber Security Ltd. Prisma Browser for Business, its version for small businesses, went on sale in the U.S. in March.

Guardz is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $84 million, including a $56 million Series B round led by ClearSky in June 2025.

#5584. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5583. MazeBolt launches native RADAR deployment for Akamai DDoS protection customers

Distributed denial-of-service testing company MazeBolt Technologies Ltd. today launched a native deployment of its RADAR validation platform for customers of Akamai Technologies Inc.

Enterprises using Akamai’s DDoS protection can have continuous testing running within hours without taking services offline. The release targets the configuration gaps that open up as a company adds services, application programming interfaces and regions behind its DDoS protection.

Akamai setups are rarely tested independently against each of those changes, according to MazeBolt, and a gap can stay hidden until an attack reaches a login page or a payment flow. Founder and Chief Executive Matthew Andriani said testing “even a few times a year cannot keep pace” now that artificial intelligence projects keep adding new services and APIs.

Akamai’s own State of the Internet report, published in March, found that Layer 7 DDoS attacks rose 104% over two years, and the company blamed part of that growth on attack tools that use AI to make web applications and APIs easier to hit.

RADAR fires simulated attacks at Akamai-protected services from inside the customer’s own environment. The attack library covers known vectors as well as the AI-orchestrated and AI-generated attacks MazeBolt added with its VectorAI module in June. When RADAR first tests a production environment, about 37% of attack vectors get past the protection already in place, based on MazeBolt’s data from initial deployments.

Each run ends in a report with remediation guidance written for the specific protection vendor, and RADAR repeats the test once a fix is in place. “Deployed protection is not proven protection,” said Eyal Rahimi, vice president of engineering at MazeBolt. Customers also need to be able to prove which gaps they have closed, Rahimi said.

Most financial institutions test far less often. In a MazeBolt survey of 300 of their security leaders last year, 86% said they test their DDoS defenses once a year or less. Akamai reported in May that the median duration of Layers 3 and 4 DDoS attacks on the sector has risen 738% since 2024.

John Grady, chief analyst at Omdia, said misconfigurations and out-of-date rules remain the source of many security incidents. “DDoS is no different,” Grady said. “It is a critical area where security teams must ensure protection is current, because successful attacks impact availability and directly affect the bottom line.”

Native Layer 7 support for Akamai environments is available today to all RADAR customers. Cloudflare Inc., F5 Inc. and Radware Ltd. are among the other mitigation vendors whose products RADAR already tests across scrubbing centers, on-premises equipment and cloud services.

#5582. Google finds ‘LLMjacking’ attackers running up $100K a day in fraudulent cloud charges

A new report out today from Google LLC’s Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that attackers who hijack enterprise access to large language models are running up fraudulent cloud charges of more than $100,000 in a single day.

The report, “The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources,” covers multiple LLMjacking cases Mandiant responded to this year. At some organizations, the cumulative bill reached $1 million before access was revoked.

Cryptojacking, the older way of stealing cloud compute, tends to drain resources gradually. LLMjacking charges can spike in a matter of hours.

Victims in North America, South America and Asia-Pacific included financial services and retail companies, along with technology and transportation businesses. GTIG has tied the intrusions to several financially motivated clusters and sees a growing split between the people who break in and the operators who resell the access.

In most of the investigations, attackers got in with cloud identity credentials that had been stolen or left exposed, including service account keys and GitHub personal access tokens. Others went after LLM endpoints left open to the internet, such as exposed Ollama servers.

A group tracked as UNC6993 broke into a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used that foothold to reach an LLM application programming interface. A fake portal it hosted posed as a sign-up page for a group of LLM users. Visitors were sent to the real LLM service and told to paste back a raw JSON payload containing an active access token. With that token, passwords and multifactor authentication no longer stood in the way.

Another actor scraped LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and tested each one with a request capped at a single output token. Requests that small slipped under the volume-based alerts in the victims’ security monitoring tools.

Routing software is a target too. In one case a follow-on cluster obtained pre-validated virtual keys from the group that had established access, then exploited a user ID rebind flaw in LiteLLM’s key regeneration endpoint. The bug, CVE-2026-40217, let it turn ordinary virtual keys into master administrator credentials for the victim’s gateway.

Some of the stolen access was burned through directly. UNC6993 tried to generate more API keys and switch on extra services inside victim cloud projects, and the charges quickly passed $100,000. A different actor signed victim accounts up for pay-as-you-go agreements on premium models. To get around rate limits, the actor used what GTIG calls a “burn and rotate” strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts.

A third went further and planted a containerized backdoor built on the Manus agent framework, which asked an upstream model to reason through instructions and then executed the resulting commands on the compromised host.

Other access ends up for sale through what GTIG calls “LLM Mixers.” These operations run stolen credentials through open-source API gateways and custom relays so usage can be metered and the origin of each request hidden. UNC6993 used tools such as new-api and gcli2api, likely to pool stolen keys, and GTIG believes the group sells access through underground storefronts.

One mixer is Jet Night, a token routing service. An actor that made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours was using stolen third-party keys to power it, and one victim organization was left with nearly $1 million in token costs.

Jet Night sells an unlimited plan claiming frontier model access for about $60 a month. Comparable consumer plans typically cost $100 to $250, and GTIG thinks prices that low only work on stolen keys. Outages advertised on the service’s Telegram channel are likely the result of victims finding the compromise and revoking keys.

GTIG expects attackers increasingly to favor LLMjacking over cryptojacking because the mixers pay out quickly and at high margins. Exposed API tokens and model routing middleware will draw more automated targeting as companies put higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production, the report predicts.

On the defensive side, the report notes that in several of Mandiant’s cases, the victim had never enabled LLM services. Attackers used stolen keys to turn on services such as Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Amazon Bedrock and Google’s Gemini API, and a bill could balloon within minutes from there.

Any unauthorized enablement should be treated as a critical security event, it says. Spending caps, API keys scoped to specific models and environments and log monitoring for the single-token pings used to validate stolen keys are among its other recommendations.

Threat actors want artificial intelligence to give them scale over defenders, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, and they are getting it with agentic tools and tokens stolen from unwitting third parties.

“Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks,” Hultquist said.
