#5580. Better founder Vishal Garg details Tinman AI platform shift

Better founder Vishal Garg said Tinman AI is driving about 60% of company activity as Better pivots from ad-driven DTC lending to partners. He also outlined a $60 million cost reduction plan and a focus on contribution margin profitability.  AI Summary

Better founder Vishal Garg sat down with HousingWire President Diego Sanchez on the PowerHouse podcast today to unpack his proxy victory, the company’s shift away from ad-driven direct-to-consumer lending and a plan to turn its Tinman AI platform into shared infrastructure for brokers, IMBs and fintech partners.

In the wide-ranging conversation, Garg talked first about his proxy fight to return to the company he founded.

“The odds of a founder CEO coming back and removing the entire board — that happens 1.7% of the time successfully in the history of proxy fights. So, I didn’t know that going in, apparently, but like 60-to-one odds against,” Garg said.

Garg was removed as Better’s CEO in early August, replaced on an interim basis by Daniel Lewis. Garg then launched a campaign to replace members of the board, winning over enough shareholders to regain control of the company.

He says shareholders backed him because they buy into Better’s mission to make homeownership “cheaper, faster and easier,” and because they see early results from Tinman AI, the company’s mortgage manufacturing engine.

In his short time away, Garg said he reflected on the mistakes he made as CEO. “The biggest thing I did wrong was not push the AI hard enough. You know, really just still kind of kept trying to convince people that this path was the best path, trying to convince people that the agent needed to be perfect, right? It did not need to be perfect.

“All of those things, big mistake. While I was doing that, there are other people out there, you know, 23-year-olds disrupting entire industries with a completely brand new perspective and just like letting the agents run.

“And so while we have this massive competitive moat of licenses, and over a hundred billion dollars of transactions on our platform that serves as learning data, the ability to rep and warrant — and all these sorts of things that your traditional 23-year-old coming out of Silicon Valley with a a mortgage startup doesn’t have the ability to do — we would very clearly lose that edge over time if we just didn’t run fast enough.”

Garg said Better has raised “almost $2 billion” to remake the mortgage manufacturing process and acknowledged the company has “lost more money than anyone else” in the space. He compared that to the long burns at Uber and Airbnb, positioning Better as early in an effort to reshape what he called a $4.5 trillion industry.

Tinman — originally built to codify agency and investor rules from 2016 to 2022 — is the foundation of that strategy. Garg said the system delivers a “six basis point critical defect rate,” which he called the lowest in the industry, and that overlaying large language models has accelerated the process and stripped out human friction.

Better’s revenue peaked at about $1.5 billion during the refi boom, then dropped to roughly $75 million in 2023. Garg said the company is now at a “$220-plus” revenue run rate, with about 60% of activity tied to Tinman AI.

Crucially, he said Better no longer cares “about the customer interaction surface.” Instead, the goal is to plug Tinman AI into whatever front end the consumer, lender or broker already uses — whether that’s a fintech app like Credit Karma, an AI agent interface, a mortgage broker’s POS or a branch loan officer’s tablet at an open house.

“We are not even seeking to disrupt the industry anymore,” Garg said. “We’re seeking to empower the entire industry and uplift the entire industry by taking Tinman and making it available to anyone and everyone in the industry to power their business.”

Garg framed Better’s first phase, from 2016 to 2023, as a DTC-heavy play. The new phase, he said, is “interaction surface agnostic” — with growth coming through distributed retail, broker and fintech partners instead of Google and Facebook ads.

He pointed to Better’s relationship with NEO Home Loans as an example of how Tinman can sit behind distributed retail brands. Garg said Neo’s loan officers went from averaging roughly 2–2.5 loans per month to closer to 5 loans per month on Tinman, with higher commissions because they can handle more business and deliver more consistent execution.

He said Tinman reviews decisions across “all 65 investors” before a loan is rejected, reducing fallout and helping attach additional products like HELOCs. The strategy, he argued, is similar to Uber’s path, where local operators plug into a central platform rather than run their own full tech stacks.

“The Uberization of retail is what happens,” Garg said, describing a model where Better supports multiple distributed retail brands and expands city by city.

Garg also confirmed that Better is already operating as a wholesale lender.

“We are a wholesale lender,” he said, noting the company currently has about 40 mortgage brokers on its platform, focused today on home equity.

He described that as a “land and expand” strategy. Over time, he envisions brokers evolving into broader “home advisors” or “loan advisors” who can also sell insurance and maintain long-term relationships with borrowers.

Garg highlighted that past investments — including title, homeowners, auto and life insurance entities under the Better Cover umbrella — didn’t produce strong unit economics when driven by Better’s own human salesforce. But he said those capabilities can make more sense when product distribution runs through brokers and retail partners who already own the consumer relationship.

“It is so powerful to tip the platform in the hands of people that know what they’re doing,” he said.

On where Better is pulling back, Garg was direct: paid, ad-driven DTC.

He said Better has already “cut D2C marketing” and questioned the logic of spending “two and a half million a month for buying clicks on Google” when he was able to mobilize tens of thousands of proxy voters himself using low-cost AI video tools and social platforms.

“I am short ad-driven D2C, brand-driven D2C, because it will die a fast and rapid death in the age of the AI agents,” he said.

He contrasted that position with lenders that have invested heavily in mortgage servicing rights and large workforces, saying those business models are effectively “long consumer friction” at a time when AI agents such as Muse, Instinct and others could make it easier for borrowers to move and refinance.

“You cannot charge people 50 basis points on a mortgage and hope to make up for it because you can bid more than everyone else on Google,” Garg said.

For lenders that still lean on digital ad spend and lead buying, his stance underscores the risk that acquisition costs continue to rise while AI tools make rate and fee comparisons more transparent.

Garg acknowledged recent layoffs at Better and called the current cost structure “unsustainable.”

He said the company needs to reduce costs by about $60 million and has identified or executed on roughly $24 million of savings so far. The goal, he said, is to move quarterly operating costs from the mid-$60 million range into the $40 millions.

“For us to be the platform for the industry, for us to be the AWS for the industry… the industry has to know that Better will always be there,” he said. “And the only way the industry knows that Better will always be there is if Better makes money every month.”

Asked whether Better will be profitable a year from now, Garg said the “core parts of the business will be contribution margin profitable,” unless the company chooses to lean into large growth or acquisition investments. He differentiated this plan from past profitability promises by emphasizing that this time Better is attacking both revenue and expense lines.

“In the past, we were keeping expenses the same and using AI to help power growth,” he said. “Now operating costs are going from that number down by 25 million… and we’re focused on still growing.”

Garg also argued that Better trades at about 1.5x revenue, a steep discount to private-market mortgage fintech valuations he said can reach 10x–50x revenue. Reaching profitability, he said, is the “best way to remove that discount” and create value for shareholders.

As part of his return, Garg has committed to hiring a CEO. He said he is looking for an executive who is “AI pilled,” has a deep understanding of credit risk and has experience building large B2B “outcome as a service” platforms — delivering specific outcomes instead of just software licenses.

He argued that mortgage is an industry that “blows itself up every 10, 20 years” and that the next CEO must be grounded in how credit cycles and product standards can go wrong.

Garg said strong people skills are also critical — and acknowledged that is an area where he has historically struggled and needs complementary leadership.

#5579. On theCUBE Pod: Stock market gets the jitters and Anthropic files IPO

The hubbub at the New York Stock Exchange was audible on theCUBE Pod last Friday, with concerns rising over the artificial intelligence bubble.

Several tech companies, including Intel Corp., Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., CoreWeave Inc. and Fortinet Inc., saw their stock fall, suggesting that investors may have doubts about all that AI infrastructure spending. At the same time, Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which looks to be a grand debut for one of the biggest AI developers out there (despite the company still not turning a profit).

Also causing a stir is the announcement that NYSE parent company, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), will partner with Trade[XYZ] to bring perpetual futures markets built on cryptocurrency trading platform, Hyperliquid, to the U.S., subject to regulatory approval.

“The whole idea of exchange is going to change,” said John Furrier (pictured, left), executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “It reminds me of cloud computing, how it re-leveled the data center. NYSE is the cathedral of capitalism. Nasdaq started as an over-the-counter bulletin board. Tech was early there and then only listed there. But now the game has changed. It’s very interesting to see how the competition between the NYSE and the Nasdaq is going to play out.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (right), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed what Anthropic’s IPO and Friday’s stock market jitters suggest about a potential AI bubble. They also explored Intel’s missteps and the opportunity for full-stack infrastructure companies.

Last week, Alphabet’s stock fell more than 12% after it reported slower growth in search revenue, presumably because chatbots are drawing people away from the browser. Amazon also had a disappointing Friday, with its stock falling 7% as the company continues to dump money into an AI infrastructure buildout.

Despite investors’ concerns, Vellante sees the AI bubble letting out a little air. He views this as a healthy sign for the AI market’s future.

“Think of the tulip bubbles in the 1600s,” Vellante said. “Think about the Japanese real estate bubble in the 1980s. And you think about the dot-com. That dot-com was actually different. Dot-com, they were all … overhyped. They drove massive valuations. But the dot-com actually played out. It actually exceeded expectations. And I think there’s some things that we can learn from there.”

Furrier sees evidence for a positive growth cycle, starting with cloud growth, which is needed to support the AI expansion. He also suggested that the infrastructure boom could coexist with the neocloud shakeout, as enterprise AI starts to create jobs rather than taking them away. Last week isn’t necessarily indicative of the AI bubble popping any time soon, he argues.

“Rationale is kicking in, common sense,” he said. “You’re starting to see the beginning of a transition. Wall Street is trying to figure it out. I think they don’t yet get it. But if you look at the language of the experts on the inside and how all the IPOs are being positioned, the value of these IPOs — they want durability. That transition from Silicon Valley tech ecosystem platforms is going to move into the markets. This is a platform game.”

Intel stock saw the steepest drop last week, almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report. The company has leaned into CPUs over GPUs, which Vellante thinks is missing the mark; the real game is not CPUs versus GPUs, but rather AI platforms. Nonetheless, he and Furrier predict Intel will make up some ground.

“Lip-Bu Tan and Intel have an opportunity,” Furrier said. “You basically lost the hyperscaler market that they once had a foothold in. You still run x86 on some clusters. But they got to look at other footprints. I think he’ll turn it around. It’s a multiyear journey, as he says. But the fact of the matter is why I don’t think it’s a bubble, is companies like Alphabet dropping major, major action, $500 billion, in a day.”

Intel is just one component in a rapidly changing ecosystem. Although the AI boom draws comparisons to the bubbles of yore, theCUBE concluded that this is still a unique phenomenon the market has to grapple with, and one that will play out over decades.

“This is just a natural adoption phase,” Vellante said. “What’s different is a lot of things. Like you said, tech is suddenly deflationary. We’re trading CapEx for labor, and that hasn’t really kicked in yet. We’re seeing individual productivity gains but it hasn’t shown up at the firm level yet. These things just take time. And, of course, Wall Street’s like, show me the money.”

#5578. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5577. Rocket Pro launches broker-built Quick Counter tool in November Power Play

Rocket Pro launched Quick Counter, a broker-built tool in Navigate that creates refinance loan estimates in real time. Brokers can adjust rates, points, terms, and closing cost options for cash-out and rate-and-term refis.  AI Summary

Rocket Pro is rolling out Quick Counter, a new tool designed to help mortgage brokers compete for borrowers by building and delivering refinance loan estimates in real time.

The rollout is part of Rocket’s monthly Power Play, an initiative that Rocket Pro promised to its business partners back in February and has announced on the first Tuesday of each month. The November initiative features the winning idea from The Big Pitch competition at Rocket Pro’s RPX event in September.

Available within Rocket Pro Navigate, Quick Counter allows brokers to generate a competitive loan estimate while a client is still on the phone, rather than risk losing business by promising a callback.

The tool supports both cash-out and rate-and-term refinances, allowing brokers to adjust interest rates, points and loan terms in real time. Brokers can also evaluate different pricing scenarios, including options for lowering closing costs, to tailor an offer to a borrower’s needs.

“Every loan matters, and conversion matters in a really big way,” said Austin Niemiec, chief revenue officer of Rocket Mortgage. “There’s so many times out there, a borrower will call a broker with a competing loan estimate and ask, ‘Hey, can you beat it?’ And Quick Counter helps that broker work through the offer, compare pricing and then build a counteroffer right through this tool while on the phone with the client.”

The tool is the first of three broker-developed ideas Rocket committed to building after its Big Pitch competition, a broker tech innovation contest announced in June. The company received hundreds of submissions from Rocket Pro partners and brokers who do not currently work with the lender.

Rocket Pro narrowed the submissions to three finalists and paired each broker with its technology and product teams to turn the concepts into working prototypes. The finalists presented their ideas at RPX, where the broker community voted on the products.

Seth Hasan of West Capital Lending submitted Quick Counter and received the $100,000 first-place prize. The other finalists were Andrew Haff of Barren Hill Mortgage, whose Rocket Pro Right Track concept provides alternatives when a loan encounters an obstacle, and George Chevalier of Clearview Lending Solutions, whose Rocket Pro Signal concept identifies potential risks before they threaten a closing.

Rocket initially planned to select one winner and build the winning concept. Instead, it was announced at RPX that the company would develop all three ideas, awarding $60,000 to Haff and $40,000 to Chevalier.

Niemiec said Rocket moved from prototype to Quick Counter’s launch in less than 60 days, with Hasan and his team involved in reviewing the final product.

“We didn’t come up with this in a boardroom or us trying to guess what brokers want,” Niemiec said. “Not only did Seth and his team come up with the idea, we worked side by side with them to make sure that every single detail was how they envisioned, and then the broker community is the one that voted on it.”

Rocket plans to build the second- and third-place ideas as well, although Niemiec did not provide a specific rollout timeline. He said development is already underway and that the company does not intend to delay the releases for an extended period.

The latest announcement follows October’s Power Play, which introduced Orbit, a platform feature intended to help brokers access and track new benefits. Niemiec said the launch generated significant activity among Rocket’s account executives, who have been fielding calls and helping brokers understand how to use the feature.

Rocket also reported more than $3 billion in locks through its Compass credit since its introduction. The credit, which runs through the end of 2026, gives broker partners a pricing incentive to build relationships with Compass real estate agents and strengthen existing partnerships.

Niemiec said Rocket plans to reevaluate the Compass credit at the end of the year but pointed to continued momentum behind the program.

#5576. Compass expands agent benefits with health and retirement support

Compass International Holdings launched healthcare navigation and retirement planning concierge services for more than 250,000 U.S. affiliated agents across 9 brands. Partners include Stride and TouchCare for ACA enrollment and billing support, plus Morgan Stanley with Vestwell for Solo and team 401(k) plans.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings has rolled out new healthcare and retirement planning concierge services for more than 250,000 affiliated real estate professionals across its U.S. franchise brands, the company announced Tuesday.

Independent real estate professionals affiliated with @properties, Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate, Century 21, Christie’s International Real Estate, Coldwell Banker, Compass, Corcoran, ERA and Sotheby’s International Realty will gain access to health coverage navigation, medical billing support and retirement plan setup at preferred pricing, according to the announcement.

The offerings are aimed at independent contractors, who typically lack access to employer-sponsored health insurance and retirement plans and must navigate Affordable Care Act marketplaces and individual advisory relationships on their own. For broker-owners and team leaders, benefits access has become a key recruiting and retention issue in a slower housing market with compressed margins.

Participating agents will have year-round access at no cost to healthcare and retirement planning experts who can provide guidance 365 days a year. Support includes comparing coverage options, estimating plan costs, finding in-network providers and reviewing retirement savings choices.

Through Stride, agents can compare health, dental and vision plans, identify available tax credits and get help from a licensed advisor to estimate plan costs and enroll. Stride reports that customers who qualify for tax credits save an average of $615 per month on coverage.

TouchCare will provide dedicated Health Assistants to help agents and their families navigate the health system throughout the year. Services include finding in-network doctors and specialists, understanding costs before receiving care, exploring prescription savings and disputing or correcting inaccurate medical bills, according to the announcement.

On the retirement side, Compass International is partnering with Morgan Stanley, with plans powered by Vestwell, to offer Solo(k) and team 401(k) plans that real estate professionals and teams can elect to establish. The program features professionally managed retirement solutions with zero setup fees, preferred pricing and dedicated support. The company said the offering can save agents up to $850 in their first year.

Independent contractors in real estate have historically been responsible for setting up their own IRAs or solo 401(k)s, often without institutional pricing or plan design support. Formal programs from brokerages and holding companies could help normalize retirement saving behavior in an industry where income is volatile and many agents remain active later in life

“One of the top requests I hear from our real estate professionals is better support and access for healthcare and retirement,” Robert Reffkin, chairman and CEO of Compass International Holdings, said in the announcement. “These offerings are about helping our real estate professionals navigate and maximize their options so they can spend more time focused on building their future, helping their clients, and spending time with their families.”

The company said the benefits program is available to all U.S.-based real estate professionals affiliated with its participating brands and that it expects to expand offerings in 2027. Compass International plans to explore additional options such as life and disability coverage, more retirement savings choices and exclusive vendor discounts on goods, services and technology used in agents’ professional and personal lives.

Reffkin said Compass International’s long-term goal is to give members of its network access to “higher-quality, lower-cost healthcare and retirement planning options” tailored to the way independent real estate professionals work.

#5575. Marvell to acquire optical component maker Lumentum in massive $115B deal

Marvell Technology Inc. today announced plans to acquire Lumentum Holdings Inc. for $115 billion, in one of the largest deals in tech history.

Lumentum investors are set to receive 4.5 Marvell shares for every unit of stock they own. That translates to about $1,132 per share, which is 23.9% higher than the company’s last unaffected stock price.

Investors, however, weren’t so sanguine about the deal. Marvell’s shares fell almost 13%, while Lumentum’s fell almost 19%. Chalk it up, again, to recent investor worry that the promised growth from artificial intelligence infrastructure may not last forever.

Marvell provides networking equipment for data centers and telecommunications infrastructure. Many of its products use fiber-optic cables to transmit data. Lumentum, in turn, makes components for fiber-optic network devices such as those offered by Marvell. The acquisition will give the latter company more control over its supply chain, which could enable it to more closely align upstream components’ design with its requirements.

Optical networks use laser emitters to generate the light which they transmit data. Lumentum sells a line of lasers based on indium phosphide, a semiconducting material that generates light more efficiently than silicon. The product family includes modular and continuous wave devices. Modulated lasers are used to physically connect servers to the host data center’s optical network, while continuous wave lasers power longer-range network links.

Lumentum also makes single-mode optical amplifiers. Such devices strengthen the laser signals that travel through long-haul carrier networks to reduce data transmission errors.

Last year, the company debuted a laser optimized for co-packaged optics, or CPO, chips. Such chips enable servers to connect to the host data center’s network without expensive modules called transceivers that are usually needed for the task. CPO technology has emerged as an important focus of Marvell’s growth strategy. Its chip design business can help customers integrate CPO modules into their custom artificial intelligence accelerators.

Lumentum doesn’t focus solely on the laser component market. It uses a material called indium gallium arsenide to make analog photodetectors, which customers can use to monitor their optical networks for errors. The company also sells optical circuit switches. Such devices use tiny mirrors to coordinate the flow of traffic, which removes the need to turn data into electrical signals and thereby saves power.

Notably, Lumentum will also give Marvell a presence in the industrial equipment market. The former company makes high-power lasers for cutting and welding machines. It’s unclear what will happen to that part of Lumentum’s product portfolio following the deal. After a large acquisition, companies sometimes spin off newly absorbed business units that don’t align with their core focus.

“By bringing together two leaders with highly complementary technologies, exceptional talent and specialized manufacturing capabilities, we intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value,” said Marvell Chief Executive Officer Matt Murphy.

The chipmaker expects to close the acquisition in the first half of 2028. The combined company will be led by Murphy, while Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston will join the board along with two of the optical component supplier’s directors.

Marvell expects the deal to become accretive to its adjusted earnings per share within a year of closing. In the longer term, the company hopes to achieve annual run-rate cost savings of more than $1 billion and accelerate revenue growth. Marvell estimates that Lumentum will expand its total addressable market to $550 billion.

#5574. Exclusive: Victor Ciardelli on merger of Rate, Compass JVs into top-10 retail lender

Rate and Compass International Holdings are combining their two mortgage joint ventures, Guaranteed Rate Affinity and OriginPoint, under the OriginPoint brand. The unified platform will include 672 loan officers and is projected to reach $13.2 billion in mortgage volume by the end of 2026, with Rate holding a majority stake.  AI Summary

Rate and Compass International Holdings are merging their two mortgage joint ventures, creating a top-10 pure retail mortgage lender, Rate CEO Victor Ciardelli told HousingWire in an exclusive interview.

Guaranteed Rate Affinity (GRA) and OriginPoint will merge under the latter brand, putting together a team of 672 dedicated loan officers that’s expected to reach $13.2 billion in mortgage volume by the end 2026 — most of it from GRA, Ciardelli said.

The move was widely expected since Compass’s merger agreement with Anywhere Real Estate last year. Anywhere and Rate launched Guaranteed Rate Affinity in 2017.

In 2021, Rate also partnered directly with Compass to create OriginPoint. And a year earlier, it launched Proper Rate with @properties, which later became part of Compass through its acquisition of Christie’s International Real Estate.

Rate and Compass had been working on the integration of the JVs for the past six months. Dave Dickey, the current president and chief production officer of GRA, and James Elliott, president and CEO of OriginPoint, will be co-presidents of the new joint venture.

“It wasn’t the current rate environment that was a driver in it at all; we happen to own both JVs under all of Compass, and so it’s something that we worked with Robert Reffkin, their team with our team, with the intent that we would always put it together,” Ciardelli said. “We just wanted to take our time and build a state-of-the-art technology stack.”

The companies said OriginPoint customers will receive a streamlined real estate experience, allowing them to find, secure and close on a home in as few as 10 days.

All of this will be connected to Compass’s owned-brokerage network of more than 80,000 real estate professionals. The companies estimate that between Coldwell Banker Realty and Compass alone, there are over 200,000 buy-side purchase transactions representing more than $200 billion in purchase volume.

“Loan officers at Guaranteed Affinity who work with Coldwell Banker are now going to be able to work with Compass agents, so that’s going to open them up into other opportunities,” Ciardelli said. “Then, you’re also going to have at OriginPoint-Compass people, loan officers, that are working with Compass are now going to be opened up to working with all the other brands — Coldwell Banker, @properties, Sotheby’s, Corcoran.”

Rate will have a majority share on the JV and expects that, if it captures 10% to 20% of the buy-side purchase transactions from its partners, it would generate $4.5 billion to $10 billion in incremental volume, along with $17.7 billion to $30 billion in annual volume.

“OriginPoint is a trusted partner of our team. By bringing our two joint ventures with Rate together, we can now serve our clients better than ever before,” Reffkin, the chairman and CEO of Compass International Holdings (CIH), said a statement. “We can connect more great real estate professionals with more great loan officers to create a simpler, more seamless and connected experience for homebuyers.”

Compass last year also announced an alliance with Redfin, owned by Rocket Companies. The partnership includes the displaying of Compass Coming Soon listings, buyers working with an agent at a CIH brand gaining access to Rocket Preferred Pricing, and opportunities for its agents to receive buyer leads directly from Redfin and Rocket.

Ciardelli said this move had no impact on the JVs’ businesses. “All they are is a marketing agreement, and their loan officers are not allowed to go inside the real estate offices,” Ciardelli said. “What they do is they’re getting traffic just off of the website of Compass.com, so they haven’t been a problem for us at all. They’re not getting any market share.”

Ciardelli said Rate is focused on growing the JV and Rate, including from a recruiting standpoint, rather than looking “as far as the strategic plan, to keep adding more JVs.” (Rate also has a joint venture with KB Homes, inherited from the acquisition of Stearns.)

“With interest rates up, it’s a purchase market,” he said. “It’s a great opportunity for good loan officers, and we’re looking for good loan officers to come into the platform and help us build and grow market share, because there’s so much opportunity to capture with the buy-side business, and there’s so many agents to build relationships.”

Rate has also been working on a strategy to keep clients closer to the company, including changing its strategy from selling to retaining mortgage servicing rights (MSRs). This strategy has led to a $50 billion book, he said.

“We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer,” he said.

#5573. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5572. Palantir beats Q3 forecasts as US commercial revenue overtakes government for first time

Shares of Palantir Technologies Inc. rose more than 1% in late trading today after the big-data analytics company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year revenue guidance for the third time this year.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Palantir reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, up from 21 cents in the same quarter of last year, on revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 41 cents per share on revenue of $2.18 billion. It was the first quarter in which Palantir’s revenue topped $2 billion.

U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time in Palantir’s history. Sales to commercial customers in the U.S. reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Government sales rose 96%, to $953 million. Together they took total U.S. revenue to $1.937 billion, up 119% year-over-year.

Palantir closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million in the quarter, including 64 worth $10 million or more. Total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, to $2.918 billion, after growing 151% in the same period of 2025. U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79%, to $6.517 billion.

Net income more than doubled, to $1.128 billion from $476 million a year earlier, giving the company a 49% net margin. On an adjusted basis, operating income came to $1.427 billion at a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. Palantir’s “Rule of 40” score hit 158%. The company ended September holding $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and U.S. Treasury securities.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Karp used the earnings release to argue that what he called the “Sovereign AI movement” is creating “the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots” he has seen in 30 years in business. Governments and companies alike are being forced into one group or the other, “voluntarily or not,” according to Karp. That shift, he said, is “purpose-built for Palantir.”

Looking to the fourth quarter, Palantir expects revenue of $2.649 billion to $2.653 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.640 billion to $1.644 billion. Analysts had forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $2.46 billion.

Full-year revenue guidance now stands at $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion, up from the $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion Palantir forecast in August. U.S. commercial revenue is expected to exceed $3.559 billion, growth of at least 143%, and the company lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to a range of $5.245 billion to $5.249 billion. Adjusted free cash flow for 2026 is now forecast at $4.8 billion to $5 billion.

#5571. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5569. The concessions field problem that breaks pay-for-listing data models

Contribution schemes that credit MLS data by listing totals overlook whether key valuation inputs are complete. A single MLS can require a numeric concessions amount whenever concessions are yes, improving downstream appraisal and model reliability.  AI Summary

Metering who uses listing data is an engineering problem with engineering answers. Deciding what a contributed listing is worth is not, and the difficulty sits in the field definitions rather than in anybody’s policy.

The proposal itself is sound, and it is gaining ground. Meter extraction, credit the organizations that supply the data, and reward the brokerages that send more of their eligible inventory into the system rather than less. Paper agreements stop working the moment data leaves the system, and an incentive attached to the record travels wherever the record goes.A contribution model based primarily on listing counts risks rewarding volume rather than the completeness and usefulness of the information. That is the obvious unit, and it is the wrong one, because two listings entered on the same morning by the same brokerage can differ by the only thing a valuation needs.

The RESO Data Dictionary permits three answers to whether a closed sale carried concessions: yes, no and call listing agent. The ‘Concessions Amount’ sits beside it as a number field, ‘Concessions Comments’ as free text. All three belong to the closing group, which RESO describes as intended to describe facts that occurred at the closing of a transaction rather than offers made before it. RESO’s own guidance says recording this data consistently is important, and notes that adopting the newer concessions fields is optional for any organization.A concession is consideration. Fannie Mae specifically says concessions adjustments should reflect their impact on the transaction price, rather than automatically deducting the full dollar amount of concessions. In some cases, the market-based adjustment may be smaller than the concession or unnecessary. Also, RESO’s concessions fields for closed transactions shouldn’t be confused with fields advertising potential seller concessions before closing.

RESO explicitly distinguishes the two uses in its April 2024 guidance. It moves the figure a buyer paid without moving the figure the deed records, and that gap is the entire reason an appraiser adjusts for it. Fannie Mae requires adjustments to reflect the market’s reaction to the difference between properties, naming paired sales as one method among statistical analysis, modeling and other commonly accepted approaches. Every one of them needs the magnitude.

It is not one field. View carries 38 category words, among them ‘Bay’, ‘City Lights’, ‘Ocean’ and ‘Panoramic’, with no amount and no rating attached. ‘Entry Level’ carries the floor as a number and nothing joins the two, while Fannie Mae’s condo section requires special attention to a unit’s location within its project and says nothing about view at all.So, a contribution model priced by record count pays for the half of the work that costs nothing. An address, bedrooms, bathrooms and a price make a record. The concession amount, the extent of the view and the condition detail make it evidence. Paying the same for both, or partial credit for the thinner one, is a reliable way to end up with more records rather than better ones.

I think requiring a number whenever the answer to the concessions question is ‘yes’ is a rules change inside a single MLS’s authority, enforceable at the point of entry, and it costs an agent the half minute it takes to read a closing statement already in front of them. Apply it to the other fields that carry magnitude rather than category and a contribution model has something worth metering.The alternative is a market that pays for volume. Records multiply, credits clear and the fields that decide what a house is worth carry whatever they happen to carry, because nothing in the scheme ever asked for them.The governance conversation is about who may read the record. What the record contains is a separate question, and it is the one that can be answered this quarter by any organization willing to make a single field mandatory.Nikola Gojkovic is the founder of CMAflow and writes on residential valuation methodology.

#5568. 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch.

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February. Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

Asked whether a brokerage could turn those predictions against its own clients, Ezra called it “a valid concern.” The founders pointed to regulation, monitoring and an internal ethics committee as checks on that kind of use.

Gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity are the next markets 42AI is exploring, with helping robots and AI agents understand people as a longer-term goal. Wherever it runs, the model loses accuracy when it misses outside influences, such as a trader acting on a colleague’s advice. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said.

The $62.5 million, which 42AI describes as seed funding, came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Amir Gal-Or, the startup’s co-founder and chairman, founded Infinity Group. Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is among the advisers to the research team. 42AI plans to raise more money.

ERA Live Moore, one of the Carolinas’ premier real estate brokerages, today announced the acquisition of Blue Door Group Real Estate, a respected and established local firm serving the Greater Winston Salem market. Moving forward, the brokerage will operate as Blue Door Group Real Estate, an ERA Live Moore Company, preserving its trusted local identity while connecting agents and clients to the expanded resources of the ERA Live Moore network.

Binance reported that the hack may have stemmed from a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which could have facilitated unauthorized withdrawals. However, they emphasized that there is no evidence of private key exposure. The exchange has vowed to cover all user losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and corporate reserves, and has temporarily suspended withdrawals while reinforcing its security measures.

Analytics firms widely suspect that North Korean actors, particularly the TraderTraitor group, are behind the attack, although Binance has not confirmed this. President Trump has commented on the Binance exploit, saying the FBI is investigating and that it also suspects North Korean-linked hackers are behind the hack.

While this incident introduces significant short-term uncertainty and reputational risk, Binance’s quick commitment to compensating users, the freezing of a large portion of the compromised funds, and the market’s overall resilience may help mitigate the situation.

If the response contains the damage effectively, the incident may ultimately be absorbed as a stress test rather than a permanent impairment to the long-term thesis.

#5565. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped from $55 billion at the end of 2025 to about $314 billion in the third quarter.

Alongside the new financial figures, Anthropic’s revised S-1 filing provides an update about its efforts to mitigate AI risks. According to the document, the company is considering “to require human review and approval of certain” research tasks that are currently performed automatically by its models. It believes that its models will soon be capable of “dramatically” accelerating AI development.

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it plans to raise through its public offering. Reuters reported that Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

#5564. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?
