#5563. Why Offerpad is getting more selective on home buys

Offerpad said faster rising mortgage rates and affordability pressures slowed home sales in Q3 2026. The iBuyer tightened acquisition criteria, leaned more on brokerage and its marketplace and guided to positive adjusted EBITDA run rate by Q2 2027.  AI Summary

Heading into the second half of 2026, Offerpad was laser-focused on “turning its buying engine back on,” however, housing market headwinds caused by rapidly rising mortgage rates and continued affordability challenges, have led the iBuyer to increase the intentionality behind its strategy.

In a call with investors and analysts to discuss the company’s third quarter 2026 earnings, Offerpad executives said that with homes taking longer to sell, the firm adjusted its acquisition criteria to require higher expected returns on a property. In addition, they said the company has become more selective about new purchases and that it adjusted its underwriting to build wider expected margins into each purchase.

Instead of providing home sellers with a direct cash offer, executives said Offerpad was looking to serve more sellers through its Cash Offer Marketplace and Brokerage Services offerings.

During the quarter, Offerpad recorded 324 total transactions, up from 295 transactions a quarter prior, but down 32% annually. Executives attributed the lower-than-anticipated number of transactions for the quarter to the overall slower housing market.

“We’ve operated with mortgage rates above 7% before,” Brian Bair, the CEO of Offerpad, said during the earnings call Monday evening. “What was different this time was the speed of the move late in our quarter and the attention it received. Housing affordability has become a national story. With headlines describing it as a buyer’s market. Buyers weighed higher monthly payments against the possibility of a better deal. While sellers faced uncertainty about how long their homes would take to sell and what price they could achieve. We believe that combination contributed to a more cautious market as the quarter came to a close.”

In total, Offerpad’s Brokerage Services and Cash Offer Marketplace represented approximately 35% of Q3 closed transactions, with the company noting that brokerage listing signings more than doubled from Q2 2026.

In total, Offerpad acquired 605 homes during the quarter, up 198% annually. According to executives, these purchases were concentrated in markets where homes were still selling at a pace that met the company’s requirements. On the sales side, Offerpad sold 210 homes during the quarter, down 43% annually, but up slightly from Q2 2026.

“Last quarter, we said we were increasing acquisitions and we did by acquiring 605 homes in Q3. We also had additional homes under contract that could have increased that total. As market conditions shifted, we reevaluated them against our wider margin requirements and chose not to proceed with homes that no longer met our criteria,” Bair, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said. “Where possible, we offered those sellers an alternative through cash offer or broker services. Buying well is only half the process.”

At the end of the quarter aged inventory represented just 2.6% of all homes on the balance sheet, well below Offerpad’s 10% aged inventory threshold. The company said that this inventory is expected to provide a pipeline of dispositions through the rest of 2026 and into early 2027. So far in Q4, leaders said 200 homes have sold or are under contract for sale.

Bair noted on the call that Offerpad’s current portfolio of homes is “healthy” and that most were bought within the last few months.

Looking ahead, Offerpad executives said that returning to profitability is the company’s primary focus. During the third quarter of 2026, Offerpad recorded $78.1 million in revenue, down 41% annually, while the company’s net loss of $11.5 million for the quarter was a 1% improvement compared to a year prior. As the iBuyer looks to get back into the black, executives said they are focused on reducing operating expenses and growing Cash Offer Marketplace and brokerage services.

While the company has cut operating expenses by more than $140 million since 2022, during Q3, executives said they identified an additional $8 million to $10 million in annualized operating expense reductions, which they expect to be implemented in 2027.

“Profitability remains our No. 1 priority. And nothing about that has changed. What has changed is the timeline. The shift in the market has pushed our path out, and we now expect to exit the second quarter of 2027 at a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate,” Bair said. “Together, these actions give us the opportunity to reach positive adjusted EBITDA with fewer transactions than before.”

Offerpad executives have noted that they believe positive adjusted EBITDA will come with roughly 1,000 transactions per quarter. In Q4 2026, the company said it anticipated 400-475 transactions, but executives are optimistic the firm will reach that 1,000 transaction threshold. On the call, executives noted that the firm is using lenders to fund a larger share of each home’s cost, meaning that less of Offerpad’s capital is tied up in the homes the firm buys.

“That makes our capital go further and it helps it return to the business faster as homes sell. At quarter end, we had approximately $251 million of undrawn capacity under our inventory financing facilities, the majority of which is uncommitted,” Andrew Piper, who was appointed interim chief financial officer, replacing Peter Knag, said. “We believe our cash, the capital we expect to return as homes sell, and our inventory financing are sufficient as we execute our 2027 plan. We also remain open to opportunities to strengthen our balance sheet, including strategic capital partnerships, and we will be disciplined about the structure and cost of any capital we add.”

#5562. State lawmaker pay in 20 states, from New York's $142,000 to New Mexico's $0

Free daily briefing on global business news.

State legislator salaries run from $142,000 in New York to $0 in New Mexico, and these 20 states show the range in base pay and per diems

A New York state lawmaker earns $142,000 a year. A New Hampshire lawmaker earns $100 a year and gets no per diem. New Mexico sits outside that scale entirely. It is the one state that sets no legislative salary, though its legislators collect a per diem of $202 a day. Those figures come from Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries. They show how far state legislator salaries spread across the U.S.

All five legislatures that Ballotpedia names as its top five by pay operate full time. Every state in the lower half of this selection runs a hybrid or part-time legislature.

States also differ in who decides the pay. Commissions play that role in 19 states. Some of those commissions produce reports that bind no one. Others make recommendations that take effect unless the legislature, the governor or voters block them. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters must approve any recommended change. Some states tie legislative pay to what other state employees earn. Others let lawmakers set their own pay. The National Conference of State Legislatures calls the political risk of voting yourself a raise the "pay problem." Inflation can then outrun that pay. When it does, real salaries shrink over time.

This slideshow covers 20 of the 50 states. It includes 10 from the upper end of the annual base salaries in Ballotpedia's 2025 table and 10 from the lower end. Ballotpedia names only a top five. The rest of the order here comes from sorting the table's annual figures. States that pay lawmakers by the day, week, month or session are left off both lists. Ballotpedia gives no session lengths, so their pay cannot be placed on an annual scale. Those states are Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, Utah, Wyoming, Vermont, North Dakota and Maine. Washington state and Wisconsin fall just below Alabama and outside this selection. Each slide gives a state's base salary, its per diem and whether its legislature is full time, hybrid or part time.

New York pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $142,000, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries. That is the largest annual base salary among the 20 states covered here.

New York lawmakers also receive a per diem of $203 a day. The two payments work differently. The salary is a fixed yearly amount. It arrives regardless of how many days the legislature meets. The per diem is a daily payment, and the 2025 table lists it separately from base pay.

The table does not give the length of New York's legislative session. It also does not say how many days members claim the per diem. Without those figures, the daily rate cannot be turned into a reliable yearly total. The $203 is a separate daily payment, not an addition to the $142,000 salary.

Ballotpedia classifies the New York legislature as full time. The National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) uses the same category in a report dated July 28, 2021. In that report, lawmakers in full-time legislatures devote about 84% of a full-time job to legislative work. That share means legislative work takes up most of a standard working year for members in this group. Average pay in that group was about $82,358.

New York's $142,000 salary sits well above that full-time average. The two figures come from different years, however. Ballotpedia's number reflects 2025 pay. The NCSL average dates to its 2021 report. Pay in other full-time states may have changed since then. A current average could sit higher or lower than the 2021 figure. The comparison shows the scale of New York's pay rather than a precise difference.

The full-time label and the salary describe the same job from two angles. One measures how much of a working year the role takes. The other measures what the state pays for it.

California pays its state legislators a base salary of $132,703 a year. Lawmakers also collect a per diem of $236 a day, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 table of state legislative salaries.

That salary places California second among the 20 states in this selection, behind New York. California is one of the five legislatures that Ballotpedia names as its top five by pay.

The two leading states differ on the daily payment. California's per diem is larger than New York's, even though its base salary is smaller.

The per diem sits outside the $132,703 figure. It is set as a daily rate rather than an annual sum. Ballotpedia's table does not say how many days it applies. That means there is no annual per diem total to report. A California lawmaker's full yearly pay cannot be read from the table alone.

Ballotpedia classifies California's legislature as full time.

Pennsylvania pays its state lawmakers an annual base salary of $110,015.54, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries. Members also receive a per diem of $198 a day.

Pennsylvania is one of the five states Ballotpedia names as its top five by legislative pay. Within this 20-state selection, only New York and California set a higher annual base salary.

Pennsylvania's legislature is classified as full time.

Ballotpedia lists the salary and the per diem as separate items. The $110,015.54 base figure does not include the daily payment. That payment comes on top of the salary.

Ballotpedia gives a single salary figure for Pennsylvania. It does not list separate amounts for each chamber, as it does for some other states.

Pennsylvania's lawmakers serve in two chambers. The General Assembly is made up of a House of Representatives and a State Senate.

Members of the General Assembly are not subject to term limits. They can keep seeking reelection without a cap on how many terms they serve.

Illinois state legislators earn a base salary of $93,712 a year. That places Illinois fourth among the five legislatures that Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries names as its top five by pay.

Within that group, Illinois sits below Pennsylvania's $110,015.54 and above Alaska's $84,000. Those two states hold the third and fifth spots.

Illinois lawmakers also receive a per diem of $178 a day. Ballotpedia lists this daily payment separately from the annual base pay. The table gives it as one flat rate, with no distance tiers or residency conditions attached.

That flat rate differs from the per diem rules in several other full-time legislatures in this selection. Massachusetts and Michigan pay no per diem. Ohio pays none during session. Alaska and Hawaii tie their daily payments to where a lawmaker lives.

Ballotpedia classifies the Illinois legislature as full time.

The table does not say how many days a year Illinois lawmakers collect the per diem. Without that count, the daily rate cannot be combined with the $93,712 salary to produce a yearly total.

Alaska pays its state legislators a base salary of $84,000 a year. Its legislature is classified as full time. Lawmakers from outside Juneau also collect a per diem of $307 a day. Lawmakers who live in Juneau receive no per diem.

That salary puts Alaska fifth among the 10 higher-paying states in this selection. It sits behind New York, California, Pennsylvania and Illinois. It sits ahead of Massachusetts, Hawaii, Ohio and Michigan.

The per diem rule creates two levels of compensation inside one legislature. Every member draws the same $84,000 base salary. A member from outside Juneau adds $307 for each day the per diem applies. A colleague from Juneau draws the salary alone.

Alaska's $307 daily rate is the largest per diem among the 20 states in this selection. South Carolina's $240.07 and Virginia's $237 come next.

The $84,000 figure covers base salary only. The per diem is a separate payment made on top of it. Eligibility for that payment depends on where a member lives.

Massachusetts pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $82,044.31. Ballotpedia's 2025 table lists no per diem for them and counts the legislature as full time.

That salary places Massachusetts sixth among the 10 higher-paying states in this selection. It sits below Alaska and above Hawaii.

Ballotpedia's own named top five ends with Alaska. Massachusetts is therefore the highest-paying state here that falls outside the source's named top five. Its sixth-place position comes from sorting the table's annual figures, not from a ranking Ballotpedia publishes.

A per diem is a daily allowance some states pay on top of a lawmaker's salary. In those states, yearly pay can rise above the base salary on the days a legislator qualifies for the allowance. The table shows no such rate for Massachusetts. Its base salary is the only pay figure the table lists for the state's lawmakers.

Massachusetts is not alone in this among the higher-paying states in this selection. Michigan also lists no per diem. Ohio lists none during session. New York and California, by contrast, pair their salaries with daily rates.

The full-time label puts Massachusetts alongside every other state in the upper group except Alabama. Alabama runs a hybrid legislature.

Hawaii pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $74,160. Members who live off Oahu also receive a per diem of $225 a day.

Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table lists both figures and classifies Hawaii's legislature as full time.

Whether a member gets the per diem depends on where that legislator lives. A member whose home is on an island other than Oahu qualifies for the $225 daily rate. A member who lives on Oahu gets no per diem and draws the base salary alone.

Under that rule, two Hawaii lawmakers with the same base salary can end up with different total pay. The difference comes from their home island.

Among the 10 states in the upper half of this selection, Hawaii's $74,160 salary places seventh. It falls below Massachusetts and above Ohio.

Ohio pays its state lawmakers an annual base salary of $72,343, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries. Ohio legislators receive no per diem during session.

That salary ranks eighth among the 10 higher-paying states in this selection. When the source's annual figures are sorted from highest to lowest, Ohio sits just below Hawaii and just above Michigan.

Ballotpedia classifies Ohio's legislature as full time. Nine of the 10 higher-paying states in this selection carry that label. Alabama, which the source lists as hybrid, is the only exception.

Ohio's per diem entry sets it apart from most of the higher-paying group. Seven of those 10 states list some form of daily allowance on top of base salary. In Alaska and Hawaii, that allowance goes only to some members. Massachusetts and Michigan are the other two that list no per diem.

The wording of Ohio's entry differs from those two states. Massachusetts and Michigan are listed with no per diem at all. Ohio's entry specifies no per diem during session. The 2025 table does not say what, if anything, Ohio lawmakers receive outside session.

For session work, that leaves the base salary as the only pay the table records for an Ohio lawmaker. In California and Pennsylvania, by contrast, a daily allowance comes on top of a larger base salary.

The table also gives Ohio a single salary figure. Virginia lists different amounts for its delegates and its senators.

Ohio's salary exceeds every base salary in the lower half of this selection. That includes Rhode Island's, the highest in that group.

A missing per diem is not limited to the higher-paying states. Rhode Island and New Hampshire, both part-time legislatures in the lower group, also list none. In those states, no daily allowance sits on top of a much smaller base salary.

Ohio's legislature is the Ohio General Assembly. It has two chambers, the Ohio House of Representatives and the Ohio Senate.

Michigan pays its state legislators a base salary of $71,685 a year, with no per diem on top. Its legislature is full time.

That salary puts Michigan ninth among the 10 higher-paying states in this 20-state selection, which is sorted from Ballotpedia's 2025 table. Ohio ranks just above it, at $72,343. Alabama ranks just below it, at $62,212.

Michigan is also the lowest-paid full-time legislature among the 20 states here. Alabama, the next state down, runs a hybrid legislature. Every state in the lower 10 is hybrid or part time.

Without a per diem, the $71,685 salary is all of the pay Ballotpedia lists for a Michigan lawmaker. A per diem is a daily payment made on top of salary. New York, California, Pennsylvania and Illinois all pay one to their full-time legislators. Michigan does not.

Two other states in the upper group take a similar approach. Massachusetts lists no per diem. Ohio pays none during session.

The absence of a per diem also means Michigan's listed pay does not change with where a lawmaker lives. In Alaska, the daily allowance depends on whether a member lives in Juneau. In Hawaii, it goes only to members who live off Oahu. Alabama's depends on distance and trip length. Michigan's entry carries no such variation. A member from any part of the state receives the same listed figure.

Alabama pays its state legislators a base salary of $62,212 a year. It is the only hybrid legislature among the 10 higher-paying states in this selection. The other nine are all full time.

The hybrid label comes from the National Conference of State Legislatures. NCSL sorts legislatures into full-time, hybrid and part-time groups based on how much of a full-time job the legislative work takes.

NCSL found that hybrid legislators spend about 74% of a full-time job on legislative work. Average pay for the hybrid group was about $41,110.

Alabama's base salary sits above that hybrid average. The two figures come from different years, though. The NCSL average dates from 2021, while the $62,212 salary comes from Ballotpedia's 2025 table.

The hybrid label does not settle where a state's pay lands. Texas, South Carolina, Nebraska, North Carolina, Louisiana and Virginia also run hybrid legislatures, and all six sit in the lower half of this selection. Alabama shares their classification, yet its salary places it among the higher-paying states.

Alabama does not pay a single flat per diem. The daily allowance depends on distance and trip length, including whether a trip involves an overnight stay.

Trips of under six hours carry no per diem at all. A trip lasting six to 12 hours pays $12.75.

A trip of more than 12 hours without an overnight stay pays $34. A trip that includes one night away pays $85.

For trips of two or more nights, the rate rises to $100 a day. The structure ties the allowance to time spent away. A short trip earns nothing, while a multi-night stay draws the highest rate.

Among the 10 higher-paying states here, Alabama is the only one whose per diem varies with trip length. New York, California, Pennsylvania and Illinois each pay one daily rate. Massachusetts and Michigan pay no per diem. Ohio pays none during session.

Rhode Island pays its state lawmakers an annual base salary of $19,817, with no per diem on top. Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table classifies the Rhode Island legislature as part time.

With no per diem, that salary is the only regular pay the table records for a Rhode Island legislator. Days spent in session do not add a separate daily payment to it.

Among the 10 lower-paying states in this selection, Rhode Island has the highest base salary. It pays more than Virginia pays either its delegates or its senators. It also pays more than Louisiana's base salary, before Louisiana's separate expense allowance is considered.

The comparison changes once daily payments enter the picture. Several states in the lower group pay smaller salaries and then add a daily payment. Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Nebraska all follow that pattern. Rhode Island takes the opposite approach and puts all of its recorded pay into the salary itself.

Rhode Island is one of two states in the lower group with no per diem at all. New Hampshire is the other. In the upper group, Massachusetts and Michigan also pay no per diem, and Ohio pays none during session. All three run full-time legislatures.

Rhode Island is also one of four part-time legislatures in this selection. The others are South Dakota, New Hampshire and New Mexico. Of those four, Rhode Island pays the highest base salary.

Politico reviewed 2018 financial disclosures from state legislators whose forms were available, and Ballotpedia cites that review. Of 117 men, 42, or 36%, had other jobs. Six of 49 women also had other jobs.

As Ballotpedia presents them, those counts are not specific to Rhode Island. They show that a share of state legislators held other jobs in 2018. They do not show how many members of the Rhode Island legislature hold outside work.

Virginia pays its delegates $17,640 a year and its senators $18,000, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table. Virginia legislators also collect a per diem of $237 a day.

Virginia is the only state among the 20 in this selection with two base salaries in its table entry. Senators receive the higher amount. Delegates receive the lower one.

Sorting the states requires one figure for each. This selection uses the delegates' $17,640 to place Virginia.

The choice of figure does not move Virginia. On either salary, the state sits above Louisiana and below Rhode Island. That makes Virginia the second-highest payer among the 10 lower-paying states covered here. Even the senators' $18,000 falls short of Rhode Island's base salary.

Ballotpedia classifies Virginia's legislature as hybrid. Six of the 10 lower-paying states in this selection run hybrid legislatures, and Virginia is one of them. The other four in that group are part time.

The table lists Virginia's $237 per diem as a single daily rate. Some states in this selection scale their per diem by how far a legislator lives from the Capitol. Virginia's entry attaches no distance or residency condition to its rate.

The per diem is a separate payment from base pay. It is not part of the $17,640 paid to delegates or the $18,000 paid to senators.

This slide falls short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives Virginia only its two base salaries, a per diem and a legislature type, and no approved supplementary details cover Virginia.

Louisiana pays its state legislators a base salary of $16,800 a year. Each lawmaker also receives a $6,000 annual expense allowance, which Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries lists apart from the salary.

The two payments serve different purposes. Salary is compensation for holding the office. The $6,000 is an expense payment, and it is unvouchered. Legislators do not have to back it with receipts or itemized claims to receive it.

That distinction shapes how Louisiana compares with other states. Its position in this 20-state selection rests on the $16,800 salary alone. The allowance plays no part in the ordering.

Louisiana also pays a per diem of $178 a day. A per diem is a third kind of payment, separate from both the salary and the expense allowance. It is paid for days of legislative work rather than as a fixed annual amount. The per diem grows with the number of working days, while the salary and the allowance stay fixed.

Illinois uses the same $178 daily rate. Illinois runs a full-time legislature with a far higher base salary, so an identical per diem can sit inside very different pay structures.

Louisiana's legislature is classified as hybrid.

Among the 10 lower-paying states in this selection, Louisiana's base salary ranks third from the top. Only Virginia and Rhode Island pay more in base salary within that group. South Dakota, at $16,348, sits just below Louisiana.

South Dakota pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $16,348. Its legislature is classified as part time, and members who live more than 50 miles away also receive a per diem of $178 a day.

The salary is the fixed part of the package. Every member receives the same base amount, whether home is a short drive from the statehouse or at the far end of the state.

The per diem works differently in South Dakota. The $178 daily rate goes only to legislators whose homes sit more than 50 miles away. Members who live closer receive the base salary alone.

That split means two South Dakota lawmakers serving in the same session can take home different totals from the job. The difference turns on where each member lives.

The per diem is also a daily rate rather than a yearly sum. What an eligible member collects depends on how many days that member is paid for. Ballotpedia's table does not give that count. Without it, the per diem cannot be converted into an annual figure.

The part-time label comes from the National Conference of State Legislatures, which sorts legislatures into full-time, hybrid and part-time groups. Its report dated July 28, 2021, found that part-time legislators devote about 57 percent of a full-time job to legislative work. That is more than half of a standard workload.

The same report put average pay for part-time legislators at about $18,449. South Dakota's base salary sits below that average. The two figures come from different years, though. The NCSL average dates from 2021, while South Dakota's salary comes from Ballotpedia's 2025 data.

The NCSL report also found that part-time legislators typically need another source of income beyond their legislative pay. That finding describes part-time legislatures as a group, not South Dakota's members in particular.

North Carolina pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $13,951 and a per diem of $104 a day, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 table of state legislative salaries. Ballotpedia classifies the state's legislature as hybrid.

The two figures measure different things. The salary is a fixed yearly amount. The per diem is a separate daily payment on top of it.

Ballotpedia does not say how many days a year the per diem covers. A North Carolina lawmaker's full-year pay cannot be worked out from these two figures alone.

The daily rate is lower than the salary ranking might suggest. Several states in this selection pay every member the same flat daily rate, without distance or residence conditions. Among those states, North Carolina's $104 is the lowest.

The base salary sits near the middle of the selection's lower group. Among the 10 lower-paying states here, North Carolina ranks sixth from the bottom. Its salary sits above Nebraska's $12,000. It falls below South Dakota's $16,348.

The hybrid label does not settle where a state's pay lands. Three other hybrid legislatures in this selection, Texas, South Carolina and Nebraska, pay lower base salaries than North Carolina. Virginia, Louisiana and Alabama, also hybrid, pay more.

The two states below Texas in the lower group, New Mexico and New Hampshire, both run part-time legislatures. North Carolina's hybrid legislature pays more in base salary than either of them.

Nebraska pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $12,000. Any recommended change to that salary must win voter approval before it can take effect.

That rule means the salary cannot rise through a commission report or a legislative vote alone. Nebraska voters hold the final say over what their legislators earn.

Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table classifies Nebraska's legislature as hybrid. Hybrid legislatures fall between full-time and part-time bodies.

Within the 10 lower-paying states in this selection, Nebraska sits in the middle. Its salary is higher than South Carolina's and lower than North Carolina's.

The salary is only one part of a Nebraska legislator's compensation. Lawmakers also collect a per diem. The daily rate depends on how far they live from the Capitol.

Legislators who live within 50 miles of the Capitol receive $68 a day. Those who live farther away receive $178 a day.

The distance line splits Nebraska's lawmakers into two groups for daily allowances. The $12,000 salary is the same for all of them. A legislator who lives far from the Capitol draws the higher rate for each day the per diem applies.

South Dakota also draws a line at 50 miles. There, the distance decides whether a legislator gets a per diem at all. In Nebraska, every legislator gets one, at one of two rates.

South Carolina pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $10,400, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table. Lawmakers also collect a per diem of $240.07 a day.

That salary places South Carolina near the bottom of this 20-state selection. Among the 10 lower-paying states covered here, only New Mexico, New Hampshire and Texas set a smaller annual base salary.

The daily allowance points the other way. South Carolina's per diem of $240.07 is the largest daily rate among those 10 states. Virginia pays $237 a day, and Texas pays $221.

The South Carolina rate also tops California's $236 a day. California pairs that per diem with a base salary of $132,703. Across all 20 states in this selection, only Alaska's rate for legislators who live outside Juneau is higher.

A per diem is a daily payment made on top of salary. Ballotpedia's table gives no session lengths. It therefore does not show how many days qualify for the payment. Any yearly per diem total for a South Carolina legislator would be a guess.

That gap shapes how South Carolina compares with other states on this list. The salary is a fixed annual amount. The per diem varies with the number of qualifying days. Ordering by base salary captures only the fixed part of the pay.

Rhode Island pays a larger base salary than South Carolina and no per diem. Salary order alone therefore cannot show which of the two states pays its lawmakers more over a year. Texas sets both a smaller salary and a smaller daily rate than South Carolina. New Mexico sets no salary at all and a lower daily rate.

The state's legislature is classed as hybrid, a category that sits between full-time and part-time legislatures. Six other states in this selection share that classification: Alabama, Virginia, Louisiana, North Carolina, Nebraska and Texas. The salary table does not say how South Carolina sets its $10,400 figure.

Texas pays its state legislators an annual base salary of $7,200 and a per diem of $221 a day, according to Ballotpedia's 2025 comparison of state legislative salaries. Ballotpedia classifies the Texas legislature as hybrid.

That salary puts Texas third from the bottom among the 20 states in this selection. Only New Mexico and New Hampshire list a lower annual base salary.

The per diem ranks higher. Among the 10 lower-paying states in this selection, only South Carolina and Virginia list a higher daily rate than Texas.

The $221 is paid per day, separately from the salary. The annual salary on its own therefore leaves out part of what Texas pays its legislators.

Ballotpedia's table does not say how many days a year Texas legislators collect the per diem. Without that number, the source does not support a yearly total for it. It also does not show how the per diem adds up against the $7,200 salary over a full year.

New Hampshire pays its state legislators $100 a year and no per diem. Its legislature is classified as part time.

With no daily allowance added, that $100 is the full amount the state pays a member for legislative service in a year.

In this 20-state selection, only New Mexico ranks below New Hampshire on annual base salary. New Mexico's place at the bottom comes from setting no salary at all. New Hampshire does set one, but it is a nominal sum.

Those lawmakers serve in the General Court, the name for New Hampshire's legislature as a whole. It has two chambers, a House of Representatives and a Senate.

Members of the General Court face no limit on how many terms they may serve.

New Mexico pays its state legislators no salary. It is the one state in Ballotpedia's 2025 salary table that sets no base pay for lawmakers. Its legislators receive a per diem of $202 a day instead.

With a base salary of $0, New Mexico sits at the bottom of the 20 states in this selection. The $202 figure is a daily allowance, not a salary. Ballotpedia lists it separately from base pay.

The absence of a salary is written into state law at the highest level. New Mexico's constitution provides that legislators are not paid a salary.

Ballotpedia classifies New Mexico's legislature as part time.

The per diem is set as a daily rate rather than a fixed yearly sum. Ballotpedia's table does not show how many days that rate is paid in a year. It therefore does not show what a New Mexico lawmaker collects in total.

#5561. Mortgage rates have a quiet week as markets digest Fed comments, Trump’s directive

Mortgage rates were mostly flat week over week, with the 30-year fixed averaging 7.38%. Jumbo and FHA rates fell modestly, while markets are still pricing a likely 25-bps Fed hike in December.  AI Summary

Mortgage rate movement was largely flat in the past week, with the downward momentum of previous weeks cooling off even as more potential homebuyers have been incentivized to seek financing.

At HousingWire’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year loans averaged 7.38% — the same as one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.62%, down 7 bps in a week, while 30-year rates for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans stood at 7.16%, down 8 bps.

The small declines in rates come a week after the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate at a range of 3.75% of 4% in a widely expected decision. But after policymakers hiked rates in September, further increases are anticipated, with the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showing that 77% of interest rate traders predict a 25-basis-point increase in December.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote this week that tighter monetary policy “has created financial pain for some AI companies.” With the Fed focusing on the inflationary aspects of AI and associated debt-financing issues, the 10-year Treasury yield has been dropping, which has placed downward pressure on mortgage rates.

Hector Amendola, president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG, told HousingWire in an interview that he believes a December hike is already baked into current rates and that drastic movement, up or down, is unlikely to happen for the rest of this year.

“It’s kind of been par for the course now for a while, that rates are continuing to rise based on the expectation that the Fed will go up a little bit more until there’s a way to figure out how to tame inflation a little bit,” Amendola said.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced last week that the central bank would be shifting to fewer policy votes in each of the next two years. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) currently meets eight times a year, with a vote scheduled after each, but the number of votes will be reduced to seven in 2027 and potentially to six in 2028.

“I think it puts a little bit more weight on each of the meetings,” he said. “I also think it’s interesting, because as Warsh kicks over, you’re kind of wondering if it’ll be like, ‘Let’s break everything and see what happens and figure it out later,’ or are we going to continue to really look at the data and do what the data tells us?

“I think what I’ve seen so far is, it’s still a wait-and-see approach. Let’s see what the data says, and that’s kind of why I think this particular decision that came out [last week] was expected, because the data is saying, ‘Slow down.’”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that targets lower costs in multiple areas of housing finance. These include proactive mortgage insurance cancellations for conventional loan servicers, an expanded title waiver program through the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), reduced rates on some government-backed loans and the creation of a manufactured housing task force.

Mat Ishbia, president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), said this week in his monthly “3 Points” video that “housing affordability continues to be front and center in Washington D.C. There’s a real focus right now on finding ways to lower the cost of homeownership, reduce friction in the mortgage process and make financing more accessible.”

He pointed specifically to the proposal to make the title insurance waiver pilot a permanent program, saying that prior waivers on some low-risk refinances have been “saving consumers thousands of dollars.”

“Some of these ideas will help; some of them won’t help,” Ishbia said of the executive order. “We’ll see how it all shakes out. But I think these are good things they’re looking at doing.”

Amendola said his company has “always been big proponents” of waiving title insurance on refi transactions with loan-to-value ratios below 80%. “Like, what are we really doing? It’s the same consumer. You know, all that stuff is still coming up,” he remarked.

He also said that allowing servicers of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans to help borrowers cancel their mortgage insurance premiums when they reach the statutory threshold “is a bigger deal than people think.” U.S. Mortgage Insurers have expressed their support for the move, while some analysts label it as “fairly benign” for the financial performance of mortgage insurers.

“That’s extra revenue that they’re making right now that they, honestly, probably shouldn’t be making — and suddenly they’re going to have an impact on their end,” Amendola said. “But it’s going to be really good for the homeowner to free up some of that cash that can then turn into something else for them.”

#5560. Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra, product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE. “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get to capitalize from.”

Dell and AMD must also accommodate a wealth of AI use cases and the accompanying demand for compute. Dell’s three-rack-unit server requires less power for cooling than a two-unit equivalent, allowing customers to pack more computing power into each rack, according to Narendra.

“By deploying servers that are slightly larger in package, you deliver more density at a rack level, which seems sometimes counterintuitive,” he explained. “As AI accelerates, inferencing and agentic AI around it will accelerate and grow faster. As these use cases scale out, you get exponential growth in the need for compute.”

Beyond server consolidation, Dell and AMD have been steadily enhancing a modular solution to simplify AI deployment and scaling: the Dell AI Platform with AMD.

The on-premises enterprise AI solution integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking and PowerScale storage for model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference. The platform is designed to let customers begin with configurations that meet current workloads and expand compute and GPU density over time, without rearchitecting.

“What we’re finding is customers want modular solutions. They want to think about [solutions] across the whole platform,” said Varun Chhabra, senior vice president of product marketing and infrastructure solutions group at Dell, in a discussion with theCUBE. “Compute, storage, networking [and] GPU. The software framework on top of it, the models: Have they all been tested? Have they all been validated?”

Dell has integrated the AMD ROCm software stack into the platform to support training, fine-tuning and serving large language models on-premises. The modular platform lets customers begin with smaller deployments and expand on the same infrastructure, according to Chhabra.

“You can start small with these composable units of storage, compute, networking, pre-integrated with AMD Instinct and EPYC CPUs with the ROCm software as well as the open ecosystem that sits on top of it,” he said. “We test it, we validate it, and the customers can use it and once they start seeing value in it, they know they can scale in a modular way with the same frameworks.”

Dell announced support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers beginning in July, giving enterprises another option for scaling agentic and generative AI deployments. It also represents an important boost in memory bandwidth which matters in time-to-first-token latency.

The MI350P offers 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, which can be a key differentiator for inference performance, according to Mike Darby, senior manager of business development, Instinct Data Center GPUs, at AMD, during an appearance on theCUBE.

“It’s a lot of memory, but it’s also HBM3E, so [it has] an amazing amount of bandwidth,” he said. “The main use case being inference: It’s all about that latency, time to first token [and] the user experience, so that your attention span doesn’t move somewhere else while you’re waiting for your response.”

AMD and Dell’s collaboration on PCIe integration has another angle worth watching. AMD’s PCIe-based GPU supports air-cooled deployments, providing users with a path to deploy AI within existing data center infrastructure.

As the tech industry has encountered resistance in recent months to the buildout of large data centers across the U.S., concerns have centered on the environmental impact and use of water-based cooling systems. Separately, Dell found that, as it deployed its next-generation PowerEdge servers, some enterprise customers were still not prepared to adopt liquid cooling within data centers.

“Working with Dell, we added a PCI card to our air-coolable roadmap for GPU Instinct so that it fit in more Dell PowerEdge servers that go to the broader enterprise,” said Robert Hormuth, corporate vice president of architecture and strategy for the Data Center Solutions Group at AMD, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Not everybody is adopting direct liquid cooling.”

Dell’s work with AMD this year has extended beyond joint product announcements. In June, the two companies announced a partnership with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (SAIL) in the United Kingdom.

The collaboration is designed to help advance the next generation of AI infrastructure and AI-powered scientific breakthroughs. It builds on Cambridge’s expanded AI research infrastructure, including the Zenith AI supercomputer, powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators integrated into Dell infrastructure.

Dell and AMD have also collaborated in recent months on a telecom initiative with AT&T Inc. Telecom data is a heavy lift when it comes to AI, with AT&T having processed over one trillion tokens to train models. AMD has provided the high-performance hardware foundation for both training and inference workloads involving the OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.

Dell integrated this technology with AI-optimized servers for telecom environments to create a production-grade foundation for operators across data-intensive, real-world network environments. OTel 2.0’s training infrastructure uses Dell’s PowerEdge XE9785 server configured with eight MI355X GPUs.

The alliance between Dell and AMD highlights a key development in the growing AI infrastructure market: There are plenty of opportunities for competition. Both Dell and AMD appear committed to building portfolios that offer enterprise choices in AI processing solutions.

“AMD didn’t present its new products … as ‘respectable alternatives,’” Vellante said. “It claimed outright leadership across CPUs, GPUs, rack-scale performance, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar. It extended the argument across enterprise AI, robotics, ultra-low-latency inference and a rapidly expanding partner ecosystem.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5559. Real Brokerage expands in Midwest with Iowa-based The Team

The Real Brokerage announced that Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit moved their 30-agent group, The Team, to Real. The Dubuque, Iowa-based brokerage covers Iowa, Illinois and Wisconsin, with reported volume of $1.2B since 2020.  AI Summary

The Real Brokerage announced that real estate leaders Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit have moved their 30-agent brokerage to Real under the name The Team. The group, based in Dubuque, Iowa, previously operated as an independent brokerage known as Unlimited.

The Team serves buyers and sellers across Dubuque; Galena, Illinois; and southern Wisconsin. Since 2020, the brokerage has closed about 5,000 transactions totaling $1.2 billion in volume, according to the company announcement.

The move gives Real, a top-ranked firm by RealTrends Verified, a larger foothold in a smaller but active Midwest market as national brokerages continue to compete for productive teams rather than individual agents. For brokers and team leaders, these platform moves can signal shifting economics around splits, stock incentives, technology stacks and administrative support.

Buchheit brings more than 30 years of real estate experience to Real and also co-owns multiple complementary businesses in property management, insurance, HVAC, cleaning and construction. That ecosystem can create cross-sales and referral opportunities while helping to stabilize revenue through market cycles.

Buchheit recruited Burger to Unlimited in 2020 to run the company, a partnership that preceded Unlimited’s merger with the region’s largest brokerage. Together they grew Unlimited into a local market leader by both agent count and production, the announcement explained.

Burger has balanced ownership responsibilities with active production. He is on track to generate about $15 million in personal sales volume in 2026, according to the announcement.

At Real, Burger and Buchheit plan to leverage the firm’s cloud-based brokerage platform to streamline operations, recruit additional agents and expand into new Midwest markets.

“Cody and Dennis have built a business with a strong regional presence and a clear vision for growth,” Joel Kirsch, senior vice president of growth at Real and a 2024 HousingWire Insider, said in the announcement. “They bring valuable operational experience, production success and an entrepreneurial mindset.”

Buchheit said the switch was driven largely by technology and long-term positioning.

“Real is light-years ahead when it comes to technology and where the industry is going,” he said, noting that the platform and community provide tools and relationships to “build a business that’s positioned for the future.”

Burger said the move will allow him to spend less time on day-to-day management and more time on production, agent development and geographic expansion. “I’ve spent years running every aspect of the business while still producing, and Real gives me an opportunity to take a lot off my plate,” he said.

#5558. What happens to leftover campaign money? 10 federal rules for surplus funds

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What happens to leftover campaign money after an election depends on federal rules that ban personal use but allow refunds, charity gifts, party transfers and future campaigns

Fundraising rarely stops as a race nears the finish. Candidates keep asking for donations through the final weeks, and many committees end election night with money still in the bank. Winners and losers face the same question when the results are in. What happens to leftover campaign money?

The candidate cannot simply keep it. Federal law treats contributions as money raised for a campaign, not as a personal fund. The Federal Election Campaign Act bars candidates from converting campaign funds to personal use. The Federal Election Commission, or FEC, enforces that rule and oversees how federal committees handle what remains.

That ban still leaves a candidate with several legal paths. A committee can hold its surplus for a future federal campaign. No federal deadline forces it to spend the money. It can move funds to political party committees or donate them to tax-exempt charities. It can give to other candidates and political action committees, within contribution limits. It can also send money back to the donors who gave it.

Other uses involve settling the business of the race. Campaign money can pay off debts, including loans a candidate made to their own campaign. It can cover legal bills, recounts and the accounting work needed to comply with federal reporting rules. Candidates who win can use it for certain costs tied to their duties in office. A committee that wants to close has to dispose of its funds and clear its debts and obligations first.

This guide covers federal candidates only — people running for president, the U.S. Senate or the U.S. House of Representatives. Their committees answer to the FEC. State and local campaigns follow their own laws, which differ from place to place. Those rules are not covered here. Races for governor, mayor or state legislature fall outside the scope of this guide.

Each of the 10 slides that follow explains one option or restriction for surplus campaign funds. Each slide stands on its own. A reader looking for a single answer can go straight to it. Together they show where unused campaign donations can end up and where they cannot.

A federal candidate cannot keep leftover campaign money as personal income. The prohibition comes from the Federal Election Campaign Act, which forbids turning campaign contributions into personal funds. The ban still applies after Election Day, whether the candidate won or lost.

The rule reaches beyond the candidate. Federal law bars any person from converting a committee's money to personal use, and that includes family members and staff. A surplus stays committee money until it goes to a permitted purpose.

The Federal Election Commission enforces the ban. Its test looks at the expense itself rather than the reason a candidate gives for it. If a cost would exist even without the campaign or the candidate's duties as a federal officeholder, paying it with campaign funds is personal use.

That test explains the FEC's standard examples. A mortgage or rent payment comes due whether or not someone runs for office. So do grocery bills and a child's tuition. The campaign does not create any of those costs, and the committee cannot pay them.

FEC regulations name other expenses treated as personal use in every case. They include health club and country club dues, vacations and tickets to concerts or sporting events with no campaign purpose. Clothing is also on the list. The exception is low-value campaign items such as T-shirts and caps.

Some spending gets a case-by-case review instead. Meals, travel and vehicle costs can serve both campaign and private ends. The committee can pay the share tied to campaign activity. It cannot pay the private share.

Paying relatives draws its own scrutiny. A committee can put a family member on the payroll only for real work at a fair market rate. Any amount above the value of the services counts as personal use.

Penalties range from civil fines to criminal charges. The FEC can pursue civil enforcement. The Justice Department can prosecute knowing and willful violations. Former California Rep. Duncan Hunter pleaded guilty in 2019 to a conspiracy charge tied to spending campaign money on personal expenses.

A federal candidate can keep leftover campaign money in the committee and spend it on a later run. Federal law sets no deadline for using the funds and no cap on how much can sit in the account between elections.

That later run does not have to be for the same seat. The money can support a bid for the same office or for a different federal office. A House member who later runs for the Senate, for example, can draw on money raised for earlier House races.

FEC regulations allow a candidate to transfer funds from an earlier campaign committee to the committee for a new federal race. The main condition is that the candidate is not running for both offices at the same time.

House members face voters every two years. Senators serve six-year terms. A senator's committee can hold a balance through an entire term and put it toward the next reelection campaign. A House member's committee can carry money through several consecutive terms.

A committee that keeps a balance stays registered with the Federal Election Commission. It continues to file regular disclosure reports showing its cash on hand, receipts and spending. Those reports are public, so anyone can see how much a candidate has banked.

Funds carried forward remain campaign funds. The ban on personal use applies the whole time, whether the next race is two years away or 10.

Carrying money forward does not lock in its final use. A committee holding a balance can later choose a different legal path for it. Nothing in federal law forces that decision soon after election day.

"War chest" is the common shorthand for this money. A large balance lets an incumbent start a reelection campaign without first rebuilding funds from zero.

The same rules apply to candidates who lost. A defeated candidate can keep a committee open and use the money if they run for federal office again.

This option applies to federal committees. Money raised for state and local campaigns falls under state law, which differs from place to place.

A federal candidate's campaign committee can move any amount of leftover money to a political party committee. Federal law sets no dollar cap on these transfers. A committee can send its entire remaining balance to a party in one transaction.

The permission covers all three levels of party organization. A committee can send funds to a national party committee, a state party committee or a local party committee. The Federal Election Campaign Act lists these transfers among the lawful uses of campaign money.

At the national level, each major party runs several committees. The Democratic National Committee and the Republican National Committee handle party-wide work. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee focus on Senate races. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee do the same for the House.

State and local parties are separate organizations. Both major parties maintain state party organizations across the U.S. Many counties and cities also have local party committees. A candidate's committee can transfer money to these groups on the same unlimited terms as to national committees.

Sitting members of Congress regularly send campaign money to their party's congressional committees. Both parties' House campaign committees set fundraising expectations for their members, a practice commonly called party dues. A member's campaign account is one source of that money.

Once the money reaches a party committee, it belongs to the party. The party decides how to spend it, within the rules that govern party committees. That spending can include voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives and support for other candidates on the ticket.

Both sides of the transaction appear in public records. The candidate's committee reports the transfer as a disbursement on its regular filings with the Federal Election Commission. A party committee registered with the FEC reports the same money as a receipt. Anyone can look up these filings in the FEC's online database.

The absence of a ceiling sets party transfers apart from gifts to individual candidates. A contribution from one candidate's committee directly to another candidate faces a federal limit. A transfer to a party committee does not.

A federal campaign committee can give its leftover money to organizations that qualify as tax-exempt charities under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. No cap applies to the amount. The candidate cannot receive compensation from the donation or use it for personal benefit.

A committee can direct its entire surplus to one organization. It can also split the money among several groups. The federal contribution limits that cap gifts to other candidates and political action committees do not apply to charitable donations.

The 501(c)(3) category covers groups organized for charitable, religious, educational, scientific and similar purposes. Food banks, nonprofit hospitals, private universities and many other nonprofits fall into it. The Internal Revenue Service recognizes that status. Its online Tax Exempt Organization Search tool lets anyone check whether a group qualifies. Gifts to these organizations from individual donors are generally tax-deductible.

A candidate cannot route campaign money to a charity that then pays the candidate a salary or fee out of that gift. The donation also cannot serve as a way to deliver goods or services back to the candidate. These limits come from the Federal Election Campaign Act's ban on converting campaign funds to personal use.

Charity also takes the money out of electoral politics. The Internal Revenue Code bars 501(c)(3) organizations from participating in any campaign for or against a candidate for public office. A charity that receives leftover campaign funds cannot spend them supporting or opposing a candidate. The IRS enforces that restriction.

The gift stays on the public record. Campaign committees report their disbursements to the FEC. Itemized entries in those reports name the recipient and the amount. Anyone can search the filings to see which organization received the money.

For a candidate with no plans to seek federal office again, charity offers a permanent exit for the money. Money saved for a future race stays in the committee. A charity gift moves it out of the committee for good. One donation can clear a large balance in a single transaction.

A federal campaign committee can give its leftover money to other candidates and to political action committees. Unlike transfers to party committees, these gifts are capped by federal contribution limits.

Federal campaign finance law lets a candidate's committee contribute to other federal candidates. That gives a candidate with money left after a race a way to support others. A winning lawmaker may back colleagues in competitive seats. A losing candidate may support allies who share the same priorities.

The ceiling sets this route apart from several other ways of disposing of surplus funds. A gift from one candidate's committee to another counts as a contribution under federal law. The receiving campaign must count it toward the limit for that donor, as it would any other contribution.

Limits on gifts to other candidates apply per election. A primary and a general election count as separate elections. A runoff or special election also counts on its own. A committee can give up to the limit for each election in which the recipient is running.

Gifts to PACs work differently. The limit on contributions to a PAC is generally counted per calendar year rather than per election. The FEC publishes the current figures in a contribution limits chart on its website. Some of those limits are adjusted every two years, so the dollar amounts can shift from one cycle to the next. A committee checks the chart for the period in which it gives.

The caps restrict how much of a large surplus this route can absorb. A committee with a big balance would need many separate recipients to spend it down this way. Party transfers and charitable gifts carry no such ceiling. A committee can combine several permitted options to close out its balance.

Both sides of the transaction are public. The giving committee reports the disbursement to the FEC, and the recipient reports the receipt. Those reports appear in the FEC's online database, where anyone can trace money moving from one campaign to another.

A federal campaign committee can return leftover money to the people and organizations that gave it. Under Federal Election Commission rules, refunding contributions is a permitted way to dispose of surplus campaign funds.

A refund sends the money back to its original source. The donor recovers what they gave, and the committee's balance drops by the same amount. No new recipient gets the funds. That sets refunds apart from gifts to a charity, a party or another candidate, where the money moves on to someone else.

Refunds can go to any kind of contributor. Individuals, political action committees and party committees all give to federal candidates. A committee can send each of them its money back.

Refunds are not only an end-of-race decision. Federal rules also require committees to deal with certain contributions they cannot keep. A gift above the federal contribution limit must be refunded, redesignated or reattributed. A gift from a source barred from giving, such as a foreign national, must be refunded. Those corrective refunds follow their own deadlines. They are separate from a choice to return surplus money after an election.

Primary races create another common refund situation. Federal law treats a primary and a general election as separate elections, each with its own contribution limit. Some donors give money designated for the general election before the primary is decided. If the candidate loses the primary, the committee cannot spend that money on a race the candidate will not run. FEC rules require the committee to refund those funds or have the donor redesignate or reattribute them.

Every refund is a disbursement the committee must report to the FEC. Refunds show up in the committee's regular disclosure reports, which are public. Anyone can search those filings on the FEC website to see which committees returned money to donors.

The IRS does not let taxpayers deduct contributions to political campaigns or candidates. A donor who receives a refund recovers money that never produced a tax deduction in the first place.

A federal campaign committee can use leftover money to pay off its debts. Since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate, money raised after Election Day can also repay a candidate's personal loans in full.

Campaigns often end owing money. Unpaid bills to vendors, consultants, pollsters or staff remain obligations of the committee after the votes are counted. Paying them is a permitted use of surplus funds. A committee that still carries debt can also keep raising money to settle it.

Candidate loans are a separate category. Federal law lets candidates lend their own money to their campaigns without a limit on the amount. The harder question has been how that money gets paid back.

The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, often called McCain-Feingold, set a ceiling. A campaign could use no more than $250,000 in contributions collected after the election to repay a candidate's loans. FEC rules added a timing requirement. Loan amounts above the threshold had to be repaid with pre-election funds within 20 days of the election.

Ted Cruz challenged the restriction. The Texas Republican lent his 2018 Senate campaign $260,000 just before the election. That was $10,000 more than the cap allowed to be repaid from post-election money. His campaign let the 20-day window pass, leaving that amount unrecoverable under the rules. It then sued the FEC.

The Supreme Court struck down the limit in a 6-3 decision issued in May 2022. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority. He concluded that the cap burdened political speech in violation of the First Amendment. The majority found the government had not shown that the limit targeted actual corruption or its appearance.

Justice Elena Kagan wrote the dissent, joined by Justices Stephen Breyer and Sonia Sotomayor. She argued that post-election donations used to repay a candidate's loan flow to the candidate personally. Donors giving after the vote also know who won, which she viewed as a corruption risk.

The ruling has the largest effect on self-funding candidates. Those who lend their campaigns large sums can now seek full reimbursement through fundraising after the election. Contributions raised to retire that debt remain subject to the standard federal contribution limits.

Campaign funds can pay legal fees connected to a federal race. They can also cover a recount, an election contest and the accounting needed to comply with Federal Election Commission reporting rules. Each of these expenses can draw on money that remains after Election Day.

Recounts and election contests take place after ballots are cast. A recount retabulates the votes in a close race. An election contest is a formal legal challenge to a certified result. Both can require lawyers and staff. A committee with surplus money can use it to cover those bills.

Legal fees must be tied to the campaign. The personal-use test in the Federal Election Campaign Act applies to legal bills as well. It asks whether an expense would exist regardless of the campaign or the candidate's duties as an officeholder. Campaign money cannot pay for a legal matter the candidate would face anyway.

Compliance costs are a steady expense for any federal committee. Every committee must have a treasurer. The committee's reports to the FEC itemize what it received and what it spent. Preparing those filings takes bookkeeping and accounting work. Campaign funds can pay for that work.

Presidential general election campaigns have used separate legal and accounting compliance funds, commonly called GELACs. These accounts hold money raised for legal and compliance expenses. That money is kept apart from the main campaign account.

Public financing adds another rule. A presidential nominee who accepts a public grant for the general election receives money from the Presidential Election Campaign Fund. Taxpayers direct money to that fund by checking a $3 box on their federal income tax returns. Checking the box does not change the filer's tax owed or refund.

Accepting the grant comes with conditions. The nominee agrees not to raise private contributions for the general election campaign. The legal and accounting compliance fund is the exception. A publicly financed presidential campaign must also return surplus public money to the U.S. Treasury.

Privately raised money left in a committee carries no such repayment requirement.

A candidate who wins federal office can keep spending campaign money on ordinary and necessary expenses connected to the duties of that office. Those costs still cannot be personal expenses.

The permission comes from the Federal Election Campaign Act. The provision, codified at 52 U.S.C. 30114, lists officeholder expenses as a permitted use of contributions. The same section also covers campaign spending, charitable donations and transfers to party committees.

A newly elected member of the House or Senate still controls a campaign committee after Election Day. Under this provision, the committee's funds can pay for some costs of the job itself, not only the costs of running for it.

Campaign money is separate from the official funds Congress provides each member. Those office allowances come from the U.S. Treasury and pay for staff and offices. Campaign funds come largely from donors and stay subject to election law.

The limit on officeholder spending is the personal use rule. A cost is personal if it would exist even if the person did not hold office. A home mortgage stays off-limits for a sitting lawmaker, just as it does for a candidate.

That leaves a judgment for each cost. The question is whether the expense arises from the work of holding federal office or from private life. The FEC interprets and enforces the personal use rule. A committee unsure about a specific expense can request an FEC advisory opinion before spending the money.

Members of Congress also answer to their own chamber. The House Committee on Ethics and the Senate Select Committee on Ethics issue their own guidance on how lawmakers may use campaign funds. A lawmaker spending committee money has to satisfy both federal election law and the rules of the chamber where they serve.

Officeholder spending does not happen out of public view. The committee reports these payments to the FEC as disbursements, the same way it reports any other spending.

A federal campaign committee can close only after it has no outstanding debts or obligations and has disposed of all its remaining money. It then files a termination report with the Federal Election Commission. Until that report is filed, the committee must keep submitting its regular disclosure reports.

The two conditions work together. A committee with cash in the bank cannot simply abandon the balance and close its books. A committee that still owes vendors, staff or lenders cannot close while those bills stand. The debts and the bank account both have to reach zero before termination is possible.

Disposing of the remaining money means sending it somewhere federal rules permit. Refunds to donors, gifts to charities and transfers to party committees are among the allowed channels. A committee that wants to wind down has to move its final dollars through one of them. Only then can it ask to terminate.

Debts can take longer to clear than cash. A campaign can finish a race still owing money to consultants, pollsters, advertising firms or the candidate. Those obligations must be paid off or otherwise resolved before the committee can end. A committee that cannot pay its creditors in full can submit a debt settlement plan to the FEC on Form 8.

The termination report is the committee's final disclosure. It accounts for the last money in and the last money out. It also shows that nothing is left in the account and nothing is still owed. Once the FEC accepts it, the committee's reporting obligations end.

Until that point, the paperwork continues. A committee that has stopped campaigning but still holds money or owes debts remains registered with the FEC. It must keep filing its regular reports on schedule, even when little happens between them.

Federal law sets no deadline for a committee to close. A committee that stays open keeps its reporting duties for as long as it remains registered. Some committees stay on the FEC's books for years after a candidate's last campaign.

The filings themselves are public records. The FEC posts committee reports on its website. Anyone can use them to follow a committee's money from its final campaign through its termination report.
