#5557. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

Jacob Bourne of Emarketer told SiliconANGLE that Apple’s stock premium is likely linked to the growing concerns some investors have over the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom, which is being driven by all of Apple’s big tech peers. “Its tepid approach to AI infrastructure spending has helped to preserve its cash flow, and through strategic partnerships Apple may be able to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers,” Bourne said. “But Apple faces its own challenges as AI-enabled devices such as smart glasses could eventually challenge the iPhone’s central role in iOS. Apple’s long-term advantage will hinge on combining its hardware strengths with compelling AI capabilities in a way that preserves its reputation.”

In the meantime, the pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.

#5556. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5555. Recessions, scandals and backlash: 10 midterms that hit the party in power

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These midterm election swings, from 1894 to 2018, show how recessions, scandals and policy fights cost the president's party control of Congress or big blocs of House seats

The party that wins the White House usually pays for it two years later. Since the Civil War, the president's party has lost House seats in most midterm elections. In some years those losses are large enough to hand a chamber of Congress to the opposition and stall a president's legislative agenda.

This list covers 10 of those larger moments, from 1894 to 2018. It is a selection, not a ranking. The elections appear in chronological order rather than by size. The yardstick throughout is the same: the net change in House seats, along with any change in which party controls the House or the Senate. Where historical tallies disagree, the slides describe a swing in general terms rather than settle on one disputed number.

Midterm election swings tend to follow a small set of triggers. Economic downturns are one. A financial panic, a depression or a recession gives voters a concrete reason to hold the party in power responsible. Several elections on this list followed an economic slump. Scandal is another. A president's troubles can weigh on House and Senate candidates who had no part in them. A third trigger is backlash against major legislation or against a president's bid to expand his authority. Voters who believe a party has overreached can use the midterm to register that view.

The midterm electorate also differs from a presidential-year electorate. With no presidential race at the top of the ballot, turnout typically falls. A smaller electorate can shift the balance toward whichever side is more motivated to vote. That helps explain how an opposition party can gain ground quickly while the president remains in office.

The consequences reach beyond the seat count. A House flip gives the new majority the speakership, control of committees and the power to subpoena and investigate. A Senate flip changes who controls confirmation votes on judges and cabinet nominees. Even without a change in control, a large loss can shrink a governing majority enough to give smaller factions more leverage.

Each slide below covers one election: who held the White House, what drove voters and what changed in Congress afterward.

The 1894 midterm gave Republicans control of the House of Representatives. They made a net gain of more than 100 seats as voters punished Grover Cleveland's Democrats for the depression that followed the Panic of 1893.

Cleveland began his second, nonconsecutive term in March 1893. His term had barely started when the panic took hold. The Philadelphia and Reading Railroad had already gone into receivership that February. A wave of bank and business failures followed. Railroads that had overbuilt during the previous boom went bankrupt, and unemployment climbed across industrial cities.

Cleveland's main response was monetary. He called Congress into a special session in 1893 to repeal the Sherman Silver Purchase Act. He blamed the law for draining the Treasury's gold reserve. The repeal passed, but it split his own party. Democrats from the South and West who favored silver saw it as a betrayal of indebted farmers.

Unrest spread in 1894. That spring, Jacob Coxey led a march of unemployed workers, known as Coxey's Army, to Washington, D.C. That summer, the Pullman Strike spread along the nation's railroad lines. Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago over the objections of Illinois Gov. John Peter Altgeld, a fellow Democrat.

Trade policy offered no relief. The Wilson-Gorman Tariff Act was meant to lower tariffs. It emerged from Congress so weakened by amendments that Cleveland let it become law without his signature.

Democrats went into the November vote carrying the depression, the silver split and the tariff fight. Republicans made heavy gains across the Northeast and Midwest. Thomas Brackett Reed of Maine returned as House speaker when the new Congress met in December 1895.

The result reached beyond a single Congress. The Democratic split over silver carried into the 1896 presidential race. That year the party nominated William Jennings Bryan, and Republican William McKinley won the White House. Republicans then held the House until Democrats won it back in the 1910 midterm.

The 1938 midterm cost Franklin D. Roosevelt's Democrats dozens of House seats, though the party kept its majorities in both chambers. The result strengthened a bloc of Republicans and conservative Southern Democrats that resisted new New Deal programs for years afterward.

The losses came two years after a landslide. In 1936, Roosevelt carried 46 of the 48 states, and Democrats entered 1937 with commanding margins in Congress. That position eroded within months.

The first setback came from the White House. In February 1937, Roosevelt proposed legislation to expand the Supreme Court. The bill would have let him appoint an additional justice for each sitting justice who passed age 70 without retiring, up to six new seats. Critics in both parties called the plan an attack on judicial independence. The Senate sent the bill back to committee in July 1937, and it never became law.

The second setback was economic. A sharp downturn, now known as the Recession of 1937-38, began later that year. Unemployment rose again after several years of recovery. Republicans used the slump to argue that the New Deal had not produced lasting growth.

Roosevelt then tried to reshape his own party. During the 1938 primaries, he campaigned against conservative Democrats who had opposed his agenda. His targets included Senators Walter George of Georgia, Millard Tydings of Maryland and Ellison "Cotton Ed" Smith of South Carolina. All three won renomination. The effort, which came to be called the "purge," succeeded mainly against Representative John J. O'Connor of New York. O'Connor, chairman of the House Rules Committee, lost his primary.

In November, Republicans gained seats in the Senate as well as the House. The incoming class included Robert A. Taft, elected to the Senate from Ohio. Harold Stassen won the governorship of Minnesota the same year. Both men became leading Republican figures in the following decade.

The legislative consequences outlasted the campaign. The Fair Labor Standards Act, signed in June 1938, set a federal minimum wage of 25 cents an hour. It also required overtime pay for work beyond a standard workweek. Few major domestic reforms followed it. After the election, the conservative coalition had enough votes to block or trim many of Roosevelt's domestic proposals. His attention turned increasingly toward the fighting in Asia and the threat of war in Europe.

Republicans won control of both the House and the Senate in the 1946 midterm elections. It was the first time since 1930 that the party had won both chambers. The result left Harry Truman facing a Congress run by the opposition after his first midterm.

Truman had not been elected to the presidency. He moved up from the vice presidency in April 1945, after Franklin D. Roosevelt died, a few months before World War II ended. The 1946 vote was the first national verdict on his administration.

That verdict came as the country shifted from a wartime economy to a peacetime one. Millions of returning service members needed jobs and housing. Wartime price controls were being loosened and fought over, and prices climbed as controls came off. Shortages of meat and other consumer goods frustrated households.

Labor unrest added to the strain. Major strikes hit the auto, steel, coal and railroad industries during 1945 and 1946. Truman clashed with union leaders as he tried to keep those sectors running. Those fights cost him support among workers who had backed Roosevelt.

Republicans built their campaign around that discontent. Their slogan, "Had enough?", asked voters whether they were tired of shortages, strikes and years of Democratic government in Washington.

The new majority formed the 80th Congress. Joseph Martin of Massachusetts became speaker of the House. The incoming class of 1946 also included Richard Nixon, elected to the House from California, and Joseph McCarthy, elected to the Senate from Wisconsin. John F. Kennedy, a Democrat, won his first House race in Massachusetts the same year.

The Republican Congress pushed back against the labor policies of the Roosevelt era. In 1947 it passed the Taft-Hartley Act, which restricted union activity, and overrode Truman's veto to make it law. It also sent the states the proposal that became the 22nd Amendment, limiting presidents to two elected terms.

Truman turned that Congress into his main campaign target. Running for a full term in 1948, he attacked it as the "Do-Nothing Congress." He won that election, and Democrats regained both the House and the Senate the same year.

The 1958 midterm gave Democrats large gains in both the House and the Senate during Dwight D. Eisenhower's second term. Voters cast their ballots after the 1957-58 recession, and the result widened majorities that Democrats already held in both chambers.

That detail sets 1958 apart from most large midterm swings. Democrats had controlled Congress since winning it back in the 1954 elections. The 1958 vote did not flip either chamber. It turned working Democratic majorities into much larger ones for the final two years of Eisenhower's presidency.

The economy shaped much of the result. The downturn that began in 1957 pushed up unemployment, and industrial states in the Midwest were hit hard. Republicans held the White House while factory jobs disappeared. Many of the party's congressional candidates carried that record into November.

Two other events shaped the political backdrop. The Soviet Union launched Sputnik in October 1957. The launch set off a debate in the U.S. over science education and national defense. In September 1958, weeks before the vote, Sherman Adams resigned as Eisenhower's top White House aide. His exit followed disclosures that he had accepted gifts from Boston textile manufacturer Bernard Goldfine.

Labor issues featured in several key contests. Right-to-work measures appeared on the ballot in states including California and Ohio, and unions organized to defeat them. Both measures failed. In California, Senate Republican leader William Knowland gave up his seat to run for governor and lost to Democrat Edmund "Pat" Brown. In Ohio, Republican Sen. John Bricker lost his seat to Democrat Stephen Young.

The Senate class elected in 1958 included several figures who went on to long national careers. Democrats Edmund Muskie of Maine, Eugene McCarthy of Minnesota, Philip Hart of Michigan and Thomas Dodd of Connecticut all won seats that year. Alaska, then on the verge of statehood, elected two Democrats, Ernest Gruening and Bob Bartlett, as its first senators.

The expanded majorities went to a Congress led by two Texas Democrats, Senate Majority Leader Lyndon Johnson and House Speaker Sam Rayburn.

Republicans won back a large bloc of House seats in the 1966 midterm, two years after Lyndon Johnson's landslide win over Barry Goldwater. Democrats kept their majorities in both the House and the Senate. Even so, the result cut sharply into the margins Johnson had used to pass much of his domestic agenda.

The size of the rebound reflected how far Republicans had fallen in 1964. Johnson's landslide that year carried many Democrats into House seats that usually leaned Republican. In 1966, those first-term members ran without a presidential contest at the top of the ticket. Many of them lost.

The Congress elected in 1964, the 89th, had passed a long list of major laws. Medicare and Medicaid became law in 1965. So did the Voting Rights Act and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. That pace of legislation gave Republicans a record to campaign against. Their message focused on federal spending and the reach of Washington.

Foreign policy also shaped the campaign. Johnson had sent U.S. ground combat troops to Vietnam in large numbers in 1965. By 1966, the war's cost was growing, and it divided the Democratic coalition. Higher prices and unrest in American cities added to voter discontent. The 1965 riots in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles were one example of that unrest.

The Republican class of 1966 included several figures who went on to national prominence. George H.W. Bush won a House seat from Houston, his first elected office. In Massachusetts, Edward Brooke became the first Black senator elected by popular vote. Howard Baker won a Senate seat in Tennessee. Mark Hatfield, then Oregon's governor, won a Senate seat in his state. Charles Percy defeated Democratic incumbent Paul Douglas in Illinois.

Republicans also gained ground in races for governor. Ronald Reagan, in his first run for office, defeated incumbent Democrat Edmund "Pat" Brown to become governor of California.

Richard Nixon campaigned across the country for Republican candidates that fall. The results helped rebuild his standing in the party ahead of his successful 1968 presidential run.

In the 90th Congress, Johnson's remaining domestic proposals faced a House with far fewer reliable Democratic votes. Republicans and conservative Southern Democrats held more leverage over which bills advanced.

The 1974 midterm gave Democrats a much larger House majority three months after Richard Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal. Voters went to the polls on Nov. 5, 1974, with Gerald Ford $F in the White House and Nixon's pardon still fresh. Republicans lost seats in both the House and the Senate.

The scandal had been building for more than two years. It began with the June 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate complex in Washington, D.C. Congressional investigators and reporters traced the cover-up back to the White House.

In July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in United States v. Nixon that the president had to hand over recordings of Oval Office conversations. That same month, the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment against him.

Nixon resigned on Aug. 9, 1974, before the full House could vote on impeachment. He was the first U.S. president to leave office by resignation.

Ford took over without having been elected president or vice president. Nixon had nominated him for vice president under the 25th Amendment after Spiro Agnew resigned in October 1973. Congress confirmed the nomination that December.

On Sept. 8, 1974, Ford granted Nixon a full, free and absolute pardon for any federal crimes he may have committed as president. The pardon ruled out a federal prosecution of the former president. Ford's public standing dropped after the announcement. The decision also pulled Watergate back to the center of the fall campaign.

The economy added to the pressure on Republican candidates. The 1973 Arab oil embargo had driven up energy prices. Inflation was high, and the country had slipped into recession. In October 1974, weeks before the vote, Ford launched his "Whip Inflation Now" campaign to rally public support against rising prices.

The election reshaped the House Democratic caucus. The large class of newly elected Democrats became known as the "Watergate babies." Many of them ran as reformers.

Early in 1975, the Democratic Caucus voted to remove three longtime committee chairmen. They were Wright Patman of the Banking Committee, F. Edward Hébert of the Armed Services Committee and W.R. Poage of the Agriculture Committee. Those votes weakened the seniority system that had long decided who led House committees.

The 1994 midterm gave Republicans a majority in the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. The party also won control of the Senate. That left President Bill Clinton facing a Republican Congress halfway through his first term.

Democrats had held the House without a break since the 1954 elections. The 1994 result ended that run in a single night.

Republican leaders built their national campaign around the Contract with America. The platform was unveiled on the steps of the U.S. Capitol in September 1994. Its central promise was procedural. If voters gave Republicans the House, the party would bring 10 bills to a floor vote within the first 100 days of the new Congress. The proposals included a balanced budget amendment, congressional term limits, welfare changes and tax cuts.

Newt Gingrich of Georgia, then the House Republican whip, was the plan's chief architect. He became Speaker of the House when the 104th Congress convened in January 1995.

Democrats entered the campaign after several contested legislative fights. Clinton's health care overhaul, led by Hillary Clinton, collapsed in Congress in 1994 without a floor vote in either chamber. His 1993 budget raised taxes and passed without a single Republican vote. The 1994 crime bill included a ban on certain semiautomatic weapons.

The defeats reached the top of the Democratic leadership. House Speaker Tom Foley lost his seat in Washington state. He became the first sitting Speaker defeated for reelection since 1862. In the Senate, Alabama's Richard Shelby switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party the day after the election. Bob Dole became Senate majority leader.

The new House majority voted on every item in the contract within the 100-day window. All but the term limits amendment passed the House. That measure fell short of the two-thirds vote a constitutional amendment requires. Several bills later stalled in the Senate.

Clashes over spending between Clinton and the Republican Congress led to two federal government shutdowns between late 1995 and early 1996. The two sides later agreed on a welfare overhaul, which Clinton signed in 1996. Clinton won reelection that November, and Republicans kept their House majority.

Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the 2006 midterm, held on November 7 during George W. Bush's second term. The result ended the Republican House majority that began with the 1994 election.

The Iraq War sat at the center of the campaign. The conflict was in its fourth year, and sectarian violence inside Iraq had escalated. Democratic candidates framed the vote as a referendum on the war and on Bush's handling of it.

Scandal added pressure on Republicans. The lobbying scandal surrounding Jack Abramoff produced guilty pleas and put members of Congress under scrutiny. Tom DeLay, the former House majority leader, resigned his seat in 2006 after an indictment in Texas.

Weeks before the vote, Rep. Mark Foley of Florida resigned over messages he had sent to teenagers who had served as House pages. Democrats campaigned against what they called a "culture of corruption" in Washington.

Control of the Senate came down to a handful of close races. Democrats defeated Republican incumbents in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Missouri, Montana, Rhode Island and Virginia. In Virginia, Jim Webb unseated George Allen by a narrow margin. In Montana, Jon Tester ousted Conrad Burns.

The new Senate split 49 to 49, with two independents holding the balance. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut both caucused with Democrats. That gave the party a working majority. Lieberman had lost the Democratic primary to Ned Lamont, then won reelection as an independent.

The political consequences arrived within a day. On November 8, Bush announced that Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld would step down. He named Robert Gates, a former CIA director, as the replacement. At a news conference, Bush described the results as a "thumping."

In January 2007, Nancy Pelosi of California became Speaker of the House. She was the first woman to hold the post. Harry Reid of Nevada became Senate majority leader.

The election did not end the war policy it was fought over. Bush announced a troop increase in Iraq in January 2007. In May 2007, he vetoed a war funding bill that included a timeline for withdrawing U.S. troops. The new majorities instead used hearings and spending bills to press the administration through the rest of his term.

Republicans won control of the U.S. House in the 2010 midterm, Barack Obama's first. The Tea Party movement and opposition to the Affordable Care Act shaped the campaign. Democrats held the Senate, but the House majority they had won in 2006 was gone after four years.

The election came less than two years after Obama took office with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress. That majority passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the stimulus package of early 2009. It also passed the Affordable Care Act, which Obama signed in March 2010. Both laws became central targets for Republican campaigns that fall.

The Tea Party movement took shape in 2009. Its supporters objected to federal spending, bank and auto bailouts, and the health care overhaul. They organized rallies, confronted lawmakers at town hall meetings and backed primary challenges against establishment Republicans. A televised rant by CNBC commentator Rick Santelli in February 2009, aimed at a mortgage relief plan, helped popularize the name.

An early warning for Democrats came in January 2010. Republican Scott Brown won a special election in Massachusetts for the Senate seat long held by Ted Kennedy. The result cost Democrats their 60th Senate vote, the number needed to break a filibuster.

The economy also weighed on the majority. The country was still recovering from the Great Recession. Unemployment stayed high through the campaign.

Tea Party energy reshaped the Republican field. Candidates backed by the movement won Senate seats in several states, including Rand Paul in Kentucky, Marco Rubio in Florida and Mike Lee in Utah. Other insurgent nominees lost races Republicans had hoped to win. Christine O'Donnell lost in Delaware. Sharron Angle lost in Nevada to Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid. Both seats stayed in Democratic hands, and Democrats kept their Senate majority.

The day after the election, Obama described the result as a "shellacking." John Boehner of Ohio became speaker in January 2011, replacing Nancy Pelosi.

The timing extended the effect beyond Congress. Republicans also made large gains in state legislatures and governorships just as states were redrawing congressional maps after the 2010 census. That put the party in charge of drawing district lines in many states for the following decade.

The new House majority quickly clashed with the White House over spending. A standoff over raising the federal debt limit in the summer of 2011 ended with the Budget Control Act. Standard & Poor's downgraded the U.S. credit rating that August.

Democrats won control of the U.S. House of Representatives in the November 6, 2018, midterm election, with a net gain of about 40 seats during Donald Trump's first term. The result ended eight years of Republican control of the chamber and produced divided government for the rest of Trump's term.

Republicans had held the House since winning it in the 2010 election. Going into 2018, the party also controlled the Senate and the White House. That gave Republicans full control of the elected branches in Washington for Trump's first two years in office.

Health care became a central issue in the campaign. In 2017, a Republican bill to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act passed the House but failed in the Senate. Democratic candidates built much of their message around keeping protections for people with preexisting conditions. Republicans campaigned in part on the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which Trump signed in December 2017.

Much of the Democratic gain came in suburban districts. Republican-held seats around cities in California, New Jersey, Virginia and Texas moved to Democrats. Several of those districts had sent Republicans to Congress for years before 2018.

The House class that took office in January 2019 included a record number of women. It also included the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan. Sharice Davids of Kansas and Deb Haaland of New Mexico became the first two Native American women elected to Congress.

The Senate moved in the opposite direction. Republicans kept their majority and added to it, defeating Democratic incumbents in Florida, Indiana, Missouri and North Dakota. That split outcome set 2018 apart from midterms in which one party gained in both chambers at once.

Nancy Pelosi of California returned as speaker of the House on January 3, 2019. She had first held the post from 2007 to 2011, becoming the first woman to serve as speaker.

Democratic chairs took over House committees in January 2019. They opened inquiries into the Trump administration. In December 2019, the House impeached Trump on two articles, abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. The Republican-led Senate acquitted him in February 2020.

#5554. The 10 highest-paid CEOs in America, according to the 2026 Equilar 100

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Elon Musk's $132.3 billion award heads this look at 10 of the 100 CEOs in the 2026 Equilar 100, where median pay hit $39.4 million.

Running a large American company means steering it through market upheaval while keeping its finances growing. The strain of that job commands lavish rewards, and those sums raise hard questions about fairness and about who captures the gains of corporate success. In 2025, the median chief executive among the 100 best-paid at U.S. public companies collected $39.4 million. No earlier year in the long-running analysis produced a higher figure, and the median climbed 35.8% from a year earlier. Anyone who owns shares, draws a paycheck from one of these firms, or wonders where corporate money flows has a stake in how boards arrive at those numbers.

The distance between the corner office and the rest of the workforce stretched at a similar clip. The median ratio of chief executive earnings to those of a typical employee reached 475 to 1 in 2025, up from 348 to 1 the year before, a 36.5% jump. The median worker at these employers took home $101,322, a solid income that looks modest beside packages worth tens of millions of dollars. Stock awards drive the surge in executive totals. Base salaries held flat at $1.3 million, while long-term equity accounts for more than 70% of total compensation in the usual package. The research credits movements in stock value with an outsized effect on what an executive receives. A share-price rally can reshape a leader's haul by a margin no salary adjustment could match.

Equilar has partnered with The New York Times for 19 years to track what chief executives earn, and its 2026 study lists the 100 richest pay deals that boards granted to CEOs at U.S.-based or listed companies. Each company needed more than $1 billion in revenue and had to file a proxy statement for its latest completed fiscal year by April 30, 2026. Total compensation sets the order, and the figures cover awards from 2025. The report includes a table of 10 executives from that roster, showing each one's total package, change in pay, and fiscal 2025 revenue. The slides ahead follow those 10 of the 100 in the order the table presents them.

Elon Musk drew a $132.3 billion pay package from Tesla $TSLA in 2025, and all of it came as a single long-term stock award. The grant hinges on aggressive goals for Tesla's market capitalization and its operations. Nothing in the reported total came from salary, bonus, or perks. The structure turns Tesla's chief into an investor whose payday rides on the same share price outside shareholders watch.

Stock awards across the full list look small beside Musk's grant. The median award rose 44.6% in 2025 to $28.4 million, up from $19.6 million. No other package in the study comes within reach of his total. Even the second-largest deal in the table, at Figma, measures in the hundreds of millions, while Musk's runs to the billions.

Musk's package held none of the cash that pads other executives' pay. Median cash compensation, which covers salaries, bonuses, and perks, rose 3.6% to $6.1 million in 2025. Every dollar of his total depends on how Tesla's shares and operations perform. A median executive on the list draws a fixed salary regardless of where the share price lands. Musk's reward rests on his targets alone.

Musk's award surpasses Tesla's $94.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, the largest sales total among the 10 companies in the table. A single grant that outstrips a full year of sales shows how equity tied to market value can lift pay beyond anything a company's revenue would suggest. Sales figures could not explain a sum of this size. The valuation goals carry that weight.

The table lists no change in pay for Musk, leaving the award without a year-over-year comparison. Readers cannot tell from the study whether 2025 marked a leap or a continuation of his earlier pay. What the grant delivers will track the market value and operating results its targets measure.

Figma chief Dylan Field collected $864.4 million in 2025, a 799% jump that gave him the second-largest package among the 100 executives in the study, behind only Tesla $TSLA's Elon Musk. Field co-founded Figma, a cloud-based design tool, and serves as its chief executive. Musk's award runs into the billions. Among the executives paid in millions, nobody topped Field. His award edged past the one Welltower granted Shankh S. Mitra by a slim margin and sits many times above the study's median.

Figma reported $1,055 million in fiscal 2025 revenue, the smallest total among the 10 companies in the table. Every other company in that group brought in more than $4 billion. The leanest firm in the table yielded one of its two biggest awards. Field's package came close to matching everything Figma sold during the year. Outside Tesla, no company in the table handed its chief a sum so large relative to its own sales.

Across all 100 companies in the study, the median company took in $22.8 billion, a mark that dwarfs Figma's turnover. Broadcom $AVGO and Goldman Sachs $GS, two of the largest businesses in the table, gave their chiefs less than Field received. Warner Bros. Discovery, another company many times Figma's size, awarded David M. Zaslav a fraction of Field's sum. Corporate scale did little to determine which executives drew the richest rewards in 2025.

Field's raise trails the gains of four peers in the table, whose increases climbed into the thousands of percent. None of those four took home as much as he did. Even the steepest of those jumps produced a package far smaller than Field's. Percentage change measures movement from a prior award. It reveals little about where an executive finishes. A steep growth rate alone did not carry any executive in this group past Field's dollar total.

Shankh S. Mitra of Welltower received $821,090,355 in 2025, a package 3,965% larger than his award from the year before. Only two executives in the table, Elon Musk and Dylan Field, earned more. Mitra's total trailed Field's by a narrow margin and topped every package listed after his, including the all-equity award to Kasra Nejatian of Opendoor.

A gain of that scale implies Mitra's previous award amounted to a small slice of his 2025 haul. Two leaders in the group posted steeper percentage increases, Niraj Shah of Wayfair and Hock E. Tan of Broadcom $AVGO, yet neither approached Mitra's dollar total. Mitra pairs the third-largest package among the 10 with the third-steepest climb, and no other executive in the table claims a top-three spot on both measures. Field, his nearest rival in dollars, logged a slower rise, and Shah, the fastest riser, finished far behind Mitra in total pay.

Welltower reported $10.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, less than half the $22.8 billion median across the full roster of 100 companies. Five companies in the table brought in more: Tesla $TSLA, Broadcom, Goldman Sachs $GS, Warner Bros. Discovery, and Wayfair. Every one of their chief executives except Musk took home less than Mitra. Welltower outsold Figma, Opendoor, Rivian $RIVN, and Palo Alto Networks $PANW, yet Figma still paid Field more than Welltower paid Mitra.

Nothing in the table explains how Welltower built the award, which leaves the distance between the company's mid-table sales and its outsized payout as the clearest feature of Mitra's year. Within this group, a company's sales offer a poor guide to the size of its leader's award.

Kasra Nejatian, chief executive of Opendoor Technologies, collected a $741.1 million package in 2025, and long-term stock awards made up the whole of it. No salary, cash bonus, or perk appears in that total. Every dollar of his reward rises or falls with Opendoor's share price, the same asset his investors hold.

Cash carried more weight for the typical executive on the list. Median cash compensation across the 100 CEOs, covering salaries, bonuses, and perks, edged up 3.6% to $6.1 million in 2025. Median stock awards climbed 44.6% to $28.4 million over the same stretch. Nejatian took none of the first category and a sum that dwarfs the second. His package pushes the list-wide tilt toward equity as far as it can go.

Opendoor's investors earned a 264.4% total shareholder return, the highest of any company in the study. The median company returned 12%. The study ties these results to Nejatian's pay, describing his equity-heavy structure as a match for Opendoor's strong market results. Owners and their chief executive profited from the same rally.

Opendoor's size does little to explain the award. The company booked $4,371 million in fiscal 2025 revenue, about $4.4 billion and below the $22.8 billion median for the 100 companies. Figma, at $1,055 million, is the lone company among the 10 largest packages with a smaller top line. Modest revenue beside an outsized award suggests that stock performance outweighed scale in setting Nejatian's payday.

The table lists no year-over-year change in pay for Nejatian. His compensation offers no growth story to measure. The case for his award rests on a single year of results. An all-stock package paired with the list's best shareholder return leaves his fortunes and his investors' moving in lockstep. If Opendoor's shares stumble, the same structure that produced this windfall would shrink his reward alongside theirs.

Robert J. Scaringe, chief executive of Rivian $RIVN Automotive, collected $402,639,080 for 2025, a 2,604% jump from the year before. Eight executives in this group of 10 show a reported change in pay, and the leaders of Wayfair, Broadcom $AVGO, and Welltower alone posted steeper climbs than his. Elon Musk and Kasra Nejatian carry no comparison figure. Scaringe's climb outpaced the increases at Figma, Goldman Sachs $GS, Warner Bros. Discovery, and Palo Alto Networks $PANW. Dylan Field's package at Figma is larger, a sign that the pace of a raise and the size of a paycheck tell separate stories. An increase of 2,604% means his 2025 award dwarfed whatever he received a year earlier. Scaringe sits in the upper half of this group on both total compensation and growth.

Rivian's $5.4 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue places it eighth among these 10 companies, above Figma and Opendoor. The automaker trails the $22.8 billion median revenue across the full roster of 100 firms. Scaringe's award exceeds what five businesses with heavier sales handed their leaders: Wayfair, Broadcom, Warner Bros. Discovery, Goldman Sachs, and Palo Alto Networks.

Tesla $TSLA, the table's other carmaker, outsells Rivian by a vast margin, and its chief collected the largest award of all. Welltower books heavier sales than Rivian and paid Shankh S. Mitra more than Scaringe. Tesla and Welltower fit the intuition that bigger companies hand their leaders bigger checks. The five other heavier sellers break that pattern, and Broadcom, Goldman Sachs, and Warner Bros. Discovery each outsell Rivian many times over.

Scale and generosity point in opposite directions at the low end of the revenue column. Figma, Opendoor, and Rivian, the three smallest businesses in the table by sales, handed their chiefs the second-, fourth-, and fifth-largest packages among the 10. Across this group, a company's revenue says little about what its leader earns, and outside Tesla, several of the richest awards gather where sales run lightest.

Niraj Shah collected $280,847,068 from Wayfair in 2025, a 99,088% increase and the largest change in pay anywhere in the table. Shah serves as chief executive, co-chairman, and co-founder of Wayfair Inc.

A gain of this size dwarfs the four-figure jumps that Shankh S. Mitra, Robert J. Scaringe, and Hock E. Tan posted. Those three increases already sit among the steepest in the group, yet none comes close to the scale of Shah's.

Shah's percentage reveals as much about his starting point as about his reward. A raise this large requires a modest base, so his prior-year pay must have amounted to a sliver of the 2025 total. The table does not disclose what he earned the year before or what form the new award took. Whatever the 2025 package contained, it marked a sharp break from what Shah had received before.

Wayfair booked $12.5 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, the fifth-largest figure among the 10 companies. It outsold Figma, Welltower, Opendoor, Rivian $RIVN, and Palo Alto Networks $PANW. Tesla $TSLA, Broadcom $AVGO, Goldman Sachs $GS, and Warner Bros. Discovery each brought in more. Across all 100 companies in the study, median revenue reached $22.8 billion, a mark Wayfair's sales failed to clear. By that measure, the company sits in the middle of this group and below the midpoint of the full roster.

Shah's haul outstrips the sums granted to Tan of Broadcom, David M. Zaslav of Warner Bros. Discovery, and David M. Solomon of Goldman Sachs. Each of those three companies generated billions of dollars more in annual sales than Wayfair. The mismatch runs the other way, too. Welltower, Rivian, and Opendoor all brought in less than Wayfair, yet Mitra, Scaringe, and Kasra Nejatian each walked away with more than Shah. Among these 10 executives, a company's top line offers a poor guide to the size of its leader's paycheck.

Hock E. Tan collected $205,278,006 as Broadcom $AVGO's chief executive in 2025, a 7,692% increase over his prior-year pay. Of the eight executives in the table with a reported change in pay, only Niraj Shah of Wayfair posted a steeper climb. Tan's raise outpaced the gains of Shankh S. Mitra at Welltower and Robert J. Scaringe at Rivian $RIVN, two leaders who still took home bigger packages than he did. A jump of that magnitude shows how small his previous award was by comparison.

Broadcom brought in $63.9 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, more than any company in this group except Tesla $TSLA. Its sales tower over the $22.8 billion median for the 100 companies in the study. The company's total still trails UnitedHealth $UNH Group, whose $447.6 billion topped the entire roster. Tan's package sits seventh in the table, well below the second-place standing Broadcom holds on revenue.

Pay and corporate scale part ways near the head of the table. Apart from Elon R. Musk, every executive who out-earned Tan runs a smaller business. Figma, Welltower, Opendoor, Rivian, and Wayfair each reported between $1.1 billion and $12.5 billion in sales. Wayfair, the largest of the five by revenue, sits a long way behind Broadcom. Company size cannot explain those five packages. Each of those leaders out-earned Tan while overseeing a smaller revenue base.

David M. Solomon of Goldman Sachs $GS and David M. Zaslav of Warner Bros. Discovery both earned less than Tan, and both of their companies generated less revenue than Broadcom. Nikesh Arora of Palo Alto Networks $PANW follows the same pattern, with a smaller paycheck and a smaller company. All three also received raises far slimmer than the one Tan collected. Among these 10 CEOs, Tan's award lines up with company size in a way the packages of Dylan Field, Mitra, Kasra Nejatian, Scaringe, and Shah do not.

David M. Zaslav of Warner Bros. Discovery collected $165,009,366 in 2025, a 218% increase over his prior-year pay.

Zaslav's raise looks restrained beside the surges around him. Shankh S. Mitra, Robert J. Scaringe, Hock E. Tan, and Niraj Shah each logged increases that ran to four or five digits in percentage terms. Dylan Field's 799% climb and David M. Solomon's 280% gain also outstripped Zaslav's. Among the eight executives in this group with a reported change in pay, only Nikesh Arora posted a smaller one.

A raise in the hundreds of percent delivered Zaslav a nine-figure sum. Only Solomon and Arora collected less, making the Warner Bros. Discovery award the third-smallest of the 10.

Warner Bros. Discovery generated $37.3 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, the fourth-largest total among these 10 companies after Tesla $TSLA, Broadcom $AVGO, and Goldman Sachs $GS. Zaslav's company brought in more than Figma, Welltower, Opendoor, Rivian $RIVN, and Wayfair, yet the chiefs of all five firms received bigger awards than Zaslav. Goldman Sachs topped Warner Bros. Discovery in sales, yet Solomon took home less than Zaslav.

Revenue scale says little about the pace of raises, either. Among the four companies with the largest sales in this table, Warner Bros. Discovery and Goldman Sachs paired their totals with triple-digit gains for their chiefs, while Tan logged a four-digit jump at Broadcom. Musk's entry lists no change in pay, which leaves Tesla out of that comparison.

The Warner Bros. Discovery total also cleared the $22.8 billion median revenue across the full list of 100 companies. Clearing that median places Warner Bros. Discovery in the upper half of the 100 companies by sales. UnitedHealth $UNH Group outsold every company on that list with $447.6 billion, and its chief executive does not appear among these 10.

Across these 10 packages, neither a company's sales nor its position by revenue offers a reliable guide to what its leader earns or how fast that pay grows.

David M. Solomon received $118.9 million in total compensation from The Goldman Sachs $GS Group in 2025, 280% more than his prior-year award. His increase dwarfed the growth in median pay across the full roster of 100 chief executives. Among the 10, no other haul cleared nine figures by a thinner margin.

Goldman Sachs generated $59.4 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, the third-largest figure among the 10 companies in the table, behind Tesla $TSLA and Broadcom $AVGO. Eight executives in that group collected bigger packages than Solomon. Broadcom's sales edged past Goldman's, and Hock E. Tan's award outran Solomon's. Warner Bros. Discovery, fourth in revenue among the 10, paid David M. Zaslav more than Goldman paid Solomon. Dylan Field, whose Figma posted the smallest revenue in the table, earned several times Solomon's total. Kasra Nejatian of Opendoor and Robert J. Scaringe of Rivian $RIVN outearned him while running companies with a fraction of Goldman's sales. Revenue offers a poor guide to executive rewards among these 10.

Critics faulted Solomon's leadership of Goldman Sachs after a stretch in which the firm's investment banking activity declined and its consumer business lost money. The setbacks did not stop Goldman's board from granting him a richer payout for 2025.

Solomon's gain sits toward the modest end of the changes in this group. The table reports no change for Elon Musk or Nejatian, which leaves eight executives to compare. Of those eight, Zaslav and Nikesh Arora logged smaller increases than Solomon. Field, Shankh S. Mitra, Scaringe, and Tan posted larger jumps, and three of them climbed by thousands of percent. Niraj Shah's increase ran into the tens of thousands of percent.

Nikesh Arora's $99,736,336 package at Palo Alto Networks $PANW makes him the only executive in this group of 10 whose 2025 pay stopped short of nine figures. Each of the other nine crossed the $100 million mark, a sweep the study counts as one more record. Arora's award rounds to $99.7 million, a sliver beneath the threshold his nine peers cleared. A single executive kept the table from a perfect run of nine-figure deals, and he missed by a margin narrower than the distance between any two neighbors on the list.

Arora's pay rose 72% from the prior year, the smallest increase among the eight executives in this table with a reported change. The other seven gains all topped 200%, and several packages swelled many times over in a single year. Arora joined the 10 on a raise that did not double his compensation. By the standards of this roster, his raise looks restrained.

Palo Alto Networks booked $9,221 million in fiscal 2025 revenue, or about $9.2 billion. Six companies in the lineup brought in more, and three brought in less. Figma, Opendoor, and Rivian $RIVN all trailed Palo Alto Networks on sales, yet each of their chief executives received an award several times larger than Arora's. Broadcom $AVGO and Goldman Sachs $GS posted the second- and third-largest revenue totals in the table, while their leaders hold packages among the four smallest. Company size offers a weak guide to where an executive lands among these 10.

Jane Fraser of Citigroup $C earned $95.8 million, the most among the four women on the full list. Her total fell below Arora's, and no woman appears among these 10. Arora's haul marks the entry point for this cohort, and the best-paid woman in the study never reached it. At the top of the 2025 study, every nine-figure package went to a man, and so did the record those nine deals set.

#5553. Rorra filtered showerhead review: Is better shower water worth $199?

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Does the Rorra filtered showerhead deliver cleaner shower water? Explore its filtration performance, price, installation, and ongoing filter costs

Your shower water may not be as clean as you think. Municipal water treatment helps make tap water safe, but disinfectants such as chlorine and chloramine can affect the water coming through your showerhead. If you've noticed dry skin, brittle hair, or simply want to reduce your exposure to certain chemicals, a filtered showerhead may be worth considering. The Rorra Filtered Showerhead is designed to make that upgrade without requiring a complicated bathroom renovation.

Priced at $199 with a filter subscription, the Rorra combines a built-in filtration system with a modern showerhead designed for easy installation and consistent water flow. Its filter uses KDF-55 media and calcium sulfite to reduce chlorine and other contaminants, including chloramine and certain heavy metals. The company also publishes third-party laboratory testing, giving shoppers more information to evaluate its filtration claims.

However, the Rorra isn't the cheapest way to filter shower water. Replacement filters cost $45 every 90 days, and the showerhead doesn't offer adjustable spray settings. Here's what to consider before buying.

The Rorra uses a two-part filtration system made with KDF-55 and calcium sulfite. Together, these materials are designed to reduce chlorine, chloramine, and other contaminants, including iron, lead, chromium, and copper.

The filter contains 240 grams of filtration media, which Rorra says is more than 30% above the average amount in comparable systems. The company also says its product has been tested by multiple NSF-accredited laboratories according to NSF/ANSI 177 protocols.

That testing is particularly important in a market where shower filters often make impressive-sounding claims without publishing much evidence to support them. Rorra is among the few manufacturers willing to share independent laboratory results.

Independent testing found that the showerhead reduced total chlorine to undetectable levels, including in water treated with chloramine. The filtration also remained more than 90% effective after three months of daily eight-minute showers for two people.

That's a meaningful advantage over filters that lose effectiveness quickly. It also gives the Rorra a stronger case than products relying primarily on marketing claims.

Still, keep the filtration claims in perspective. A shower filter isn't a substitute for a drinking water purification system, and evidence that it reduces certain contaminants doesn't automatically mean it will resolve skin or hair concerns. The most relevant question is whether it addresses the specific substances in your water.

The Rorra is designed to replace your existing showerhead rather than attach as an additional inline filter. It measures 6 inches in diameter and height, weighs 1.9 pounds, and fits standard U.S. shower connections.

Installation is intended to be straightforward. The package includes a wrench and thread tape, and the company's built-in thread-stop design helps create a secure connection. You shouldn't need to hire a plumber for a typical installation.

The showerhead has an optimized jet design intended to provide broad coverage and consistent flow. Its standard flow rate is 2.5 gallons per minute, and an optional 1.8-gallon-per-minute restrictor is included for markets with stricter water-use requirements.

The showerhead has a sturdy, modern design and comes in several finishes, including chrome, glossy black, and brushed nickel, making it easy to match with different bathroom styles.

The biggest practical advantage is that the filter is integrated into the showerhead. You don't have to install a separate filtration unit between the pipe and your existing fixture, and Rorra designed the filter to be replaced without removing the entire showerhead.

That makes the Rorra a relatively simple upgrade for anyone who wants filtered shower water without a complicated setup.

The biggest drawback is the ongoing filter expense. Rorra recommends replacing the filter every 90 days, or approximately every 200 showers. Replacement filters cost $45, which works out to $180 annually if you follow the recommended schedule.

Replacement filters cost more than some competing options, though the Rorra maintained its filtration effectiveness longer in testing.

The upfront price also depends on how you buy it. Rorra lists the showerhead at $199 with a filter subscription, compared with $239 for a one-time purchase. Check which option you're selecting and factor in the cost of future filter replacements before buying.

Another limitation is the lack of adjustable spray settings. The Rorra focuses on its filtration system and optimized jet design rather than offering multiple spray patterns. If you prefer switching between a wide rainfall spray, massage setting, or concentrated stream, this showerhead may feel restrictive.

Finally, filtration performance depends on your water supply. Different municipalities use different disinfectants, and a filter that performs well in one water system may produce different results elsewhere. Check your local water quality report before assuming you need this particular type of filtration.

The Rorra Filtered Showerhead is worth considering if reducing chlorine and chloramine in your shower water is a priority. Its combination of KDF-55 and calcium sulfite filtration, published laboratory testing, and positive independent testing results gives it a stronger foundation than many competing shower filters.

It's less compelling if you're primarily looking for an inexpensive showerhead or want multiple spray settings. The $199 starting price and $45 quarterly filter replacements also make it a more expensive commitment than some alternatives.

Before buying, check your local water quality, compare the ongoing filter costs, and decide whether the fixed spray design suits your preferences. If you want a well-tested filtered showerhead and are comfortable paying more for it, the Rorra makes a convincing case. Its strongest selling point isn't just the promise of cleaner shower water—it's the testing that helps back up that promise.

#5552. Robotics startup Tutor Intelligence nabs $75M investment

Warehouse automation provider Tutor Intelligence Inc. today announced that it has raised $75 million in funding.

Andreessen Horowitz led the Series A investment. It was joined by Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led Tutor’s previous two rounds.

The merchandise that a warehouse processes often arrives on pallets, flat wood structures capable of holding up to several tons. Tutor sells a mobile robotic arm called Cassie that can take packages off a pallet and place them in containers. It’s also capable of performing the opposite operation.

Cassie can process up to 18 items per minute depending on the package type. Its robotic arm is equipped with a vacuum gripper designed to pick up more than 50 pounds. The arm is mounted on a four-wheeled platform that enables Cassie to autonomously travel between different sections of a warehouse.

Automating pallet processing is challenging because the merchandise that a warehouse receives changes over time. Historically, adapting a robotic arm’s workflow to a new item involved manual coding. Cassie uses built-in artificial intelligence models to learn how to pick up new package types automatically.

Tutor also ships its AI models with a second wheeled robot called Sonny. It uses a pair of robotic arms to take items off warehouse shelves and place them in packages. The robot finds the needed items using an array of time-of-flight and stereo cameras. Both camera varieties collect depth data, which makes it easier to determine the distance of an object.

Tutor plans to apply Sonny to additional use cases in the future. In particular, it sees industrial companies using the system to assemble products and perform equipment maintenance. Tutor teaches Sonny’s AI models new tasks in a facility that hosts more than 100 robots. Human experts demonstrate how to perform a task using a remotely controlled robot and the AI models learn by imitation.

“Sonny’s manufacturability at scale makes it an ideal robot not just for most handwork in manufacturing and logistics, but for arbitrary business-critical applications across the physical economy,” Tutor co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Josh Gruenstein wrote in a blog post. “Data collected by our Sonny fleet trains our largest and most capable robot foundation models at the frontier of rate and reliability.”

Tutor sells its robots under a usage-based pricing model. It removes the need for customers to make a large upfront purchase, which lowers the entry barrier. The company disclosed today that the number of facilities where its robots are used has nearly quadrupled over the past year.

Tutor will use its newly raised funding to enhance its AI models and speed up robot production.
