#5551. How to fall asleep fast: science-backed tips from the Sleep Foundation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

From the military method to stimulus control, 10 relaxation techniques and bedroom habits that can help you drift off sooner at night.

Few nights feel longer than the ones spent watching a clock creep past midnight. The day is over, the lights are off, and yet thoughts keep sprinting through conversations, deadlines, and tomorrow's to-do list. Each glance at the time brings a fresh calculation of how little rest remains before the alarm. The problem has many roots. Trouble drifting off can stem from physical factors, psychological ones, or both, and medical conditions can interfere too. Insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless legs syndrome can each stand between a person and a quick slide into sleep. Sleeplessness that turns into a regular problem deserves a closer look at evening habits and a visit to a health care provider, who can rule out an underlying sleep disorder or another health concern.

Worry sits at the center of the struggle for many people with insomnia. They cannot switch off their concerns, and the mental churn blocks complete relaxation. The body keeps pace with the mind. People who have a hard time falling asleep may show stronger bodily signs of stress, among them tense muscles, a higher body temperature, and a faster heartbeat. Sleep latency is the term for the stretch between lying down and nodding off, and an ideal window runs 15 to 20 minutes. The wait responds to change. Small behavioral adjustments and relaxation methods with scientific support can improve it, which gives a frustrated sleeper something concrete to work on.

Sleep Foundation gathers its advice for anyone stuck awake in an explainer it updated June 3, 2026. Austin Meadows, a sleep product tester, wrote the piece, and Dustin Cotliar, MD, MPH, reviewed it for medical accuracy. The article leans on outside medical references, among them the National Library of Medicine, and reports no original study, survey, or ranking of its own. Its guidance spans calming strategies, sleep hygiene, bedroom setup, and steps to take when nothing works. A comparison table matches five of its techniques with the concern each suits and the time each requires, without naming a source for those times. The 10 items below draw from across the article. They form a selection of its advice in no ranked order, and they describe what each approach asks of you without promising how fast it will work.

The military method set out to put soldiers to sleep within two minutes, a goal built for people with little say over where or when they rest. The Sleep Foundation notes that service members contend with irregular schedules and bed down in conditions far from ideal, and both pressures can scramble their sleep patterns. A routine designed for those circumstances has to function without a quiet room, a favorite pillow, or a predictable bedtime.

The two-minute figure describes what the technique's creators aimed for. The guide offers no evidence that sleepers hit that mark, and its table of time required per technique leaves the military method out. Treat the target as an ambition, and gauge the method by how your body responds over several nights.

The sequence travels through the body from top to bottom. It begins once you settle into a comfortable position and let every part of the face go slack. Your shoulders drop, and your arms lie at your sides. Deep breaths loosen the chest and the remainder of the torso. The unwinding continues below the waist, passing from the hips through each section of the legs to the feet.

The final step shifts from the muscles to the mind. The guide observes that quick sleep comes hard on nights when thoughts keep racing after a long day. With every limb at ease, you picture a calm scene, such as open countryside. Stray thoughts may intrude. The technique asks you to acknowledge each one and let it pass.

The Sleep Foundation names relaxation as the force behind fast sleep onset. In its view, letting go of tension prepares both body and mind for sleep. The military sequence follows that logic in a fixed order, clearing bodily strain first and mental chatter last. Its steps require nothing beyond a place to lie down. Anyone whose nights resemble a service member's, with shifting hours and imperfect surroundings, can carry the routine to any bed.

Progressive $PGR muscle relaxation has you clench one muscle group for 10 seconds, release it, and take deep breaths before moving to the next. The method pairs breathing work with deliberate tightening and loosening to drain physical stress from the body. It travels through every major muscle group in turn. Calm builds in stages, one group after another.

The routine starts in bed, with eyes closed and a few long, full breaths in and out. Your face comes first. Squeeze those muscles for 10 seconds, let go, and take several deep breaths. The shoulders follow with the same 10-second hold, the same release, and another round of full inhales and exhales. From there, the pattern repeats group by group down your frame until it reaches the feet.

Pain carves out the one exception to the sequence. You skip any area that hurts and continue without it. The Sleep Foundation's comparison chart matches the technique to physical tension and lists five to 10 minutes as the time it requires. A full pass from face to feet fits inside that short block.

The technique goes by a second name, Jacobson relaxation. Practitioners tend to combine it with guided imagery and breathing exercises. Calming methods of this kind carry a reputation for safety among healthy people. Yet a small number of users have described unpleasant reactions, including heightened anxiety, unwanted thoughts, and a fear of losing control. Anyone with a heart condition should talk with a health care provider before trying the technique.

Among the five techniques in the table, progressive muscle relaxation stands alone in answering physical tension. The other four take aim at anxiety, racing thoughts, stress, and general relaxation. Its steps skip any request to picture a scene or quiet a thought. The clench-and-release cycle keeps its focus on muscle from start to finish, which makes it the logical pick for nights when a tight body, more than a busy head, holds sleep at bay.

Guided imagery answers a specific bedtime problem, a mind crowded with racing thoughts, and the technique takes 5 to 10 minutes to complete. The method starts with a calm memory or an imagined peaceful place. Settling into that scene can drain off the day's accumulated stress and ready the mind and body for rest. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health defines the practice as picturing objects, scenes, or events linked to tranquility while trying to summon the same feeling in the body.

Sight, sound, and smell carry the exercise. You notice what the place looks like, how it sounds, and what scents drift through it, all while drawing slow, deep breaths. You aim to sink into the surroundings until every sensory layer feels present. You picture tension leaving in stages as the soothing space sharpens. The same federal center groups guided imagery among relaxation techniques, a family of methods meant to trigger a physical state of ease marked by slower respiration, lower blood pressure, and a reduced heart rate. The unhurried breathing the exercise demands matches one hallmark of that condition.

Recordings hand the scene-building to someone else, a relief for a restless brain that struggles to construct a setting alone. A soundtrack can steer your thoughts, and guided imagery tracks are simple to find online. The NIH Patient Library chose audio programs of guided imagery and meditation, which it says can lessen distress and pain, lower anxiety, encourage sleep, and give a sense of well-being. The National Institute of Mental Health published its own guided visualization for coping with pressure. Listeners sit in a comfortable position, take deep breaths, shut their eyes, and picture a walk through a rainforest to an ocean beach. A listener who picks a track that, like the institute's beach walk, builds breathing into its script covers both halves of the technique at once.

Meditation claims 10 to 15 minutes in the Sleep Foundation's comparison table, which pairs the practice with stress. The estimate exceeds every breathing, muscle-tension, and imagery exercise the table lists. The added minutes pay for a distinct mental task. Mindfulness meditation holds attention on what is happening now and asks the practitioner to set judgment aside, and the source credits those two moves with producing calm.

Bedtime anxiety gives meditation its clearest job. A session before sleep may soothe that unease and make negative emotions easier to release, the guide notes. Fixing focus on the current moment offers a churning mind somewhere to rest besides the day's frustrations and tomorrow's chores. The guide's prose names anxiety while its table names stress, and the overlap suggests meditation reaches both a hard day's lingering pressure and the sharper dread that arrives at lights-out.

Mindfulness meditation may ease chronic insomnia, a small study in the journal Sleep indicates. A version tailored to insomnia, called mindfulness-based therapy for insomnia, showed the most promise. The findings hint that meditation may prove a practical treatment. Participants in the tailored program learned behavioral tactics aimed at the condition, including sleep hygiene and sleep restriction therapy. The insomnia-focused approach folded meditation into a broader plan that also reshaped how and when people sleep. The result positions meditation as a tool for entrenched sleeplessness, beyond its role as a nightly wind-down.

Newcomers face a slower start. Reaching a settled state may take longer during the first few tries, according to the Sleep Foundation. With familiarity, the same person can unwind faster and drift off sooner. A beginner may overshoot the chart's window, and a regular may finish inside it. Each repeat night lowers the effort the next one demands. A weary sleeper who quits after one sluggish evening judges the method by its clumsiest attempt.

Anxiety is the condition 4-7-8 breathing targets, and the method asks for two to five minutes, the shortest time among the five techniques the source assigns an estimate. Its draw comes from that brevity and from a structure simple enough to recall in a dark bedroom.

The technique borrows from pranayama, an ancient yogic discipline of breath control. Its purpose is to calm the nervous system, and the guide names bedtime as a moment when the practice can help in particular. Deliberate pacing does the work. The measured rhythm slows the heart rate, quiets the mind, and readies the body for sleep.

The table ties anxiety to 4-7-8 breathing and to no other technique, handing stress to meditation and racing thoughts to guided imagery. The slower pulse the method produces answers one of the physical signs of strain common among people who struggle to drift off.

The routine opens with a full exhale. Next comes an inhale through the nose for four seconds, then a seven-second hold and an eight-second exhale through the mouth. A person repeats the cycle three to four times. The method calls for no recording, playlist, or prop. A silent count carries the whole exercise.

Each round of the sequence lasts 19 seconds. Three rounds add up to 57 seconds, and four reach 76. Both totals land under the two-minute low end of the estimate. The timed breaths occupy a fraction of the window the guide budgets for the method.

The out-breath stretches to twice the length of the in-breath, which gives every cycle a slow release at its close. The hold between them runs seven seconds, one second shy of the exhale. At 19 seconds a cycle, the pattern works out to a little more than three breaths per minute.

A cycle under 20 seconds and no equipment let 4-7-8 breathing start the instant anxiety surfaces in bed, which suits nights with little patience for a longer routine.

A soothing playlist running 15 to 20 minutes gives music the longest time requirement of the five techniques in the Sleep Foundation's comparison table, which pairs it with general relaxation. The other four methods in that chart each target a named problem, from anxiety and physical tension to racing thoughts and stress. Music casts a wider net and asks for more patience in exchange.

Noise gives the advice its purpose. A loud bedroom stands between a person and restful sleep, and the Sleep Foundation recommends cutting needless or grating sounds. Calm tracks pull double duty. They help a listener unwind, and they mask the clatter that drifts in from outside.

The playlist's length carries its own logic. The guide suggests building one that fills the window it considers ideal for falling asleep, then putting the same list on every evening. Repetition turns a set of songs into a routine, which the article names as the goal. A listener still awake when the final track fades has outlasted the target, which turns the playlist into a rough clock as well as a soundtrack.

Music can backfire on some listeners, who find the songs more distracting than calming. The article points those sleepers toward white noise, which some people champion as a sleep aid.

Michael Gradisar, a clinical psychologist at Flinders University, said music might help people who fret while lying awake in a dark, quiet bed. In his view, a song might pull attention away from worries and make bedtime feel more pleasant.

Dr. Junge said the Sleep Health Foundation offered no recommendation to play music during sleep and advised against the practice, children included. Junge described the evidence on music and sleep as undecided.

Junge's caution targets music that keeps playing after a person falls asleep. The Sleep Foundation's playlist has a built-in stopping point, which prevents the audio from running until morning.

Paradoxical intention reverses the usual bedtime aim with one sentence you repeat to yourself: "I'm not going to fall asleep." The Sleep Foundation concedes the idea sounds counterintuitive and says the reversal can help a person drift off faster. Its guide stops there, with no steps, no timing, and no account of how the trick works. The technique also stays out of the guide's comparison table, which leaves it without a time estimate or a matched concern.

A treatment chapter by Colin A. Espie of the University of Glasgow Sleep Centre supplies the reasoning the guide leaves out. Espie treats sleep as an involuntary physical process and warns that trying to control it by force of will is likely to make the problem worse. The body resists effort in other ways too, the chapter observes. People blush when they try not to, stammer when they try to stop, and stay awake when they try to sleep. Patients often describe straining to stay up "just a few minutes longer" and then waking to find the morning had arrived.

The method has a clinical history behind its single sentence. Michael Ascher and others adapted it for insomnia in the late 1970s, drawing on Viktor Frankl's work from 1955 onward, according to Espie. They noticed that people with insomnia fell asleep more successfully when they tried to stay awake than when they tried to nod off. The chapter's instructions to patients grow out of that observation. One asks a patient to hold off sleep and stay awake as long as they can.

People with insomnia disorder who fixate on sleep, on losing it, and on its fallout make an ideal fit for the therapy, the chapter argues. Its exit from that vicious cycle is to stop trying. The Sleep Foundation's lone line echoes the advice in plain words. A vow to stay awake turns the sleeper away from chasing rest. Repeating the phrase requires no equipment, recording, or set block of time. The guide's six other numbered techniques work on the muscles, the breath, attention, or the soundscape of the room. This one targets nothing but a person's stance toward sleep.

No formal clinical trials have shown the therapy works better for insomnia patients who try harder to sleep, the chapter notes. Two studies tie its effect to lower sleep-related anxiety and less effort to perform, so its case for the hardest-trying sleepers rests on that mechanism and awaits trial evidence. The chapter also counts the approach a poor match for patients whose thinking runs concrete in the extreme or who have cognitive impairment. Paradoxical intention suits a sleeper consumed by worry over lost hours and offers little to someone who takes words at face value.

Twenty minutes of wakefulness marks the point where the Sleep Foundation recommends leaving the bed, whether the trouble starts at lights-out or after waking in the middle of the night. The cutoff lands at the far edge of the span the organization considers a normal wait for sleep. Anyone still alert past it has slipped outside the healthy range. Staying under the covers to stew carries its own cost. The guidance warns that lying there trains the brain to pair the bed with alertness and frustration instead of rest.

Stimulus control is the name the Sleep Foundation gives this approach, a behavioral sleep strategy that strengthens the bond between the bed and sleep. It also loosens the grip of tossing, turning, and worrying. With time, the organization says, the practice can support more consistent, restorative sleep.

A different room gives the sleepless person somewhere calm to wait out the restless spell. The organization suggests reading, deep breathing, or gentle stretching to fill the gap. Screens and bright lights stay off during the break. The return to bed waits until drowsiness arrives, which keeps the mattress tied to the moment sleep feels within reach.

Reserving the bedroom for sleep and sex carries the same principle into waking hours. The Sleep Foundation contends that keeping work, entertainment, and stress out of the room deepens the mental connection between the bed and repose. Each activity that creeps onto the mattress erodes the conditioning the nighttime exits try to build.

Pressure to sleep rises once a person lies down in bed, according to the Sleep Foundation's answer on why people nod off on the couch. The higher stakes sharpen awareness of racing thoughts, a weight the sofa does not place on a tired mind. Couch sleepiness and bedtime vigilance in the same person point to a learned reaction to the bed itself, which explains why the remedy starts with walking away from it.

Most people sleep best in a room that stays between 60 and 67 degrees Fahrenheit, and the Sleep Foundation pairs that cool setting with darkness and quiet as the three conditions a bedroom should meet. The group describes the ideal room as a sanctuary, a calm place for rest. It argues that modest adjustments to that space can produce a noticeable gain in sleep quality. A well-arranged bedroom eases both falling asleep and staying asleep.

Blackout curtains or a sleep mask can shut out unwanted light, and earplugs or a white noise machine can dampen sounds from outside. Each pairing offers a choice between changing the space and changing what the sleeper wears. Curtains and a noise machine alter the surroundings themselves. A mask and earplugs go wherever the sleeper goes, which suits anyone who cannot rework their surroundings.

Breathable cotton or bamboo bedding carries the cooling effort past the thermostat by helping the body regulate its temperature overnight. The mattress and pillows deserve the same attention. The group advises choosing both to match a person's sleep position and body type, so no single setup suits every sleeper.

Falling asleep with the TV on undercuts these efforts in most cases. A screen's glow and sound can hold the brain back from deeper stages of sleep, and sudden volume jumps may trigger brief awakenings. Some people find background sound relaxing. A white noise machine, a fan, or sleep-focused audio may deliver that comfort with fewer interruptions. The same white noise machine that muffles outside sounds can replace the TV's background chatter. Anyone who depends on the TV to doze off can set a sleep timer that switches the set off after they drift away.

Each recommendation answers one specific disruption, whether warmth, light, noise, a mismatched mattress, or the TV. A sleeper can audit the bedroom one problem at a time and address whichever ones it has.

Sleep hygiene caps daytime naps at 20 to 30 minutes and moves them out of the late afternoon and evening. The Sleep Foundation groups this rule with a handful of other habits that shape rest before a person turns out the light. Its guide argues that the right conditions for sleep stretch past the moment of lying down, with habits, surroundings, and evening rituals all playing a part.

Good sleep hygiene, in the guide's definition, means practices and an environment that support steady, high-quality sleep. Adopting it can involve changes to the hours before bed, daily conduct, or broader lifestyle. The Sleep Foundation stops short of a single template and notes that the ideal approach differs from person to person. The nap cap is the lone tip in this group to carry a number, which makes it the simplest to track.

A wind-down routine draws its power from repetition. Doing the same calming activities each night tells the body that sleep is approaching. The article leaves the choice of what to include to the reader. Consistency, in its account, does the signaling.

Chronic stress can disrupt sleep, and the Sleep Foundation urges readers to handle it during daylight hours. Journaling, therapy, and breathwork give people outlets for working through emotions. Breathwork ties this habit to the breathing methods earlier in the list, letting one skill serve day and night. Dealing with stress before dark leaves bedtime relaxation techniques with a lighter load of tension to undo.

Late-day fluids round out the advice. Too much water close to lights-out can mean repeated nighttime bathroom trips. The guide's remedy is to drink less in the hours before bed. This tip protects the stretch after sleep arrives. Each trip pulls a person from bed and interrupts the night.

Each of these steps happens before a person reaches the pillow. Falling asleep fast, by the guide's logic, starts with a decision about the afternoon nap and runs through the last glass of water.

#5549. How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Every September, Climate Week and Global Citizen Week in New York bring together policymakers, investors and innovators focused on the world’s most pressing problems.

It’s also when Cisco Systems Inc. and Global Citizen recognize the winner of the Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award. Cisco and Global Citizen created the award in 2018 to honor a young leader who uses technology to help end extreme poverty, and this year’s recipient may have the most compelling story yet.

Diana Virgovicova (pictured) is the founder and CEO of Xatoms (pronounced “X-Atoms”), a Toronto-based company that uses artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to design sunlight-activated materials that break down pollutants in water. The award comes with a $250,000 grant, and Xatoms was chosen from more than 2,000 applications.

Most of the AI conversation at Climate Week focused on what AI takes from the planet: power, land and, increasingly, water. Xatoms offers a positive counterpoint, a case study in AI giving back.

Most founders find a market. Virgovicova found a problem the hard way. She grew up in a village of about 800 people in Slovakia, surrounded by farms that used heavy amounts of pesticides. “I got sick when I was 14 years old,” she told me. “I was diagnosed with ovarian cancer because of the water I drank.”

After her diagnosis, she persuaded her mother to go backpacking across Asia. On trains in India, she heard from women facing the same thing. “I learned that there is a girl in Slovakia who got sick. There is a girl in India who’s getting infections. There is a girl in Africa who has to spend long hours every single day searching for clean water,” she said. “So, we need to find a solution, and it is affecting mainly women across the globe.”

Globally, women and girls spend 250 million hours a day collecting water, more than three times the time men and boys spend. “While boys go to school, the girls are responsible for bringing a bucket of water home, and they start missing school very early on,” Virgovicova explained. “It’s an educational, economic and health problem.”

And it’s growing. “We have 2 billion people that don’t have access to clean drinking water, and this number is actually growing because of flooding, climate change,” she said.

One of the more interesting aspects of Xatoms is where it chose to play. Many water treatment efforts target bacteria such as E. coli because the effects are immediate. Xatoms goes after the harder problem: complex industrial pollutants such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, forever chemicals and heavy metals.

“I think we are forgetting about these complex contaminants because they don’t make us sick tomorrow. They make us sick in 10 years,” she said. “They give us chronic diseases. They cause infertility.” She made a point I hadn’t considered: Scientific progress is making it worse.

“We are able to create better antibiotics, but these better antibiotics are more complex, thus more difficult to destroy in water,” she said. That’s a second-order problem traditional treatment wasn’t built for, and exactly where advanced computational design has an edge.

At 17, while working with a university professor in Slovakia, Virgovicova used quantum chemistry software to design a new molecule that harnesses sunlight to break down water pollutants. That work earned her a Diploma of Excellence from the Swedish Royal Family and a full scholarship to the University of Toronto.

“What is so exciting about this science is that we can use computers to design new materials, and we don’t have to create them in the lab,” she said. “We can see these materials, how they react, and what their properties are before we even synthesize them.”

Quantum chemistry gets far fewer headlines than quantum computing, so I asked her to explain it. “Quantum helps us understand these molecules at a fundamental level, including how the atoms within the molecule interact,” she said. “When we know these fundamental properties, we can understand what makes each molecule good at something, and that helps us design an even better molecule, a better material.”

The output is a photocatalyst powder. “Initially, it was a molecule in a computer, but we were able to synthesize it in a lab,” Virgovicova said. “We put this photocatalytic powder into water. It splits water into OH radicals, and the OH radicals then destroy contaminants.”

Because it’s a catalyst, it isn’t consumed, so a small amount can treat “hundreds of gallons,” she said. Earlier photocatalysts required ultraviolet light; her design works with visible light, such as sunlight or LEDs, eliminating the need for expensive UV reactors.

AI is the accelerant. “It would take a decade if we did it without AI,” she said. “We can do it in 30 days.” That’s the real story for business leaders. Materials discovery has historically been slow, expensive and lab-bound, and Xatoms has transformed it into a computational pipeline.

Here’s where it matters for technology buyers. Data centers consume enormous volumes of water for cooling, and the AI buildout is making that worse. I asked Virgovicova whether Xatoms can flip the script. “There are a lot of problems with contaminants within the data center,” she said. “The data center water needs to be completely clean for cooling,” she said. “We are able to use this catalyst to help reuse the water in data centers.”

This is an underappreciated opportunity. Hyperscalers and neoclouds face mounting pressure over water use, and the industry’s response has largely focused on cooling design. Reuse through improved treatment is a different and more planet-friendly solution.

Xatoms works with Indigenous communities in Canada under longstanding boil-water advisories, as well as in Kenya and South Africa. Virgovicova told me the footprint now includes Japan and Azerbaijan. Every engagement is customized.

“We collect a water sample. Recently, we shipped the sample from Azerbaijan all the way to Canada,” she said. “We identify the contaminant and then determine which of these 88 options would be the best.”

Customers define the outcome. “Some of them want to take yellow water and decolorize it. Some of them have a specific contaminant in mind that they want to remove or reduce,” she said.

Next up are Turkey, where co-founder Kerem Topal Ismail Oglou grew up, and the broader Middle East, driven by textile manufacturing and oil and gas. She also met South Africa’s water minister during Climate Week ahead of a trip to Cape Town.

Being named a global winner of the World Economic Forum’s Water Resilience Challenge opened doors with large enterprises. “We had the chance to interact with some of the biggest Fortune 500 companies, which helped us create pilots and partnerships,” she said.

The Cisco grant is moving directly into execution. “We have more than six major projects coming up, so we need help with lab work,” she said. “We need to figure out the best way to manufacture more materials.” The goal is to “commercialize this technology as fast as we can.”

When I joked that billionaires are hunting for water on Mars while we haven’t solved it here, she pointed out a funding gap. “About 3% of climate VC funding goes to water only,” she said. Water underpins industry, agriculture and now AI infrastructure, yet it remains capital-starved.

Virgovicova mentors young founders, especially women in science and climate, and her advice is very direct. “There’s always going to be skepticism in every single room you go into at first,” she said. “It’s very important that you know how to present yourself and that you’re confident. You can really prove everyone wrong as long as you know your stuff.” With women still scarce among Fortune 500 CEOs, she added, “If I can do it, you can do it as well.”

Her favorite piece of advice: “If you focus on watering your grass, you don’t care about someone’s grass being greener.” And the AI myth she wants gone? “That it’s going to destroy the world. I think it’s a tool for improving the world.”

Cisco uses this award to make a point it rarely gets credit for: technology’s value is measured by what it does for people. Xatoms applies two of the decade’s most hyped technologies, AI and quantum, to a tangible, urgent problem.

For technology leaders, there are three key takeaways. First, AI’s biggest payoff may come from scientific discovery, where compressing a decade of work into 30 days can reshape an entire industry’s economics. Second, AI’s water problem has solutions beyond cooling design, and data center builders should be evaluating treatment and reuse partners now. Third, water deserves far more capital than it receives.

In 10 years, Virgovicova wants Xatoms to be “a global leader in discovery of these materials,” with solutions for many toxic contaminants worldwide. Given how far she has come from a village of 800 people, I wouldn’t bet against her.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5548. The states with the lowest unemployment rates, according to the BLS

Free daily briefing on global business news.

South Dakota, North Dakota, Vermont, New Hampshire, Hawaii, and Nebraska held jobless rates under 3% in September 2026.

People hunting for work, angling for a raise, or weighing a move across state lines are betting on a labor market they can glimpse but not measure. The odds shift with geography. A job seeker in a state where few residents are out of work competes against a smaller crowd for each opening. Workers who hold jobs gain leverage in those places as well. A manager who loses an employee in a tight market may struggle to find a replacement, and the threat of a vacancy can make a raise easier to win. The reverse holds in places with plenty of idle workers, where every posting draws more applicants and employers feel less pressure to bid up pay. The statewide jobless rate offers one of the clearest gauges of that pressure, and it can tell a family more about its prospects than any headline about the economy as a whole.

A single national number hides how far apart the states sit. The U.S. unemployment rate stood at 4.2% in September 2026, yet 20 states came in below it and 28 differed from it by too little to matter statistically. Two states ran higher, California at 5.1% and Michigan at 5.0%, along with the District of Columbia at 5.6%. The map changed over the prior 12 months. Unemployment dropped in 20 states and the District between September 2025 and September 2026. New Jersey posted the steepest decline, falling 1.3 percentage points to 4.2%. Seven states went the other way. Connecticut climbed the most, adding 0.9 percentage point to reach 5.1%. Rates in 23 states showed no notable change. Two Americans in different states can face local conditions that diverge by more than a full percentage point.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled these state figures for September 2026 from its Local Area Unemployment Statistics program. The numbers carry seasonal adjustment, and the agency labels the most recent month preliminary. Later revisions could shift the September estimates. The agency's chart includes only states whose distance from the U.S. figure clears its significance threshold and leaves out the rest. The chart, as a result, falls short of a complete 50-state ranking. The list below draws from that chart and features the six states that kept unemployment under 3% in September 2026, ordering them from smallest rate to largest across five slides. Two of those states tie and share one entry.

South Dakota held its unemployment rate to 2.0% in September 2026, a mark no other state in the data matched. The figure sits 2.2 percentage points beneath the national level. Across the U.S., joblessness ran 2.1 times as high as in South Dakota.

One in every 50 members of South Dakota's labor force lacked a job. Put the other way, 98 of every 100 were working. California's share of idle workers ran more than twice as high, and the District of Columbia's reached 2.8 times the South Dakota level. A 3.6-point gulf separates South Dakota from the District, which occupies the opposite end of the chart. An employer with an opening in South Dakota fishes in a shallower pool of jobless residents than one in California or the District.

South Dakota finished 0.2 point under North Dakota, its closest rival in the chart, and 0.6 point under Vermont and New Hampshire. Nebraska, the last of the six states below 3%, lands 0.9 point higher. Wyoming, at 3.0%, stands a full point above South Dakota. The six states under 3% span less than a single point from bottom to top. Among those low-unemployment states, South Dakota's edge comes in tenths of a point. Measured against the U.S. figure and the states above it, the cushion swells to whole points.

Farming and ranching form the bedrock of South Dakota's economy and remain its largest industry. Services, retail trade, and manufacturing supply most of the state's jobs. South Dakota's rate lies nearer to zero than to the U.S. figure.

North Dakota's 2.2% unemployment rate in September 2026 sat 2 percentage points beneath the U.S. figure, a margin only one other state in the chart surpassed. The report built its headline around this state and South Dakota, grouping the two Dakotas among the country's lowest jobless rates. No other state earned a place in that title, which singles out the pair as the standouts of the month.

South Dakota stands as the lone other state in the chart below 2.5%. North Dakota clears the next tier by 0.4 percentage point, the distance to the 2.6% that Vermont and New Hampshire share. The state lands nearer its neighbor below than the tied pair above. Hawaii and Nebraska, also under 3%, trail North Dakota by even wider margins. The two Dakotas form a cluster of their own, with a clear break before any other state appears.

Michigan's rate runs more than double North Dakota's, and California's does as well. The District of Columbia comes in 3.4 percentage points higher. Job seekers in those places face a much larger crowd of unemployed rivals for each opening. An out-of-work North Dakotan competes in a far thinner field, where employers may feel the shortage of applicants more than candidates feel the shortage of jobs.

The North Dakota Department of Commerce describes energy as the largest industry in the state. The energy detail profiles the economy and proves nothing about why so few residents lack work. The September report ties no industry to North Dakota's jobless rate, and it supplies no year-earlier reading for the state either. Whether the state's rate fell, rose, or held steady since September 2025 remains unknown from these numbers.

Halving the U.S. rate would leave it 0.1 percentage point beneath North Dakota's. North Dakota's unemployment, in effect, runs a shade above half the national level.

Vermont and New Hampshire each posted a 2.6% unemployment rate in September 2026, the lone shared figure among the six states that kept joblessness under 3%. At that level, fewer than three of every 100 people in each state's labor force were out of work. A job seeker comparing the two states would find no edge for either one on this measure.

Both states finished 1.6 percentage points beneath the U.S. rate. The margin separates them from the many states whose readings landed near the national mark without a meaningful difference. Workers in the pair faced a tighter labor market than their counterparts in the states clustered around the national figure.

Their shared reading sits in the middle of the under-3% group. South Dakota and North Dakota came in 0.6 and 0.4 point lower. Hawaii's rate ran 0.2 point above the pair, and Nebraska's ran 0.3 point above. The gaps on either side measure only tenths of a point, so the six states form a tight band at the low end of the chart.

Maine's 3.3% rate exceeded the Vermont and New Hampshire level by 0.7 point and missed the under-3% cutoff. Maine still beat the U.S. rate, yet its distance from the pair outstripped the spread between the pair and South Dakota. The District of Columbia, which posted the chart's highest rate, more than doubled the pair's mark.

Workers in Vermont or New Hampshire faced joblessness closer to South Dakota's 2.0% than to the national rate.

Hawaii's unemployment rate came in at 2.8% in September 2026, 1.4 percentage points under the national figure and one-third below it. Of the 20 states that sat beneath the U.S. rate, Hawaii undercut 15. Four states logged lower readings, and Vermont and New Hampshire, the closest of them, landed 0.2 point beneath Hawaii. Nebraska finished 0.1 point above Hawaii. A band 0.3 point wide, running from 2.6% to 2.9%, contains four of the six states under 3%.

Hawaii's cushion beneath the 3% line measures 0.2 point. An increase of two-tenths of a point would lift the state to 3.0% and out of the group. Both Dakotas hold wider margins. North Dakota sits 0.8 point below the line, and South Dakota a full point under it.

The District of Columbia's jobless rate ran at twice Hawaii's in September 2026, the widest spread between Hawaii and any place in the chart. California and Michigan, the two states above the national figure, posted rates 2.3 and 2.2 points higher than Hawaii's. New Jersey, despite the steepest one-year decline of any state, ended September 2026 1.4 points above Hawaii. South Dakota, at the chart's opposite end, registered a rate 0.8 point lower than Hawaii's. California's gap above Hawaii stretches nearly three times as wide as South Dakota's gap below it.

Hawaii's state business development division describes military-related spending as the second-largest sector of the state's economy, behind tourism. Visitors and defense form the two biggest pieces of Hawaii's economic base.

Construction, health care, and professional services were the leading contributors to Hawaii's growth, according to the state's Department of Business, Economic Development and Tourism. The department reports that fields outside tourism, such as information, helped offset an uneven rebound in visitor-related industries. It projected a slower but steady recovery for tourism. Hawaii's job market rests on a broader foundation than travel spending.

Nebraska kept its jobless rate at 2.9% in September 2026, one-tenth of a point beneath the 3% line. No state in the under-3% group posted a higher figure. Nebraska marks the seam between that cluster and the rest of the chart.

Wyoming came in at 3.0%, a tenth of a point above Nebraska and outside the group. Montana followed at 3.1%, and Iowa and Wisconsin each reached 3.2%. The five states fit inside a band three-tenths of a point wide. A sliver that narrow divided Nebraska from four states that landed at or above the line.

Inside the group, Nebraska stood 0.1 point above Hawaii and 0.3 point above Vermont and New Hampshire. The 3% line separates Nebraska from Wyoming by the same margin that separates it from Hawaii. A round-number cutoff can make two states with near-identical rates look like members of different tiers. Nebraska's place at the edge reflects where the line falls more than any gap between its labor market and Hawaii's.

Nebraska's margin beneath the U.S. rate came to 1.3 percentage points, the thinnest cushion among the six states this list features. Pennsylvania and Virginia, the highest-rate states on the chart's below-national side at 3.6% each, cleared the U.S. figure by 0.6 point. Nebraska's cushion ran more than twice as wide. Even the weakest showing in the under-3% group left Nebraska far ahead of states that slipped under the national rate by slimmer margins.

Nebraska finished 0.9 point above South Dakota, the state at the bottom of the chart, and 0.7 point below that pair. Its rate falls near the midpoint of the span that states below the national figure occupy. A spot among the six lowest rates still leaves Nebraska in the middle of the states that beat the national figure. Even at the group's outer edge, Nebraska's rate remained closer to South Dakota's than to the national figure.

#5545. VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.

Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.

By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.

Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.

“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”

Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.

Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

#5544. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Predicts an XRP Explosion as Binance Resumes Withdrawals Following Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Something potentially massive could be coming for Ripple XRP, according to Mark Zuckerberg’s AI bot. Meta AI predicts that XRP could be the market leader across Q4 and into 2027, with an explosive move into double digits, but only if an over-the-top scenario built around a hypothetical landmark catalyst lands.

The idea centers on a major global payments consortium and several large commercial banks formally adopting the XRP Ledger as a preferred liquidity and settlement layer for next-generation cross-border corporate treasury and trade-finance flows.

In this framework, significant volumes of institutional payment activity would migrate onto the XRP Ledger, creating structural demand for XRP as a bridge asset at a scale far beyond previous cycles.

On the higher timeframes, XRP has been consolidating in the $1.20–$1.30 region following recent market volatility. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $1.35–$1.45 zone.

In a standard bull market, a sustained breakout above $1.60–$1.80 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path toward a retest of the prior all-time high near $3.65–$3.66.

Under the extreme corporate treasury and trade-finance adoption scenario outlined above, clearing that previous high would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections from the long-term base.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-corrective territory with significant room to run into the extreme overbought levels typical of parabolic advances.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $1.18–$1.22 and $1.10–$1.15; holding those levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact.

Binance has announced it will resume phase one of withdrawals on November 1, 2026, in a controlled, phased manner after completing security assessments.

The exchange has reiterated that user funds remain safe, that it will absorb the full financial impact of the stolen assets (rather than passing losses to users), and that it has already covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount.

Deposits remained open throughout, and the company continues working with partners and law enforcement on recovery efforts. The relatively orderly response, combined with the market’s ability to absorb the largest exchange hack on record without a cascading collapse, suggests a constructive signal of growing industry resilience.

For risk assets more broadly, including XRP, a successful, transparent restoration of services and containment of the incident may help restore confidence and reduce one major overhang on sentiment as the market looks ahead.

#5543. 6 ways to trim a rental car bill, from insurance to EV recharge fees

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Consumer Reports flags pricey rental add-ons, from insurance that can top $30 a day to EV recharge fees, plus ways to keep costs down.

A rental counter at the end of a long flight makes a poor setting for money decisions. The traveler wants to reach the hotel, the line keeps growing, and the agent has a list of extras to pitch before handing over the keys. Every choice a renter makes in those few minutes lands on the final bill. The stakes have risen with the market. Rental car prices have climbed about 35% since before the pandemic, according to NerdWallet. A rental has become a major trip expense, and the damage compounds for anyone who overpays on the daily rate and piles add-ons on top of it.

The amount a company quotes per day marks a starting point, and the tally at drop-off can climb past it. Counter coverage, strings on discounted bookings, and charges tied to the fuel or battery level at return all sit outside that headline number. A renter who compares companies on the per-day quote alone misses part of the eventual cost. Choices a traveler makes before the trip, such as where to book, what kind of vehicle to reserve, and whether a traditional rental fits the need at all, also shape what the renter ends up paying. Some extras deliver genuine value. Others duplicate safeguards a driver may hold through other channels, and certain bargains swap a smaller upfront sum for restrictive terms. Sorting one from the other takes homework that can spare a traveler from paying twice for the same protection.

Consumer Reports tackles these pitfalls in a service guide on saving money when renting a car, which Benjamin Preston wrote and Jeff S. Bartlett updated Oct. 22, 2026. The piece offers practical advice and does not rank its tips or rely on a survey. The guide draws on a recent staff comparison of options for a weeklong Hertz rental in Los Angeles, along with outside figures from NerdWallet and coverage guidance from the Insurance Information Institute. Its scope stretches from insurance and credit card benefits to discounted deals, booking channels, electric vehicles, and car-sharing and peer-to-peer services such as Zipcar and Turo. The six entries below present a selection of that advice and follow the order in which the guide lays it out.

Counter coverage can cost more than $30 a day, and rental agents pitch it to nearly every customer who reaches the desk. Consumer Reports judges that most renters probably don't need it. Over a seven-day trip, a daily charge above $30 adds more than $210 to the bill before the car leaves the lot. The charge grows with every added day of the rental. A longer trip turns a reflexive yes at the counter into a bigger expense.

Many drivers already carry protection that can follow them to the counter. A personal auto policy may extend to a rented vehicle, according to the Insurance Information Institute. A renter who holds such a policy and also buys the counter product may pay twice for the same safeguard. The second purchase raises the bill without adding security.

Assumptions about coverage can backfire. Credit card benefits can shift over time, and a perk that protected one trip may not apply to the next. Consumer Reports urges travelers to check their protection before every rental. A fresh review keeps a driver from declining a safeguard that no longer exists. It also stops a traveler from buying a policy that duplicates one already in hand.

Some travelers have good reason to buy at the desk. Paying for the rental company's damage coverage keeps personal insurance out of the picture. The driver files no claim with an auto insurer, pays no deductible, and faces no risk of a premium increase after a damage incident. Travelers $TRV who prize peace of mind over savings may judge the daily charge worth it. The trade-off weighs a certain cost today against a possible one after an accident.

A driver without outside protection, or unsure of its terms, faces a different calculation. A driver with confirmed outside protection buys little at the counter beyond insulation from a future claim and the costs that claim could trigger.

Many credit card issuers cover collision damage on rental cars charged to their cards, yet certain cards drop that protection in Ireland, Israel, Italy, Jamaica, and a handful of other foreign countries. A traveler who counts on a card abroad could reach the rental desk in one of those places with no collision benefit in hand. The exclusions turn a familiar perk into a conditional one. A card that shields a rental at home may offer nothing on a drive through Ireland or Italy. Coverage follows the payment. It attaches to the card the renter charges for the rental, so a traveler who settles the bill with a different card leaves the benefit behind.

Confirmation gives renters grounds to decline the company's damage policy. Consumer Reports advises checking with the auto insurer or the card issuer that the specific rental qualifies before saying no to the agent. A call to the issuer or a read through the card's terms before departure settles the question ahead of the sales pitch. The check carries the most weight on international trips, where the list of excluded countries determines whether the card helps at all. A renter who skips the step could learn of the gap after the car takes damage, long past the moment to accept the counter policy.

AAA opens a separate route for its members. Those who reserve through the club's website can buy rental insurance, and its policy tends to cost less than what rental companies charge for their own. The offer hinges on the booking channel, which ties the savings to where the reservation begins. The club's policy gives members a fallback if their card carries no rental benefit.

A renter with an eligible card or a AAA membership holds two alternatives to the rental company's plan, provided the card's terms reach the country where the trip takes place.

Paying up front, accepting a mystery car, or agreeing to both can unlock steep discounts at many rental companies and at third-party sites such as Priceline. Consumer Reports warns that the cheapest cars often come with strings. Each bargain asks the renter to give up something in return: either the chance to pay later or the power to select a vehicle.

The Manager's Special, Hertz's mystery car offering, cut the cost of a weeklong Los Angeles rental in a recent Consumer Reports check. The electric edition of the same deal undercut most alternatives on the menu. Surrendering control over the vehicle shrank the bill in both cases.

An electric rental trades a lower price for a bigger time commitment. A driver who takes the EV version may need to hunt down chargers along the route and block out time to plug in. Anyone on a tight schedule covers the difference in hours spent waiting.

Free cancellation may disappear from these reduced-rate reservations. A traveler whose plans shift could lose the money already paid. The exposure grows with every dollar a renter hands over in advance, which puts prepaid bookings at the greatest risk.

Consumer Reports advises reading the small print and reviewing restrictions at whatever company or site handles the booking. These offers reward travelers with fixed itineraries and no strong attachment to a particular model, and they can backfire on anyone whose travel dates remain uncertain.

Shortfall: Slide 3 runs about 245 words, under the 300-word minimum. The source gives no prices, dates, or percentages for the Hertz Manager's Special or EV Manager's Special comparison and offers only a few sentences on Priceline and prepaid or mystery car terms. No supplementary evidence was supplied, so the slide carries only what the source supports. An unsupported claim that a forfeited prepayment exceeds the deal's savings was removed.

AAA, Costco $COST, and Priceline may turn up the lowest rates on a rental car, but reserving through one of them hands the deal to a middleman. The guide expects extensions and other adjustments to run through the third party's website, which cuts the renter off from a direct line to the rental company.

Consumer Reports cautions that sorting out changes through an intermediary could prove more fraught than working with the company that holds the car. Two parties now sit in the chain. One manages the reservation, and the other holds the keys. A traveler who wants an extra day must work through the site, even though the vehicle belongs to the rental firm.

Firm travel dates shrink the exposure. A traveler with a set return time can pocket the savings and leave the reservation untouched. The discount shows up at checkout, and any friction surfaces after plans shift. Someone who expects to stretch the trip or rework the details faces the extra steps the guide describes.

The guide hedges its price claim with "may," so the cheapest quote stays a possibility and falls short of a guarantee. A renter who checks the rental firm's direct price alongside the third-party figure can see what the middleman saves. A slim margin buys little and gives up the simpler route to changes. A wide gap may justify the extra hassle on a trip with fixed dates. A trip that might run long can tip the math toward reserving direct.

This slide runs about 250 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives this topic about three sentences with no figures, and no approved supplementary evidence was supplied, so it was not padded.

Electric rentals can be the cheapest cars on the lot, yet a DC fast charger needs 30 minutes to add about 150 miles of range. Filling a gas tank takes a fraction of that wait. Some renters land in an EV without asking for one. An electric car may be the only vehicle the lot has ready at pickup. Those drivers inherit the charging schedule along with the low rate.

Level 2 units turn up in more places, but they supply 10 to 20 miles in the same half hour. A DC fast charger covers 7.5 to 15 times as much ground over that window. Matching one 30-minute fast session at Level 2 speeds would take between 3.75 and 7.5 hours. A short break on a road trip can stretch into an afternoon parked beside a plug. The easier charger to locate is the slower one. Renters who settle for the nearest plug pay in hours.

Topping up the battery before drop-off takes longer than five minutes. The quick stop gas drivers make on the way to the return lane will not work for an EV. Renters need to build charging time into the final day of the trip or pay the company to recharge the battery. At Level 2 rates, adding a modest amount of range can consume hours before the return deadline.

Hertz estimates its recharge fee at $30 for renters who prepay and $65 for those who pay later. The final amount hinges on how much energy the battery needs. The pay-later estimate runs more than double the prepaid one, a $35 difference between the two figures. A driver who expects to return the car low on power, with no time to plug in, secures the smaller estimate by committing in advance. Renters who wait until drop-off to decide have already lost the cheaper option.

Zipcar charges $5 to $19 a month for membership, and every new member pays a $25 application fee. A full year at those monthly rates comes to $60 to $228 before any hourly billing. Adding the application fee pushes the first-year outlay to $85 to $253. None of that money pays for time behind the wheel. It buys access, and each trip adds to the tab.

Short-term services such as Zipcar rent by the hour and station cars in many cities. A traveler who needs wheels for an errand or a single afternoon can spend less this way than on a standard daily rental. The math favors repeat users. Each extra outing spreads the fixed membership expense thinner, while a one-time user absorbs the whole sum for a single drive.

AARP members get $40 off the annual fee. The discount exceeds the $25 application charge. A traveler who already belongs to AARP recovers the signup expense and then some.

A long list of add-on charges trails the membership price. Zipcar bills for lapses ranging from a late return to a car handed back with a low tank of gas. An afternoon errand that runs past its reserved window or ends near empty can cost more than the hourly rate implied. Reserving a cushion of extra time and leaving room for a fuel stop guards against both penalties.

Turo links renters with owners who list their own vehicles. The deal runs between renter and owner, with no rental company standing in the middle. Peer-to-peer platforms such as Turo may offer low prices. Consumer Reports singles out a different strength as their top advantage, the ease of getting behind the wheel of a classic or exotic car. Turo's draw lies in the car itself, which makes the platform a fit for a milestone trip or a dream drive.

Zipcar's pricing rewards brief, repeated trips that end on schedule and with fuel in the tank.

#5541. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)
