#5540. 11 common airport scams and how to avoid them, according to AAA

Free daily briefing on global business news.

From fake QR codes to rigged USB ports and bogus taxi drivers, AAA outlines 11 airport scams and the habits that help travelers avoid them.

Anyone who has hurried toward a departure gate knows how little attention the moment leaves for anything beyond the next checkpoint. A traveler in that state gives scams scant thought. Fraudsters know how far a hurried mind drifts, and they treat the airport as a place where distracted people make easy marks. Their targets include cash, personal information, and the belongings a passenger carries. Losing any one of them can turn a routine trip into a costly ordeal, with emptied wallets, exposed personal data, or missing bags to sort out.

Fatigue deepens the problem. A long flight leaves arriving passengers worn out and eager to reach their destination. Exhaustion dulls the instinct to question a stranger, a sign, or an offer. Scammers count on that lapse. The risk opens before boarding and lingers after landing. Threats arrive through the phones and gadgets passengers carry, and through the cash, cards, and paperwork they hand across counters. A single slip in either realm can compromise a bank account, private records, or a suitcase. Vigilance has to stretch across the whole journey, from the curb at departures to the arrivals hall.

AAA Club Alliance laid out 11 common airport scams in its publication The Extra Mile. Beryn Orera wrote the guide, which ran Jan. 13, 2025. Each entry explains how a scheme works and pairs that explanation with steps for spotting and avoiding it, with expert input shaping the advice. The article offers practical guidance and presents no survey, dataset, or incidence figures. Its numbering follows the sequence of the piece and makes no claim about which scams occur with the greatest frequency or inflict the heaviest losses. The full feature runs as an 11-minute read. Orera closes by arguing that readers who stay informed and alert can recognize a scam, sidestep it, and respond well if one gets through. The list below keeps the source's order.

Thieves running QR code phishing, a scheme known as "quishing," place malicious codes in public spaces or deliver them through email, text messages, and mail. Scanning one sends a phone to a fraudulent website. From there, the site can harvest personal information, install malware, or divert a payment to the scammer. The mailed, emailed, and texted versions reach travelers far from any terminal. The attack depends on one action from the victim, the scan itself.

Some rogue codes hide on top of genuine ones. Scammers paste their own stickers over real codes on parking meters, posters, and similar spots. Scraping a fingernail across a code can reveal whether a sticker covers the original. One expert warned against scanning any code fixed to a bare wall or light post with nothing else around it.

Urgency offers another tell. Experts treat any lure that manufactures a rush, such as a code promising last-minute concert tickets, as an immediate red flag. A code that hurries the scanner leaves less time for the checks that expose it. An airport generates that pressure on its own, with travelers racing to a gate and few spare moments to question a scan.

The landing page leaves clues. Any page demanding more details than a task requires deserves suspicion, and airport staff can confirm whether a code is legitimate. Secure sites begin with HTTPS, and any site a traveler opens at the airport should carry that prefix. Reading the full URL a code points to can expose a scam before any data changes hands.

The safest move bypasses the code. Typing the address into a browser, or paying by another method such as cash, leaves a fake code nothing to exploit. A traveler who reaches a site without scanning shuts out every version of the con, from doctored stickers to codes sent by mail.

Scammers can stand up an "evil twin" Wi-Fi network whose name echoes the airport's own, then capture the data of anyone who joins it. Criminals pull a parallel trick over Bluetooth by posing as a device the victim recognizes. Public Wi-Fi and Bluetooth make airport waits easier, and that ease exposes travelers to cyberattacks.

The evil twin belongs to the broader family of "Man in the Middle" attacks, in which a hacker or group creates a counterfeit Wi-Fi network in public settings that draw many users, according to CNBC. IT consultant Brian Alcorn said such a device can serve a convincing replica of a valid login page. The fake page invites a username and password, which the attacker collects for later exploitation. The stolen credentials can resurface long after the traveler has boarded. Authorities in Australia charged a man over this kind of attack on domestic flights and at airports in Perth, Melbourne, and Adelaide. The charges accuse him of building a bogus network to harvest email or social media login details.

Travelers $TRV can blunt the threat by switching Wi-Fi off before they reach the airport. One expert the guide consulted advises confirming the official network on the airport's website or with staff after arrival. Skip any public network that requires no login or requests personal information it has no use for. Sensitive activity such as online shopping belongs on cellular data.

Brian Callahan of the Rensselaer Cybersecurity Collaboratory points to a phone's mobile hotspot as a way around evil twins. Its owner knows the network name and can set a strong password. Callahan added that a VPN offers some protection when a hotspot is unavailable. Traffic to and from the VPN should travel encrypted.

Bluetooth should stay off inside the airport. Travelers who need it can set the device to "non-discoverable" mode and pair only with trusted gadgets.

An official connection can sit beyond an airport's own control. A Dallas Love Field Airport spokesman said the airport's IT team cannot access the systems of Boingo, the company that supplies its Wi-Fi. The checks travelers run before connecting carry much of the burden that the terminal itself cannot shoulder.

Juice jacking turns a public USB port into a hidden route for malware, and the data breach it triggers can slip past the phone's owner without a trace. A draining battery creates the opening. Travelers $TRV watching their charge fall reach for the nearest USB slot, and nothing on the outside of a compromised one reveals the malicious code inside. The guide counts this trick among the common scams that target people passing through airports.

Phone software supplies one layer of protection against the attack. Denver International Airport said it had received no reports or alerts of juice jacking. The airport called the smartphone itself the strongest safeguard at any public charging port. Apple $AAPL and Android have released updates that block such attacks or warn users about them, the airport noted. The airport also said it can check whether someone altered a public charging port and pull any tampered unit from use. The FCC advises anyone who plugs into a free USB port to watch the screen for prompts or pop-ups and to decline the links and permission requests those messages display.

A wall socket and a personal charger spare a phone any contact with public USB hardware. The FBI's Denver field office urged people to skip free charging stations in airports, hotels, and malls. Its guidance told travelers to pack their own charger and USB cable and plug into a wall outlet. The office framed the warning as an advisory and tied it to no specific case.

Power-only cables shut the data channel at the wire. A standard USB cable carries both electricity and data. A power-only version carries electricity and nothing else, which blocks a tampered port from reaching the phone's contents. AAA Club Alliance credits this design with cutting the risk of juice jacking. The FCC recommends carrying a charging-only cable along with personal chargers and power cords, and it favors an AC outlet over a public USB station.

A USB data blocker gives travelers a fallback when a public port is the sole source of power in reach. The device halts data transfer and lets power, and nothing more, flow from the port into the phone. By stripping out the data link, the blocker shields the device from malware lurking in a compromised slot. Personal chargers, power-only cables, and data blockers all work by severing the data connection, and a port with no data path to the phone has no means of delivering its payload.

Payment card fraud can begin with a small unauthorized charge, the scammer's opening move before larger transactions follow. A declined ATM withdrawal can point to the same problem. Either signal can look trivial on a hectic travel day, and a traveler juggling gates and connections might write it off as a glitch. Treating it as a warning gives the cardholder a chance to act before the thief moves on to bigger sums.

Widespread use makes credit and debit cards a natural target for fraudsters. One card can cover purchases and pull local currency from a cash machine in another country. The same reach draws thieves hunting for money and financial details. The more a traveler leans on a single card abroad, the longer the trail of swipes grows, and the easier an unfamiliar entry becomes to miss.

Card details can also leak through hidden hardware. The U.S. Department of Agriculture describes a skimmer as a device that thieves fit onto payment terminals or PIN pads to capture card numbers and other data from credit, debit, and EBT cards. Criminals design skimmers to blend in as an ordinary part of a card reader or keypad. Thieves have used card numbers and PINs harvested this way to take SNAP benefits from recipients, the agency reports. Its guidance tells retailers to lift their payment machines by the top more than once a day and check for loose pieces that don't belong.

Steady attention to account records gives travelers a direct defense. Reviewing bank and card statements on a regular schedule during a trip can expose a modest purchase the cardholder never made. Transaction alerts on bank and credit accounts add a second safeguard by flagging fresh activity. Catching the pattern at its first minor charge spares a traveler the heavier losses a thief would pursue next.

A boarding pass photo shared on social media can expose a traveler's name and booking reference number, and scammers could use those two details to cancel the return flight. A printed pass holds more than the eye catches. Travel security guidance cautions against posting pictures of plane tickets or other travel documents online. Hiding the flight number leaves the leak open, and the ticket can reveal more than it appears to. Barcodes and QR codes on tickets can pack in a lot of data, sometimes including details about the returning flight, according to Sanchez-Rola.

A posted boarding pass also broadcasts an absence. Such an image can tell thieves that nobody is home, which shifts the danger from a disrupted itinerary to an unguarded house. One expert the guide cites adds a third threat. Criminals, he warns, can turn details travelers share into counterfeit documents.

Guarding the paperwork itself forms the first line of defense. The same expert recommends keeping travel documents secure, posting as little as possible on social media, and throwing away used documents at home instead of at the airport. "Shoulder surfers," people who try to photograph documents in plain view, pose one more hazard in public spaces.

Bogus flight alerts that arrive by text present a related trap. In one common version, fraudsters send an urgent message claiming the airline canceled or delayed a flight, then pose as helpers who will rebook the traveler for an added fee. Travelers $TRV who get such a text should confirm the flight status through the airline's portal and rebook only with the airline or the booking system they used at the start. They should also skip any link inside those messages.

A single posted photo can hand strangers the means to cancel a trip, copy its paperwork, and target the empty home left behind.

Fake lounge pass apps give scammers a way to drain money and personal information from travelers looking for a quiet seat before their flight. Airport lounges offer a comfortable place to rest, along with food, drinks, and other amenities. Some lounges require a dedicated pass app for entry. Scammers exploit that requirement by building counterfeit versions that steal from the people who download them. A genuine need for an app makes a fake one look routine. Travelers $TRV who expect to download something at the lounge door have little reason to doubt whatever link turns up.

A fraudulent Android app called "Lounge Pass" turned the scheme against air travelers at Indian airports, according to CloudSEK's Threat Research Team. Deceptive websites such as loungepass.in distributed the app, which posed as a legitimate lounge access tool while carrying malware. After a traveler installed it, the app intercepted incoming text messages in secret and forwarded them to servers under the fraudsters' control.

The operators left a Firebase endpoint exposed, and CloudSEK researchers used that opening to read the messages the app had siphoned off. Domain analysis and passive DNS data led the team to related sites spreading similar malicious APK files, including loungepass.info and loungepass.online. Each of the addresses shares the loungepass name with loungepass.in and differs in its ending alone. A traveler searching for the app by name could land on any of them.

CloudSEK urged travelers to obtain lounge access apps from trusted app stores alone, ignore unfamiliar QR codes posted around airports, and refuse SMS permission requests from lounge or travel apps. Two of those steps answer the routes the fake Lounge Pass app used: the copycat sites that pushed it and the SMS traffic it harvested. The QR code warning carries the same caution into the terminal itself. A traveler who declined the SMS request would have denied the Lounge Pass app the messages its makers set out to collect.

A stranger who asks a traveler to carry a bag through the airport, even for pay, presents a luggage scam worth refusing. The bag could hold prohibited items. Anyone who agrees ends up hauling whatever someone else packed, and a cash offer reveals nothing about the contents. Whoever accepts the bag carries those contents through screening alongside their own gear.

Bag wrapping promises more protection than it delivers. Security checks can strip the wrap off and leave the suitcase as exposed as it was before. A reusable cover can stand in for the plastic, and waterproof bags can shield the belongings inside. Unlike wrap, a reusable cover can return for the next trip.

A case without external pockets gives thieves fewer openings to work with. TSA-approved locks shut the main compartment to outside hands. Each of these precautions narrows how many people can reach what sits inside, from the person offering cash for a carrying favor to the thief probing an outer pocket.

Taxi drivers who overcharge, steal luggage, or skim payment cards can lie in wait at the end of a long flight, and car rental companies may tack on fees nobody expected. Each of those tricks hits a different target: the traveler's cash, bags, and card details. Fatigue hands these operators an advantage. Travelers $TRV stepping off the plane want to reach their destination, and the urge to get moving leaves them exposed to transportation scams. The guidance urges staying alert at this stage, however drained a passenger feels.

Impostors go after pre-booked rides. A fake driver can stand in the arrivals area holding a placard with a customer's name, posing as the person the customer hired. A name on a sign proves nothing about who holds it. The sounder test compares the driver and the vehicle against the information supplied at booking. A mismatch on either count is reason enough to walk away.

Rental cars carry a separate risk: charges for damage the renter never caused. A close inspection of the car before leaving the lot, backed by photos, builds a record of its condition at the start. The renter should tell the agency about any existing damage before driving off, which shuts out a later charge for harm someone else did.

Illegal taxis have drawn government scrutiny at Perth Airport in Australia. ABC News reports that Western Australia's transport minister, Rita Saffioti, said authorities would step up compliance checks on unlawful operators there and at the Crown Casino complex. Investigators compared fares in digital card records with distance traveled, and a court fined one driver after that work. Saffioti said other investigations were continuing and that officials were examining vehicle roadworthiness and whether drivers and companies held authorization. Perth's case shows that a card payment leaves a trail of fares and distances investigators can use to expose inflated pricing.

Scammers can pass as official airport or airline staff with nothing more than a fake uniform and a counterfeit badge.

The short list of props lowers the barrier for anyone attempting the trick. Impostors copy the clothing and credentials travelers associate with employees, and those visual signals do the persuading on their behalf.

A uniform or badge on its own cannot prove that the wearer works for the airport or the airline.

Currency exchange kiosks expose travelers to three distinct tricks: unfavorable rates, shortchanging, and counterfeit bills that vendors swap for genuine money. AAA Club Alliance calls scams at these counters common. A poor rate trims the value of every unit of cash a traveler trades, and the loss hides inside the posted price. Shortchanging strikes at the handoff, as a vendor counts out less money than the deal promised.

Counterfeit notes do the most damage of the three. The traveler surrenders real currency and walks away with paper worth nothing. A short count or a stingy rate leaves some value behind. A fake bill leaves none.

Kiosks in airports and train stations tend to offer the poorest rates, according to experts cited by CBC News. Most airport exchange houses tack on a charge for convenience, a markup that can lift service fees, according to Visit Florida. A traveler at the terminal counter can face a weak rate and a steeper fee in a single transaction.

ABC News reports a caution from Australia's competition regulator. A provider advertising the lowest rate may turn out costlier once its charges enter the tally. The headline number leaves part of the cost out of view. What matters is how much foreign cash lands in the traveler's hand after every fee.

Tourist districts beyond the terminal promise no bargain either. Visit Florida warns that some exchange houses in those areas can prove expensive. It advises researching rates in advance and keeping a currency converter app close at hand. The site also points international visitors with time to spare toward a home bank or another financial institution for the swap, citing a clearer process. A bank deserves the same scrutiny. CBC News reports that bank rates can beat those of other providers or trail them. A traveler who arrives knowing the going rate can spot a lopsided offer at the counter and walk away.

Distraction scams depend on teamwork. One person stages a diversion, such as dropping an item or stirring up a commotion, and an accomplice lifts belongings in the moments that follow. The guide places the tactic among the classic airport scams.

The trick requires no technology, no fake app, and no counterfeit badge. Its tools amount to a partner and a staged spectacle. A dropped item or a raised voice pulls a traveler's eyes away from a bag, and the accomplice moves before those eyes return. The low barrier helps explain why the guide treats the scheme as a classic. Any pair of thieves can run it in a crowded corner of a terminal.

Screening order offers a defense at the checkpoint, where travelers part with their bags. Travelers $TRV can send bags and bins into the screener first and walk through the metal detector or scanner afterward, even if the detector or scanner frees up sooner. Keeping bags in sight adds a second safeguard. A traveler who looks watchful tends to discourage most would-be thieves.

Checkpoint theft often follows a simple lapse. A traveler walks off toward the gate and leaves a laptop or another item behind.

Both threats exploit the same opening, the stretch when a bag sits beyond its owner's view. A staged commotion near the screening belt would land at the moment travelers hold the least control over their belongings.

#5537. 15 Grand Theft Auto games, expansions, and ports ranked ahead of GTA 6

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A countdown of 15 Grand Theft Auto games, expansions, and handheld ports, from worst to best, as fans wait on GTA 6.

Every long gap between major game releases sends players back to their shelves, digging through older titles to find out which ones hold up. Few franchises put that habit to a harder test than Grand Theft Auto, a crime series with a reputation as one of the most praised, and most disputed, in video game history. Its catalog stretches past the numbered games. Expansion packs, spin-offs, and versions built for portable machines all carry the name, and each one arrived with its own ambitions and its own compromises. Sorting through that history helps players deciding where to spend a free weekend. The same exercise rewards anyone curious about how one series changed shape across so many machines and so many years.

The wait for the sequel sharpens the question. As of mid-2021, GTA 6 looked distant, with rumors pointing to a 2025 launch that no one had confirmed. Speculation swirled around where the game would unfold, which characters would take the wheel, and what features it might introduce. None of that chatter gave fans anything to play. A rumored date four years out leaves a lengthy stretch to fill, and the earlier installments offer the only Grand Theft Auto experiences available in the meantime. Picking among those installments takes more thought than a quick glance suggests. The lineup spans top-down originals, 3D sandboxes, downloadable episodes, and handheld adaptations, and each format asks something different of the person holding the controller.

TechRadar took on that choice with a countdown of 15 entries its editors regard as keystones of Grand Theft Auto, ordered from worst at 15th to best at first. Gerald Lynch wrote the piece, which ran on July 17, 2021. The list mixes core games with add-ons and ports, and the editors acknowledge that not every port made the cut. No scores, ratings, or numeric metrics determine the order. Editorial judgment sets each placement, and this article covers all 15 in that sequence, beginning at the bottom and climbing toward the editors' favorite.

The Game Boy and Game Boy Color versions of Grand Theft Auto and GTA 2 close out the countdown as ambitious, flawed ports that pushed the series onto aging handhelds. TechRadar's editors argue that coaxing even the top-down entries onto those machines took guts. Their verdict credits the attempt before it weighs the result.

Engineering earns these conversions their praise, and the feel in the hand explains their low standing. The editors call the pair impressive technical efforts yet judge them neither the smoothest nor the most enjoyable way to play Grand Theft Auto. Anyone curious about the series' history can admire what the developers pulled off on such limited hardware. Players hunting for a comfortable way to revisit these early games will find better routes elsewhere in the lineup.

The editors treat the top-down perspective as the easier case, and they still describe fitting it onto Nintendo's older screens as an act of nerve. Their wording implies that anything more demanding sat beyond what these machines could handle.

Tarantula Studios built the Game Boy Color edition of Grand Theft Auto. Rockstar Games published it.

The distance between the editors' praise and the slot they assigned suggests they valued these cartridges as proof that the top-down design could travel, more than as games worth returning to.

Shortfall: Slide 1 (Grand Theft Auto / GTA 2 on Game Boy / Game Boy Color) runs about 205 words, under the 300-word minimum. The source offers only four points on these ports (ambitious but flawed, took guts on aging handhelds, impressive technical efforts, not the smoothest or most enjoyable way to play), and the approved web details add only the developer and publisher. Details about toned-down violence, language, and scale appear in neither the source notes nor the approved web details, so they stay out. No further genuine facts exist to expand the slide without padding.

GTA Advance packs a large Grand Theft Auto sandbox onto a tiny Game Boy Advance cartridge, a feat the editors praise even though the title sits 14th of the 15 spots. A slot this low signals no failure. The editors insist GTA Advance is by no means a bad game, and they reserve their admiration for how much world the developers fit into so small a format. Their verdict separates a humble placement from a weak one, and the distinction matters for anyone weighing which handheld chapter deserves a few hours.

Speed and surprise drive the experience on the portable screen. The editors credit GTA Advance with holding on to the quick, unpredictable fun that defined the series' earliest entries. The loose, anarchic spirit of those original outings survives the move to a weaker machine. GTA Advance keeps its violence intact as well, pulling no punches on the Game Boy Advance, according to Old School Gamer Magazine.

A modest story, in the editors' view, lifts GTA Advance beyond a proof of concept by giving its pocket-sized chaos a purpose. The plot unfolds in Liberty City and follows Mike, a thug looking into the killing of Vinnie, his partner in crime. Mike's search for answers gives each burst of mayhem somewhere to go. A hook this slight marks the boundary between a finished product and a technical showcase.

Hardware limits leave the controls short on precision, a cost of shrinking the formula onto the Game Boy Advance. Even so, the editors set GTA Advance above the Game Boy and Game Boy Color ports of the first two games. Rough handling did not sink a release the editors prize for its capacity and its energy. The game's lasting value lies in showing how much of Grand Theft Auto survived the squeeze onto so cramped a device.

GTA: Liberty City Stories holds 13th place as a PSP prequel that reworks GTA 3, and its standing rests on the handheld that hosted it.

The editors call the game a reheat, a label that concedes how much of it returns to ground GTA 3 had already covered. Most players, they note, recall it as a dazzling showcase for Sony $SONY's portable. Steering a Rockstar open world across that small screen in the years before smartphones struck the team as something close to magic.

Late 2005 marks the window when the game counted most. Anyone holding a PSP then, in the editors' view, would have played it. A prequel built on an older console game still reached that whole audience. The pull came from carrying a Rockstar city in a pocket, and new content mattered less to those early owners.

The placement lifts it above the Game Boy, Game Boy Color, and Game Boy Advance efforts at the foot of the list. It still trails GTA: Vice City Stories, a second prequel that also reached the PSP. The gap between the two points to what this one lacked. Vice City Stories earned a higher slot with its empire-building system, while Liberty City Stories leaned on the hardware. Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars, shaped around the two screens of the Nintendo DS, sits six places higher at seventh. A handheld entry can climb far up the order when its design grows out of the machine it runs on. Liberty City Stories borrowed its design from a console game, so its spot preserves a moment in portable hardware more than a lasting piece of game design.

This slide runs about 250 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives GTA: Liberty City Stories only three facts (a PSP prequel that reheats GTA 3, a dazzling showcase for the PSP that felt like magic before smartphones, and near-universal play among PSP owners in late 2005), and no approved web details cover the game. Expanding further would require padding.

GTA: Vice City Stories earned 12th place on TechRadar's list through one feature, an empire-building system its editors call innovative and credit with giving the prequel a stamp of its own. The game arrived on both the PSP and the PS2. Its hero, Victor "Vic" Vance, comes from the cast of Vice City. In this outing, he tries to assemble a criminal organization alongside his brother, Lance.

The editors stop short of putting the game on equal footing with Vice City. They call it a fun prequel that falls a step below the original Vice City. GTA: Liberty City Stories, the list's other PSP prequel, occupies the next rung down, and the comparison between the two clarifies the verdict. The editors treat the Liberty City entry as a reheat of GTA 3 and a showcase for Sony $SONY's handheld. Vice City Stories earns its edge with a mechanic the editors consider its own. Its management layer carries the case for the higher spot.

GameSpot reports that every gang in the game controls several businesses across Vice City. Those properties can host rackets such as prostitution, loan sharking, smuggling, and drug dealing. A player seizes one by goading the gang members inside into a brawl, then buys the property and installs any illegal operation they choose. Each business generates cash every day and doubles as a save point, according to GameSpot. Owners can upgrade a location over time, either by pouring more money into it or by completing missions that raise its reputation.

Daily earnings from seized rackets supply the cash that upgrades demand, so each takeover helps fund improvements across the rest of the network. Every new property also adds a place to save progress, which gives a growing operation more footholds around the city. The Vance brothers' syndicate expands one seizure at a time, at a pace the player controls.

DMA Design rode the late-1990s Austin Powers craze by moving the top-down Grand Theft Auto formula to 1960s London. Its expansion pack dressed the series' crime sandbox in cockney accents and Minis. Under the new costume, the play itself matched the familiar overhead entries. The studio borrowed its backdrop from a passing fad, and the choice showed the series could soak up outside trends.

Local touches gave London 1969 its personality. The editors single out a "tank" players could steal, which turns out to be a taxi with a cannon strapped to it. The joke trades military hardware for a London cab. Homegrown radio stations round out the details the list's authors remember, so each commandeered car came with a soundtrack rooted in the city. Both touches live in objects and sounds a player meets in passing. The setting registers on every drive, even with the rules unchanged.

GTA: London 1961 followed as a PC-only prequel that stacked a second add-on on top of the first. The follow-up introduced drive-by shootings and nitro speed boosts, giving players a new way to attack from behind the wheel and a new burst of acceleration. London 1969 reworked the game's look and sound, and the prequel delivered the only mechanical changes the editors report for the London games. Its release on PC alone confined those upgrades to computer players.

At 11th, the London pair outranks every Game Boy and PSP release on the list. The two London games changed little beyond their scenery and two new driving moves, yet the editors placed them above standalone handheld efforts such as GTA Advance and GTA: Liberty City Stories. The editors credit both of those games with bringing a Grand Theft Auto open world to small hardware. The ordering suggests the list's authors prized a sharp sense of place over a technical feat on a tiny device.

GTA 2 landed in 1999 with a near-future setting, cyberpunk leanings, and a garage of science-fiction vehicles, and the editors suggest the mix may make it the strangest Grand Theft Auto of all. They describe the game as an odd swerve for a franchise in its infancy. The action plays out in Anywhere City, a dystopian metropolis dressed in retro-futuristic style.

Players could pick up GTA 2 on platforms ranging from the PC to the Dreamcast. It marked the final stop before Grand Theft Auto reinvented itself as an open world in full 3D. Its top-down camera, carried over from the 1997 original, belongs to that opening era. Any mechanic it tested had to survive the jump into three dimensions to last.

Car customization debuted in GTA 2, alongside city residents who react more to the player's behavior. Both features cleared that hurdle, and the editors count them among the traits subsequent releases held onto. Customizing cars resurfaces among the side activities in San Andreas, which shows how far the early experiment traveled.

A gang affiliation system decided which missions the player could take on. Helping a criminal faction opened its work, and hurting one sealed those jobs off. The design tied loyalty to opportunity. Missions became a resource earned through alliances. Every choice about whom to aid and whom to attack reshaped the campaign's path.

Each of GTA 2's three additions handed players more say over their surroundings: the look of a car, the reaction of a crowd, and the menu of available jobs. GTA 2 followed the first Grand Theft Auto by two years yet sits two places behind it in the editors' order. The verdict favors the founder over the inventor. Later entries kept the machinery GTA 2 introduced and returned to Liberty City, Vice City, and San Andreas, leaving Anywhere City behind.

GTA 4: The Lost and Damned grew out of a deal Rockstar struck with Microsoft $MSFT around the Xbox 360's launch, an agreement covering two premium downloadable episodes. The biker-themed chapter became one half of that arrangement, and The Ballad of Gay Tony filled the other. Each episode carried a price tag. The model let Rockstar sell new stories set inside a game its audience owned, stretching one map across more than one campaign.

CNBC reports that Take Two pointedly withheld sales figures for a downloadable add-on for the Xbox 360. The silence fed speculation that the results had disappointed.

A biker gang supplies the new lens. The expansion returns to the intricate Liberty City of GTA 4 and follows a different protagonist through its streets. The geography stays fixed while the perspective shifts. The base game's story belonged to another character, and the biker theme now frames the roads that figure once crossed. The setting comes from the game the editors placed first in their countdown, so the episode opens on the map they admire most. A city of this much detail can carry a second narrative, and a new lead character gives players a reason to cross it again.

The editors call the campaign short but thrilling, and its missions steer players toward locations that got less attention in GTA 4's central story. Familiar territory gains a sense of discovery as a result, with corners that sat at the edges of the earlier plot moving to the center. The brevity suits that goal. A compact campaign can spend its hours on overlooked spots and leave the well-worn districts alone. A brief outing on a borrowed city finished ninth, one spot behind the 1997 original that founded the series and first put Liberty City on the map. The verdict suggests Liberty City held enough untapped ground to support a separate tale inside the same borders.

Grand Theft Auto, the 1997 original, introduced Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City, the three settings the franchise would return to again and again. Players worked for gangsters in each city, taking on objectives from the local underworld. The structure gave the series a durable premise. A city served as the stage, and criminal bosses supplied the reasons to tear across it.

Four later entries on this list borrow those place names for their titles: GTA: Liberty City Stories, GTA: Vice City Stories, GTA: San Andreas, and GTA: Vice City. GTA 4 and its two downloadable episodes, The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, head back to Liberty City as well. The handhelds return there too. GTA Advance drops its hero into Liberty City, and Chinatown Wars stages its gang battles on the same streets. Counted together, at least nine of the 15 entries here unfold in a city the first game named. More than half the countdown runs on a 1997 atlas. Three of the editors' top four picks, GTA 4, GTA: Vice City, and GTA: San Andreas, take place in those same cities. The places the original named ended up hosting the series' best-regarded work.

The game's graphics lagged behind other 1997 releases. Its overhead camera rendered the streets in flat 2D, a crude look by the standards of its own year. The editors single out attitude as the quality that lifted the game past competitors. Gangster jobs gave that swagger a home. With visuals unable to impress, the tone had to carry the original.

The original's eighth-place finish leaves it two spots above GTA 2, its 1999 sequel, and seven above the Game Boy and Game Boy Color ports of both games, which sit at 15th. The handheld versions share the bird's-eye design yet land last. The gap suggests the formula alone cannot explain the 1997 game's standing. In the editors' order, the original earns its place through what it founded, with three cities and a defiant tone outweighing its rough presentation.

Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars earns its spot through a design shaped around the two screens of the original Nintendo DS, and the editors argue it belongs among the finest games that handheld hosted. Its overhead camera fit the hardware's stacked layout. Rockstar repeated an earlier portable feat by packing a massive sandbox onto a tiny cartridge. No other entry on the list ran on the DS.

The top-down angle reaches back to the franchise's roots. Reviewers at Good Game noted that the view recalls the first Grand Theft Auto games. The 1997 original presented its streets in flat 2D from above, a look that appeared primitive beside other releases of that year. Chinatown Wars took the same vantage point and gave it a second display to work with.

The touchscreen handles the map and lets players plot the arc of a thrown grenade. The same critics praised the stylus for hijacking cars, defusing bombs, and smashing windshields. Each of those inputs puts the DS's signature feature at the center of the action.

Connected play exposes where the game falls short. Good Game found multiplayer restricted to local sessions. Online features extend no further than sending messages and trading spots and gear with friends. The outlet judged the police presence excessive. Players can shake officers by ramming their vehicles or switching cars out of sight. Head-to-head matches required a friend close by.

A seventh-place finish puts Chinatown Wars above every release made for the Game Boy, Game Boy Advance, or PSP, and one spot ahead of the 1997 original whose overhead view it shares. GTA Advance managed a similar cartridge squeeze yet finished seven places lower, a gap the dual-screen design helps explain. The ordering suggests the editors reward handheld games tailored to their machine's strengths over adaptations that shrink a console formula.

GTA 4: The Ballad of Gay Tony answered a grievance players kept voicing about GTA 4, a game many of them found too grounded and short on silliness. San Andreas had set expectations for absurdity with fighter jets, alien Easter eggs, and a burger habit that slowed its hero's running speed. Food could alter how its hero moved, a measure of how far that game indulged its taste for the ridiculous. Against those indulgences, the sober Liberty City of GTA 4 left fans hungry for mischief.

The add-on kept GTA 4's world intact and changed what happens inside it. Its plot follows the hapless nightclub owner who gives the episode its name, and the stakes stay low from start to finish. The editors say the level design shook off restraint too, so the missions carry a playfulness the main campaign withheld. A smaller story suited the experiment. Freed from heavy drama, the expansion could chase gags and chaos through streets familiar to GTA 4 players.

The editors slotted The Ballad of Gay Tony sixth, ahead of The Lost and Damned, the other downloadable chapter set in GTA 4's Liberty City. Both episodes share a map and a parent game, so the distance between them hints that tone carried real weight in the editors' judgment. The looser chapter finishes ahead of the original Grand Theft Auto and Chinatown Wars, a strong showing for an add-on built on another game's foundation. GTA 4 itself claims first place on the same list, so the editors appear to value both the restraint players resisted and the release valve this expansion supplied.

The editors credit the episode with clearing the way for GTA 5 to return to daft, large-scale antics. The Ballad of Gay Tony bridges the excess of San Andreas and the sprawl of GTA 5, evidence that the series recovered its humor inside a familiar city before carrying it to a bigger stage.

GTA 3 bears much of the credit, in TechRadar's view, for selling millions of PlayStation 2 consoles early in the system's lifecycle. The game stood as a technical achievement for its era. A 3D crime world running on a home console gave buyers a concrete reason to pick up Sony $SONY's machine, and the console's early momentum owed a large debt to it.

The leap into three dimensions masked a structure that looked backward. GTA 3 marked the series' first 3D entry, yet the list's authors argue it shares more with its PS1 predecessors than with Vice City or San Andreas. Its protagonist, Claude Speed, never speaks. Claude Speed's silence leaves players to supply the motive for every rampage. The plot serves as an excuse to blow things up and offers little meaningful commentary. Both of those successors moved further from the old roots, and both finish above GTA 3 on the list, at third and fourth. The comparison leaves GTA 3 as a bridge between eras, with new technology wrapped around old instincts.

GTA 3's chaotic sandbox set the bar that later open-world titles had to clear. The ranking's compilers trace a direct line from its anything-goes mayhem to sillier games such as the Saints Row series. A whole strand of goofy games grew from the seed GTA 3 planted. The game's carefree destruction, more than its story, became its chief export to the rest of the genre.

GTA 3 has not held up against today's standards, TechRadar's team concedes, yet its pull on free-roaming design persists. The gap between those two verdicts explains its fifth-place finish. Its spot puts it ahead of The Ballad of Gay Tony, a GTA 4 expansion, and Chinatown Wars. Its placement suggests TechRadar gives historical impact enough weight to lift a game whose moment-to-moment play has dated.

GTA: San Andreas squeezed an enormous map onto limited hardware, linking three major areas with desert locales in what the editors call the biggest technical leap of its era. The scale of that world set the frame for everything else the game attempted. Desert terrain between those hubs stretched the play space past the bounds of any single city.

Carl Johnson, or CJ, gives the sprawl a human center. He comes back to San Andreas after an extended stay in Liberty City and finds his old neighborhood torn by turmoil and gang violence. His return ties a vast setting to the trouble on one familiar block. The plot keeps its focus tight while the scope widens, centering on a homecoming to the streets CJ once knew as his own.

Side pursuits put CJ himself in the player's hands. Players can customize cars, buy him clothes, form relationships with non-player characters, and train at the gym to build up his stamina and strength. The options let each player shape the hero across the game, from his wardrobe to his physical stats. Downtime between missions can leave a lasting mark on the character. Each of those activities touches a different part of CJ's life: his garage, his closet, his social circle, and his body.

San Andreas became the best-selling game on the PS2, and the editors credit it with fitting a great deal of content onto a constrained console. Topping PS2 sales while packing in so many systems indicates buyers rewarded how much the game let them do. Even so, the editors set three other entries above the console's top seller, so commercial dominance did not decide the order by itself. Breadth carried San Andreas to fourth place, and the distance left to first suggests the editors valued qualities that sheer size could not deliver.

GTA: Vice City carries what the editors consider perhaps the most memorable aesthetic in the series, with Hawaiian shirts, hot pink convertibles, and sun-soaked bust-ups set in a Miami-like version of the '80s. Their praise centers on the game's look and sound, and those qualities lift it above every entry except GTA 5 and GTA 4.

A classic soundtrack completes the period picture. Music, clothing, and cars form one portrait of a decade, and the editors treat the era as the game's signature. Their write-up names no mission, character, or side activity as a reason for the placement. The visuals and the music carry the whole argument.

San Andreas, one spot below, made its case with an enormous map and a long list of diversions on limited hardware. GTA 4, the editors' top pick, wins on story and city design. Vice City outranks San Andreas on mood, and the order reveals the weight the editors give a world that captures a specific time and place. Size and systems lose to period detail in their judgment.

Fans have met rumors of a GTA 6 return to Vice City with excitement. The '80s city whose style raised this entry to third place sits at the center of speculation about the next main game. The excitement suggests the setting's pull extends past a single game.

Shortfall: this slide runs about 222 words, under the 300-word minimum. The source gives GTA: Vice City only its aesthetic (classic soundtrack, Hawaiian shirts, hot pink convertibles, sun-soaked bust-ups, an '80s Miami-like setting) and the GTA 6 return rumor. No approved web details cover this game. The remaining related facts (Vice City Stories and Vic Vance, the 1997 original introducing Vice City, GTA 3's closeness to PS1 roots) already appear in other slides, so the draft's Vice City Stories paragraph and its unsupported claim about the creators' judgment were cut.

GTA 5 still commanded a huge audience nearly eight years after its release, and GTA Online held its own crowd across the same span. The editors grouped both under one slot, so the multiplayer mode shares credit with the base game for the entry's staying power. Neither half carries the placement alone.

GTA 5 also carries the largest number of any game in the countdown, and its endurance reflects a long stretch with no newer main installment on shelves. Players who stuck with it across those years had no numbered successor to move on to. Its audience held without competition from a fresher Grand Theft Auto.

Only GTA 4 kept the pair from first place, and the editors describe the margin as narrow. A huge following did not settle the contest. The older game claimed the top spot, a sign the editors weighed qualities beyond how many people kept playing.

GTA 4 also holds a wider footprint across the list. Its two downloadable episodes earned places of their own at ninth and sixth, giving GTA 4's world three entries in total. GTA 5 fills a single position and splits even that one with its online mode. The finalists differ in how they spread across the countdown as well as in where they finished.

With GTA 4 and GTA 5 holding the top two spots, the series' two most advanced numbered games took both of the editors' strongest verdicts.

Niko, an Eastern European war veteran trying to shake off his past, drives the 2008 game that TechRadar's editors picked as the best Grand Theft Auto. His struggle to move on gives the series what the editors suggest may be one of its most human stories.

The narrative reaches deeper than any earlier installment, in Lynch's view, and it presses players to weigh whether the jobs they carried out as Niko served any greater good. A crime game that asks its audience to second-guess their own choices turns each mission into a moral test as well as a task. Eleven years after the 1997 original sent its hero on errands for gangsters, the franchise had arrived at a lead character weighed down by memory and doubt.

Liberty City spreads across three islands. The team credits this version of the city with setting a new standard for open-world design, describing a place that felt alive and never grew stale to explore. A map that stayed fresh across an entire campaign gave Niko's personal journey a convincing stage.

Lynch calls GTA 4 one of the darkest entries in the lineup and one of the best built. The game probes the grimy workings of organized crime and refuses to look away from what it finds. He offers no hedging on where he stands, writing plainly that the team loves it.

Darkness won the countdown's top spot. TechRadar's staff put one of Grand Theft Auto's grimmest games above GTA 5, the sunny Vice City, and San Andreas, which became the best-selling PlayStation 2 game. Their choice favors gravity and urban detail over spectacle and sales.

Both downloadable episodes for GTA 4 later returned to this Liberty City with new protagonists of their own. One three-island map went on to host three separate campaigns, evidence of how much its streets could hold.

#5536. PagerDuty debuts Paige AI agent with renamed PD Reliability Platform and PD Labs

Operations management software company PagerDuty Inc. today introduced Paige, an artificial intelligence agent for site reliability engineering that is built to work as a member of operations and engineering teams.

Paige runs on the company’s flagship product, which as of today is called the PD Reliability Platform. Alongside both, PagerDuty opened PD Labs to put early features in front of customers while they are still being built.

The launch is aimed at a problem PagerDuty says is getting worse as AI coding tools write more production software, much of it shipped with little human review. Applications built on AI models also break in their own ways. Chief Executive John DiLullo pointed to model drift, token runaway and leaked personal data as examples. The only way to stay resilient, he said, is “to fight fire with fire, using AI itself as part of how we keep systems running.”

Customers set Paige’s permissions team by team. A team that keeps a person in the loop gets faster triage with remediation held for approval, and the agent acts on its own only in well-understood, low-risk scenarios the team has explicitly authorized. In March, PagerDuty said its SRE Agent would start joining escalation policies as a “virtual responder.” Paige, billed as the company’s next-generation SRE agent, can now be put on call that way. A lower-priority incident may never reach a human at all.

Paige’s recommendations arrive with evidence and a confidence level attached. By the time a responder reads one, many possible causes have been ruled out already. PagerDuty argues the bigger payoff comes later, once a resolved incident has been written into a shared memory that Paige consults whenever something similar fails. In a benchmark report released with the launch, the company says Paige did better than leading AI coding agents at diagnosing simulated information technology incidents.

The renamed platform, known until today as PagerDuty Operations Cloud, is where Paige gets its operational context. Incident commanders and team managers also get a new PD Reliability Platform Console, which puts incidents, on-call rotations and AI agents in one view. The console shows which agents are switched on and what each one is doing. Paige’s suggested fixes can be acted on from the same screen.

Responders can run an incident end to end in Slack or Microsoft Teams. A trigger opens a dedicated channel and a conference bridge without anyone having to set them up.

Steve Miller, director of business development at Slack, said having Paige and the platform inside Slack gives responders speed and visibility, which he called critical as “agentic and human teams operate side-by-side in the same channel.” Nobody has to write the post-incident review, which is generated as soon as the incident is resolved, and its follow-up actions come with owners and due dates already assigned.

Canadian telecommunications company Telus Corp. has wired the platform into its own centralized internal incident tool. Kulvir Gahunia, director of the Site Reliability Office at Telus, said PagerDuty’s Scribe Agent now runs through every incident, so responders “don’t have to stop and document what is happening.”

The earlier-stage work runs through PD Labs, which PagerDuty is building in the open with design partners who get early access and a direct line to the engineers writing the code.

Three experiments are in preview to start. Topology keeps a live map of an organization’s services, assembled from its code, infrastructure and runbooks. No configuration management database is needed, and the map scopes the blast radius of a problem automatically as conditions change.

Deep Investigation has Paige test several root-cause hypotheses at once while showing its reasoning on each as new evidence comes in. SRE Workbench gives people and agents one workspace to tackle a problem side by side, and whatever they find is saved to the same memory Paige learns from.

IT teams want measurable results from their spending on AI agents, according to Snow Tempest, research manager for IT service management at International Data Corp. Better uptime counts, as does time handed back to responders who would otherwise be “chasing logs and assembling the right people for an incident.” More organizations also want to prevent incidents, Tempest said.

Paige and the PD Reliability Platform are generally available today, and SRE Workbench is open to try through PD Labs. The platform is sold for a fee tied to operational scale that comes with a starting allotment of ingested events, automation actions and user seats. Customers who outgrow it can buy flexible credits without having to forecast usage ahead of time.

#5534. Google is cutting off Search for schools that restrict AI

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Google said AI is built into Search and cannot be switched off, leaving schools that want no AI without Search access

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Google $GOOGL is telling school districts that want no AI on school devices that they must give up Google Search, according to Chalkbeat.

Google on Tuesday announced changes to its school products, including Guided Learning features in Search and Google Classroom and a new approach to school controls. The company said access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators turn them on. Google said it will share specifics with schools in the coming months, ahead of the rollout.

"If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have Search on at all," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said, according to Chalkbeat. Phillips described AI as so thoroughly woven into Search that it can't be switched off.

Phillips also told The New York Times that students at schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Google said the Guided Learning feature in Search is meant for student accounts and walks students through homework problems step by step instead of giving the answer directly. The company will start with a pilot in select U.S. schools later this month, then expand to other districts in the coming months. Guided Learning also became available globally in Google Classroom on Tuesday, where teachers can assign activities and see real-time insights on where a class needs support.

Guided Learning will take the place of AI Overviews for students who search while signed in to school accounts, according to Chalkbeat. Chalkbeat also reported that Google intends to pilot the changes in a handful of U.S. schools this month, with a wider rollout set for early next year.

Eisha Bush, head of teaching and learning at the advocacy group Common Sense Media, said it is “slim to none” that schools and students will steer clear of Google Search, according to Chalkbeat. Google has also never let schools disable AI Overviews, and getting rid of AI Mode has meant working around it with tricky technical fixes. Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute has labeled both AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search an “unacceptable risk” to students, according to Chalkbeat.

The changes arrive as parents press for greater control over school technology and as big districts, including New York and Los Angeles, impose heavy limits on how students can use AI, according to Chalkbeat.

#5533. How the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem Could Accelerate Scientific Discovery

CU Anschutz researchers play a major role in evaluating research data from 18 programs to help scientists uncover relationships across studies and make better use of existing research.

AURORA, Colo., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Scientists generate vast amounts of research data, but connecting information across studies can be difficult. The NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem is working to change that by making research datasets from 18 NIH programs easier to find, connect and analyze.

The initiative brings together research resources spanning human genetics, the microbiome and emerging technologies, helping scientists explore relationships that might otherwise remain hidden across separate studies.

A new paper published in Patterns describes the ecosystem's development, infrastructure and tools, as well as efforts to evaluate its impact.

"The challenge is no longer just generating more scientific data. It's making the data we already have work together in ways that help researchers answer questions they couldn't tackle before," said Casey Greene, PhD, professor of biomedical informatics at CU Anschutz and study senior author. "When information is connected across research programs, scientists have more opportunities to identify patterns, explore new relationships and build on discoveries made by others."

The goal is to make complex datasets easier to find, interpret and analyze, including for researchers without advanced programming or bioinformatics expertise.

How Can Connecting Research Data Help Scientists Make New Discoveries?

Understanding a disease or identifying a promising drug target may require scientists to connect genetic information with molecular measurements, tissue data and results from drug-screening experiments. A drug target is a molecule or biological process that researchers investigate as a potential point of action for a treatment.

When these resources can be explored together, researchers may be better equipped to understand biological mechanisms, identify meaningful patterns and investigate promising directions for further study.

"Scientific discovery rarely happens in isolation. A finding in one dataset may become much more meaningful when it can be examined alongside evidence from another study or another area of biology," said Julie A. Jurgens, PhD, associate director of scientific delivery for the Knowledge Portal Network at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard and study corresponding author. "Building the connections between these resources can help researchers spend less time navigating fragmented systems and more time asking important scientific questions."

By making existing research easier to access and combine, the ecosystem aims to help scientists build on findings from multiple programs rather than examining each dataset in isolation.

Researchers at CU Anschutz contribute to the initiative's coordination and evaluation efforts, helping assess how effectively the shared research infrastructure supports scientists and delivers value across research programs.

The work examines whether connecting datasets across programs helps researchers find and use information in ways that separate public repositories cannot.

The team is also evaluating indicators of research engagement and impact, including how often scientists use the ecosystem's online resources and cite related publications. Preliminary findings suggest that related research publications may receive more citations than comparable papers, although additional analysis is needed to understand the significance of those differences.

These evaluation efforts are intended to help determine how the ecosystem can remain useful, accessible and valuable to researchers over time.

How Could Connected Research Data Support Artificial Intelligence?

As artificial intelligence becomes more prominent in scientific research, well-organized and connected datasets could also help computational tools analyze scientific information more effectively.

The ecosystem offers an opportunity to explore how infrastructure designed to help people navigate scientific evidence might also support emerging AI-driven approaches to research.

"The long-term opportunity is to create a research environment where valuable data don't sit in separate repositories waiting for someone to make the right connection," said Sean Davis, MD, PhD, professor of bioinformatics at CU Anschutz. "By making those connections easier to discover and explore, we can help scientists get more value from existing research and create new opportunities for future discoveries."

By making existing evidence easier to find, interpret and combine, the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem aims to help researchers uncover meaningful connections, explore new scientific questions and make more effective use of the research investment already made.

The Common Fund Data Ecosystem and corresponding publication are the product of a multi-institutional, multidisciplinary collaboration across 5 centers, 18 programs, and multiple partnerships.

About the University of Colorado AnschutzThe University of Colorado Anschutz is a world-class academic medical campus leading transformative advances in science, medicine, education and patient care. The campus includes the University of Colorado's health professional schools, more than 60 centers and institutes, and two nationally ranked independent hospitals - UCHealth University of Colorado Hospital and Children's Hospital Colorado - which see nearly three million adult and pediatric patient visits each year. Innovative, interconnected and highly collaborative, CU Anschutz delivers life-changing treatments, exceptional patient care and top-tier professional training. The campus conducts world-renowned research supported by $890 million in funding, including $762 million in sponsored awards and $128 million in philanthropic gifts for research.

#5532. Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI

Athena Circle Corp., an artificial intelligence-native legal technology startup that’s automating the nitty gritty of commercial real estate deals, said today it has raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun. No other investors were named.

Legal AI technology is nothing new, but its adoption in the industry has been somewhat haphazard, for the technology has exposed an awkward problem: Most law firms are still billing their clients by the hour, and that makes automation less lucrative. If a law firm can use AI agents to get a 10-hour contract review done in just a couple of minutes, then it’s going to let an awful lot of billable revenue slip through its fingers, killing any incentive there might be to adopt them.

Athena’s co-founders Cem Ucan (pictured, left) and Kieran John Keenan (right) and founding engineer José Braz all cut their teeth at the pioneering legal AI tech startup Legora AB, where they quickly realized how AI conflicts with the industry’s standard business model. They came up with an entirely different business model to convince legal firms of the benefits of automation. Instead of selling software tools directly, it provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm, charging a fixed fee per transaction that’s typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates. In this way, it ensures that revenue is better aligned with efficiency.

“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but we took a different approach,” Ucan said. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”

The startup is focused on automating the intricacies of commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its AI agents are designed to automate the creation and review of purchase agreements and loan documents, and will handle all of the due diligence and administrative closing hurdles needed to get deals done, while ensuring human lawyers remain fully in the loop to make all of the final legal determinations.

In this way, Athena basically takes care of the grunt work, giving commercial real estate firms much more agility. That’s a real advantage, because commercial real estate is an industry where speed is of the essence: The faster a law firm gets things done, the more likely it is to actually secure the deal, which is the end result that everyone wants. With investors often submitting dozens of bids for each property listing, the ability to get the paperwork done in a matter of hours rather than weeks or days means buyers can lock in a deal before their rivals know what’s happened.

Keenan, who serves as the startup’s chief technology officer, explained that each new workflow begins with an incoming agreement that’s ingested by its AI agents. They cross-reference the terms of the deal against their standard deal sheets in order to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications.

This work is informed by historical transactions, which allow its agents to adapt to each client’s negotiating style, Keenan said. Human attorneys then review this work, make strategic judgment calls when required, and approve all deliverables before they’re sent to clients.

“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” Keenan explained. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect.”

Athena’s agents are already proving their worth, with the startup having signed up 22 legal firms as clients so far, just two months after launching its service. By learning continuously from attorney’s edits and client’s preferences, its agents have reduced review times by an average of 70%.

L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based multifamily real estate and property management firm Mox Living, said Athena was able to deliver a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has ever seen. “A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” he said. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and Athena gets us both.”

Keenan said Athena is primed to strike while the iron is hot. He said the industry is bracing itself for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 hit their refinancing deadlines, and he’s hoping that the startup can win a significant amount of that business. In any case, growth is on the horizon, for Athena also plans to expand into new markets and property classes and even new legal domains.

A16z Speedrun’s Troy Kirwin said AI automation is all well and good, but clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work that gets done. “Athena is building around that need with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team that’s obsessed with scaling fast,” he said.

#5531. 2026 holiday shipping deadlines for USPS, UPS and FedEx

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ground, two-day, and overnight cutoffs from USPS, UPS, and FedEx, plus the closures and tips that help holiday gifts arrive by Christmas.

A wrapped present sitting on the kitchen counter in December carries its own kind of pressure. Somewhere across the country, a parent, a grandchild, or an old friend expects that box to appear under the tree, and the person holding it has a shrinking stretch of days to get it there. Missing the window turns a thoughtful gift into an apology. The gift becomes a phone call explaining the delay, a card promising the real present later, or a photo of something the recipient cannot hold. Shoppers who order online and shoppers who browse in stores share the same final hurdle. Someone has to hand the package to a carrier in time, and the calendar decides whether all that effort pays off.

Every carrier keeps its own clock, and each service level within a carrier runs on a separate cutoff. A parcel on the slowest option needs the most lead time. Faster tiers push the last possible send date closer to the holiday, which gives procrastinators some breathing room but narrows the margin for anything to go wrong. The result is a patchwork of dates that shifts with the counter a sender visits and the option that sender picks on the shipping form. Anyone who assumes a single deadline applies everywhere can guess wrong and lose days without noticing. Each passing week in December removes another choice, until the quickest services stand alone and the question of speed turns into whether anything will arrive by the big day.

CBS Chicago laid out the final mailing dates for the U.S. Postal Service, UPS, and FedEx $FDX in a short consumer roundup for holiday mailers. The story covers ground, two-day, and overnight deadlines for delivery by Christmas, a note on carrier closures, a recommended date for anyone who wants a cushion, and advice on addresses and tracking. It passes along a seasonal package volume estimate from unnamed officials. The roundup lists no prices, international dates, or reasons behind any carrier's schedule. The list below sticks to the dates and tips the roundup reports.

Officials estimated that about 2.3 billion packages would ship during the 2025 holiday season, a 5% increase. Every gift held until the final days before that Christmas added one more box to a swelling stream.

The 5% rise pointed to a growing holiday period. Each parcel a late shopper dropped off joined a larger flow of mail, and every carrier handled more freight across the same December calendar.

Officials framed the volume as an expectation, a December 2025 forecast for that season's shipments. The final count could have landed above or below it.

CBS Chicago builds its roundup around urgency. The story opens by warning anyone mailing presents to head to the post office without delay. The cutoff dates, it notes, sit close at hand.

A heavier load of shipments lent the alert extra weight. More items moving through the system gave every sender a stronger reason to beat the crowd at the counter.

The U.S. Postal Service lists Dec. 17 as the last day to send a package by ground and have it land by Christmas. The date falls eight days before the holiday and marks the earlier of the two Postal Service deadlines CBS Chicago reports. Gift givers who pick ground shipping need their boxes packed, wrapped, and labeled by that day. Anyone hunting for a present in the middle of the month has little slack left.

Two-day delivery stretches the USPS window to Dec. 20. A sender who misses the ground date can rescue a Christmas arrival by switching to the faster tier and mailing the box on Dec. 18, 19, or 20. The switch turns a blown cutoff into a recoverable mistake, as long as the parcel reaches a post office counter before the second date passes. The later date sits five days before Christmas. No USPS service in the roundup extends into the holiday's final days.

Ground shipping carries its own appeal for people who plan ahead. USPS Ground Advantage costs less than Priority Mail and offers comparable delivery expectations and features. Ground Advantage handles domestic shipments only. A present headed to another country cannot travel that way. Ground Advantage pricing climbs or falls with a package's weight and the zone of its destination. The savings go to senders organized enough to mail by the earlier date.

The three-day gap between the USPS dates gives gift senders a choice between an early send and an upgrade. Anyone who aims for Dec. 17 keeps both Postal Service options in reserve. The ground date works as the target, and the two-day date works as the backstop. Missing the first narrows a sender's USPS choices to one. A shipper who lets Dec. 20 pass has exhausted every USPS speed the outlet names for Christmas arrival.

UPS and FedEx $FDX accept two-day shipments through Dec. 22, and both carriers run an overnight service on Dec. 23 that delivers on Christmas Eve.

The two private carriers keep matching calendars. CBS Chicago states the two-day cutoff and the overnight option a single time and applies both to the pair. A shopper comparing the companies meets the same dates at either counter. The schedule gives no grounds to favor one carrier over its rival. Whichever location sits closer to home or work can settle the choice without costing a sender any time.

The roundup lists no ground cutoff for UPS or FedEx, which leaves Dec. 22 as the earliest send-by day it gives for either company. A sender who wants a slower tier at either carrier has to find that deadline somewhere else. The story treats both carriers as a fast lane for the final days before the holiday.

Overnight service buys one more day past the two-day cutoff. A sender who misses Dec. 22 can hand off a gift the next day and watch it arrive on Christmas Eve. No deadline in the roundup falls later. The pair's two-day window stays open two days beyond the Postal Service's version, and the overnight handoff trails the final USPS deadline by three days. A sender who lets every USPS deadline pass still has a way out with UPS and FedEx.

Christmas Eve delivery leaves no margin. A box that shows up that day reaches its recipient with hours to spare before Christmas morning, and a one-day slip would push it past the holiday. Anyone choosing this route surrenders every spare day December once offered. Any hiccup between the drop-off and the doorstep has no backup day to absorb it. Waiting until Dec. 23 turns a holiday gift into a one-day bet with no second try at either carrier.

The U.S. Postal Service, UPS, and FedEx $FDX all shut down on Christmas Day. None of the three companies in the roundup will bring a gift to a doorstep on the holiday itself. A sender who pictures a Dec. 25 drop-off will find nothing open. The shutdown erases any chance of a last-minute rescue on the 25th. A shopper who remembers a forgotten relative on Christmas morning cannot hand a box to any of these carriers and expect it to arrive that day.

The holiday closure turns Christmas Eve into the hard stop on the gift calendar. Overnight shipping from UPS and FedEx produces the latest arrival the article describes for any of the three carriers. A box that misses its carrier's final send date has no holiday-morning delivery to fall back on. It reaches the recipient after Christmas, once operations resume.

CBS Chicago recommends mailing every gift by Dec. 15 for anyone who wants a buffer against a present showing up late. The outlet gives no rationale for choosing that day. The Dec. 15 mark falls two days before the USPS ground deadline, the earliest cutoff the roundup lists. It sits 10 days ahead of Christmas.

A single target spares shoppers the work of juggling separate dates for each carrier and each speed tier. A gift mailed by Dec. 15 clears every date in the article, whether it travels by ground, two-day, or overnight. The suggestion leaves USPS ground shippers the thinnest margin, two days, compared with eight for anyone relying on UPS or FedEx overnight.

The gap between those margins shows where the advice matters. A sender who plans on the slowest Postal Service option has little slack beyond the suggested date, while an overnight customer could wait more than a week and make it in time. Anyone unsure which service a gift will travel by gains the most from treating Dec. 15 as the true deadline.

A correct address on every package forms the final safeguard CBS Chicago urges on holiday senders, and the outlet warns that the season leaves no room for error. The advice covers each box in a shipment. A sender with a stack of gifts checks every label, one at a time.

Little slack remains in the holiday calendar to fix a mistake. The latest overnight service marks the closing chance to send anything before Christmas Eve. A box that goes astray late in the season leaves its sender with no listed service to try again before the carriers shut down for the holiday.

An email address supplies the second precaution. Entering one lets a sender receive tracking updates as a package heads toward its recipient. The updates give the sender a way to follow a gift between the counter and the doorstep. A shopper who skips the email line gives up that view of the trip.

Both steps rest with the sender. Neither depends on the carrier a shopper picks or the delivery speed a shopper pays for. A ground parcel mailed early and an overnight box sent at the last minute need the same accurate label and the same email for tracking. The carriers set the dates, and the sender controls the details on the form.
