#5529. When newly elected officials take office: 10 parts of the post-election calendar

Free daily briefing on global business news.

When do newly elected officials take office? This guide walks through 10 key dates and rules, from Election Day and the Electoral College to inaugurations and swearing-in ceremonies

Winning an election and holding power are two separate events in the U.S., and the gap between them is set by law. Election Day falls on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. For most federal winners, the actual start of the job arrives about two months later, in January.

That waiting period is not a formality. It contains a sequence of legal steps. Electors cast their ballots in their home states in December. Congress counts those electoral votes in a joint session in January. A federal transition process prepares an incoming administration to run the government. Each step has a fixed place on the calendar.

Anyone asking when newly elected officials take office will find that the answer depends on the office. Federal start dates are set by the Constitution. The president and vice president begin their terms at noon on January 20. Members of the House and Senate begin at noon on January 3, unless Congress sets another date by law. Both dates come from the 20th Amendment.

State and local offices follow a different logic. Each state sets its governor's start date in its own constitution or law. Many governors start in January, but not all of them. Cities set their own calendars as well, and some hold elections in the spring rather than November.

The calendar also has quirks and a history. When January 20 lands on a Sunday, the president takes the oath twice — once privately on the day itself and again in public the next day. A closing slide explains where the January start dates came from and what schedule they replaced.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of offices and the mechanics behind them. They are not a complete list of every elected position in the U.S. The slides explain the key federal dates, the Electoral College timeline, the presidential transition and a handful of specific state and local examples. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can go straight to the office or step they want to understand.

A newly elected U.S. president takes office at noon on January 20. The 20th Amendment to the Constitution sets both the date and the hour.

The handover takes place in a single moment. The outgoing president's term expires at noon, and the incoming president's term begins at that same instant. There is no window in which the office sits empty. There is also no stretch in which two people hold it at once.

Election Day runs on a different kind of rule. It falls on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Because the rule is a formula rather than a fixed date, the calendar day moves from one election to the next. The earliest possible date is November 2. The latest is November 8.

Inauguration Day does not move with it. The new term begins on January 20 no matter which November date voters went to the polls. One end of the post-election calendar floats, and the other is pinned in place. As a result, the wait between the vote and the start of the term runs a few days longer in some cycles than in others.

The fixed date gives everyone involved the same deadline. A winning candidate, the departing administration and the public all know the endpoint before a single ballot is cast.

The words of the swearing-in are fixed too. The presidential oath of office appears in Article II of the Constitution and runs 35 words. Its wording does not change from one president to the next.

Noon marks the exact cutoff. A candidate who wins in November carries the title of president-elect until that moment. A president-elect does not hold the powers of the office. Until then, the outgoing president still holds the office and all of its powers. Those powers pass only when the clock reaches noon on January 20.

When January 20 lands on a Sunday, the president takes the oath of office privately that day. A second, public swearing-in follows on Monday, January 21.

The calendar quirk changes the ceremony, not the term. A presidential term begins at noon on January 20, whatever the day of the week. A Sunday does not push that start date to Monday.

The private oath keeps the swearing-in on the constitutional date. Holding it on Sunday means the oath and the start of the term fall on the same day. The president does not wait an extra day to take the oath that comes with the office.

The Monday event is the inauguration most people see. The president recites the same oath a second time, this time before a public audience. By then the term has already begun. The second oath does not start anything new. It repeats in public a step already completed in private.

The result is one term with two oaths. A Sunday inauguration therefore involves two dates: January 20 for the private oath and January 21 for the public ceremony.

Ronald Reagan followed this pattern in 1985. He took the oath privately on Sunday, January 20. He repeated it in public the next day, Monday, January 21.

Barack Obama did the same in 2013. His private oath came on Sunday, January 20. His public ceremony followed on Monday, January 21.

In both cases, the official start of the term stayed on January 20. Only the public ceremony moved to Monday.

The vice president's term begins at noon on January 20, the same moment the president's term begins. That start time comes from the 20th Amendment, which covers both offices.

The shared start follows from how the office is filled. Voters do not pick a vice president in a separate race. The vice presidential candidate runs on the same ticket as the presidential candidate.

The Electoral College treats the two offices as a unit. The same electoral votes that decide the presidency also decide the vice presidency. A winning ticket therefore takes both offices together, and the two terms open at the same hour on the same day.

The oath of office is where the two jobs part ways. The presidential oath is written into Article II of the Constitution. The vice president's oath does not appear anywhere in the constitutional text.

Its wording is set by statute instead. That means Congress, through federal law, supplied the words a vice president recites. A reader searching the Constitution for the vice presidential oath will not find it there.

The difference in legal source has no effect on timing. Whoever wins the vice presidency takes office at noon on January 20, alongside the president elected on the same ticket.

Newly elected members of the U.S. House of Representatives take office at noon on January 3. The 20th Amendment sets that start date and lets Congress choose a different day by law.

A House term lasts two years. That short term puts every seat in the chamber before voters every two years. No member serves beyond a single term without winning another election.

Each term runs from noon on January 3 until noon on January 3 two years later. One House ends at the same moment the next one begins.

The House has 435 voting members. All of them start a new term on the same date. A first-term member and a member returning for another term begin at the same hour. The chamber does not bring in its members in staggered groups.

A new House handles two pieces of business when it first convenes. Members begin by electing a Speaker. The swearing-in of the members follows that vote.

The House opening falls on the same day newly elected senators begin their terms. It comes 17 days before the president's term begins at noon on January 20. Members of a new House are already in office when the presidential inauguration takes place.

Newly elected U.S. senators take office at noon on January 3, the start time the 20th Amendment sets for congressional terms. Once sworn in, a senator serves a six-year term.

The Senate term is three times as long as a House term, which lasts two years.

Senate terms are staggered. The seats are split into three classes, and each class comes up for election in a different cycle. As a result, about one-third of the Senate is on the ballot every two years. It takes three election cycles, or six years, for every Senate seat to come up for a vote once.

That structure means the chamber never turns over all at once. On January 3, only the senators who won that cycle's races begin new terms. Members of the other two classes keep serving without interruption. Their six-year terms are still running.

The six-year term also sets a senator's calendar for the years ahead. A senator who takes office on January 3 will see two more Senate elections pass before the seat appears on the ballot again. Those intervening elections decide the seats in the other two classes.

A senator who wins re-election follows the same schedule as a newcomer. The old term ends at noon on January 3, and the new six-year term starts at the same moment.

The oath is typically administered by the vice president, who serves as president of the Senate, or by a designee. That role gives the vice president a formal part in seating each incoming class of senators.

The Senate and vice presidential calendars do not line up. The vice president's term runs until noon on January 20. Senators sworn in on January 3 after a presidential election therefore take office while the sitting vice president is still serving, even if voters chose a successor in November.

Electors cast the formal votes for president in their own states on the first Tuesday after the second Wednesday in December. Congress then counts those votes in a joint session on January 6.

The popular vote in November is the first step on this calendar. Because Election Day follows a rule tied to the first Monday of the month, it always lands between November 2 and November 8.

The electors' meeting also follows a rule rather than a fixed date. The second Wednesday in December always falls between December 8 and December 14. The electors' meeting therefore lands between December 14 and December 20. There is no single national gathering of electors. Each state's electors meet in their own state.

Both dates are tied to days of the week, so the gap between them never changes. The electors meet exactly 42 days after Election Day, six weeks to the day.

States must resolve disputes over their results before that meeting. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 set the deadline for settling those disputes at six days before the electors meet. Counting back from the meeting dates, the deadline falls between December 8 and December 14.

After the electors vote, the process moves to Washington. The joint session on January 6 is where the electoral votes are formally counted. Members of the House and Senate begin their terms at noon on January 3. That means the newly sworn-in Congress, not the outgoing one, conducts the count.

The 2022 law kept January 6 as the date for the joint session. It also clarified that the vice president's role in the count is ceremonial.

The count leaves 14 days before the next fixed point on the calendar. The president and vice president take office at noon on January 20. From the electors' December meeting to that noon start, between 31 and 37 days pass, depending on the year.

There is no national start date for governors. Each state sets the day its governor takes office in its own constitution or state law. Many governors begin their terms in January, but the exact day varies from one state to the next.

That patchwork means a governor's swearing-in can land on a Monday, a Tuesday or a Saturday, depending on the state. Four states show how wide the spread runs.

Ohio's governor takes office on the second Monday in January. The rule is tied to a weekday rather than a fixed calendar date. As a result, the actual day moves from year to year. The second Monday in January always falls somewhere between January 8 and January 14.

Texas uses the third Tuesday in January. That puts the Texas start date between January 15 and January 21. Like Ohio's rule, the Texas rule is pinned to a day of the week. The calendar date therefore shifts each year within that seven-day window.

Virginia's rule has more steps. The governor takes office on the Saturday after the second Wednesday in January. The second Wednesday falls between January 8 and January 14. The Saturday that follows therefore lands between January 11 and January 17. Of these four states, Virginia is the only one where the swearing-in always falls on a weekend.

Alaska is the outlier. Its governor takes office on the first Monday in December, weeks before the other three states seat theirs. Counting forward from the November Election Day, an Alaska governor-elect has either 27 or 34 days between the vote and the start of the term. The exact gap depends on how the calendar falls that year. That is a much shorter wait than in the three states with January start dates.

Alaska's rule also puts its start date in a different calendar year from the others. An Alaska governor begins the term in the same year as the election. Governors in Ohio, Texas and Virginia begin theirs in the year after the vote.

These four dates do not predict any other state's schedule. Readers checking a different state can find the governing rule in that state's constitution or state law.

Start dates for mayors and state legislators vary by state and by city. No single national rule decides when these officials begin their terms.

That makes a local start date a separate question from a federal one. A winner in a city or statehouse race begins on a date tied to that place. The January 3 and January 20 dates that govern Congress and the White House do not apply.

New York City follows a January schedule. Its mayor takes office on January 1, the first day of the calendar year. On the calendar, that start comes ahead of both federal start dates.

Chicago runs on a different timetable. The city elects its mayor in the spring, and the winner takes office in May. Brandon Johnson took office as Chicago's mayor on May 15, 2023.

A Chicago mayor therefore starts governing in late spring. That falls outside the November-to-January pattern that shapes federal offices. A New York City mayor, by contrast, starts on the year's opening day.

These two examples come from just two cities. They show that a local start date cannot be assumed from a federal one or from another city's practice.

State legislators follow no common calendar either. Their start dates differ from state to state.

For anyone tracking when a mayor or state lawmaker takes power, the answer depends on the specific city or state. That place's own rules set the date.

The presidential transition runs from Election Day in November to noon on January 20, when the new president's term begins. The Presidential Transition Act of 1963 governs the federal support an incoming team receives during that window.

The winner does not take power on election night. The outgoing administration stays in office until its term runs out. The incoming team uses the weeks in between to prepare to govern.

The 1963 law sets the rules for how the federal government backs that preparation. It defines what an incoming administration can receive before it takes office. That support includes transition funding and access to federal resources.

The General Services Administration, or GSA, handles a gatekeeping step in the process. Its administrator formally ascertains who the apparent winner of the presidential election is. That ascertainment unlocks the funding and resources for the president-elect's team.

Ascertainment is separate from casting or counting votes. It is an administrative determination made by the head of a federal agency, not by voters, electors or Congress. Until the GSA administrator makes it, the incoming team cannot draw on the support the transition law provides.

The handover is complete at noon on January 20. At that moment, the outgoing president's term ends and the new president's term begins. The transition period closes, and the new administration takes over the executive branch.

Presidential terms once began on March 4, months after voters had already picked a winner. The 20th Amendment, ratified on January 23, 1933, moved the start of the term to noon on January 20 to shorten that long lame-duck stretch.

A lame duck is an officeholder who keeps serving after a successor has been chosen. Under the old calendar, that overlap was built into every presidential election. Voting took place in early November. A defeated or departing president then stayed in office until March 4 of the following year.

That left roughly four months between the vote and the handover. During that stretch, the outgoing administration still held power. The incoming one had won the election but had no authority to act yet.

The amendment cut that gap by about six weeks. Moving the start date from March 4 to January 20 removes 43 days in a year without a leap day and 44 days in a leap year. Under the current calendar, the wait from Election Day to the January 20 handover runs between 73 and 79 days. The change did not eliminate the lame-duck period, but it compressed it. The four-year length of the term stayed the same. Only its start and end dates moved.

The amendment fixed both ends of the handover at the same moment. The outgoing president's term ends at noon on January 20, and the successor's term begins at that instant. No gap opens between the two administrations.

The new date did not apply to a presidential inauguration right away. Franklin D. Roosevelt's second inauguration, on January 20, 1937, was the first held on the January date. His first term had started under the old March 4 calendar. That term ran about six weeks short of four full years.

Ratification on January 23, 1933, and that first January inauguration were just under four years apart. Every four-year presidential term since then has started at noon on January 20.

#5527. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s VR-1.1 model outscores Claude Code and Codex on vulnerability repair

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today released VR-1.1, a new version of its frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

On a public repair benchmark, the model outscored Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex.

The release goes after the part of vulnerability management that has not sped up. In July, research group Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. counted about 2,500 high- and critical-severity disclosures from major organizations, roughly five times the monthly record set before Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview in April.

Each repair still needs an engineer who understands the flaw well enough to change the code without breaking something else. Co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti called that stage “where security teams are stuck.”

To test the model on that repair work, Cogent turned to LiveCVEBench. Researchers at Harbin Institute of Technology and Kuaishou Technology built the benchmark from vulnerabilities disclosed in recent months and add new ones regularly. VR-1.1 produced a working repair for 57.9% of the benchmark’s 190 tasks. Claude Code and Codex tied at 45.3%.

Each task drops an agent into a real development environment with a vulnerability report and the affected codebase, in one of 14 programming languages. To pass, a patch has to close the vulnerability without breaking the software, which the benchmark checks with separate security and functionality tests.

Cogent blocked outbound network access during repairs and hid the grading tests until each agent was done. Inference budgets differed across the three systems, according to the full methodology Cogent Research has published.

Where the environment allows, VR-1.1 starts by writing its own proof of concept that triggers the reported flaw. From there the model follows the vulnerability through the affected code, including related paths that share the same weakness. The fix itself stays small, for example checking an index before use.

Every patch goes to a separate review that starts from a fresh context and hunts for a way around the fix. New bugs introduced by the change are part of that check. The model also leaves behind regression tests, which fail if a later code change reopens the flaw. When an attempt fails, the diagnosis and failure details carry into the next try.

“A patch might block the exact payload from a bug report, but leave the same vulnerability open via a different endpoint or break core functionality for users,” said Geng Sng, co-founder and chief technology officer of Cogent. “We designed VR-1.1 to check its own work for both problems before it finishes.”

Cogent introduced VR-1 in July to find and prove the attack paths an adversary could reach inside an enterprise. The new release extends the remediation capabilities that model introduced.

Founded in 2025, the company sells artificial intelligence agents that detect and fix vulnerabilities, with customers choosing whether a human signs off on each change. According to Cogent, Fortune 500 users have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%.

Greylock Partners backed its $11 million launch round in July 2025, and Bain Capital Ventures led the $42 million Series A in February that took total funding to $53 million.

#5526. Cerbo Expands AI Scribe to Virtual Visits, Bringing Native AI Charting to Telehealth

AI Scribe now drafts the structured note inside the chart for Cerbo Telemedicine and Zoom visits, so telehealth doesn't mean extra time spent on documentation.

ATLANTA, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cerbo, a leading electronic health record (EHR) platform forcash pay, personalized care practices, today announced that AI Scribe, its native clinical documentation tool, now works on virtual visits. AI Scribe captures the conversation on native Telemedicine and Zoom visits, then drafts a structured note inside the chart for the provider to review, edit, and sign.

Cerbo brings its native AI Scribe to telehealth, drafting structured notes during Telemedicine and Zoom visits

AI Scribe launched in August this year as a scribe built directly into the Cerbo EHR, with no separate login, no dictation app, and no copy and paste between systems. Extending it to telehealth brings that same experience to every way an independent practice sees patients. In the exam room or on a screen, AI Scribe follows the clinical conversation and drafts the structured note inside the chart, ready for review after the visit ends, requiring signoff before anything commits to the chart.

For many independent practitioners, telehealth days carry the same hidden cost as in-person ones. The appointments end, and the documentation waits until the evening, a pattern providers often call "pajama time." Cerbobuilt the native AI Scribe to close that gap in the exam room, and bringing it to virtual visits closes it on video too, so a full schedule of telehealth appointments does not follow a provider home.

"Our goal is to take the barriers out of a provider's day, the time-consuming administrative work that pulls them away from the patient in front of them," said Nishant Phadnis, Chief Product Officer at Cerbo. "AI Scribe was built to do exactly that, and we keep extending it so it helps across more of the moments that matter. Telehealth was a natural next step. A provider on a video visit deserves the same focus on their patient, and the same relief from charting, as one in the appointment room."

For practices, AI Scribe on virtual visits means:

AI Scribe is available to Cerbo customers today in Settings > AI Scribe. For AI Scribe users with Cerbo Telemedicine or the Zoom integration, virtual visit support is included at no additional cost, capturing the same comprehensive notes on telehealth visits that AI Scribe already captures in person. More information is available at www.cer.bo/ai-scribe.

Bringing AI Scribe to telehealth is part of how Cerbo keeps building for independent practices, putting more of the provider's time back where it belongs, with the patient.

Cerbo is a leading EHR built for independent practices, including functional medicine, integrative medicine, longevity, wellness, direct primary care, and concierge practices. Founded in 2011 and headquartered in Atlanta, GA, Cerbo gives practitioners a single, flexible platform for clinical documentation, scheduling, billing, and patient engagement, built around the way independent, personalized-care practices design their visits and workflows rather than a one-size-fits-all system designed for institutional medicine. Cerbo is part of Providi, the company behind Cerbo and OptiMantra. Learn more at cer.bo.

#5524. 10 things to know about bear markets — how often they happen and how long they last

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The S&P 500 has faced 27 bear markets since 1928. Learn how deep they cut, how long they last, and how often they return.

A portfolio that climbed through a long winning run can surrender its gains within a few days, and few investors watch a balance shrink with calm. Markets behave like athletes after a grueling season. Even the strongest competitors need time off to recover, and stocks can stall after a streak of record highs. The pause feels different from the inside. Each red day on a brokerage screen invites the same question: sell now or hold on? Fear pushes many people to sell, and a panicked choice can shadow their savings for decades. Money set aside for retirement, a child's tuition, or a first home can hinge on how an investor handles those days.

The hardest part of a downturn is the blindness. Nobody watching a decline unfold knows whether it will stop at a modest dip or carve deep into an account, or whether it will last weeks or drag on for more than a year. Headlines raise the stakes by declaring a new bear market the moment losses cross a familiar line, and the label alone can rattle people who hold equities without tracking the market's every move. Without context, every slide looks like the start of a collapse. History supplies the missing frame, an accumulated record of how deep, long, and frequent past slumps have been. It cannot predict the next one. Someone who knows those patterns can judge a falling market against a broad baseline instead of one bad afternoon.

Hartford Funds gathered the essentials in a 10-point explainer on bear markets in the S&P 500 Index, a market capitalization-weighted price index of 500 widely held common stocks. The firm draws most of its statistics from Ned Davis Research, with figures current through March 31, 2025, and a view reaching back to 1928. An accompanying table catalogs every drop of 20% or more in the index from 1929 through 2024. The recession count comes from the National Bureau of Economic Research, and a separate Ned Davis analysis tracks the index's best trading days over the past two decades. The guide below works through all 10 points, covering how far stocks sink, how long and how often bear markets strike, and how patient shareholders have fared across them.

A slump becomes a bear market once the S&P 500 closes at least 20% below its most recent peak, and a drop of 10% to 19.9% stays a correction. The cutoff turns a vague mood of gloom into a fixed number anyone can check against the day's final price. A rough afternoon does not qualify on its own. The index has to finish trading beyond the mark, so a midday plunge that recovers by the closing bell leaves the label untouched.

A decline near the top of the correction band and one a hair past 20% can look alike on an account statement. Only the second earns the heavier name, though a fraction of a percentage point may separate the two. The threshold measures depth and nothing more. It says nothing about how long a slide will last or how far it will reach.

The S&P 500's mildest bear market shows how slim that margin can run. From June 15, 1948, to June 13, 1949, the index lost 20.57%, a sliver past the line. The downturn stretched across 363 days, a shade under a full year. Its shallow depth bought no speed, and a gentle loss can grind on for months. Depth and duration move on separate tracks.

The same 20% yardstick marks the recovery's start. A new bull market begins once the index closes 20% above its low. Gains and losses compound from different bases, so a 20% rebound from a trough does not restore a 20% loss from a peak. The all-clear can sound before the old high returns. Both milestones rest on closing prices, and neither tells an investor whether the worst has passed or whether a rebound will hold.

Investors who hear analysts declare a new bull market may hold portfolios short of their prior highs, a gap the twin 20% rules build in from the outset.

Stocks surrender 35% of their value in the average bear market, and the S&P 500 slumps recorded from 1929 to 2024 produce a mean drop of 35.24%. Any recovery starts from a smaller base. A portfolio that sheds 35% needs a percentage gain larger than 35% to return to its old peak.

Bull markets supply that repair with room to spare, lifting stocks 112% on average. An advance of that size dwarfs the typical loss. An ordinary bull market carries the index beyond the peak it held before an ordinary bear struck.

The averages mask a brutal tail. The worst collapse in the record cut the index 61.81% between Nov. 9, 1931, and June 1, 1932, a 205-day span. Two other episodes broke through the 50% mark. The index skidded 54.50% from March 6, 1937, to March 31, 1938, and it plunged 51.93% from Oct. 9, 2007, to Nov. 20, 2008, a slide that unfolded over 408 days.

Depth and duration followed separate paths across these crashes. The 1931-32 collapse cut deeper than the 2007-08 rout in far fewer days. The first slump in the table shows how fast a severe loss can land. The index fell 44.67% in 67 days, from Sept. 7 to Nov. 13, 1929.

The early 1930s piled one severe slump on top of another. A 44.29% drop ran from April 10 to Dec. 16, 1930. The index then shed 43.10% between June 27 and Oct. 5, 1931, and another 40.60% from Sept. 7, 1932, to Feb. 27, 1933. Shareholders in those years absorbed loss after loss deeper than the average bear market, with little time between them.

The average blends those early catastrophes with far milder episodes. A single bear market can stop short of it or blow past it by a wide margin. The benchmark describes the record, and it offers little guidance on how deep the next downturn will cut.

The S&P 500 Index has endured 27 bear markets since 1928, and it has strung together 28 bull markets over the same stretch. Steep declines belong to the ordinary experience of owning stocks. A slump arrives, runs its course, and hands off to a fresh advance.

Upswings outnumber downturns by one, and the long-term climb survived every reversal. Stocks have posted substantial gains over the decades across those 27 separate plunges. Investors who judge the market by its worst stretches miss the larger arc the full record traces.

The 27 episodes stretch across generations of shareholders. The earliest entry in the source's table, a 44.67% collapse from Sept. 7 to Nov. 13, 1929, played out in 67 days. The postwar years brought a 28.78% slide from May 29, 1946, to May 17, 1947, and a 21.63% retreat from Aug. 2, 1956, to Oct. 22, 1957. A 33.51% drop struck between Aug. 25 and Dec. 4, 1987, over 101 days. Others ground on longer, such as the 27.11% loss that stretched 622 days from Nov. 28, 1980, to Aug. 12, 1982.

The newest of the 27 began Jan. 3, 2022, and bottomed Oct. 12, 2022. It cut the index 25.43% across 282 days. Twenty years earlier, a 33.75% fall from Jan. 4 to Oct. 9, 2002, lasted 278 days, four days short of the 2022 episode. The pair shows the cycle persisting into the 21st century.

Depth and duration vary across the 27 by wide margins. A setback from Feb. 9 to Oct. 7, 1966, trimmed 22.18% in 240 days. The bear market from Nov. 29, 1968, to May 26, 1970, stripped 36.06% over 543 days. The later one ran more than twice as long and cut deeper. No single profile fits every member of the list. The count of 27 shows how routine these sell-offs are. It reveals nothing about how deep or long the next one will run.

The average bear market runs 289 days, or about 9.6 months, from the S&P 500's peak to its trough. Inside a decline, each losing week can feel open-ended. Measured against the full market cycle, the typical slump amounts to a short interruption.

Bull markets outlast them by a wide margin, averaging 988 days, or 2.7 years. A downturn of ordinary length wraps up in less than a year, and the average advance carries into its third. An investor who endures a typical slump trades months of losses for an upswing that lasts years on average.

The longest decline in the record stretched 630 days, from Jan. 11, 1973, to Oct. 3, 1974, and wiped out 48.20% of the index's value. The selloff from March 24, 2000, to Sept. 21, 2001, also outran the norm by months, spanning 546 days and costing 36.77%. A slump from Nov. 29, 1968, to May 26, 1970, lasted 543 days and took 36.06%. Investors caught in any of the three waited more than a year for a bottom. Even the record-length slump fell short of the span of an average bull market.

The S&P 500 shed 33.92% in 33 days between Feb. 19, 2020, and March 23, 2020, the briefest bear market on file. Rapid collapses have struck in other eras too. A 101-day plunge from Aug. 25, 1987, to Dec. 4, 1987, erased 33.51%. Both crashes packed a loss of about one-third into a few months or less, and speed offered no shield against severity.

Length and depth do not move in lockstep. The bear market from Nov. 28, 1980, to Aug. 12, 1982, and the 2009 rout from Jan. 6 to March 9 produced near-identical losses of 27.11% and 27.62%. The first dragged on for 622 days, and the second ended after 62. A decline's age reveals little about how deep it will cut. An investor cannot gauge the remaining damage from the calendar.

The S&P 500 has tumbled into a new bear market about once every 3.5 years over the long term. Across a decade, the pace adds up to close to three downturns. A 20% slide belongs among the routine costs of owning stocks.

The 3.5-year figure smooths over intervals that differ by years from one era to the next. In 1931, one slump bottomed on June 2, and the next began on June 27, leaving investors less than a month of relief. Seventy years later, a decline that ended on Sept. 21, 2001, gave way to a fresh one on Jan. 4, 2002, less than four months afterward. The most recent pair also sat close together. After bottoming on March 23, 2020, the index needed less than two years to set the Jan. 3, 2022, peak that preceded its next bear market.

The index went five years and 13 days without a bear market between the Aug. 12, 1982, low and the Aug. 25, 1987, peak. A second five-year lull separated the Oct. 9, 2002, trough from the Oct. 9, 2007, peak. The 1987 bear market that ended the first quiet spell erased 33.51% in 101 days and bottomed on Dec. 4. From there, the S&P 500 climbed without a 20% break until March 24, 2000.

Hartford Funds credits the run from December 1987 to the dot-com crash in March 2000 with the technical title of longest bull market, a span of more than 12 years. Many observers hand the crown to the bull that ended in 2020. The later uptrend ran from the March 9, 2009, low to Feb. 19, 2020, a span of 10 years and 11 months. The 1987 advance outlasted it by more than a year.

A 19.9% drop in 1990 came within a tenth of a percentage point of ending the 1987 run. The slide stayed a correction, and the bull's streak survived. A full 20% decline would have cut the rally into two pieces, each shorter than the bull that ended in 2020.

The 3.5-year mean blends reprieves of weeks with stretches of more than a decade. Investors can count on the rhythm across a career and still find no timetable for the next decline.

The S&P 500 absorbed 12 bear markets between 1928 and 1945, close to one every 1.5 years, and has endured 15 since 1945, about one every 5.1 years. The postwar tally runs higher, yet it stretches across a longer span of history. The typical gap between downturns has more than tripled as a result.

Seven bear markets opened between September 1929 and July 1933, a window of less than four years. Three of them began in 1931, in February, June, and November. The September 1929 decline erased 44.67% of the index's value in 67 days. The pre-1945 sequence closed with a 535-day grind from November 1940 to April 1942 that cost 34.47%.

Depth divides the two eras as much as frequency does. Six of the 12 bear markets before 1945 wiped out more than 40% of the index's worth. Two of the 15 postwar episodes crossed that line. The shallow end tells the same story. Eight sell-offs since the war stopped short of a 30% loss, compared with two in the earlier period. The first postwar bear market, from May 1946 to May 1947, set the tone with a 28.78% drop.

Long quiet spells marked the decades after the war. One retreat ended in June 1962, and the next did not begin until February 1966. Another closed in August 1982, and investors waited until August 1987 for the next one, a five-year lull. The 1987 slump shed 33.51% in 101 days. An extended calm before a bear market offers no protection against a swift one.

Some postwar bear markets dragged on past anything the earlier years produced. The 1980 to 1982 slide lasted 622 days, and the 1968 to 1970 stretch ran 543 days. Both outlasted every bear market before 1945. The postwar pattern swaps frequent, severe collapses for rarer and milder ones, and duration stands as the one measure where the later decades offer no clear relief.

Roughly 42% of the S&P 500's best trading days between Jan. 1, 2003, and March 31, 2025, arrived during a bear market. The index posted many of its sharpest single-day gains in the stretches that leave shareholders most anxious. The market's best and worst moments crowd into the same turbulent periods.

Only four declines of 20% or more fell inside that 22-year window. They began in October 2007, January 2009, February 2020, and January 2022, and together they lasted 785 days, a little over two years. Slumps that covered less than a tenth of the calendar still produced about two in five of the top sessions. The four also ran shorter on average than the long-run norm for bear markets. Their share of standout days looks even more concentrated as a result.

Selling after a steep drop and waiting for calm leaves a portfolio on the sidelines during many of the days that rebuild lost value. An investor who exits in a panic must also pick a moment to return. Many of the biggest rallies arrive while the index still sits in bear territory, before anyone can confirm a bottom. A seller who waits for proof of a rebound risks forfeiting a large slice of the most rewarding sessions in this record. The exit carries one cost, and the delay before reentry carries another.

Hartford Funds argues that staying invested may offer the strongest way through a downturn. Its reasoning rests on one practical problem. Pinpointing when a recovery begins is hard. The brevity of those four slumps gave anyone who sold a short span to spot the turn and buy back in. The February-to-March decline of 2020 left the slimmest window of the group. A shareholder who held through all four episodes collected every one of those banner days without guessing at a single turning point.

The economy slipped into recession 15 times in the years since 1928, a stretch in which the S&P 500 fell into 27 bear markets. Stock losses and economic contractions do not march in step. Investors who treat the two as a single event misread the historical record.

Slumps in share prices tend to coincide with a cooling economy. Hartford Funds draws the connection, observing that many bear markets have arrived alongside slowing growth. The overlap helps explain why a sharp drop in the index stirs talk of hard times ahead. A shrinking portfolio and a faltering economy can show up in the same season, and the timing makes them look inseparable.

Hartford Funds stops short of treating a falling market as a forecast. A slide in stock prices, by itself, offers no proof that a recession is on the way, the firm argues. The two can travel together, yet a price decline cannot reveal where the economy is headed.

The index has crossed into bear territory on many more occasions than the economy has contracted over the same span. A longer list of bear markets than of recessions means the two tallies cannot pair off one for one. Bear markets, by this tally, have proved the more frequent of the two shocks.

Shareholders who sell at the first bear market headline in expectation of a recession are betting on a link the counts do not support. A drop in stocks signals that prices have fallen, and it leaves the question of the wider economy open. A brokerage statement and an economic report track different things, even in the same rough year. Keeping the two readings apart lets an investor weigh a sell-off on its merits.

Anyone who read every bear market as a recession warning would have braced for more contractions than the economy delivered.

Someone who keeps money in stocks for 50 years should plan on living through about 14 bear markets, give or take, by Hartford Funds' estimate. The projection recasts a downturn as a recurring feature of a long financial life. Across decades of saving and the years of drawing on savings in retirement, a slump will come back again and again. An investor who expects 14 or so has less reason to treat any single plunge as a verdict on the market's future.

Some bear markets clear the 20% threshold by a slim margin, and a lifelong investor can count on meeting a few. The S&P 500 gave up 22.18% between Feb. 9 and Oct. 7, 1966, a span of 240 days. A shallow bear market can linger. The index shed 21.63% over 446 days from August 1956 to October 1957, more than a year of sagging prices for a modest total hit.

Other episodes gouge deeper. Between October 1939 and June 1940, the S&P 500 lost 31.95% in 229 days. A 27.97% decline from December 1961 to June 1962 took 196 days. The index surrendered 33.51% in 101 days between Aug. 25 and Dec. 4, 1987. The 1980-to-1982 slide needed 622 days to inflict a smaller 27.11% loss, and the 2002 bear market subtracted 33.75% over 278 days. The heaviest blow of this group came between November 1968 and May 1970, when the index relinquished 36.06% across 543 days. Depth and duration follow separate paths in these episodes, so a bear market's depth says little about how long it will last.

Hartford Funds acknowledges that watching a portfolio shrink is uncomfortable. It frames downturns as a short-lived part of investing. Every entry in the table carries an end date. An investor who absorbs that record can meet each new bear market knowing none in the index's history has proved permanent.

Stocks have climbed 78% of the time over the past 95 years, a record that shrinks even the worst slides to a fraction of market history. Bear markets occupied about 21.4 of those years. Hartford Funds grants that such stretches can be painful, and it still describes the full record as one in which stocks spend most of their time gaining ground.

Some of the longest declines the S&P 500 has suffered fit inside those 21.4 years. The 1980 to 1982 slump dragged on for 622 days and pared prices 27.11%. The 1968 to 1970 drop lasted 543 days and wiped out 36.06%. The 1940 to 1942 retreat stretched across 535 days and cost 34.47%. Each tested shareholders for well over a year, and each forms a piece of a span where rising prices prevail.

Milder episodes filled out the tally in the decades after World War II. A 353-day fall from 1946 to 1947 took 28.78% off the index. The 1956 to 1957 setback ran 446 days and trimmed 21.63%, and the 1966 downturn lasted 240 days and subtracted 22.18%. The 1961 to 1962 sell-off needed 196 days to strip away 27.97%. None of them approached the depths of the early 1930s, yet each still counts toward the 21.4-year total.

The 21.4 years of losses arrived in installments. The table's entries run from a 67-day plunge in the fall of 1929 to the 2022 slide, and bull markets filled every gap between them. The earliest years packed the slumps close together. One decline ended on June 2, 1931, and the next began June 27. The pattern repeated at the end of the 1930s. A downturn that ended April 8, 1939, gave way to another starting Oct. 25.

Every bear market in the table ended in a recovery. Selling during a downturn trades a temporary loss for a seat outside a market whose past tilts toward gains.

#5523. Joseph Rabinowitz, CPA selects Michael Zaidman, CPA and ZBS Group LLP as Succession Partner for Tax & Accounting Practice

ZBS Group LLP selected for fourth CPA practice transition, reinforcing the firm's position as a trusted succession partner for accounting professionals and their clients

PLAINVIEW, N.Y., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ZBS Group LLP, led by Michael Zaidman, CPA and financial advisor, is pleased to announce the acquisition of the tax and accounting practice of Joseph Rabinowitz, CPA. The transaction provides a thoughtful succession solution for Rabinowitz while ensuring continuity of service and expanded capabilities for the individuals, families, and businesses his practice has served.

Rabinowitz has built his practice around long-standing client relationships and the delivery of tax and accounting services. As he considered the future of the firm, identifying a successor capable of preserving those relationships while providing clients with additional resources was a central priority.

Following the transaction, Rabinowitz will remain actively involved during a diligent transition period, working alongside the ZBS team to help ensure continuity, facilitate introductions, and maintain the high level of service his clients have come to expect.

"Selecting a successor is about much more than completing a transactionâit is about determining who you trust with the relationships you have spent a career building," said Joseph Rabinowitz, CPA. "ZBS has the accounting and tax capabilities to serve my clients well, along with a broader team and additional services that can provide meaningful value as their needs evolve. I am looking forward to working closely with Michael and his team throughout the transition."

The Rabinowitz practice will complement ZBS Group's established tax and accounting capabilities while giving existing clients access to the resources of a larger, efficiently structured professional team.

A key differentiator for ZBS is its understanding of the intersection between tax strategy and financial advisory services. Rather than viewing tax preparation, accounting, investments, and financial planning as entirely separate disciplines, ZBS seeks opportunities to coordinate these areas when appropriate.

For financial advisory clients, this approach can include greater attention to tax-efficient investing, investment and account structure, and the potential benefits of consolidating professional relationships. For tax and accounting clients, joining ZBS provides access to additional capabilities should their financial needs expand over time.

"Joe has built something valuable: a practice based on trusted relationships and years of service to his clients," said Michael Zaidman, CPA and financial advisor at ZBS Group LLP. "Our responsibility is to protect what Joe has built, make the transition as seamless as possible, and demonstrate to his clients that they will continue to receive attentive tax and accounting service while gaining access to the broader capabilities of the ZBS team."

The Rabinowitz transaction marks the fourth time Zaidman and his team have been selected to facilitate the succession of a CPA practice, reflecting ZBS Group LLP's growing experience in helping accounting professionals transition their firms as they approach retirement or the next stage of their careers.

CPA practice transitions present challenges that extend well beyond valuation and deal structure. Clients may have worked with the same accountant for decades, making continuity, communication, trust, and service quality critical to a successful succession.

Zaidman and the ZBS team have developed experience navigating these transitions from both sides of the relationship: providing retiring practitioners with a structured path toward succession while giving their clients a professional home designed to preserve existing relationships and expand available services.

"Every successful transition starts with trust," Zaidman added. "The retiring CPA needs confidence that the team stepping in understands the responsibility that comes with taking care of longtime clients. Our goal is to give practitioners a thoughtful retirement and succession solution while giving their clients confidence about what comes next."

Expanded Resources Without Sacrificing Relationships

For Rabinowitz's clients, the transition is designed to provide continuity rather than disruption. Rabinowitz's continued involvement will allow relationships and institutional knowledge to transfer deliberately to the ZBS team.

At the same time, clients will gain access to a broader organization with professionals across tax, accounting, and financial and investment advisory disciplines. This combination of additional services, an experienced team, and an established transition process helped make ZBS a compelling succession choice for Rabinowitz.

The transaction also reflects ZBS Group's broader strategy of partnering with CPA firm owners seeking a responsible long-term home for their practices. ZBS is particularly focused on transitions where maintaining client relationships, providing high-quality tax and accounting services, and offering access to broader financial capabilities can create value for both the retiring practitioner and the clients being served.

ZBS Group LLP is a tax & accounting CPA firm led by Michael Zaidman, CPA and financial advisor specializing in tax efficient investment solutions. The firm combines tax and accounting expertise with an understanding of financial planning and investment strategy, helping clients consider financial decisions through a coordinated, tax-aware lens.

#5522. Novee’s External Surface Testing checks which exposed assets attackers can actually exploit

Artificial intelligence penetration testing startup Novee Cyber Security Ltd. today added External Surface Testing to its platform so its AI-driven attacks can reach a customer’s entire internet-facing footprint.

External Surface Testing is aimed at the scramble after a critical vulnerability is disclosed, when security teams have to work out which exposed assets are affected and whether any can actually be exploited. Novee argues that attackers see a target as a single environment with many ways in, including forgotten subdomains and staging servers someone left exposed.

Conventional external attack surface management products catalog a company’s exposed assets and score them by severity. Netta Rager Dan, vice president of product at Novee, said those products “show you what’s exposed, but don’t give you the full picture of real risk.” In the company’s telling, security staff are left to validate long lists of exposures on their own.

Novee’s version needs nothing more than a domain name to get started. From there the software works outward the way an outside attacker would, and it keeps track of what it learns about each asset and service as it goes. A newly disclosed vulnerability gets run against a customer’s live systems to see whether anyone could actually exploit it.

Findings exported from other vendors’ attack surface tools go through the same check. Novee says the testing also catches flaws nobody had logged, chained attack paths among them, and the customer ends up with a short, prioritized list of validated issues backed by evidence.

Until now Novee’s testing has stopped at the application layer. External Surface Testing runs on the same platform as the company’s Application Pentesting product, so a host found during external discovery can be promoted straight into a full gray-box or white-box pentest. Whatever the discovery phase learned carries over. Novee claims no other fully autonomous AI pentesting platform covers the external attack surface as well as web, mobile and AI applications.

Limits are built in to keep the testing safe. Customers approve the scope before anything runs, and the probes come from outside the perimeter without agents or customer-supplied credentials. Exploit attempts don’t use destructive payloads. Traffic is held under configured caps so testing doesn’t cause load spikes or bury the security operations center in noise.

Former national-level offensive security operators Ido Geffen, Gon Chalamish and Omer Ninburg founded Novee in May 2025. YL Ventures LP, Canaan Partners and Zeev Ventures LP backed the company when it launched in January with $51.5 million in funding.

External Surface Testing is available now as part of the Novee platform.

#5521. Binance Withdrawals Top FTX Levels in November, but Crypto Liquidity Defies Panic

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance withdrawals surged into the billions after a record-breaking $6.3 billion hack, bringing back memories of FTX’s November 2022 collapse. Yet the world’s largest crypto exchange is showing a resilience that could barricade the industry from its darkest chapter.

Binance processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits during the first nine and a half hours after reopening services on November 1, resulting in $3.64 billion in net outflows. According to its October 28 Proof of Reserves data, the exchange held $171 billion in total assets, so the withdrawal wave accounted for just 2.1% of its reported holdings.

Binance withdrawals are BACK!BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, DOGE, USDT, USDC and more are being re-enabled across supported networks.Binance also says 95% of the stolen assets have already been replaced.Bears were screaming FTX 2.0, desperately hoping for another collapse.

This puts the outflows in perspective: despite the initial rush following the $6.3 billion hack, Binance retained assets worth 47 times the net amount withdrawn. The exchange said withdrawals had begun stabilizing, while deposits remained substantial.

The figures initially look alarming, especially against the backdrop of FTX. The failed exchange suffered $6 billion in net withdrawals over 72 hours before suspending customer withdrawals in November 2022.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

“98% choose to stay. Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times.” – Changpeng Zhao, Binance Founder

Binance has previously said that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the incident, including $5 billion in the affected token assets. It also reported that partners had frozen approximately $3 billion linked to the attack.

So how does this compare to FTX? This current crisis is fundamentally different from FTX’s collapse. FTX’s withdrawal run exposed a liquidity shortfall tied to customer funds and its relationship with Alameda Research. Binance, by contrast, says it will cover the stolen assets rather than pass the losses to users.

Bitcoin’s reaction offers one of the clearest signs of crypto’s resilience compared with the FTX collapse. Following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, BTC briefly slipped toward $76,700 but held above the closely watched $75,000 support level before recovering toward $79,000. The contrast with November 2022 is stark. Bitcoin fell nearly 10% on November 8 as FTX’s withdrawal crisis intensified, then plunged another 14.4% on November 9 to close near $15,877, after briefly hitting $15,632.

While Binance’s hack triggered billions in withdrawals and market-wide liquidations, Bitcoin has so far avoided the cascading selloff that followed FTX’s implosion. Its ability to defend $75,000 suggests investors are treating the incident as a major exchange security failure rather than evidence of a systemic liquidity crisis across crypto.

Binance has already faced a major financial and regulatory reckoning. In November 2023, the exchange agreed to pay more than $4 billion to resolve U.S. investigations into anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. Founder Changpeng Zhao also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. He resigned as CEO and paid a separate $50 million fine.

Despite that enormous settlement, Binance continued operating as the world’s largest crypto exchange. The latest hack now presents another test of its financial strength, operational resilience, and ability to maintain customer confidence.

Crypto markets have still felt the shock. Bitcoin and Ethereum fell following the breach, while spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded huge outflows and leveraged positions faced heavy liquidations. However, both major cryptocurrencies partly recovered after hitting lows.

Now, can Binance withdrawals continue to ease? The exchange publishes updated Proof of Reserves data and completes its security review. The comparison with FTX shows the scale of investor concern, but not necessarily the same outcome. Binance has absorbed a major hack, committed to covering customer losses, and resumed withdrawals after billions left the platform.

November has brought back memories of 2022. Binance’s response shows crypto’s largest exchange is determined to keep this crisis from becoming another industry-wide collapse.

#5519. Katie Lee Shares "The Power of Your Story" at New York Public Library Event

St. Louis restaurateur and author discusses building success on losses, not wins, in a free in-person and virtual event on Nov. 18

ST. LOUIS, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The New York Public Library's Thomas Yoseloff Business Center will host "The Power of Your Story," a presentation by restaurateur, entrepreneur and author Katie Lee, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, from 3:00 to 4:00 p.m. ET. The program is hybrid, with attendees able to join in person at the library or online via Zoom.

Lee's path to business success was anything but conventional. A high school dropout who battled addiction, she went on to build one of the country's fastest-growing Italian food brands. In her talk, Lee will share how her success was built not on the wins, but on her losses, and how embracing your own story, including its hardest chapters, can become your greatest strength.

"For a long time, I thought my past was something to hide and be ashamed of. It turned out to be the foundation of everything I've built," said Lee. "Every setback taught me something I couldn't have learned any other way. I want people to leave this event knowing that their story, all of it, is their superpower."

Today, Lee is the founder and owner of a consumer-packaged goods business of fine Italian foods, with products sold at more than 8,000 retail outlets nationwide. She also owns four locations of KATIE'S Pizza & Pasta in her hometown of St. Louis. Her new book, Unemployable, is her first, and she has also commissioned an album, One Night at Katie's, with a documentary and cookbook in the works. The book recently sold out Target stores across the country after an exclusive month-long retail presence. The book is now available on Amazon and at Katies.com.

Katie Lee is the founder and CEO of Katie's Pizza & Pasta, a four-location restaurant group that has been operating for 18 years in St. Louis. She is also the founder and CEO of Katie's Fine Foods, an artisan Italian consumer packaged goods company leading four categories with 18 SKUs in 8,000 retail stores nationwide. Katie's is one of 20 brands in Target's Innovation Collective. She is an author and speaker whose new memoir, Unemployable, chronicles her struggle with addiction and her unconventional path to building one of the fastest-growing pizza companies in the nation. The book is available nationwide at Target and on Amazon. Katie leads a team of 500 employees, including a C-suite, a chef collective and an in-house media company of artists, designers and musicians. She owns her manufacturing plant and imports single-ingredient products from Italy. Katie's is 100% women owned.

About Katie'sKATIE'S is a chef-driven Italian restaurant and consumer packaged goods brand based in St. Louis. Founded by Katie Lee, the company is built on handmade techniques, rigorously sourced ingredients, and a belief that food should nourish both body and soul. Its restaurants are known for wood-fired pizzas and house-made pastas, while its fast-growing national retail line brings the same standards to grocery stores across America. KATIE'S is a WBENC-certified 100% women-owned business. To learn more, visit Katies.com and follow on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Facebook to see the latest.

#5518. Groundcover turns its Wand acquisition into a Kubernetes rightsizing beta

Observability company groundcover Inc. today added Autonomous Infrastructure to its platform in beta to rightsize the processor and memory requests automatically on customers’ Kubernetes workloads based on how each workload behaves in production.

The technology comes from Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd., which groundcover acquired in September.

The release is aimed at the processor and memory requests Kubernetes has engineers set for each workload up front, usually before it has handled any real traffic, and groundcover said most teams seldom return to those numbers. When one is set too low, the first sign is often a service throwing out-of-memory errors. Padding that goes unused ends up on the monthly cloud bill.

Because the groundcover sensor has been collecting production history all along, a customer on a supported version can open Autonomous Infrastructure for the first time without installing anything and find the data the feature needs already in place. Requested processor and memory for each workload appear next to actual usage. Estimated monthly savings sit beside a count of under-provisioned workloads, and a chart tracks over time how much of the potential saving has been realized.

Dollar figures in the beta are based on a price per processor and memory unit that customers enter themselves. Public cloud pricing is the next step, according to groundcover, and billing data such as the Cost and Usage Report from Amazon Web Services Inc. will come after that.

Most resource optimization tools size each workload in isolation, groundcover argues, so a request that looks right for one service can still starve its neighbors on a crowded node. Stability is the first constraint in groundcover’s own software. Before Autonomous Infrastructure raises a request, it checks how tightly the node is already packed so one workload’s increase does not leave the rest short of resources.

Shahar Azulay, groundcover’s co-founder and chief executive, said customers can check what their clusters stand to save, from data already held in their own cloud accounts, before they let Autonomous Infrastructure “change anything.” The feature stays off until an engineer turns it on and picks the deployments, namespaces or clusters it manages.

During the beta the software touches requests only and leaves limits where they are. Each policy carries minimum and maximum bounds for processor and memory, and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. Groundcover suggests starting with lower-risk workloads such as development namespaces and leaving alone something like a production database that needs room to grow.

The beta is available now at no additional cost to every groundcover customer running its sensor on Kubernetes, and the company is also recruiting design partners to work with its product team while it runs. Demonstrations are scheduled for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City Nov. 9-12.

Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

#5517. Corporate Technologies Offers Free IT and Cybersecurity Assessments to New Jersey Small Businesses

2026 MSP 501 MSP of the Year offers New Jersey businesses a no-cost, 30-minute review of IT setup, security gaps and per-user pricing

FAIRFIELD, N.J. , Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Corporate Technologies, a managed IT services and cybersecurity provider for businesses with 10 to 200 employees, today announced free IT and cybersecurity assessments for small and mid-sized businesses in New Jersey. The offer is backed by the company's Fairfield office at 55 Lane Road, which serves businesses in Fairfield, Newark, Paterson, Wayne, Parsippany, Morristown, Clifton, Montclair, Livingston, Caldwell, Hackensack and Jersey City.

Each assessment is a 30-minute review with a Corporate Technologies IT services specialist. It covers what the business runs today, where its security and compliance gaps are, and what fully managed IT would cost at a flat per-user, per-month rate, with onboarding and any hardware on the same proposal. A specialist calls back the same business day, and there is no obligation.

"Most business owners we meet don't know where their real IT risk is until something breaks," said Jim Griffith, CEO of Corporate Technologies. "A half hour with one of our IT services specialists gives a New Jersey business a straight answer on what's covered, what's exposed and what it costs, with no commitment."

The offer comes as confidence in recovery outpaces reality. Veeam's 2026 Data Trust and Resilience Report, cited in Corporate Technologies' Q2 2026 SMB Technology & Cyber Resilience Index, found that 90% of security leaders are confident they can recover from an attack, yet only 28% of organizations hit by ransomware fully restored their data.

Across the environments it manages, Corporate Technologies reports about 2.6 hours of downtime per client per year, compared with roughly 14 hours for the market. #5516. Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools

Snowflake Inc. today announced a sweeping collection of artificial intelligence capabilities designed to bring business context, governance and autonomous development into the same environment, as enterprises increasingly hand over software engineering and everyday operations to AI agents.

The announcements, during the company’s Expedition 2026 virtual conference, include a new Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering capabilities that allow AI agents to build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention.

The company is betting that more coders and engineers will use AI throughout the software development lifecycle as creation moves even faster, while other back-end departments begin to adopt agents in their day-to-day work. For example, sales operations are creating agents that can analyze sales risks and prepare customer outreach without writing code.

“AI is industrializing software creation. Actually, it’s industrializing intelligence,” Chief Executive Sridhar Ramaswamy said. “What once took months can now take hours, days, or even minutes.”

Ramaswamy noted that while AI is changing the economics of software development, as agents take over tasks usually relegated to specialized developers, business users become developers. This is changing the competitive landscape, meaning that the advantage no longer goes to specialists, but to proprietary knowledge.

Snowflake is taking the field by helping ordinary AI models understand and contextualize that business knowledge. It does this with Business Ontology, an extension of its existing semantic views that lets organizations establish approved definitions used across the organization. Without a standard definition, two agents could respond to the same business-related question with incompatible answers, even when both agents have accurate underlying data.

Using information from Business Ontology, Snowflake CoCo, the coding agent for data teams, and Snowflake CoWork, the personal work agent for knowledge workers, use these approved business concepts to ground their responses.

This new feature is currently in private preview, but is headed to public preview soon.

Cortex AI Gateway arrives to become a single front door for agents within an organization. It is not entirely new; Snowflake introduced it in July 2026 as a centralized way to govern and monitor agents.

Today’s announcement expands its capabilities rather than introducing the gateway for the first time. The new updates include agent abuse detection, observability and tracing, Cortex sandboxes, AI cost governance, dynamic model routing and tools integration using technology from Snowflake’s Natoma acquisition.

“An agent that acts on your business has to be trusted, and it has to know three important things: what the data means, which data to trust, and what it’s allowed to do,” said Ramaswamy.

The platform most importantly applies existing security mechanisms, including data masking and access restrictions, to agent-driven operations while adding capabilities to monitor activity, detect potential abuse and maintain records of what agents do. The information technology and security teams can also apply cost controls, select models based on efficiency or accuracy and restrict which external tools agents can access granularly.

The underlying role of this governance, control and transparency is aligned with giving agents the same sort of role observation granted to employees. Treating them similarly in terms of autonomy.

Snowflake’s push comes amid a broader industry race to establish the control layer for enterprise AI agents. SAP has been expanding its Autonomous Enterprise architecture and governed Joule agents, while Salesforce has introduced its Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane to secure autonomous workflows. Snowflake is approaching the same problem from the data platform side, seeking to become the foundation through which agents access trusted business information and operate under enterprise policies.

Snowflake also announced the public preview of Cortex Training, which will allow customers to tailor open-weight AI models with their own proprietary information.

The service is designed to make it simpler to create specialized models using post-training without needing vast arrays of graphics processing units. Snowflake lets them train models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Specialized, smaller models that come with more efficient responses, faster responses, and frequently cost benefits in terms of tokens,” Executive Vice President of Product Christian Kleinerman said.

Many enterprise companies will require sovereign control of their own AI models as increasing restrictions on foreign open-weight AI or regulations on handling sensitive information. It’s easier to audit what passes through an AI model on your own hardware than in a third-party vendor’s cloud.

Separately, Snowflake announced an expanded partnership with Oracle Corp. to make its platform available as a first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The integration will give customers easier access to Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities while allowing them to work directly through Oracle databases and applications.
