#5514. What 3 court rulings say about ballot selfies and photos at polling places

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ballot selfie laws vary by state, and court rulings, secret-ballot history and polling place rules explain what voters should know before posting a photo

A marked ballot is meant to stay private, and a phone camera makes it easy to share. That collision sits at the center of ballot selfie laws. A voter who wants to show support for a candidate can snap a picture in seconds. Whether that picture is legal depends on where the voter lives.

No federal statute settles whether a voter may photograph a ballot. States write the rules on photographing or sharing a marked ballot, and those rules differ from one state to the next. They have also changed over time. Legislatures rewrite statutes, and courts weigh in. Advice that was accurate in one election cycle may not hold in the next one.

The concern behind many restrictions is older than the smartphone by more than a century. The secret ballot spread across U.S. states in the late 1880s, and Massachusetts adopted it statewide in 1888. Its purpose was to curb vote buying and voter intimidation. A photo of a completed ballot could serve as proof of how someone voted. That proof is what a vote buyer would want before paying. Federal law already prohibits paying or offering payment for votes in federal elections. States have their own vote-buying laws as well.

Courts have shaped the edges of what states can do. In 2016, the First Circuit decided Rideout v. Gardner and struck down a 2014 New Hampshire law that barred voters from sharing images of their marked ballots. The court found that the law restricted speech based on its content and failed First Amendment review. The U.S. Supreme Court has addressed speech at the polls more broadly. In Burson v. Freeman in 1992, it upheld a Tennessee ban on campaign activity within 100 feet of polling place entrances. In Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky in 2018, it struck down a Minnesota ban on political apparel inside polling places by a 7-2 vote. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion, which found the ban's standard too vague.

The 20 slides that follow cover that history, those three cases and the practical questions voters face. Those questions range from wearing a campaign shirt to photographing a mail-in ballot at home to posting an "I voted" picture. This guide does not replace the current rules where you vote. A state or local election office is the place to confirm what is allowed before casting a ballot.

No federal law bans or allows ballot selfies. Each state decides whether a voter may photograph a marked ballot or share that image online. The answers vary across the country.

That split follows from how the U.S. runs elections. Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution, known as the Elections Clause, gives state legislatures the power to set the times, places and manner of congressional elections. Congress can alter those rules. In practice, it has left most of the day-to-day mechanics of voting to the states.

Congress has passed major election laws. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 targeted racial discrimination in voting. The National Voter Registration Act of 1993 set rules for registering voters, including registration at motor vehicle offices. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 set standards for voting equipment and created the Election Assistance Commission. None of these laws addresses whether a voter can take a picture of a completed ballot.

Because of that gap, ballot selfie rules come from state statutes and from the procedures of election officials. Secretaries of state or state election boards generally oversee voting statewide. Local offices, usually at the county or municipal level, run polling places. A rule about phones or cameras can come from a law passed by a legislature or from instructions issued to poll workers.

State rules also reach federal races. A voter choosing a president or a member of Congress usually marks the same ballot that lists state and local contests. That ballot falls under the photo rules of the state where it is cast, not under a national standard.

The practical result is that a ballot selfie allowed in one state may break the rules in another. Before taking out a phone in the voting booth, check with your state or local election office for the rules that apply where you vote.

Ballot photo rules are not fixed. Each state sets its own limits on photographing or sharing a marked ballot. Those limits differ across state lines, and some have been rewritten or struck down over the years.

The state-by-state approach means a voter who moves also moves into a different set of rules. A picture that was allowed at a polling place in one state may be restricted at a polling place in another.

These rules can change in two main ways. A legislature can pass a new law, amend an old one or repeal one entirely. A court can also rule that a law violates the Constitution, which bars officials from enforcing it. Either route means a rule in force during one election may not apply in the next.

A court ruling does not erase a statute's wording. The text of a law struck down by a judge can stay in a state's printed code until lawmakers formally remove it. Reading the statute alone can point a voter to a rule that officials can no longer enforce.

That history has practical consequences. A news article or social media post from a past election may describe a rule that no longer applies. A friend's advice may reflect the law where that friend votes, not where you vote. Even your own memory of a previous election can be out of date.

The details of a rule can matter as much as its existence. A state's limits may focus on taking a photo inside the voting booth, on sharing an image afterward or on both. Two voters in different states could take the same picture and fall under different rules.

The most current source is the guidance published by your state or local election office. Check it shortly before you vote rather than relying on what applied the last time you cast a ballot.

The secret ballot, adopted across U.S. states in the late 1880s, is the historical root of limits on photographing a marked ballot. Its purpose was to keep each vote private so that no one could buy it or force it. That goal still shapes ballot photo rules today.

Before the reform, American voting looked very different. Political parties commonly printed their own ballots, often called tickets, and handed them to supporters to cast. Tickets from rival parties could differ in color, size or paper. Anyone standing near the ballot box could often tell which party a voter backed.

That openness created leverage. A party agent who paid for a vote could watch to confirm that the voter followed through. An employer or local political boss could see whether people under their influence voted as told. The choice belonged to the voter on paper, but it was frequently made in public view.

The fix American reformers borrowed is often called the Australian ballot. The colonies of Victoria and South Australia introduced it in 1856. Under that system, the government prints a single official ballot listing every candidate. Voters receive it at the polling place and mark it in private.

Massachusetts adopted the secret ballot statewide in 1888. Other states moved to the same model in the years that followed. Private, government-printed ballots became the standard way Americans vote.

A phone photo of a completed ballot can restore the evidence the reform was designed to eliminate. The image shows each choice and can be sent to anyone in seconds. That possibility is the concern behind bans on photographing or sharing a marked ballot, even when the voter only wants to celebrate.

Courts have since weighed that historical interest against voters' free-speech rights, and the resulting rules differ by state. Before photographing a ballot, check the current rule with your state or local election office.

A photo of a completed ballot can show another person exactly how a voter marked it. That turns a private choice into a checkable record. This is the central worry behind rules that limit ballot photos: the image could prove a vote to someone paying for it or pressuring the voter.

The secret ballot works by making each vote impossible to confirm. Once a voter marks a ballot alone and casts it, no one else can know for certain which candidates were chosen. A voter can tell a friend, a relative or an employer anything about that choice, and no one can check.

That uncertainty is the point. A person who wants to buy a vote has no way to know whether the deal was kept. A voter offered money can take it and still vote freely. The arrangement cannot be reliably enforced. That removes much of the reason to attempt it.

A clear image of a marked ballot changes that. If a buyer demands a picture as a condition of payment, the voter can no longer quietly vote another way. The photo becomes a receipt.

The same logic applies to intimidation. Someone with power over a voter — a boss, a landlord or a family member — could insist on seeing a ballot photo. Without that option, the voter can say whatever keeps the peace and still vote privately. With it, that protection weakens.

The proof-of-vote concern does not mean every ballot selfie is tied to wrongdoing. A voter who photographs a ballot may simply want to share that choice publicly. Courts have weighed that kind of personal expression against a state's interest in preventing fraud. The balance has not always favored a ban.

Ballot photo rules come from state law. A state or local election office can confirm the current policy before a voter takes out a phone in the voting booth.

Federal law makes it a crime to pay someone, or to offer to pay someone, for their vote in a federal election. The ban targets the deal itself, not the camera. A ballot photo matters to this law only when the picture is used to prove that a vote was cast as promised.

Federal elections are the contests for federal offices, including president, the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House. Many ballots list those races alongside state and local contests on the same sheet of paper. A single picture of a marked ballot can capture choices in races covered by the federal ban and in races governed only by state law.

The federal prohibition says nothing directly about photographing a ballot. Its focus is payment for a vote. A voter who takes a picture of a ballot without any payment or offer involved is not making the kind of exchange that this law describes.

The offer alone can be the violation. A payment does not have to change hands, and no photo has to exist, for an offer to pay for a vote to fall under the ban. A picture of a marked ballot sent to the person paying would work as a receipt for the transaction. That receipt scenario is the link between the federal ban and the wider debate over ballot pictures.

States have their own vote-buying laws. Each legislature sets the wording and scope of its own statute. As a result, the details are not uniform from state to state. A voter cannot assume that the rules in one state match those in another.

Questions about how vote-buying rules and any ballot photo restrictions apply in a particular place are best directed to the county or state office that runs elections there. Anyone offered money for a vote, or for proof of a vote, can report the offer to those officials.

Rideout v. Gardner is the 2016 federal appeals court decision that struck down New Hampshire's ban on sharing images of marked ballots. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit held that the law could not survive review under the First Amendment.

New Hampshire law had long barred voters from showing a marked ballot to others in order to reveal how they voted. The legislature extended that rule in 2014. The new language barred voters from sharing images of their own completed ballots, including on social media. That covered the act most people mean by a ballot selfie: showing a filled-in ballot to other people.

The case name reflects the two sides. Leon Rideout, a New Hampshire state representative, was the lead challenger. Gardner refers to William Gardner, then New Hampshire's secretary of state and the state's chief election official.

Rideout was not a hypothetical plaintiff. He posted a photo of his own marked ballot on Twitter $TWTR during New Hampshire's 2014 primary, after the new law had taken effect. Another challenger, Andrew Langlois, photographed a ballot on which he had written in the name of his dog, Stella, as a protest vote. Both men had shared the kind of image the statute targeted.

The ACLU of New Hampshire represented the challengers. A federal district court in New Hampshire ruled against the law first. The state appealed, and the First Circuit affirmed that decision. Judge Sandra Lynch wrote the appeals court's opinion.

The challenge was a free speech case, not a dispute over vote counting or election results. Neither challenger argued that any ballot had been miscounted. The question was whether the state could punish voters for showing others how they had voted.

Anyone voting in New Hampshire today should confirm the current rule with the secretary of state's office or a town or city clerk. The 2016 decision describes what the court held about one law at one point in time, not what applies at the polls now.

The First Circuit treated New Hampshire's ballot selfie ban as a content-based restriction on speech. In Rideout v. Gardner, decided in 2016, the court concluded that the 2014 law failed First Amendment review and struck it down.

A content-based law singles out speech because of what it says or shows. New Hampshire's measure did not stop voters from taking photos in general. It targeted one category of image — a picture of a voter's own marked ballot — and barred voters from sharing it. The subject of the picture was what made sharing it illegal.

That label carries weight in First Amendment cases. Courts sort speech restrictions into categories, and the category shapes how hard the government must work to defend a law. Content-based rules generally face the most demanding review, often called strict scrutiny. Under that test, the government has to show that the law serves a compelling interest. It also has to show that the law is narrowly tailored to that interest.

Content-neutral rules sit in a different category. A limit on the time, place or manner of speech, such as a cap on loudspeaker volume near a building, applies no matter what message the speaker carries. Rules of that kind usually face a less exacting test.

Narrow tailoring is often where a speech restriction runs into trouble. A law can fall short when it reaches far more speech than the problem it targets. It can also fall short when it burdens people who pose no risk of the harm the government describes. A state's goal can be legitimate while the law written to serve it still sweeps too broadly.

Placing the ballot photo ban in the content-based category did not erase New Hampshire's interest in protecting the integrity of voting. It meant the state had to justify banning the image itself under heightened review. The First Circuit held that the state had not met that burden, and the ban on sharing marked-ballot images fell.

For a voter outside New Hampshire, the ruling shows the kind of argument that can be raised against a ballot photo ban. It does not describe the law in any other state. The agency that runs elections where you vote can tell you the rule that currently applies.

A federal appeals court decision binds only the courts within its own circuit. Rideout v. Gardner, the First Circuit's 2016 ruling against New Hampshire's ballot selfie ban, did not automatically strike down similar laws in other parts of the U.S.

The federal court system has 13 courts of appeals. Eleven are numbered circuits, and each one covers a group of states and territories. The other two are the D.C. Circuit and the Federal Circuit. The Federal Circuit hears certain specialized cases, such as patent appeals. A ruling from one circuit sets binding precedent for the federal district courts inside its boundaries. It does not bind district courts or appeals courts in other circuits.

That geography matters for anyone reading about Rideout. The case involved a 2014 New Hampshire law that barred voters from sharing images of their marked ballots. New Hampshire sits within the First Circuit. The ruling applied there directly.

A court in another circuit may treat Rideout as persuasive authority. Judges often read how other circuits worked through a similar question. They can adopt that reasoning if they find it convincing, and they are also free to reject it. When two circuits reach opposite answers on the same federal question, lawyers call the result a circuit split. A conflict among the circuits is one of the reasons the Supreme Court weighs when deciding whether to hear a case. The Supreme Court is the only court whose rulings on federal constitutional questions bind courts across the whole country.

A court ruling also addresses the specific law in front of it. A statute with different wording, a different purpose or a narrower scope would have to be challenged and judged on its own terms. A state law that no court has struck down remains in effect.

For voters, a news story about one court case is not a reliable guide to the law where they live. The state or local election office is the place to confirm which ballot photo rules apply on voting day.

In Burson v. Freeman, decided in 1992, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a Tennessee law that banned campaign activity within 100 feet of the entrance to a polling place. The ruling is a leading case on how far a state may limit political speech just outside the polls.

The Tennessee law barred soliciting votes and displaying or distributing campaign materials inside that zone on Election Day. Mary Rebecca Freeman, a campaign treasurer, challenged it under the First Amendment. The Tennessee Supreme Court sided with her and struck the law down. Charles Burson, the state's attorney general, took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The justices reversed that decision by a 5-3 vote. Justice Clarence Thomas did not take part. Justice Harry Blackmun wrote a plurality opinion joined by Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justices Byron White and Anthony Kennedy.

Blackmun's opinion treated the law as a content-based restriction on political speech in a public forum. That classification triggers strict scrutiny, the toughest standard of First Amendment review. The plurality held that Tennessee's buffer zone passed that test. It found that the state had compelling interests in protecting voters from intimidation and in preventing election fraud.

To support those interests, the plurality traced the history of election reform in the U.S., including the adoption of the secret ballot. It concluded that some restricted zone around polling places was necessary to serve those goals. It also declined to make Tennessee prove that a smaller zone would have worked just as well.

Justice Antonin Scalia agreed with the outcome on different grounds. He argued that the area around a polling place is not a traditional public forum. Justice John Paul Stevens dissented, joined by Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and David Souter.

The case dealt with campaigning, not cameras. It did not address photographing a ballot or posting that image online. The 100-foot figure comes from Tennessee's statute, and other states write their own buffer rules. A county or state election office can confirm the distance and the activities covered where you vote.

States have considerable power to limit speech at and around polling places, but that power has limits. The U.S. Supreme Court has upheld a buffer zone against campaigning near polling place entrances. It has also struck down a polling place rule written too vaguely to apply fairly.

The broad authority traces to Burson v. Freeman, a 1992 Supreme Court case. The Court upheld a Tennessee law that banned campaign activity in a zone around polling place entrances. Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the plurality opinion. It treated the law as a content-based restriction on political speech. It applied the strictest level of First Amendment review and still let the law stand.

That outcome matters because content-based limits on political speech are usually the hardest kind of law to defend in court. The plurality accepted that a state has a compelling interest in letting people vote freely for the candidates they choose. It also recognized the state's interest in protecting elections from intimidation and fraud. Those concerns are sharpest right outside the door where voters enter.

The principle has a physical boundary. The Tennessee law covered the area near polling place entrances, not public speech in general. Burson does not give states a general license to restrict political talk. The 100-foot distance came from Tennessee's statute, and it is not a national standard.

The power also has a drafting limit. In Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, decided in 2018, the Supreme Court struck down a Minnesota ban on political apparel in polling places. The problem was a standard too vague to apply reasonably. The Court did not reject the idea of regulating expression inside a polling place.

Limits on photographing a marked ballot touch the same interests Burson recognized: a secret vote cast free of pressure. Courts can still reject a specific rule. In 2016, the First Circuit struck down New Hampshire's ban on sharing images of marked ballots in Rideout v. Gardner. That law targeted what voters shared, rather than activity in a zone around the polls.

Each state writes its own polling place rules. Their reach differs from place to place. A voter unsure what is allowed at a particular polling site can confirm it with the state or county election office before voting.

In Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, decided in 2018, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Minnesota's ban on wearing political apparel inside polling places. The vote was 7-2.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion. The Court found the Minnesota ban unreasonable. The deciding problem was the standard the state used to define political apparel, which the Court held was too vague.

The Minnesota law barred voters from wearing a political badge, political button or other political insignia at the polling place. The challenge came from the Minnesota Voters Alliance and voters including Andrew Cilek. Cilek went to vote wearing a Tea Party Patriots shirt and a button reading "Please I.D. Me." A poll worker told him the items broke the ban.

The Court treated the inside of a polling place as a nonpublic forum. In that kind of government space, a state may limit speech if the limit is reasonable and does not target particular viewpoints. The majority accepted that Minnesota had a legitimate interest in keeping the polling place orderly.

The trouble was the undefined word "political." Election judges had to decide what fit that word on the spot. The Court found that discretion too open-ended to be applied evenly from one voter to the next.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justice Stephen Breyer. She would have asked the Minnesota Supreme Court to interpret the state law before the justices ruled on it.

The ruling did not give voters an unlimited right to wear anything they choose while casting a ballot. The flaw lay in how Minnesota drew its line, not in the decision to draw one.

The case concerned clothing, not cameras, and it did not address ballot selfies. Its link to ballot photo rules is a principle: a limit on expression at the polls can fail when its terms are too loose to apply consistently. The decision addressed one state's law. Rules elsewhere, and any later changes in Minnesota, are questions for the election office that serves a given voter.

The Supreme Court's 2018 ruling in Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky did not strip states of the power to limit expression inside polling places. It struck down one Minnesota ban on political apparel because the ban's standard was too vague.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion for the Court. It found the Minnesota ban unreasonable. The flaw lay in how the ban was written, not in the idea of regulating what voters display at the polls.

The distinction shapes how the case is read. A headline saying the Court struck down a polling place apparel ban can sound like a broad win for voters who want to wear political messages to vote. The opinion did not go that far. It did not say that states may never regulate expression inside polling places.

The decision turned on vagueness. A vague standard can leave much to the judgment of whoever enforces it on election day. The Court treated the vagueness of Minnesota's standard as the reason its ban was unreasonable.

The ruling also leaves lawmakers a path. A state that wants to limit apparel at the polls can try to write a standard that spells out more clearly what is covered. A clearer rule gives poll workers and voters a firmer guide to what is allowed.

Mansky also fits with an earlier Supreme Court ruling. In Burson v. Freeman, the Court upheld a Tennessee law that limited campaign activity near polling place entrances. Read together, the two cases show that states keep room to regulate speech at the polls. How a rule is drafted can still decide whether it survives a challenge.

Mansky concerned clothing, not cameras. It did not address ballot selfies or photos taken inside a voting booth. Rules on those questions come from state law, and they can differ from one state to the next. Voters with questions about what they may wear or photograph can get a current answer from the election office that runs voting where they live.

Whether you can wear a campaign shirt, hat or button while you vote depends on the rules where you cast your ballot. No national standard settles the question. The answer comes from state and local election law.

The U.S. Supreme Court addressed political clothing at the polls in Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky in 2018. It struck down Minnesota's ban on political apparel inside polling places. The ban failed because its standard was too vague. It did not give voters or poll workers a clear way to tell which items crossed the line.

The ruling was narrow in an important sense. It did not give voters an unlimited right to wear political messages while voting. It also did not bar states from regulating expression inside polling places. The decision leaves room for a state rule on campaign gear that draws its line more clearly than Minnesota's did.

Burson v. Freeman, a 1992 Supreme Court case, came at the question from another angle. The Court upheld a Tennessee law that created a campaign-free zone around polling place entrances. That case involved campaign activity rather than clothing. Its distance applied only to Tennessee's law. The case does show that the Court has accepted limits on campaigning right at the polls.

Neither case hands voters a single national rule on what to wear. The two decisions mark the outer limits of state power. The specific rules on shirts, hats and buttons are written closer to home, and they can vary from place to place.

A precise question gets a precise answer. Before voting day, ask your state or local election office whether clothing, hats or buttons that name a candidate, party or ballot measure are allowed inside the polling place. If the answer is unclear, leaving campaign items at home avoids the issue.

A photo that captures another voter or another person's marked ballot raises a different problem from a selfie with your own ballot. A voter can choose to reveal their own vote. Exposing someone else's vote takes that choice away from them.

The secret ballot exists to keep each person's vote known only to that person. Its aim was to curb vote buying and intimidation. That protection belongs to every voter in the room, not only to the one holding the camera.

A stray image can undercut that protection for someone who never agreed to it. A wide shot of a voting area could catch a marked ballot on a nearby table or a screen in the next booth. The person in the frame may also be identifiable from their face or clothing. That ties the visible ballot to a specific individual. Once posted online, an image can be copied, saved and shared far beyond the person who took it.

The intimidation concern applies here as well. A voter who believes they are being watched or recorded may feel pressure about how they mark their ballot. Removing that kind of pressure was one of the reasons the secret ballot was adopted.

Rideout v. Gardner, a First Circuit case that struck down New Hampshire's ban on sharing images of marked ballots, centered on voters' own ballots. It did not decide how a court would treat a photo that exposes another person's vote.

Rules on photographing other voters, or on taking any pictures inside a polling place, are set by states. The answer is not uniform nationwide. A poll worker on site or the local election office can say what is allowed before a phone comes out.

Keeping the frame on your own ballot, or skipping photos inside the polling place entirely, avoids capturing anyone else's vote.

No single national rule covers photographing a mail-in or absentee ballot at home. The answer depends on the state that issued the ballot and on how that state's law is worded.

A ballot marked at a kitchen table is still a marked ballot. Many ballot photo limits rest on one worry: an image could show someone else exactly how a person voted. That worry does not go away when the voting happens on a couch instead of inside a booth.

Home voting also removes a layer of oversight. At a polling place, election workers staff the room and voters mark their ballots in a private booth. At home, no official is present while the ballot is filled out. A photo is one of the few ways another person could confirm the choices on a mailed ballot.

Vote-buying laws do not turn on where a ballot is marked. A picture of a finished absentee ballot handed over in exchange for money or a favor can raise the same legal problem as one taken at the polls.

A separate question is whether a state treats a private photo of a home ballot differently from one taken at the polls. The answer turns on the exact wording of that state's law.

Voters who want a firm answer can start with the instructions that came with the ballot. If those instructions say nothing about photos, the county or state election office that mailed the ballot can explain the current rule. Asking before taking the picture matters. A ballot image that has already been posted or sent cannot be made private again.

Whether you can post a photo of your marked ballot online depends on the state where you vote. No federal law answers the question. Each state's own rules control instead.

The sharing of a ballot image, not just the act of taking one, was the conduct at issue in Rideout v. Gardner. New Hampshire had passed a law that barred voters from sharing images of their marked ballots. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit struck that law down.

The court classified the ban as a restriction on speech based on its content. It found that the New Hampshire law failed review under the First Amendment. The case treated a voter's posted ballot image as a form of speech.

That decision came from one regional federal appeals court. It did not set a national rule for what voters everywhere may post online.

The concern behind limits on sharing is proof. A picture of a completed ballot shows exactly how a person voted. That image could serve as evidence for someone who paid for the vote. Federal law bars paying or offering payment for votes in federal elections, and states have their own vote-buying laws.

Posting a ballot photo also differs from keeping one on a phone. A social media post can reach people the voter never intended to show it to. Other users can save or copy it. Deleting the post later does not remove copies that others have already made.

Rules on ballot photos can also treat taking a picture and sharing it as separate acts. New Hampshire's law was aimed at sharing images of marked ballots. A state's rules could address the photo, the post or both.

Before you post, ask your state or local election office whether its rules cover photographing a ballot, sharing one or both. Ask too whether those rules differ for ballots cast in person and ballots returned by mail.

No single national rule decides whether a voter may use a phone or camera inside a polling place. State and local election rules set those limits. Before taking out a device, ask a poll worker or your local election office what is allowed where you vote.

Courts have given states wide room to regulate expression at voting sites. In Burson v. Freeman, the Supreme Court upheld Tennessee's ban on campaign activity near polling place entrances. In Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, it struck down Minnesota's ban on political apparel inside polling places. The court's objection was the vagueness of the ban's standard. It did not bar states from regulating expression inside polling places.

Neither case involved cameras or phones. A device rule still operates inside the legal space those rulings describe. That space allows limits on conduct at the polls, but it expects them to be written clearly enough to apply.

Taking a picture is a separate act from posting it. Rideout v. Gardner involved a New Hampshire law against sharing images of marked ballots. A rule about using a device in the voting area raises a different question. A ruling about what voters may post online does not answer whether a phone may come out in the room.

A phone raised in a crowded voting area can capture more than one ballot. The secret ballot exists so that no one else can see how a person voted. A camera pointed across the room can expose the choices of nearby voters, not only those of the person holding it.

Poll workers apply the rules at each site on voting day. They are the people to ask in the moment. Read any posted notices at the entrance or near the booths before voting. A voter who is unsure can keep the phone put away while marking a ballot.

The most reliable answer on ballot selfies comes from the government office that runs elections in your state. Start with your state's chief election official, then confirm the details with the county or local office that manages your polling place.

In many states, the chief election official is the secretary of state. Other states give that job to a state board of elections or a similar commission. Whatever its name, that office usually publishes voter guides, answers to common questions and the text of state election law on its website. A search for your state's name plus "election office" or "secretary of state elections" will generally surface the official site. Look for a government web address rather than a campaign, advocacy or commercial page before relying on what it says.

Several national directories point voters to those offices. Vote.gov, a federal website, routes visitors to their own state's election information. The U.S. Election Assistance Commission maintains contact details for state election offices. CanIVote.org, run by the National Association of Secretaries of State, links to official state voter resources.

Day-to-day election administration in the U.S. happens closer to home. Counties run elections in most states, while cities or towns handle the job in some others. That local office staffs polling places, trains poll workers and can explain how a state rule is applied at a specific site. Its phone number often appears on sample ballots and mailed election notices.

When a question involves the law itself, ask the office to point you to the specific statute or written guidance. A written source can be checked. A recollection from a neighbor or a post on social media cannot. Written guidance also gives you something concrete to show a poll worker if a question comes up on Election Day.

Timing matters too. Legislatures can amend election laws between voting cycles. Courts can also strike down rules that remain on the books, as the First Circuit did with a ballot photo ban in Rideout v. Gardner. Checking shortly before you vote gives the best chance of finding the current rule rather than an outdated one.

A short call or email to your county or local election office can settle what general guides cannot. Ask three things: whether you may photograph your own marked ballot, whether you may share that image and whether your phone may be out at all inside the polling place.

Those three questions are separate, and the answers may not match. A rule may allow a phone in the building while barring its use in the voting booth. A rule may also treat taking a picture differently from posting one. The New Hampshire law struck down in Rideout v. Gardner targeted the sharing of marked-ballot images. That case shows why the distinction is worth raising.

Ask next whether the answer changes with the way you vote. Early voting sites, Election Day precincts and mail or absentee ballots filled out at home may fall under different rules or different interpretations. If you plan to vote by mail, ask the office directly how it treats a photo of a ballot marked at your kitchen table.

Clothing is worth a question too. Ask whether a campaign shirt, hat or button is permitted inside your polling place. Ask how far from the entrance campaign activity is restricted. The Supreme Court upheld Tennessee's campaign-free zone in Burson v. Freeman, but that case did not set one distance for every state.

If you plan to bring a child or another person into the booth, ask whether that is permitted and whether a photo that includes them is allowed. Ask as well whether other voters may appear in the background of a picture taken in line or inside the building.

Ask whether the office has its answer in writing, such as a page on its website or a section of state election law. Written wording lets you read the exact rule rather than rely on a summary.

Write down the date of the conversation and the name or title of the person who answered. Rules can change between elections. An answer from a previous cycle may not hold this time. Repeat the questions before each election you vote in.

A photo that shows you voted, rather than how you voted, avoids the main concern behind ballot photo limits. An "I voted" sticker selfie or a picture taken outside the polling place records none of the choices on your ballot.

That difference ties back to the secret ballot. Its purpose was to keep each voter's choices private. Private choices make vote buying and intimidation harder to carry out. A sticker on a jacket reveals participation, not preferences.

Someone paying for votes would want evidence of how a ballot was marked before handing over money. A picture with no ballot in view gives that person nothing to verify.

Where the photo is taken still matters. Rules on phones and cameras inside polling places come from states and local officials. A sticker selfie snapped inside the building falls under those rules like any other picture. Waiting until after leaving the building takes the rules written for the voting room out of the equation.

The area just outside the entrance can carry its own limits. In Burson v. Freeman, the Supreme Court upheld Tennessee's ban on campaign activity near polling place entrances. The ruling confirmed that states have room to restrict electioneering at the polls. A plain "I voted" photo carries no campaign message. A shot that includes candidate signs, campaign shirts or buttons is a different kind of image. Where campaign-free areas begin and end depends on state law.

Campaign clothing worn inside the polling place raises a related question. In Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, the Supreme Court found Minnesota's political apparel ban too vague. The ruling did not bar states from regulating expression inside polling places.

Court rulings on ballot photos have focused on marked ballots. Rideout v. Gardner, the First Circuit case over New Hampshire's law, concerned images of completed ballots, not stickers. None of these cases addresses sticker photos directly, and none guarantees that a given voting photo is allowed.

Framing the shot to show only yourself and your sticker also keeps other voters and their ballots out of the picture. A county or local election office can confirm where photos are allowed at a specific polling place and whether the building posts its own restrictions.

#5512. LiveX brings engaging, AI-powered intelligent human-sized avatar kiosks to retail and airport sites

Palo Alto-based LiveX AI Inc., a company building interactive experience artificial intelligence agents for retail and hospitality environments, today announced AI City, its kiosk-driven, life-size, human-like AI hosts.

The company’s products, currently deployed in more than 100 sites, engage guests through life-sized human avatars across retail, technology, hospitality and entertainment. Customer sites include PUMA stores, San José Mineta International Airport, SAP Center, the San Jose Sharks stadium, El Camino Hospital, and Marriott and Hilton hotels.

“We believe intelligence of this nature should meet people wherever they are, live and in person, where life happens,” said President and Chief AI Officer Jia Li. “AI should be greeting travelers at the airport, guiding a grandmother through the hospital, helping every shopper like the best employee in the building or answering sixty thousand fans at once.”

A traditional interactive kiosk relies on rigid menus and doesn’t converse with the user; it also doesn’t automatically translate into the user’s native language by simply listening to them speak. An AI City kiosk can see and hear the other person and react almost like another person, using real-time discovery to provide personalized help.

The company added that these kiosks are coming as companies try to bring other physical AI products, such as general-purpose robotics, to market, but these are still years away from widespread deployment.

As a kiosk, a user could walk up and see a projected AI person who can assist with navigation, product recommendations, event guidance or answer questions about the venue. According to LiveX, the City kiosk products have been expanded with interactive 3D maps for location-aware navigation and discovery, 3D products and multilingual translation.

LiveX said such a system could assist customers with product, venue and event questions, enabling staff to walk around with more customers at the site and handle more complex problems requiring deeper oversight.

“AI that can understand people and their surroundings is opening new ways to make everyday spaces more helpful and accessible,” said Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia Corp.

The LiveX Interactive Intelligence platform runs on Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition graphics processing units and uses the Metropolis VSS Blueprint to build visual AI agents powered by Nvidia Cosmos, an open world model builder. Nvidia also provided a surface for supplying libraries from Omniverse, which delivers digital twins for location-aware applications.

LiveX said its platform brings together proprietary models it developed and trained for human interaction, shaped on real-world interaction data and experience through live deployments. Its Omni Model provides multimodal understanding and responses, while a noise management model lets it assist users even with significant background noise.

#5510. Starbucks is pulling its plant-based breakfast sandwich from U.S. menus

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Impossible Foods sausage sandwich, introduced in 2020, was the only item on Starbucks' advertised U.S. menu with plant-based meat

Starbucks $SBUX is dropping the breakfast sandwich built around Impossible Foods' plant-based sausage patty, according to Bloomberg. The sandwich will be retired over the course of this month.

Starbucks introduced the sandwich in 2020, according to Bloomberg. It was the lone offering on the company's advertised U.S. menu to include plant-based meat. Starbucks also sells meat-free choices, among them a sandwich of egg, pesto and mozzarella.

"While we no longer offer the Impossible Breakfast Sandwich, our baristas would be happy to recommend an alternative sandwich," Starbucks said in an email, according to Bloomberg. The company also said it regularly reviews what it sells and applies "various criteria to ensure we are meeting the needs of our customers and our business," according to Bloomberg.

Impossible Foods said in a statement that it was "proud to have partnered with Starbucks for more than six years" and is "committed to making delicious, nutrient-dense meat from plants more accessible," according to Bloomberg.

The move joins a growing list of restaurant chains that have backed off plant-based meat, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg said the industry has been hurt by shrinking consumer appetite, as diners step back from items that replicate how meat tastes and feels and restaurants cut them over sluggish sales. Many consumers have also become distrustful of heavily processed foods, among them certain plant-based meats that carry lengthy ingredient lists.

#5508. IBM puts agentic workloads at the heart of its AI operating model

Agentic workloads present a new operating challenge for enterprises putting artificial intelligence into production. As autonomous systems take on ongoing responsibilities, organizations must support decisions and actions across their data, applications and infrastructure.

IBM Corp.’s approach draws on the experiences of clients scaling AI across their organizations. That work helped identify the requirements underpinning its AI operating model, according to Ritika Gunnar (pictured), chief performance marketing officer of IBM.

“As you’re more successful in using AI, especially as AI is taking action, you now have workloads that are continuously being utilized,” she said. “You are incented to be always on because those agents are always taking action for you.”

Gunnar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier for IBM’s AI Operating Model interview series in an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed enterprise integration, data governance, human oversight and evaluating AI against business outcomes in preparation for IBM TechXchange 2026. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM’s AI operating model brings together four components that enterprises may already obtain from different providers. Applying them means accounting for established applications and business processes alongside emerging AI systems, Gunnar explained.

“You need to be able to integrate with your existing systems,” she said. “People aren’t going to run away from their SAP systems that exist, from their Salesforce systems that exist. What does it mean to integrate with those and have workloads that are representative of your past and your future together?”

The components have distinct roles: Data supplies current enterprise knowledge, workloads encompass applications and workflows, automation supports oversight and optimization, and hybrid cloud accommodates distributed operations. Their effectiveness depends on how they function together across agentic workloads, according to Gunnar.

“If you have your data and that data is feeding your systems, but you’re not really taking care of automation in a way where you have complete observability of all of your workloads with that AI infused, then you’re not necessarily having an optimal way of picking the right model or picking the right agents for those kinds of workloads,” she said.

The information supporting an agent’s decision may span operational systems, edge devices and context generated by other agents. Providing governed context requires enterprises to consider both the completeness of that information and how permissions travel with it, Gunnar explained.

“Our belief is if you can take data and if you can shift left a lot of the governance — a lot of the who has the right access to the right data at the right time — it becomes important because you flow that data in real time with the context and provenance of who actually has ownership of that data,” she said. “Therefore, the agents make much better decisions.”

Enterprises also depend on knowledge employees develop through experience rather than explicitly recording it in their systems. Prompts and other context can help convey that judgment, but capturing it remains an ongoing challenge, Gunnar pointed out.

“When you think about workloads today … there is a lot of it that will be autonomous in nature,” she said. “But in most cases, if you’re talking about your essential systems, you do have humans in the loop to be able to bring some of that tacit knowledge in place where the AI has not yet matured to be able to even get there.”

Agent activity generates logs of decisions and actions, while prompts record the instructions supplied to those systems. Together, that information supports an ongoing feedback loop between enterprise data and AI workloads, Gunnar explained.

“You can actually have multiple different permutations of that agent making a decision and having another set of eval loops actually doing an evaluation of, ‘Did that agent actually make the decisions?’” she said. “Would there have been a more performant way, a more accurate way, a more cost-effective way to be able to do that?”

Performance encompasses accuracy, timeliness and cost, with the intended business result guiding how those measures are assessed. Putting AI into production therefore requires organizations to examine the work itself alongside the technology supporting it, according to Gunnar.

“Make sure that you have all of these elements and that you’re really thinking about the outcomes, and you’re willing to start with what it means to take a look at the business process transformation,” she said. “That’s really where it’s at.”

#5507. 11 states compared on health care in 2026, from New Hampshire to Alaska

Free daily briefing on global business news.

See how New Hampshire, Minnesota, Iowa, Alaska, and seven other states fared in a 2026 study of health care cost, access, and outcomes.

A routine checkup can turn into a budgeting exercise the moment the bill arrives. Millions of Americans live with that tension, trying to get the treatment they need without draining their savings. Affordable options remain hard to find, and the search does not stop at one appointment. Premiums, prescriptions, and follow-up visits keep coming long after the first exam. A careful family can plan every expense and still feel squeezed by the total. The stakes stretch past money. A bill that strains a budget can force difficult choices about which visits to keep and which to postpone.

Geography shapes much of the answer. Medical charges differ across the country, and some places deliver care for less than others. Two households with identical needs can pay different amounts based on nothing more than their address. Spending tells part of the story. A cheap appointment means little if the nearest clinic sits hours away or no provider can fit a patient in for weeks. Access carries as much weight as the price tag. Results deserve equal attention. Residents want to live long lives and avoid serious illness. A state that keeps charges low while its people grow sick has solved half the problem. Any fair verdict on a health system has to weigh what residents pay, whether they can reach a provider, and what shape they end up in.

WalletHub, a personal finance website, set out to measure those three dimensions in a new report on the best and worst states for health care in 2026. The analysis compared all 50 states and Washington, D.C., across 44 key metrics. Each measure belongs to one of three categories: cost, access, and outcomes. Every metric received a grade on a 100-point scale, and a perfect score represents the best care at a reasonable price. The report named 10 states at the top of its list and 10 at the bottom. This article examines 11 of them.

The analysis rates New Hampshire's health care first in the country, and its residents have fewer strokes than people in any other state. Stroke is one of several measures on which New Hampshire beats every rival. Residents pay the lowest average monthly health insurance premium in the country, at $469, and the state counts the most urgent care centers per capita certified by the Urgent Care Association of America. First-place marks in outcomes, cost, and access show that the state's top finish draws on every category the study weighs.

Heart attacks and type 2 diabetes show the same favorable pattern in New Hampshire. Only three states have fewer residents who have had a heart attack, and the same number post a lower prevalence of type 2 diabetes. Low rates across three separate chronic conditions suggest the state's edge in outcomes reaches beyond any single disease. On each of these indicators, New Hampshire sits among a small cluster of states at the healthy end of the scale.

New Hampshire patients can draw on a deep pool of trained clinicians. The state has the fifth-most physician assistants per capita in the U.S. and the 10th-most nurses per capita. Both professions land inside the top 10, so the state's staffing advantage does not rest on one occupation. Each count scales to population, which means it reflects how many caregivers stand ready for every resident. Ample staffing and strong health results appear side by side in New Hampshire, though the study does not link one to the other.

New Hampshire households hold on to more of their money when they seek treatment. Only one other state's residents spend less out of pocket on medical care. Modest personal costs leave more room in a family budget after each appointment. Smaller bills give residents less reason to postpone a visit to protect their savings. Rare strokes, few heart attacks, and limited diabetes alongside low spending and a well-stocked clinical workforce show that New Hampshire residents do not have to trade affordability for good health.

Minnesota, second in the study, moves emergency room patients to treatment faster than any other state. The speed reaches past the ER doors. The analysis rated Minnesota's public hospital network eighth best in the U.S. The country's quickest emergency intake sits inside one of its stronger public systems. A patient who walks in with an urgent problem avoids the long wait, and the hospital system behind that first encounter carries its own strong marks.

Out-of-pocket medical spending stays modest in Minnesota, where only six states post a smaller average. Monthly insurance premiums come in eighth-lowest. The analysis pointed to inexpensive dental visits as another point in its favor. Residents face light charges at each stage, from the premium that buys coverage to the bill after a cleaning. Savings at the front end, through premiums, and at the back end, through out-of-pocket bills, add up for a family that uses care throughout the year. Low costs at both ends leave less room for a single expense to upend a household budget.

Minnesotans can expect longer lives than residents of most states, with the seventh-highest life expectancy in the analysis. Affordable care and lengthy lifespans appear together here. The data cannot prove that one produces the other. Residents here keep more of their money than people in most of the country and enjoy more years to spend it.

Six of the eight measures the study cited for Minnesota carry a top-10 placement, spanning convenient care clinics, spending, premiums, hospital quality, longevity, and emergency waits. Two of them are outright firsts. Minnesota has more convenient care clinics per capita than any other state, and its emergency rooms post the shortest waits. Dental costs and maternal mortality, the remaining two measures, drew praise as low without a specific position. Minnesota's runner-up finish rests on consistency, with no weak spot among the figures the analysis highlighted. Both of its first-place marks concern a patient's first contact with care, which suggests easy entry into the system sets Minnesota apart even among the strongest states.

Iowa extends health insurance to about 93% of its adults, the eighth-highest share in the country. Children post a higher rate. About 97% of young Iowans hold a policy, the seventh-highest mark among the states. A gap of about 4 percentage points leaves Iowa children likelier to carry coverage than the adults raising them. Both figures sit near the top. Iowa's strength spans generations and does not rest on a single age group.

Hospital capacity backs up those enrollment numbers. Iowa holds the 10th-highest count of hospital beds per capita, and its hospital system rates third best in the U.S. Volume and quality arrive together in Iowa's hospitals. A patient who needs an overnight stay has better odds of finding an open bed than in most states. A health plan pays for the stay. The beds give the patient a place to recover. A plan without enough beds would leave patients holding a card and waiting for a room.

Iowa's emergency rooms move patients through faster than those in most states. The state posts the fifth-shortest wait, and Minnesota is one of the four places ahead of it. The analysis credits Iowa with quality access to medical care, and quick emergency treatment gives that phrase a measurable meaning. A short wait turns those earlier strengths into help on the day a patient arrives.

Cost keeps few Iowans from seeing a doctor. Residents of few other states prove as unlikely to skip a visit over price. Wide coverage offers one likely reason. An insured patient carries less of the bill at the desk. None of the details the study highlights for Iowa measure health outcomes. The case the study makes for Iowa centers on getting residents insured, admitted, and seen.

Rhode Island finishes fourth in the 2026 study, ahead of 47 of the 51 places compared. New Hampshire, Minnesota, and Iowa are the only states to finish higher, and Hawaii comes next on the best list.

The result puts Rhode Island inside the top 8% of the field. At least 37 places separate it from any state in the bottom 10, a group that Alaska anchors at the foot of the list.

Wisconsin holds the eighth slot among the 10 best states for health care in 2026, sitting behind Maine and ahead of Colorado. The finish puts Wisconsin above 43 of the 51 places the study compared, a margin that separates it from the 10 states at the bottom of the list.

The news report on the analysis gives no figures for Wisconsin alone, even though the researchers prepared an assessment of every state. The coverage leaves out Wisconsin's spending, insurance coverage, medical workforce, and patient outcomes, so its readers cannot tell which area gives the state its edge.

Colorado claims ninth place among the 10 states the analysis rates best for health care in 2026, one spot behind Wisconsin and one ahead of Nebraska. The finish puts the state ahead of 42 of the 51 places compared. Eight states earned a higher verdict.

Sponsors of the Colorado Option told a state House committee in 2021 that the bill would also benefit rural Coloradans, according to The Gazette. The sponsors pointed to the burden those residents carry, with some of the highest health insurance costs. Colorado's public option plan was designed to require hospitals to accept the coverage.

Nebraska claims the last of the 10 spots the study reserves for its best health care states in 2026, with 41 of the 51 places compared finishing behind it.

Its finish keeps Nebraska clear of every state on the study's list of 10 worst, a group that includes Alaska, Texas, and Tennessee. Colorado sits one position higher, and Wisconsin holds the slot above Colorado.

The news report on the study gives no cost, access, or outcome figures for Nebraska. The study analyzed every state, but the report spells out individual strengths for New Hampshire, Minnesota, and Iowa alone. Nebraska's place shows that its combined results beat those of most of the country, without revealing which category carried it there.

A family weighing a move to Nebraska for its care can confirm the state's standing from the report but would need the study's own analysis of each state to learn which strengths earned it.

Alaska finished as the worst state in the country for health care in the 2026 analysis, behind every other state and Washington, D.C.

Nine other states joined Alaska among the 10 weakest: Mississippi, Georgia, Texas, West Virginia, Alabama, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, and Tennessee. The study identified Alaska as the single worst and left the order of the other nine unstated.

Alaska and New Hampshire occupy opposite ends of the same scale. A move from one state to the other would carry a resident from the top-rated health care system in the country to the bottom-rated one.

#5506. ISU Specialty Chemical and Ares Materials to Co-Develop Polymer Materials for Solid-State Batteries

Partnership pairs ISU's lithium sulfide and specialty-chemical production with Ares' closed-loop AI framework for application-driven formulation

PLANO, Texas and SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ISU Specialty Chemical, a lithium sulfide producer and member of Korea's ISU Group, and Ares Materials, a materials-AI company based in Plano, Texas, and Guadalajara, Mexico, said Wednesday they will jointly develop polymer materials for solid-state batteries, along with the AI tools used to optimize them.

Under the agreement, Ares will develop the polymer formulations and the AI framework used to tune them against cell-level battery test data. ISU will contribute its specialty-chemical and lithium sulfide manufacturing and lead production and commercial supply.

Developing polymers for solid-state cells typically requires building and cycling test cells for each change to a formulation. Battery makers have cited the length of that cycle, and the difficulty of attributing a result to a specific ingredient or process step, as a constraint on commercialization timelines. Cell specifications also continue to change as the technology matures, so a formulation qualified against one target is often re-opened when the target moves.

AI tools for materials fall broadly into two categories: discovery, which screens candidate molecules to identify new materials, and formulation optimization, which adjusts the composition and processing of a chosen chemistry until it meets targets in a working device. The partnership covers the second. According to Ares, its framework is trained on measured device-level performance and decomposes each test result into the contribution of individual formulation and process variables, then uses that model to select the next set of experiments. The companies said the performance data and models generated in developing the first material will carry forward into the next generations of the product, so that each one starts from an existing performance model rather than from scratch.

"The combination of AI-based materials intelligence and established specialty-chemical manufacturing can help address a key industry challenge: developing and commercializing better materials with fewer iterations and less time," said Liz Lee, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research. "As battery and electronics manufacturers seek improved performance, partnerships connecting predictive materials design with industrial-scale expertise could become an important source of competitive advantage, particularly for next-generation battery materials where quality, cost and scalability are critical."

ISU Specialty Chemical, a member of Korea's ISU Group, reported 2025 revenue of approximately â©411.5 billion (about US$290 million). It produces molecular-weight regulators, including TDM, NOM and NDM, and completed a commercial lithium sulfide plant this year. ISU Group, headquartered in Seoul, dates to the founding of ISU Chemical in 1969; its three listed affiliates reported combined 2025 revenue of more than â©3 trillion (about US$2.2 billion).

"Lithium sulfide gives us a position in the solid-state supply chain. This partnership is about what sits next to it," said Lyu Seung-Ho, CEO of ISU Specialty Chemical. "Each generation we develop this way makes the next one faster, and that is the kind of capability our customers in Korea, Japan and the United States are asking us for."

Ares Materials develops polymers and the closed-loop AI infrastructure used to formulate them against real-world performance. It has been selected for the Apple Impact Accelerator and the Amazon Climate Tech Accelerator.

"Every materials supplier in this space knows the pattern: you hit the spec, the spec moves, and you start over," said Dr. David Arreaga, CEO of Ares Materials. "What we're building with ISU is meant to break that cycle. When a model already knows how each formulation variable drives device performance, a new target is an adjustment, not a restart."
