#5504. USA Today readers pick the 10 best new breweries in the U.S. for 2026

Free daily briefing on global business news.

From a Milwaukee gas works campus to a former New Jersey gym, meet the 10 new breweries USA Today readers named the best in the U.S.

Every weekend getaway reaches the same debate over which taproom deserves the afternoon. The familiar names offer comfort, a beer you know and a room you have sat in a dozen times. A brewery that opened its doors last year offers something different. It gives you a chance to taste a recipe before the crowds arrive, to talk with the people behind the bar, and to watch a young business steady itself. New owners compete for every visit. Each one has bet money and a reputation on the hope that strangers will walk in, order a flight, and return with friends. Where you choose to drink helps decide which young taprooms survive.

Tracking down a worthwhile upstart takes more effort than returning to an old favorite. A brewery with two or three years behind it has had little time to build a following, and its brand may mean nothing outside its own ZIP code. Travelers $TRV end up guessing. They lean on a glimpse of a storefront, a tip from a stranger in the hotel lobby, or a map pin with a handful of ratings. A good guess can produce a memorable glass in an unexpected building. A bad one wastes an evening and a designated driver's patience. The risk climbs for anyone who plans a trip around beer. One missed stop can mean skipping the most interesting pour in a region. A trusted shortlist shrinks the field. It points curious travelers toward breweries that have impressed both beer experts and ordinary patrons.

American Craft Beer reported on the 10 Best New Breweries list that USA Today announced March 4. A panel of beer specialists nominated breweries in operation since 2023, and readers voted on that slate to pick the winners. The report numbers each entry but publishes no vote counts or scores, and it does not name the panelists. The list below covers all 10 winners in the report's sequence. Each entry describes what sets the brewery apart and, where the record allows, who founded it and the space it occupies.

A massive two-story fireplace gave Hearth Brewing its name, and the hearth sets the tone inside the family-owned brewery in Harrison, Ohio. A rustic, lodge-style interior wraps around the chimney. The brand and the building share one centerpiece. A first-time guest learns where the name came from on walking through the door.

Greg Otis $OTIS and his son, Cory, started the business with their friend Andy Plogsted. The founding trio joins a father and son with a partner from outside their family. The lineup gives the brewery family roots and a third founder who arrived through friendship.

Stone-fired pizzas earn as much attention as the beer at Hearth. The brewery sets out to pour excellent beer for good people and to match it with food worth the drive on its own. A guest who stops in for a pint can stay for dinner without moving to another table, and the kitchen gives people a reason to linger beyond a single glass.

Fire ties the whole operation together. The same element warms the lodge's centerpiece and bakes the crust under every pie, so the name describes the menu as much as the room.

Night School packs three businesses under one roof, working as a brewery, a pizzeria, and a cocktail bar in the riverside village of Athens, New York. The setup lets a group split between beer fans and people who prefer mixed drinks settle at a single table, with dinner on hand for both. One stop covers the whole evening. Nobody in the party has to bargain over a second destination.

Night School serves large New York-style pizzas alongside its own beers and craft cocktails. Guests order food at the bar and claim any open seat in the taproom. Counter service keeps the visit informal and puts the bar at the center of every order. The brewhouse sits inside the pizza parlor. The beer and the pies share a single room.

The venue doubles as the home base and taproom for Deep Fried Beers, an offbeat craft label that brewer Johnny Osborne founded. Osborne built his reputation on double IPAs loaded with hops, which he brews under the Deep Fried Beers name. The label lends its name to the brewing style behind Night School's house beers. Anyone curious about the label can taste it where it lives, in Athens. First-time visitors chasing the label's signature should start with one of those double IPAs.

Osborne frames the name as a philosophy, likening a drink of his beer to a trip to the fair. The comparison fits the rest of the menu. Hop-heavy double IPAs and oversized New York-style pies both trade restraint for excess. Deep Fried Beers borrows its name from the vocabulary of fair food. The kitchen and the taps tell one fairground story, giving the pizzeria, the cocktail bar, and the brewery a shared identity.

Elder Piper Beer & Cider opened in early 2024 in Petoskey, Michigan, as an artisanal brewery and cidery operating out of a manufacturing building that dates to the early 20th century. Eeva and Trace Redmond own and run the business, and each has spent more than 10 years in the beer trade, according to petoskeyarea.com. The venture brings the pair back to Eeva's home region. Their résumés pair a young business with seasoned operators. Visitors take less of a gamble here than at most newcomers.

The cider program starts at the owners' family apple orchard in Bliss, Michigan. Northern Michigan inspires the flavors across both lineups. One sampler flight held Beach Grass Helles Lager, Pillows & Blankets Cider, Thimble Weed American IPA, and Fairy Slipper Vanilla Milk Stout. Names such as Beach Grass and Thimble Weed borrow from the landscape and carry the regional theme onto the menu board. A single tray of four pours spans both halves of the operation, from a helles lager to a vanilla milk stout. Pouring cider beside beer also widens the audience. A guest who skips hops can order a glass made from family-grown apples.

Original wood floors line the taproom, and large windows brighten it. Its cozy, unpretentious mood suits its billing as a "neighborhood hangout." A space this plain puts attention on the glass and the company at the table. The preserved floorboards keep the building's industrial past underfoot.

Picnic tables and cornhole boards extend the casual setting outdoors. Lawn games and open-air seating give a group reason to linger past one round. Food trucks such as Stiggs BBQ Wagon park on site at times. Their visits put a meal within reach at a venue built around drinks.

Each element, from the Bliss orchard to the cornhole lawn, aims Elder Piper at Petoskey regulars first and passing travelers second.

Lombardi Brewing Company runs its microbrewery and taproom on the West Side Works campus of the Milwaukee Gas Light Company, a historic utility property in the city's Menomonee River Valley. The address places a young beer business on grounds that belong to the city's industrial past.

Founder John Lombardi gives the venture a surname that football fans recognize on sight. His grandfather was Vince Lombardi, the famed coach of the Green Bay Packers. The brewery's name belongs to the founder by birth. Most newcomers must earn recognition one pint at a time. This one opens with a family story that travels well beyond the taproom door.

Freshness shapes the brewery's stated plans for its taps. Chris Gethers said Lombardi wanted to devote newly acquired equipment to fresh, varied beers, most of them brewed in Milwaukee, according to OnMilwaukee. Under that plan, those beers would pour only in the taproom. Czech and German lagers stood as the exceptions to the taproom-only rule.

The plan divides the lineup into two tracks. The Czech and German lagers could reach drinkers outside the building, while the fresh, varied releases would stay behind the brewery's own bar. The arrangement would turn the gas company campus into the single place to sample the full range of Lombardi's beer. A drinker hunting the newest pours would need to make the trip to the Menomonee River Valley to find them.

Future Days Beer Company makes its home in a renovated two-story carriage house in Philadelphia's Northern Liberties neighborhood. Tall ceilings open up the interior, and the décor leans rustic and industrial. A vintage pool table stands among the furnishings. The brewing space shares the ground floor with a smaller bar, and the main bar occupies the upper level. The layout gives each floor a job, with production and a compact counter downstairs and the larger bar upstairs. The building sits back from the street and has a large patio for outdoor pints. The setback buffers the carriage house from sidewalk traffic, and the patio pushes seating past the building's walls.

Ownership stays with the brewers who make the beer, and the company remains independent. Nick Mata and Sean McGuire founded the business after a friendship that dates to college, where the two shared a room. The friendship held for years after those dorm days ended. The pair started out as homebrewers. Their path ran from hobby batches to a commercial brewhouse of their own. Brewer ownership puts the recipes and the business decisions in the same hands. The people who design each beer choose what the taproom serves and how each glass arrives.

Lagers claim a spot on the tap list, including Come to Terms Munich Helles and Pils & The Wolf German Pilsner. Both flow through a Lukr side-pull faucet. Townline Porter comes off a nitro line. Each of those three beers gets its own serving hardware, matched to its style. Two German-style lagers routed through a specialized faucet suggest a team that treats the pour as part of the recipe. The amateur start and brewer ownership point in the same direction, toward a small group that controls each step from the kettle to the customer's hand.

Terranaut Beer has won awards for the small batches of creative, experimental beer it produces in Bend, Oregon. The brewery's lineup has run from hazy and American IPAs to beers brewed with Mexican chocolate and pineapple. A drinker after a familiar pour and one chasing an odd ingredient can order from the same board.

Hazy and American IPAs ground the menu in styles most craft drinkers know. Mexican chocolate and pineapple pull it the other way, toward ingredients borrowed from the kitchen and the produce aisle. The spread lets one taproom serve both a cautious first-timer and a regular hunting for something new. The awards indicate the inventive streak yields beer that holds up to scrutiny. Small batches also turn each release into a limited run, which suits a brewer testing ideas one recipe at a time.

The taproom extends that sense of play to its furnishings. Old vinyl records, bright artwork, and comfortable used furniture fill a cozy, eclectic room with a hipster edge. Nothing about the space suggests a showroom. The secondhand pieces echo the beer list, pairing worn comfort with the surprise of whatever album or piece of art catches a visitor's eye.

Terranaut's place among the 10 winners shows that a young brewery can earn national notice by building its identity around invention in the glass and in the room.

Blue Jay Brewing Co. built its name in St. Louis on one family of beer, small-batch lagers, and VinePair named it 2025 Brewery of the Year. The brewery keeps its runs small and holds each one to a high standard.

Jay and Nicole Thompson, a married couple, opened Blue Jay in December 2023. Praise from beyond Missouri followed fast, and the VinePair honor stands as its most prominent example. The award covered 2025, only the second full calendar year the brewery had operated.

A narrow menu gave the Thompsons a clear identity to present to drinkers and critics alike. Few of the young breweries on this list can point to a named national honor, and Blue Jay earned its own with a single style at the center of the business. Its quick climb suggests a newcomer can win attention far from home by doing one thing well instead of offering a little of everything.

Buena Connection Brewing Company pours its beer inside an 18,000-square-foot former fitness facility in Buena, New Jersey. The owners opened the doors in April 2025. Only one winner with a reported opening date arrived later. Lombardi Brewing opened in its Menomonee Valley space in September 2025, according to OnMilwaukee.

Scale defines a visit here. The room has drawn the description "colossal," and its unusual floor plan bears marks of the building's years as a workout center. The property once housed a Nova Care gym. The main tasting room fills the floor where weight machines once stood, according to The Press of Atlantic City. Cornhole and other free games now occupy the old racquetball courts. Guests drink in a room whose odd shape follows the building's earlier purpose, and the layout makes the gym's past part of the experience.

Turning the gym into a taproom took nearly six years and a renovation of more than $1 million, The Press of Atlantic City reports. Owner David Obando, a Camden County pathologist opening his first brewery, seized the chance when the Wheat Road property went up for sale in 2019. The COVID-19 pandemic halted construction in 2020, and a contractor had the work underway by 2021, according to the paper.

A family owns and runs the business, and the brewery welcomes households that want to visit together. Buena Connection is also the first brewery the borough has had, according to the paper. Until it arrived, a brewery outing meant leaving town. Buena residents now have a hometown taproom open to whole families.

The tap list stretches across many styles, from light, clean lagers to IPAs heavy with hops. Head brewer Freddy Schwindt crafts the recipes for a little under a dozen beers on tap, the paper reports. A range that wide gives first-time visitors in a town new to breweries an entry point at either end of the flavor scale.

Buena Connection earned a national honor less than a year after opening.

The Test Brewery in Brooklyn's Williamsburg neighborhood calls itself a "think-tank," a label that frames the business as a place for trying out ideas. The name on the door makes the same point. A brewery called Test signals to visitors that experimentation drives the enterprise.

The company also carries the description of a "test-kitchen" brewing company, a phrase borrowed from the world of recipe development. A test kitchen tinkers with a dish until it works, and the brewery's use of the term casts each beer as a draft open to revision. The tag and the company name tell one consistent story about a lab for new beer.

Ben Clayton founded the brewery after working the bar at Blue Hill. His résumé shows time behind another business's bar before he launched a brewery of his own. He moved from serving drinks to making them.

Brooklyn claims one of the two New York breweries among the 10 winners. Night School, the state's other entry, pours in the small village of Athens. The pair shows a young brewery can win recognition in a small village or in a big-city neighborhood.

Siblings Brian and Colleen Quinn set up Atomic Clock Brewing Co. inside a historic Durham, North Carolina, building where the city used to maintain its vehicle fleet. The property stands in Durham's Warehouse District. Municipal vehicles once rolled in for repairs, and the same building now serves people who stop by for a pint.

The brother-and-sister partnership joins a field of winners rooted in family. Hearth Brewing in Ohio began with a father, his son, and a friend. A married couple opened Blue Jay Brewing Co. in St. Louis, and Buena Connection in New Jersey runs as a family-owned business. Relatives working side by side started several of this year's picks.

A full-service kitchen operates next to the brewhouse, which lets the taproom work as a restaurant too. Visitors can stay through a meal. The bar pours wine and cocktails in addition to house beer, according to Discover $DFS Durham. Drinkers who skip beer still have options. Guests can pick an indoor table or a seat outside.

Food plays a role at other winners as well. Hearth Brewing bakes stone-fired pizzas, and Night School houses a pizzeria alongside its brewery. Atomic Clock's kitchen puts it in that company, evidence that a menu has become part of the draw at a number of this year's newcomers.

Atomic Clock shares a history of reuse with fellow winners, among them a former gas company campus in Milwaukee, an early 20th-century manufacturing building in Michigan, a carriage house in Philadelphia, and a onetime gym in New Jersey. Across this list, the newest breweries keep settling into structures first built for different work.

#5503. Mail ballots, signature checks and recounts: 10 reasons vote counts run long

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Why vote counting takes days in some states comes down to state law, from mail ballot processing limits to signature checks, curing periods, recounts and certification timelines

A slow vote count is usually a sign that election offices are following the law, not that something has broken. In the U.S., the pace of tabulation depends heavily on rules written by state legislatures. Those rules decide when workers may open mail ballots, how late an envelope can arrive and how voters fix paperwork errors.

The country has no single national election system. Each state runs its own elections, and counties or municipalities often handle the actual counting. That structure means two neighboring states can report results on very different schedules in the same election. One state may post nearly complete totals within hours. Another may still be processing envelopes days later.

Mail ballots take more steps to count than ballots cast in person. A ballot cast at a polling place is usually scanned on the spot. A mail ballot has to be received, logged and checked against voter records before it can be tabulated. Workers then remove it from its envelope and prepare it for scanning. Many states also give voters a chance to correct a missing or mismatched signature. Those ballots wait until the fix arrives or the deadline passes.

Some of these rules are policy choices that lawmakers revisit. Michigan changed its law in 2023 to give clerks some time to process mail ballots before Election Day. Pennsylvania and Wisconsin still hold that work until Election Day itself.

Election-night totals are also unofficial. The figures reported in the hours after polls close show what has been counted so far, not a final result. Official numbers come only after each state completes its canvass and certifies the outcome on a timeline it sets for itself.

Knowing why vote counting takes days helps explain why an early lead can narrow or flip. Mail ballots, late-arriving envelopes and provisional ballots are often added to the totals after election night.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of the reasons some states take longer than others. They are not a complete list or a ranking. They range from mail ballot processing limits and signature checks to ranked-choice tabulation, recounts and certification.

Pennsylvania and Wisconsin do not let election workers start processing mail ballots until Election Day itself. In Pennsylvania, counties cannot begin pre-canvassing until 7 a.m. that morning. That rule pushes a large volume of hands-on work into a single day.

Pre-canvassing is the preparation that comes before any votes are tallied. Workers open the outer return envelopes and remove the inner secrecy envelopes. They take out the ballots and flatten them so tabulating machines can read them. Each ballot passes through human hands at several stages. Under Pennsylvania's rule, none of that labor can start early.

Pre-canvassing is not the same as counting. Pennsylvania law keeps the results of that preparation from being reported before polls close. The restriction applies to when the physical work can begin, not only to when numbers can be shared.

Wisconsin takes a similar approach. Its absentee ballots wait until Election Day before clerks can process them. Local election workers there handle returned envelopes on the same day they are also running polling places for in-person voters.

The timing shapes how results arrive. Votes cast in person on machines can be tallied soon after polls close. Mail ballots in these two states often lag behind. In both states, opening and sorting begins only that morning. Counties with large stacks of mail ballots can still be counting well after election night.

Other states handle the timing differently. Florida lets election officials process mail ballots before Election Day. That preparation allows its counties to report many mail votes shortly after polls close.

Michigan shows that the start time is a policy decision rather than a technical barrier. The state changed its law in 2023 to give clerks some time to process absentee ballots before Election Day.

Changing the start time in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin would require action by state lawmakers. Under current law, the processing work in both states still begins on Election Day.

Some states count mail ballots that are postmarked by Election Day even when they reach election offices afterward. Officials in those states cannot finish the count until that arrival window closes.

The rule separates two moments in a ballot's trip. A postmark deadline asks when the voter sent the ballot. A receipt deadline asks when the ballot reached the election office.

States with a receipt deadline stop accepting mail ballots when polls close. States with a postmark deadline keep accepting ballots that were still in the mail on Election Day.

California is one of the postmark states. It accepts mail ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive after polls close, up to a deadline set in state law. A ballot mailed on Election Day is valid there as long as it arrives in time. Until that window closes, counties cannot know how many valid ballots are still in transit.

Alaska also accepts late-arriving ballots that carry an Election Day postmark. Its rules give ballots from overseas voters a longer window than domestic mail ballots. That second deadline means some Alaska ballots can enter the count after the domestic window has already closed.

Overseas and military voters have a distinct legal status across the U.S. The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, passed in 1986, protects their right to vote absentee in federal elections.

Late arrivals also add a step to processing. Workers must confirm that each envelope received after Election Day carries a qualifying postmark before the ballot moves forward. Envelopes with missing or unclear postmarks are handled under each state's own rules.

The effect shows up in close races. A contest can stay open after every ballot on hand has been processed. Margins can still move as valid late ballots arrive and enter the tally.

The deadline is set by state law, not by any technical limit of mail voting. A receipt rule closes intake when polls close. Under that rule, ballots mailed before Election Day but delivered afterward are not counted.

In many states, election workers must compare the signature on each returned mail ballot envelope with the voter's signature on file before the ballot can be counted. That review takes time, and it takes the longest in counties that receive large volumes of envelopes.

The signature on file usually comes from the voter's registration record. Depending on the state, it may also come from earlier election paperwork or a driver's license record. Workers view the envelope signature beside that reference. They decide whether the two appear to come from the same person.

The comparison happens in one of two ways. Some offices rely on staff who review each signature by hand. Others use signature-matching software to screen envelopes first. Where software is used, envelopes the system cannot confidently match are generally routed to human reviewers for a closer look.

The check comes before anyone touches the ballot itself. The ballot stays sealed inside its envelope while the signature is reviewed. Only after the envelope is accepted is it opened. That order protects the secrecy of the vote. Once separated from its envelope, the ballot can no longer be linked to the name on the outside.

Volume shapes how long this step lasts. A small rural county may handle a modest stack of envelopes. A large urban county handles far more. Every one of those envelopes passes through the same review before it can move on to tabulation.

Signatures also change over time. Age, injury or a rushed scrawl can make an envelope signature look different from one written years earlier at registration. Reviewers have to weigh those differences. Close calls take longer to resolve than clear matches.

Not every state uses this method. Some verify mail ballots through a witness signature, a notary or an identification number written on the envelope instead. Where signature matching is the rule, it adds a step that in-person voting does not require. A voter at a polling place is checked in before receiving a ballot. That verification is finished before the ballot is cast.

Envelopes that fail the comparison are set aside rather than counted. What happens to them next depends on state law. That follow-up adds its own stretch of time before the count is complete.

Ballot curing lets a voter correct a missing or mismatched signature on a mail ballot envelope so the vote can still count. Those ballots stay uncounted until the voter responds or the state's cure period ends. That keeps final totals open after Election Day.

Curing starts where signature review leaves off. Once an election office flags an envelope, the ballot inside is set aside rather than opened. Typical problems include an unsigned envelope and a signature that does not match the one on file.

Many states give voters a chance to fix those problems instead of rejecting the ballot outright. The process depends on contact. Election offices must reach each affected voter, explain the problem and wait for an answer. Offices typically use letters, phone calls, email or text messages, depending on the contact details in the voter's registration record.

The fix itself usually involves a short form. The voter signs a statement affirming that they cast the ballot, and in some places provides identification or a fresh signature. The office then matches the response to the flagged envelope before the ballot moves on to tabulation.

Arizona and California both run cure processes that continue for days after Election Day. In both states, flagged ballots remain outside the count while that window is open. A close contest in either state can stay unresolved until officials know how many voters returned their paperwork.

Campaigns and political parties watch this stage closely in tight races. They often contact their own supporters whose ballots were flagged and urge them to complete the cure. That outreach does not change the rules. It does affect how many ballots are eventually fixed.

Curing is not universal. Some states offer no cure process, and a ballot with a defective envelope is rejected. Others set different notification rules and deadlines. A ballot that is never cured is not counted.

The trade-off is between speed and inclusion. A state that lets voters repair envelope errors accepts a slower finish in exchange for counting ballots that would otherwise be thrown out.

Arizona lets voters return a mail ballot in person on Election Day, at a polling place or a drop box. Those envelopes need signature verification before they can be counted. Maricopa County handles a large share of them.

Arizona election law calls these mail ballots "early ballots." A voter who receives one does not have to mail it back. The voter can carry the sealed envelope to a polling place or drop box, including on Election Day itself.

That option shifts work to the end of the election. An early ballot returned weeks ahead can move through verification before polls close. An envelope dropped off on Election Day arrives along with the in-person vote, but it cannot go straight into a tabulator.

The difference lies in how each ballot is checked. A voter casting a ballot at a polling place has already checked in with poll workers. An early ballot envelope arrives without that step. Election staff must confirm the signature on it before the ballot inside can be removed and counted.

Envelopes returned on Election Day must first be collected from voting sites and drop boxes. They are then brought to the county's central processing facility, and verification begins only after that. A county with fewer voters can work through that queue faster.

Maricopa County is Arizona's largest county. It includes Phoenix and is home to more than half of the state's residents. When many of its voters return early ballots on Election Day, the county receives a large volume of envelopes at once. None of them can be counted until each signature is reviewed.

Arizona releases results in batches, and the effect shows up in the timing of those updates. Election-night totals mostly reflect early ballots received before Election Day, along with in-person votes. Ballots dropped off on Election Day tend to appear in later updates as verification moves forward.

California mails a ballot to every active registered voter, and it is the most populous state in the U.S. That combination puts a very large number of envelopes in front of county election offices after every statewide election. State law gives counties 30 days after a general election to certify their results.

Volume is the core issue. Every ballot mailed to a voter is an envelope that may come back for review. When all active registered voters receive one, the number of returns tracks the size of the electorate itself. In states where voters must apply for a mail ballot, only those who apply receive one.

California runs its elections through 58 counties. Each county registrar handles its own intake, review and tabulation, and then reports its own totals. Los Angeles County, the most populous county in the U.S., carries a far heavier workload than a small rural county such as Alpine County.

Voters in California do not have to return ballots by mail. They can also use drop boxes or bring the ballot to an in-person voting location. Ballots returned on or near Election Day arrive at county offices together. That adds to the work that remains once polls close.

The 30-day window shapes how counties pace that work. Counties are not required to finish on election night. They use the certification period to complete the full count and the official canvass. Totals posted in the days after the election can change as more ballots are processed.

After the counties certify, the Secretary of State certifies the statewide results. Statewide totals are the sum of 58 separate county canvasses. A statewide contest is not official until every county's numbers have been finalized and combined.

The length of California's count follows from two policy choices: broad mail voting and a defined certification period. Close statewide and county races can stay unresolved for days while that process runs its course.

Ranked-choice voting can delay final results in Alaska and Maine because a race without a majority winner must be tabulated again in rounds. Those extra rounds cannot start until officials have the first-choice totals in hand.

Both states use the system in some contests, though the offices covered differ between them. Voters rank candidates in order of preference rather than marking a single choice. A candidate who wins more than half of the first-choice votes is the winner, and no further tabulation is needed.

When no one clears that bar, the process continues. The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Each ballot that ranked that candidate first then moves to the next candidate the voter ranked. The totals are recalculated, and the cycle repeats until one candidate holds a majority of the ballots still in play.

Some ballots drop out along the way. A ballot becomes exhausted when every candidate the voter ranked has been eliminated. It no longer counts toward any remaining candidate in later rounds.

The timing problem comes from the order of operations. Officials cannot reliably decide who finishes last until they know every candidate's full first-choice total. A candidate in last place on a partial count could move up once more ballots are added. Eliminating the wrong candidate would send votes to the wrong places in every round after that.

As a result, the numbers released on election night in these races show first choices only. A candidate who leads on first choices does not always win. Once eliminated candidates' ballots are redistributed, a second-place finisher can overtake the leader.

Maine adds a logistical step. Its ranked-choice tabulation is handled centrally in Augusta, the state capital, rather than in each town. Ballots must first be gathered from municipalities across the state before the rounds can be run. That collection work happens before any second-round result exists.

Close races take longer to settle because recounts and audits begin only after the initial count is finished. Pennsylvania holds an automatic recount when the margin is 0.5% or less, while Georgia lets a candidate request one when the margin is within 0.5%.

The two approaches differ in who sets the process in motion. In Pennsylvania, the law triggers the recount once a race falls inside the threshold, and no candidate has to ask. In Georgia, the decision belongs to a candidate. Either way, the final result waits until the second count is done.

A small percentage can still mean a meaningful number of ballots. In a hypothetical statewide race with 1 million votes cast, a 0.5% margin works out to 5,000 votes. In a smaller local contest, the same threshold covers far fewer.

There is no national standard. Each state sets its own thresholds and procedures, including whether a recount happens automatically or only on request. Some states have no automatic recount provision and leave the choice to candidates. Some also require a candidate who requests a recount to cover part or all of the cost.

The method matters for timing too. Officials may run paper ballots back through tabulating machines or count them by hand. A hand recount is slower. Workers must examine each ballot and agree on how the voter marked it.

Audits serve a different purpose. A post-election audit checks whether voting equipment counted ballots correctly, typically by comparing a sample of paper ballots with the machine totals. A risk-limiting audit uses statistical methods to decide how large that sample must be. The narrower the margin, the more ballots auditors generally need to review before they can confirm the reported winner.

Both steps depend on paper records. Ballots must be retrieved from storage and kept under chain-of-custody rules while officials review them.

Results become final only after these reviews end and the state certifies the outcome.

The Help America Vote Act of 2002 requires that a voter whose eligibility is in question be allowed to cast a provisional ballot. Officials count that ballot only after confirming the voter was eligible. That check happens after Election Day.

Congress passed the law after the disputed 2000 presidential election. Problems with voter rolls and voting equipment in Florida drew national scrutiny that year. President George W. Bush signed the act in 2002. Before it, practices varied, and some states offered no ballot to a voter whose name was missing from the rolls.

The provisional ballot works as a fallback. A voter's name may be missing from the poll book at their precinct. A poll worker may be unable to confirm the voter's registration on the spot. Some voters lack an identification document required under state or federal rules. In each case, the voter can still mark a ballot rather than leave without voting.

Under the law, the voter signs a written affirmation stating that they are registered and eligible to vote in that jurisdiction. The ballot goes into a separate envelope and is kept apart from regular ballots. It is not added to the tally on election night.

The delay comes from the follow-up work. Election staff must review each provisional ballot individually. They check registration records and look for clerical errors. In some cases they wait for the voter to bring in identification. Each ballot is its own small investigation. A county with many of them needs time to resolve every case.

States set much of the detail. Rules differ on whether a ballot cast at the wrong precinct counts in full, in part or not at all. Deadlines for voters to supply missing identification also vary from state to state.

The act also covers voting during extended hours. When a court orders polls to stay open past their normal closing time, votes cast in that extra period must be cast provisionally. Those ballots are held apart in case the order is later reversed.

Voters can find out what happened to their ballot. The act requires states to offer a free access system, such as a toll-free phone line or a website. Through it, a voter can learn whether their provisional ballot was counted. If it was rejected, the system must give the reason.

In a close race, provisional ballots can affect the outcome. Until officials finish reviewing them, the final margin is not settled.

The vote totals posted on election night are unofficial. They become official only after local election officials complete a canvass and the results are certified. Each state sets its own timeline for both steps.

Election-night numbers are early snapshots. Counties post them as batches of ballots are tabulated. Those first figures can contain mistakes that the formal review later catches. A data entry error in a precinct total, for example, can appear in early reporting and be corrected before results are certified.

The order of reporting also shapes what the public sees. A state may release in-person Election Day votes first and mail ballots later, or the reverse. Different groups of voters often favor different voting methods. The candidate who leads early can then fall behind as other batches are added. That shift reflects the sequence in which ballots are tallied, not a change in how people voted.

The canvass is the formal process of reviewing and confirming the count. Officials reconcile the number of ballots cast with the number of voters recorded as having voted. They check that totals from each precinct or voting center add up correctly. They also fold in ballots that could not be counted on election night. The canvass ends with a final tally for each contest.

Certification follows the canvass. In many states, a county or local board signs off on its results first. A state official or state board then certifies the statewide outcome. The bodies involved and the deadlines they must meet differ from state to state.

News organizations often project winners before any of this is complete. A projection is an estimate based on the votes counted so far and other available data. It carries no legal weight, and it does not replace the certified result.

For presidential contests, certified state results feed into the Electoral College. Each state's governor issues a certificate of ascertainment naming the state's electors. That document depends on the state finishing its certification first.

#5502. The 10 best winter jackets of 2026, tested and ranked by OutdoorGearLab

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Testers wore parkas through Arctic cold, gusty city streets, and snowy driveways. Here are the 10 award winners for 2026.

A coat that looks cozy on a store rack can turn into a liability at a windy bus stop on a January morning. Cold slips in at the cuffs, the hood flops back, and the coat rides up and leaves the thighs exposed. People pull on the same winter coat most days for months, through commutes, grocery runs, and the long minutes spent clearing a driveway. A poor choice follows its owner through all of it. The racks hold no shortage of contenders. Fjallraven, Canada Goose, The North Face, Patagonia, REI, Columbia, and L.L. Bean all compete for one hook in the hall closet.

Much of what separates a good coat from a bad one stays hidden inside the baffles. Down delivers heat for little weight, yet it loses loft under compression or moisture, and repeated squeezing breaks the feathers down over time. Its fill power runs from 300 to 900, and higher numbers pack smaller and give more heat for the weight. A 900-fill coat stuffs into a tiny space but costs a fortune. Synthetic fill, made from spun filaments that are polyester in most cases, holds its loft in wet weather and shrugs off compression damage. It tends to cost less, though it weighs more and bulks up more than down at the same level of heat. Some makers blend the two. Cut matters as much as stuffing. A coat that binds across the shoulders limits every reach and swing of the arms, and how far a coat extends down the leg trades freedom of movement against coverage. No shopper can judge any of this from a hanger, and a bad guess reveals itself in the first deep freeze.

OutdoorGearLab has bought more than 160 top-rated winter jackets since its testing began in 2012, and it pays for every product it reviews. The site accepts no freebies from brands, though it may earn a commission through its links. Men wore men's models and women wore women's, because fit through the body, sleeve length, and hem length vary even where warmth stays similar. The testers took the coats into sub-zero Arctic temperatures, through strong winter winds around town, and out to shovel snow from driveways. Friends weighed in on comfort and appearance. The team judged each jacket on six measures: warmth, weather resistance, comfort, style, features and versatility, and construction quality. The review centers on parka-style coats that join insulation and a shell, with most falling between mid-thigh and mid-calf. These coats serve daily life in freezing weather, and they get in the way on a hike or a climb. A March 11, 2026, update added long-term testing results for several favorites. The 2026 edition hands out 10 category awards, each naming the best coat for a given use, budget, or wearer, without sorting the jackets into a single ranked order.

The Fjallraven Nuuk Parka kept one tester comfortable through -15°F nights on a hunt for the northern lights in the remote north of Sweden. The $535 coat took the award for best overall winter jacket for men, and its male testers count it among the warmest and most protective jackets they have worn. Its classic, understated styling suits nearly any setting, from errands in town to a frozen night under the aurora.

A size 2XL weighs 4.6 pounds and closes around the body with a cocoon-like feel. A drawstring at the waist shapes the garment and holds heated air close to the vital organs of the upper body. A double-layered storm flap lays an extra band of insulation over the front zipper.

One tester counted more pockets on the Nuuk Parka than on a fishing vest. The same tester singled out a fur-lined hood with Arctic vibes and construction that made the wearer feel invincible in snowstorms. The parka's long cut and tough outer shell handle snow and rain alike, which keeps it useful on wet days as well as dry, frigid ones.

Nearly four years of wear have left the parka with little damage, most of it cosmetic. Velcro on the cuffs has lost some of its grip, and a few stray fibers poke through the inner lining. Neither flaw reaches the core of the jacket. The fill and the outer fabric both came through those winters intact.

Bulk heads the parka's list of drawbacks. The Nuuk Parka resists packing and proves awkward to carry, and testers found its main zipper hard to work. One tester conceded that the bulk rules the coat out for travel, but the same tester grabs it first whenever a day calls for warmth and durability. A shopper who can live with the bulk and the stubborn zipper gets a parka built to outlast many seasons of hard use.

The Outdoor Research Coze Down Parka drops its hem to mid-calf, the most coverage of any jacket in the test, and it won the best overall award for women's winter jackets at a $500 list price. Its extra length wraps the legs along with the torso. Daily winter commutes, the apres scene after skiing, and full days out in the cold all sit within its intended use.

Insulation of 700-fill down gives the Coze its heat, and a high collar, an oversized hood, and a baffled neck close off the top of the coat against wind. The outer shell uses 100% recycled nylon. Despite its long cut, the parka weighs two pounds, and its down compresses enough to stuff into a backpack. The review likens pulling the coat on to strapping into a favorite down sleeping bag. The review credits the parka with high build quality and plenty of adjustability.

Thumb-loop gaiters extend from the cuffs to the knuckles. Bike commutes drew no complaints of restriction from testers. One tester, wrapping up a season on the Search and Rescue Team in Yosemite Valley, grabbed the Coze before anything else on getting out of bed in below-freezing temperatures.

The coat's face fabric surpassed one tester's expectations in shower trials, with water beading on the surface though it carries no DWR coating. Even so, the review counts limited water resistance among the parka's weak points.

The same mid-calf hem that guards the shins also limits leg movement on inclines. A two-way zipper or a pair of side zippers lets wearers open the bottom of the coat to free their legs. Testers also judged the look of the baffles unflattering.

Level ground suits the Coze best. Its mobility complaints surfaced on inclines, while its full-body warmth serves anyone who stands still or strolls. Those traits point it toward town sidewalks and ski lodges over trails.

The Rab Neutrino Pro wraps 800-fill down inside a jacket that weighs about a pound and a half, and testers on both the men's and women's teams called it one of the warmest jackets they wore this year. The $450 Rab claimed the Best for Lightweight Warmth award by keeping wearers cozy without the bulk that burdens heavier winter coats. One tester described the sensation as feeling "wrapped in a puffy dream of weightless warmth."

An internal dump pocket turns into a stuff sack, and the Neutrino Pro compresses with less fuss than a parka. Its light build makes it a more reasonable travel companion than the bulkier coats that won other awards. A jacket that shrinks into its own pocket leaves suitcase room for the rest of a winter wardrobe.

The Neutrino Pro runs shorter than most parkas. Its hem lands around mid-hip on both the men's and women's models, with a dropped tail at the back, and the body leaves plenty of room to move. A fleece-lined chin cuff rises to the nose, and the hood cinches tight. Few other down jackets in the review carried a two-way zipper. The Neutrino Pro's version suits wearers clipped into a climbing harness.

The Neutrino Pro gives up some weather defense to stay featherweight. A DWR-treated shell and hydrophobic down let damp feathers keep most of their loft, and the fabric sheds water better than most traditional down jackets. Long exposure to moisture still soaks through, and the write-up names this weakness as both the main downfall and part of what keeps the ounces down.

The Neutrino Pro's heat narrows its calendar. The jacket may run too hot for shoulder season, and it does its best work once temperatures drop below zero. Nor'easters, icy city streets, and alpine winds all fall within its range.

Wearers who pack their winter gear into luggage, along with those facing dry, below-zero winters, stand to gain the most from the Neutrino Pro. Buyers in rainy, milder regions would collide with both of its limits at once.

The shell of the REI Co-op Stormhenge Down Hybrid Parka all but stops high winds and wet snow, and the jacket won the Best Value Coat for Men award at a $299 list price. No other award pick lists for less. The Fjallraven Nuuk Parka, the men's overall winner, costs $236 more, and the Canada Goose Expedition Parka Heritage runs more than six times the Stormhenge's price.

Blended down and polyester insulation keeps the parka affordable without leaving the wearer cold. The women's testing team gave the Stormhenge a strong endorsement for anyone shopping on a tighter budget, and the men's team agreed once its members tried the men's version of the jacket.

The Stormhenge offers more toughness than a down puffy while weighing less than a traditional winter parka. Testers counted the lower heft among its strengths, along with enough interior room to wear extra layers underneath. The jacket suits winter hikes as well as basic errands.

Heavy, wet snowstorms paired with few days below zero Fahrenheit describe the climate where this parka belongs. Its outer layer turns back water and snow, and testers listed wet-weather handling among its pros. Shoppers in places where winter brings more slush than deep freezes get the most from that design. Residents of regions with long stretches of subzero cold would find the longer parkas among the picks a better match.

A shorter hem sacrifices some heat compared with jackets that fall to mid-thigh. Testers flagged generic styling and a hood with no fur trim, unlike the fur-lined hood on the Fjallraven Nuuk Parka. The reviewers judged these drawbacks minor next to the savings. The Patagonia Jackson Glacier draws the same complaints about a short cut and a hood without a ruff, yet it lists for $220 more. A buyer who faces more wet storms than bitter cold loses little that matters by choosing the Stormhenge.

Steady rain during a stretch of outdoor chores never reached one tester inside the women's REI Co-op Stormhenge Down Hybrid Parka, a $299 coat that took the Best Value for Women award. "I was seriously impressed by how well the outer shell performed in wet conditions," the tester said. The face fabric wetted out over time, yet no water crossed into the interior. Some testers preferred it to every other jacket in the lineup. The women's team recommends it for shoppers working with a tighter budget.

Two plies of cloth form the outer wall, and a durable water repellent coating treats the face. Inside sits 850-fill goose down. The review calls 500 to 800 a reasonable fill power for most buyers, which lifts this inexpensive coat above the suggested band. No other pick with a published fill power goes higher, including the Canada Goose parka that costs more than six times as much. Fill power alone does not settle warmth. A coat with a lower rating and more down can match one with a higher rating and less stuffing. Recycled materials go into the build, and a baffled collar wraps the throat.

Sizing runs true, and stepping up one size leaves room for extra layers beneath. A chest pocket holds a phone. The coat targets commuters, travelers, and everyday winter-weather enthusiasts. Reviewers credited it with solid construction and a sleek design packed with features.

Protection around the head trails the coverage on the torso. The hood sits shallow and lacks a ruff, and the neck baffle is small. The zipper stops at the chin and leaves the face exposed. The verdict warns that the coat may not hold up in a blizzard.

Milder, humid coastal regions see wetter winters than frigid zones, where snow dominates. A sustained soaking never penetrated this coat, yet its unprotected face and ruff-free hood leave a wearer vulnerable in a whiteout. Damp coastal winters suit it best.

The Patagonia Jackson Glacier keeps a wearer comfortable down to 15°F on its own, through long stretches of standing still, and it took the men's award for warm and casual wear at a list price of $519. A motionless body produces little heat of its own. The 15°F mark reflects the coat's insulation more than the wearer's effort. High-loft down fills the body beneath a waterproof shell. Testers credited the coat with delivering heat without much weight, and one compared pulling it on to "slipping into a warm cloud."

A relaxed cut leaves space for extra layers underneath on frigid days. One broad-shouldered tester felt no restriction through the torso. The testers judged the design free of overbuilding, which suits its award category.

Drawstrings at the front and back of the hood pull the opening in and keep the field of vision clear, a help on a bike. A fleece lining surrounds the zipper where it reaches the nose. The pockets swallow a gloved hand. Watertight zippers seal the front closure and the pockets against wet weather.

Open cuffs expose the jacket's clearest weakness. Nothing cinches the cuffs, and one tester felt air rush up his arms on e-bike rides. The gap undercuts the hood's value for cyclists, who retain a clear view ahead while their wrists go cold. The hood lacks a fur ruff, and the cut runs short. The review team expects residents of the far north to need more protection than this coat provides.

The complaints cluster at three openings: the wrists, the face, and the hem. None of them targets the filling or the outer fabric, which suggests the money buys a sound core that weakens at its edges. The temperature floor and the drafty sleeves point to a coat for chilly cities and two-wheeled commutes, with sub-zero regions left to longer, heavier parkas.

The women's Fjallraven Nuuk kept testers warm in temperatures and wind chills down to -30°F, and it won Best Combo of Style and Weather Protection for Women at a list price of $535. A durable outer shell wraps thick synthetic insulation, and testers described the fill as "incredibly warm." Synthetic fill needs more volume than down to match its heat, which helps explain the dense layer packed inside the Nuuk.

One of the largest adjustable hoods in the test crowns the Nuuk, and a removable faux fur ruff rims its opening. The reviewers single out the ruff as a strong shield against the elements. A waist cinch pulls the coat in at the midsection, and a smooth lining covers the interior. The fit runs a little big, and the reviewers credit the coat with a relaxed style. One tester said "the stylish, heavyweight design and thoughtful features inspire confidence in the longevity of the design."

The Nuuk's heavy build becomes a burden once the weather warms. One tester loves the coat through the coldest months of the year but found it more than the job required in spring and autumn, when temperatures climb. The reviewers judged that it falls short as a three-season jacket, and it feels bulkier than down coats in those shoulder months. Snapping the storm flap shut without zipping the front all the way lets the wearer release some heat on milder days.

The two-way main zipper drew the sharpest complaints. Testers found it hard to engage, and the frustration sent them to other jackets whenever the weather allowed. The flaw left the coat's heat retention intact. The Nuuk also resists packing down, a drawback for anyone who wants to stuff a coat into a bag for travel.

The reviewers recommend the Nuuk to shoppers in colder climates who want as much heat as a coat can hold short of a full technical winter jacket. Its drawbacks surface in mild weather and on the go, and its hood, ruff, and fill earn their keep in the deepest cold. The $535 price pays off best for buyers whose winters stay frigid from start to finish.

The Patagonia Tres 3-in-1 Parka, winner of the Most Versatile Men's Parka award at a $699 list price, works three ways, and its waterproof H2No outer layer can serve on its own as a rain jacket. Owners can wear the shell alone, the liner alone, or both pieces as one full winter parka. The down-insulated liner supplies solid warmth without its outer partner, which turns the inner piece into a complete coat of its own.

One tester called the parka a "daily go-to" and assigned each layer a job. The tester wore the bare shell for wet errands, the liner on cool mornings, and both pieces together once the cold turned serious. The routine shows the design earning its keep in ordinary weekday weather, with the wearer matching the coat to each morning's forecast.

Cold fall rain, mild winter afternoons, and snowy commutes all sit within the parka's range, and each condition lines up with one of its configurations. Urban dwellers and travelers who face unsettled weather across three seasons stand to benefit most. Testers praised the coat's looks and found it toasty with both layers in place.

The Tres leaves both its hood and its pockets uninsulated, so wearers heading into a freezing day need gloves and a beanie. Some wind sneaks past the collar, and the outer fabrics prove more prone to snags. These gaps around the hood, pockets, and collar bite hardest at the cold end of the coat's spectrum, under the same conditions that call for the full two-layer build.

A higher price counts among the drawbacks testers listed. Of the 10 award entries, only the Canada Goose splurge pick carries a steeper list price, and the women's Tres matches the men's at $699. Shoppers in wet, changeable climates can extract the most value from the outlay, because the standalone shell lets the coat earn wear on rainy days.

The women's Patagonia Tres 3-in-1 Parka, listed at $699, won the Most Versatile Women's Parka award by stretching one purchase across fall, winter, and spring. The review aims it at women in warmer or unpredictable climates, along with anyone who wants a single coat to carry them from the first chilly weeks of autumn to the spring thaw.

Two pieces drive the design. A satiny, down-filled liner zips into a rugged waterproof shell, and either half can go out alone. Together and apart, the pieces function as three separate jackets. Each setup holds a clean cut and reads as polished whether it serves as a full parka or a lone layer. The hood offers generous adjustment, and the combined layers kept testers warm.

One tester put all three modes to work in different settings. The full parka handled a snowstorm, the shell took on a downpour, and the liner went out to dinner. Each configuration matched a distinct kind of day, and one coat covered all three without a trip back to the closet.

The modular build leaves gaps in deep cold. The liner lacks a hood and closes with one zipper. Neither the hood nor the shell's pockets contain insulation, which forces the wearer to rely on a hat and gloves once temperatures plunge.

Fit poses a second hurdle. Testers found the sizing tricky. Shoppers should try the Tres over the clothes they wear on an ordinary winter day before settling on a size.

Price adds weight to those trade-offs. Among the 10 award picks, only the Canada Goose splurge carries a higher list price than the Tres. The waterproof shell earns its keep in milder, humid coastal regions, where winters run wetter than in frigid zones where snow dominates. A shell built to stop water also blocks wind in nearly every case. Women along those damp coasts stand to collect three working jackets for one outlay, while buyers facing months of hard freeze would pay for flexibility their winters leave unused.

At $1,895, the Canada Goose Expedition Parka Heritage carries the steepest list price among the 10 picks, and both its men's and women's versions earned one of the highest warmth scores the site has ever awarded. The women's team called the coat "a fortress against biting cold." Its sticker runs more than six times the price of the $299 value picks and sits $1,196 above the next-costliest award winner, the $699 Patagonia Tres 3-in-1 Parka.

Mild weather turns all that insulation into a liability. Testers broke a sweat once temperatures climbed past about 15°F. The parka suits extreme cold in places such as northern Canada, Alaska, and Scandinavia, along with long days of standing still outdoors. Strong weatherproofing features back up the warmth in those conditions.

A thick polyester-cotton shell wraps 650-fill-power down, and the trim seals the gaps where frigid air creeps in. Extra-long rib-knit cuffs close off the wrists, and a generous hood shields the head. A built-in snow skirt and a cinchable waist stop drafts from rising under the hem. Backpack-style carry straps round out the feature list and give the wearer a way to haul the parka once it comes off.

The testers' own Expedition parkas show scant signs of wear after a few years of use. The Heritage model in the review came with a coyote-fur ruff. A February 2026 update notes that newer fur-free versions drop the ruff, and Canada Goose confirmed that every other aspect of the design remains unchanged.

The heavy, bulky shell restricts movement and resists packing. The reviewers questioned whether most people need a coat this heavy-duty, and some settings call for something lighter. People who live, work, and play in sub-arctic temperatures may find the expense a sound investment, in the reviewers' view. Anyone whose winters stay above 15°F would pay more than for any other pick and spend much of the season sweating inside it.

#5501. Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:19 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:52 am

Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas, Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.

The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.

Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch. Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.

While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.

Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

#5500. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.

#5499. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.
