#5498. The most common grammar mistakes — and how to fix them, according to Grammarly

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Grammarly's explainer covers 30 grammar errors. Here are 20 of them, from your vs. you're to dashes, with the rule behind each fix.

Few moments sting like a colleague, teacher, or friend catching a slip in something you wrote. The embarrassment arrives in an instant, and it can linger after someone fixes the error. Yet no writer is immune. Everyone makes grammar mistakes, in a school essay and a note to a client alike. The stakes run higher than pride. A misplaced word or stray punctuation mark can leave a reader stuck on a sentence, rereading it to work out what the author meant. Prose that demands such effort strains the patience of its audience. Clean writing keeps attention on the ideas instead of the mechanics.

Grammar rules exist to help readers grasp a text, so a writer who breaks one risks confusing the audience. Language keeps shifting, and a phrase that once counted as wrong can settle into ordinary usage over time. Some departures from the rules don't qualify as faults at all. In certain cases, a writer who bends a rule on purpose produces a better result. The catch lies in the phrase "on purpose." Deliberate rule-breaking demands knowledge of the rule itself, along with why people stumble over it and how to repair the damage. Without that grounding, a stylistic choice and a careless blunder look identical on the page.

Grammarly published an explainer by Lindsay Kramer that walks through 30 common grammar mistakes writers should avoid, and the company's blog updated it on June 20, 2023. The piece defines a grammar mistake as a misused word or punctuation mark, a break from an established convention. Its entries span flawed punctuation, tangled syntax, and poor word choices. Most pair a short guideline with example sentences, and the article acknowledges that style guides split on some points. The explainer ranks nothing and measures nothing. It cites no survey, frequency count, or error rate, so its sequence reveals nothing about which problems turn up most. It closes with a pitch for the company's own writing assistant. This article draws 20 of those 30 entries, following the explainer's original order, and lays out the principle behind each one along with its fix.

Your and you're make up a homophone pair, two words that share a sound when spoken but carry separate meanings. To and too belong to the same family of sound-alikes. Speech conceals the difference between the two spellings. Writing exposes it, and a reader sees at a glance which version landed in the sentence. The wrong choice produces a genuine word, so the slip can survive a hasty reread.

Your works as a possessive pronoun, and it marks ownership. Grammarly's example has someone leave a backpack at school the day before, and your ties the bag to the listener who forgot it. The word sits in front of backpack, the item it modifies. Grammarly links this pronoun to a single second person, so the example sentence addresses one owner.

You're squeezes "you are" into one word, and an apostrophe stands in for the missing letter. Your carries no apostrophe, so the mark flags the contraction. The line "You're expected to arrive no later than 6 p.m." reads the same with both words written out. Nothing in it changes hands. It voices an expectation aimed at the listener, complete with a deadline.

Your hooks onto a noun and needs one to follow, such as backpack. You're carries a subject and a verb, so it can launch a clause on its own, as "You're expected" does. Dropping the possessive into the deadline sentence would strip the line of its main verb and leave an owner with nothing owned. The word after the blank offers a first clue. A thing owned points to your, and a description or action points to you're.

Expansion supplies a quick test. Swap in "you are" and reread the passage. The deadline sentence still holds together after the swap, so the contraction fits. The backpack sentence turns to nonsense once the two full words replace the pronoun in front of the bag, so your wins. The check takes seconds and requires no grammar vocabulary. The two words share no definition, which lets one substitution settle every case.

Who belongs in the subject position of a sentence, and whom belongs in the object position. The question "Who will be hosting the party this weekend?" shows the first pattern at work. The pronoun stands in for the unknown host, the person who will carry out the hosting, so it takes the subject form.

Whom takes over once the pronoun names someone on the receiving end. In "To whom should I send the package?" the missing person would get the delivery. The preposition to sits before whom, a spot that marks the pronoun as an object. Position near the front of a question offers no clue on its own. Whom lands second in the package question, ahead of both the verb and the subject, yet it names the person getting the parcel.

Swapping in he or him gives writers a fast check, a test the CDC's Clear Writing Hub recommends. He points to who, and him points to whom. To fill the blank in "____ wrote the report?" the hub recasts the line as a plain statement with he as the author of the report. He fits that slot, so the question becomes "Who wrote the report?" A second blank, "____ should I vote for?", draws an object pronoun in the trial answer "You should vote for them." The hub's verdict for that one is "Whom should I vote for?"

The same swap confirms both of the earlier sample questions. He will be hosting the party, which fits the subject form and keeps who in place. Nobody would send the package to he. The phrase to him sounds right, and it lines up with whom. The test works because he shares the subject role with who, and him shares the object role with whom.

Formal correctness and plain language can pull writers in different directions. The hub also offers "For whom should I vote?" and calls it correct by formal standards but probably not the best choice for plain-language writing. The package example uses the same construction, with to leading the sentence ahead of whom. The hub's other version of the voting question sidesteps that opener by parking for at the end of the sentence. The pronoun choice follows a fixed rule, while the preposition's placement remains a matter of style.

Who's compresses two words, "who is," into one, and whose names an owner as the possessive form of the relative pronoun who. Grammarly files the pair among the slips that trip up writers, and each spelling handles a separate task.

The apostrophe in who's marks the spot where the letter i dropped out of "is." Grammarly's sample question, "Who's ready for the exam on Friday?" survives when a writer spells out "who is" in place of the contraction. The longer version asks the same thing about the same test, with no shift in meaning. Any sentence that passes this expansion test calls for the contraction.

Whose collapses under the same swap, and the collapse points to the right choice. Grammarly pairs the possessive with the question "Whose laptop is this?" which asks who owns the computer. Put "who is" in the possessive's place, and the question turns into a string of words with two verbs and no owner, something no reader can parse. A sentence that breaks under the test needs whose.

Word order offers a second clue, with whose parked in front of the noun it claims in the laptop question. The possessive and "laptop" form a unit that matches a holder with the thing held. In the exam question, who's leads into "ready," which describes a person's state and assigns nothing to anyone. A noun in the next slot hints at the possessive, though the expansion test stays the surer check.

The spelling of whose sets a trap of its own. The word signals possession with no apostrophe, and the apostrophe in who's stands in for a missing letter. A writer who links apostrophes with ownership may reach for who's in the laptop question and end up asking something nonsensical. Your and you're follow the identical pattern, with the bare form showing possession and the apostrophe marking a contraction. Ownership in this pair travels without an apostrophe, the reverse of the habit Grammarly ties to many possessive nouns.

Affect names an action and effect names its result, a split Grammarly captures by defining the verb affect as "to cause an effect." The definition binds the two words together. One describes the push, and the other describes what the push leaves behind. A writer who swaps them hands the reader an action where an outcome belongs, or an outcome where the sentence needs something to happen.

Grammarly's examples tie each word to its slot in a sentence. In one, a heat wave could alter someone's vacation plans, and affect does the acting. In the other, a bigger budget yields a major effect on hiring, with effect standing as the consequence of the spending. The surrounding words in each example offer a quick check. Effect follows the article "a" and the adjective "major," the signals of a noun. Affect trails a subject, the heat wave, that acts on the plans.

Affect works in its usual role as a verb for producing a change in a person or thing. Effect, by contrast, serves in most cases as a noun naming the end result of something. Each word holds a narrower second job as well. Affect can name an emotion or feeling as a noun, a use that belongs to psychology and psychiatry and sits outside typical everyday English. Effect can act as a verb meaning to bring about, an uncommon choice that turns up in formal settings.

Grammarly's entry sets those specialist senses aside and confines itself to the verb affect and the noun effect. Both of its sample sentences hold to that division. Across general English, affect turns up more as a verb and effect more as a noun. The explainer's narrow scope mirrors the dominant usage. Outside a psychology paper or a formal document, a writer who pairs affect with action and effect with outcome lands on the correct word.

Grammarly assigns "who" to people and "that" to inanimate objects. The right pick comes down to whether a human being stands behind the clause. Each of the explainer's samples uses the pronoun to open a clause describing the noun it follows. One features a brother who solved the mystery, and "who" introduces what he did. Swapping in "that" would break Grammarly's guideline by handling the brother as an item. A second example runs the other direction. A course that changed someone's perspective on climate change has no personhood, and "that" suits it.

Groups of people supply the one exception Grammarly permits. The company accepts "that" for a collection of humans when a sentence stresses the group as a whole instead of its individual members. Grammarly's illustration involves an organization that promotes native plant cultivation. People fill the organization, yet the sentence cares about the body as a unit, and the unit takes "that." Emphasis decides the pronoun here, and the makeup of the group stays the same either way. A writer who shifts attention to the members can return to "who" under the same logic.

Federal style advice draws a matching boundary. The NIH style guide reserves "who" for people and "that" for things. The guide carries the principle over to countries, which take "it" along with "which" or "that." It bars "he," "she," and "who" as references to a country. A country lands on the thing side of the divide under that guidance, even though a population lives inside its borders.

A single name covering many people marks the point where "who" gives way to "that." The organization and country cases suggest a working test. A sentence that spotlights a named individual, such as the brother who cracked the mystery, calls for "who." A course, a physical object, or an institution acting as one body calls for "that." The NIH fixes the choice for countries. Grammarly leaves collective nouns to the writer's focus. Under that approach, a noun such as organization can take either pronoun.

The word that introduces a clause the sentence needs to make sense, and which opens one carrying extra detail the sentence could lose without harm. Grammarly treats the pick between them as a test of necessity. A wrong choice signals to readers that a piece of information matters more, or less, than it does.

Grammarly's first example uses the clause to single out one patient from among several dogs. The speaker identifies the pet bound for the vet as the one that ate a rock, and the swallowed stone does the identifying. Remove the clause, and the sentence points to one of several dogs with no way to tell which. A clause doing such work stays bound to its noun with no comma between them.

The terrier in Grammarly's second example draws which. The breed adds color without distinguishing one pet from another, and the phrase "my other dog" handles the sorting on its own. Drop the breed, and the sentence still tells readers that a second dog needs a trip to the vet. Commas flank the clause on both sides, marking the breed as an aside.

Commas give the distinction a visible form on the page. The EERE Style Guide tells writers to set off nonessential clauses with commas. The guide bars commas around restrictive phrases, the elements a sentence's meaning depends on. Both rules match Grammarly's dog examples. No comma splits the rock-eating clause from the word it modifies, and a pair of commas surrounds the terrier clause. A federal energy office and a writing company's blog settle on the same convention.

Any writer stuck between the two words can run the deletion test the dog examples model. A sentence that keeps its meaning without the clause calls for which and a pair of commas. A sentence that can no longer pin down its subject calls for that, with the clause left unpunctuated. The test turns a grammar question into a reading question. A writer can settle it by rereading the sentence, with no need to memorize labels such as restrictive or nonessential.

I.e. pins a statement down to the one thing the writer means, and e.g. offers a few samples from a broader pool, a split rooted in two Latin phrases, id est and exempli gratia. The first abbreviation clarifies. The second illustrates. A CDC style guide for health hazard evaluation reports translates id est as "that is" and exempli gratia as "for example." The same manual urges writers to handle the pair with care because their meanings diverge.

Grammarly's late-arrival sentence puts i.e. to work. A speaker warns of running late again tomorrow, and the parenthetical that follows, opened by i.e., explains that the car is still in the shop. The aside spells out the cause of the delay and leaves no other explanation open. E.g. plays a looser role in a line about a year of reading. There, the parentheses hold "A Tree Grows in Brooklyn" and "The Fault in Our Stars" as two picks from a larger stack of novels, and the reader can tell the list is partial.

Smoking, drinking, and overeating carry two senses in the CDC document, depending on the abbreviation in front of them. Its i.e. example refers to three harmful behaviors under study and then names those three as the complete set. Its e.g. example calls certain behaviors harmful and offers the identical trio as possibilities. The words stay fixed, yet the first version closes the group and the second invites additions.

NIH's STRIDES program frames the distinction as specific versus possible. Its communication guidelines describe i.e. as introducing something precise and e.g. as introducing something that might hold true. An author who reaches for i.e. commits to a single answer, while e.g. makes room for alternatives.

Grammarly calls for a comma after each abbreviation and places both inside parentheses. The NCBI Style Guide adds that e.g. takes periods and a trailing comma and needs no italics. It exempts both abbreviations from italic type because they are common and are not written-out forms. Flawless commas and periods cannot rescue the wrong abbreviation. The sharper check asks whether the aside completes the thought or offers one case among several.

Then marks the moment when something will happen, and than compares people or things, according to Grammarly. The two words sit one vowel apart, yet each answers a different question about a sentence. The first question is whether the line tracks time. The second is whether it weighs one subject against another. A writer who swaps them forces readers to guess whether a line describes a sequence of events or a contest between two rivals.

Grammarly's timing example lays out a two-step plan. The speaker and others start with the homework and move on to a presentation, with then marking the handoff from one task to the next. Grammarly opens that sentence with the word first, which establishes the order, and then completes it. Swap in than, and the line stops making sense as a plan.

Grammarly's comparison example needs no clock at all. In it, the cousins stand taller than the people speaking, and than sets one height against the other. Both parties in the example are human, and Grammarly's rule lets than measure people and objects alike. The comparative taller precedes than, a signal that the sentence registers a difference instead of following a schedule.

Then functions as an adverb in most sentences. Its territory covers time and the succession of actions. Than, in its typical use, appears when a writer sets two things side by side. The pair differs in spelling and pronunciation. Rapid speech erases that gap, and the words blur together in quick conversation. Ears make a poor guide to the right choice. Meaning has to decide it.

A spelling trick ties each word to its job. Then and time share the letter E. Than and comparisons share the letter A. Grammarly's homework sentence carries a point in time, and its cousins sentence holds a matchup between relatives. A writer stuck between the two can scan a draft for one of those signals and let the vowel follow from the answer.

Less belongs with amounts that resist division into units, such as time or plastic, and fewer belongs with items a reader could tally. The noun makes the call. Ask whether the thing arrives in separate pieces. If it does, fewer fits. If it comes as a mass or an abstraction, less takes over.

Students with less time to work on an assignment have a shorter window, and the wording treats that window as a single quantity. Nobody reading the sentence pictures individual minutes stacked on a desk. Swapping in fewer would force the reader to imagine discrete chunks the sentence never mentions.

Both words can share a sentence without clashing. Fewer people buying disposable water bottles would mean less plastic piling up in landfills. People exist as distinct individuals, and each one adds to a headcount. They take fewer. Plastic in a landfill forms a heap with no natural unit, and it takes less. Each noun picks its own word, even with the two sitting side by side.

Reader's Digest frames the same split around water and its containers. Water pours as one continuous substance, so a writer would ask for less water. Bottles stand apart from one another, and the same writer would ask for fewer water bottles.

Spans of time, distance, and money bend the pattern. Reader's Digest reports that less than fits those measures even with a noun a writer could enumerate. A concert that lasted less than two hours offers one case, according to Reader's Digest. The phrase treats the two hours as one lump.

The supermarket express lane puts the slip on public display. Reader's Digest flags the sign reading "ten items or less" as a grammatical error and holds that it should read "ten items or fewer." Groceries reach the belt as objects a shopper can number one by one. Paired, the concert and the checkout sign show that the piece-by-piece test needs a second step, a check on whether the noun measures duration, distance, or money.

The choice between me and I follows from the job the pronoun does in its sentence, and Grammarly makes the split visible through two short examples. In the first, someone explains, "It was almost midnight, so I didn't stop to pick up my shoe." I fits there. The narrator performs the action, in this case skipping the shoe.

The other sample reverses the roles. In the question "You want me to dance with you?" the listener does the wanting, and the speaker is its target. Me occupies the slot after the verb. Trading the pronouns between the two lines breaks both of them. Me in the shoe sentence would leave the skipping without a proper subject, and I after want would wedge a subject form into a spot that calls for an object.

A second person beside the pronoun can leave writers unsure, and the CDC's Clear Writing Hub offers a test for that moment. Strip out the other noun or pronoun, read what remains, and keep whichever version sounds right alone. The hub's line about cousins coming to visit "my sister and me" shrinks to a visit to me, and me survives the cut. Its next case, about "My cat and I" on camera before a meeting, reduces to I on camera, which keeps I in place.

Comparisons built on than open a choice. The hub presents "My brother is taller than I" as the traditional phrasing for formal prose. The stricter option casts than as a conjunction, with an unspoken am trailing the pronoun. In informal, plain language writing, the hub grants that "My brother is taller than me" may sound more natural. The looser wording treats than as a preposition.

Grammarly's pair and the hub's stripping method work as one tool. Removing the extra name leaves a lone pronoun, which faces the question the shoe and dance lines raise about whether it drives the verb or absorbs it. The cousins visit me, so me takes the object position. The cat and I appear on camera, so I takes the subject position. A writer who checks what the bare pronoun does can handle any pairing with a friend, sibling, or pet without guessing.

Farther handles literal distance, and further means "more," according to Grammarly. The choice comes down to one question about the sentence. Does the word describe space between two points, or an added amount of something? The explainer's first example covers the physical case, with an island that looks more distant than it ever has. The gap between the viewer and the shore decides the word there. Its second example involves no map at all. A writer tells a company to stop any further communication, and the word fits because the sentence measures no space. It refuses more messages.

Dictionary.com traces the same split to a traditional rule, one that pairs farther with literal distances and further with figurative distances or metaphorical extents. Figurative distance explains why the company line needs further. Nobody can measure off a conversation with a tape measure. The rule bends in everyday speech, where people often trade one word for the other, according to Dictionary.com. Further tends to turn up beside literal distances in that loose usage, and farther tends to mark a more advanced point or a large extent.

Further holds a job of its own at the head of a sentence. Dictionary.com reports that the word can open a sentence or clause in the sense of furthermore, in addition, or moreover. Someone who starts a clause with "Further," to add a point draws on that sense. The company example sits closer to the "more" meaning Grammarly assigns the word. Its speaker rejects any extra contact, and the sentence never touches physical space.

British English often lets further cover physical distance as well, according to the Collins Dictionary Language Blog. Further can step into farther's territory, and Collins limits farther to physical distance alone. Dictionary.com notes that in everyday use farther can signal a greater degree or extent too. The island line could take further and pass in British prose. Grammarly's guidance would steer the same sentence back to farther. Reserving farther for physical gaps keeps writing safe under every standard cited here, from Grammarly's to the British habit.

Like draws a comparison between two things, and such as introduces concrete examples, according to Grammarly's explainer. Both phrases can occupy the same slot in a sentence while delivering different meanings. A writer who grabs the wrong one hands readers a resemblance where a list belonged, or a list where a resemblance belonged.

Grammarly illustrates the first job with a couch that has black and white spots like a dalmatian. The furniture and the dog stay separate objects in the sentence. Like tells the reader the couch shares a pattern with the animal's coat, and nobody pictures a dog lounging on the cushions. The likeness rests on one shared trait between two different things.

Such as handles a distinct task in the second sentence, which concerns pizza toppings. The speaker announces many toppings before naming peppers, pineapple, and pepperoni. Each named item belongs to the larger category the sentence describes. The word many signals that the selection runs past those three, so the list samples the options without exhausting them.

Group membership decides which phrase fits. Peppers count as pizza toppings, so such as works. A dalmatian does not count as a couch, so like works. Swapping the words muddles both sentences. Spots such as a dalmatian would cast the dog as one kind of spot, and toppings like peppers would read as toppings that resemble peppers.

The EIA Writing Style Guide defines "like" as "similar to" and "such as" as "for example." Its sample sentence for like sets natural gas beside coal in the Southwest Power Pool, where coal cycling makes room for wind power. Its sample for such as names ethanol and biodiesel within the wider class of biofuels. Natural gas and coal remain two fuels, and ethanol and biodiesel both qualify as biofuels, so the energy examples mirror the couch and the pizza.

The same check travels across subjects, from pizza toppings to power grids. A writer who asks whether the named items belong to the set under discussion gets an answer that picks the phrase before any reader meets the sentence.

Past works as a noun naming earlier times in Grammarly's first example, where a grandfather tells his grandchildren stories about the past. The word marks a stretch of history in that sentence. Nothing acts on it or through it, and it sits in the slot a noun fills, following the preposition "about" and the article "the."

The grandfather sentence has its own verb doing the work. "Told" carries the action, so past has no motion to supply. Its job is to name what the stories cover. Dropping passed into the spot after "the" wrecks the phrase. An article introduces a noun, and a verb can't fill the position it opens.

Passed signals motion in the second sentence, which describes an SUV that passed on the speaker's right. The term reports something the vehicle did. It functions as a verb, and the SUV serves as its subject. Strip it out and the line loses its only verb, leaving a vehicle with nothing to do.

The "-ed" ending offers a visible clue. It marks passed as a past-tense verb, one describing a maneuver the SUV finished before the speaker mentioned it. Spelling the word as past in the SUV line erases that marker and leaves the sentence without a predicate. The spelling also preserves the base word pass, the action the SUV performs on the road.

Grammarly spells out the principle behind both sentences. Past refers to something that has already happened, and the explainer lists four roles it can fill: noun, adjective, preposition, and adverb. Passed works as a verb. The grandfather's stories show past in one of those four roles, and the SUV shows passed in its single one.

The lopsided split hands writers a quick test. Past can take four jobs, and passed takes one. A word that reports a movement, such as one car overtaking another on the road, carries the action of its sentence and calls for passed. A word that names a period, or fills any slot besides the verb, calls for past.

Grammarly names "based on" as the correct phrasing for now and builds its only model sentence around it. The explainer saves its sternest ruling for a longer variant, the one that tacks "of" onto "based off," and calls that version never correct.

The guide gives "based off" and "based on" a shared job. Each phrase points to the facts or circumstances behind a particular decision or conclusion. The two-word "based off" still falls short of approval. Grammarly allows that it may one day count as grammatically correct, yet for the present it grants that standing to "based on" alone. The explainer attaches no timeline to the shift and hedges it with a perhaps. Its verdict casts the shorter form as a usage in waiting, an example of the language drift the explainer describes, in which wording once judged an error can settle into accepted use.

The sample reads: "Based on the rain in the forecast, I decided not to water my garden today." The forecast supplies the grounds, and the skipped watering is the choice those grounds produced. The phrase opens the sentence and ties the cause in its first half to the action in its second. The garden case covers a decision. Grammarly supplies no companion sentence for a conclusion, the other use the entry names. Swapping in the three-word variant would keep the meaning yet trade the sample's phrasing for one the explainer rejects.

Grammarly rules out the three-word version in every context and offers no example of it in use. Side by side, the three variants fall into tiers. One earns a model sentence and present-day approval. One holds out hope of future acceptance. The third stands forbidden. A writer who settles for "based off" lands in the middle tier, on wording the explainer stops short of endorsing. A writer who trims the longer form to "based on" moves from the forbidden end of that scale to the only option the explainer both endorses and demonstrates.

Compliment and complement differ by one letter, and Grammarly separates them with a pair of sentences about a person named Dara. In the first, a writer enjoys Dara's presentation and pays her a compliment. In the second, Dara's background in UX design complements the writer's own experience in front-end development. Each sentence demands its own spelling, and a swap would turn praise into a statement about fit, or the reverse.

Writers confuse the two words because they sound identical, even though their meanings have little in common. To compliment someone is to express admiration or say something kind about them. The noun names an expression of that admiration. Paying someone a compliment involves no money. The verb pay in that phrase means handing over the kind words themselves.

Dara's presentation sentence shows the flattering sense at work. The writer liked what Dara delivered and answered with a warm remark, so the i form belongs there. Nothing in that sentence involves two things merging, which rules out the e form.

Complement applies to two things that go well together, with each one improving the other once they connect. Dara's UX design background and the writer's front-end development experience match that description. Neither skill set stands in for the other in the example. Together, the two cover more ground than either reaches alone.

One memory trick ties complement to complete. The e word suits any union that produces a finished look or feel. The adjectives follow the same divide. Complimentary can mean supplied free of charge, and it can describe a person who voices approval. Complementary refers to things that mesh and make each other whole.

A writer stuck between the two can ask one question about the sentence at hand. If it applauds someone, the i wins. If it describes two parts completing each other, the e does. The same question settles complimentary versus complementary, since those longer words mirror the split.

A misplaced modifier can hand a reader a picture the writer never meant, and Grammarly's example gives one sister a pair of cats called Ghost. The faulty version reads, "My sister adopted another cat named Ghost." Grammarly answers with a deadpan question about whether she now owns two cats with that name. The joke works because the sentence's literal reading supports it.

The words "named Ghost" cause the trouble through their position. Sitting beside "another cat," the label seems to describe a name the first cat also carried, so "another" implies an earlier Ghost. The sentence contains no misspelling, and each part of speech does a legal job. Its meaning breaks because the modifier latches onto the wrong neighbor. A reader has no way to tell from the words alone whether the writer meant one Ghost or two.

Grammarly's repair adds a verb and rebuilds the line: "My sister adopted another cat and named her Ghost." The fix splits one tangled description into two actions, the adoption and the naming, in the order the sister performed them. "Another" still signals a second cat, yet the name now belongs to the newcomer alone. The pronoun "her" ties the name to the new arrival and tells the reader the cat is female. One extra verb, one conjunction, and one pronoun clear the confusion without cutting a single detail from the original.

Grammarly's faulty modifier also trails at the end of its sentence. End-of-sentence tack-ons form the most common type of misplaced modifier in scientific writing, according to the CDC. The agency's guidance calls the dangling modifier, a phrase that opens a sentence, the most embarrassing variety. Under what the guidance calls the rule of proximity, that opening phrase appears to describe whatever subject starts the main clause after it.

Both patterns trace back to placement, which means a writer can catch either one by checking what word sits beside each descriptor.

Passive voice hands the subject slot to the meal in Grammarly's sample, which reads, "Breakfast was prepared by me." The cook trails in a closing phrase. The person who did the work arrives last, after the audience has met the food and the verb. Grammarly stops short of labeling passive voice a flat error. Its example shows what that ordering costs a sentence.

The repair takes three words. "I prepared breakfast" returns the cook to the front, puts the verb second, and lets the meal land as the object. Nothing drops out in the swap. The active sentence carries every fact the passive one held, with two fewer words and a straight line from actor to action.

A passive build reverses who does what. The NIH style guide explains that the subject acts in active voice and is acted upon in passive voice. Grammarly's breakfast line fits the pattern, with the meal on the receiving end and the cook doing the work from the back of the sentence. A clear writing tool from the CDC offers a sentence built the same way, in which a driver hitting the brakes on a downhill run shows up only after the brakes and the verb. Its active rewrite puts the driver first. Writers who spot an actor tucked behind "by" have found a candidate for revision.

Passive phrasing earns a place in some sentences. The NIH guide singles out three situations that suit the passive: an actor who is unknown, unimportant, or obvious. The CDC tool extends the same latitude when the performer is unknown or irrelevant. It also urges writers to hold passive sentences to 15% or less of a document. Both guides tie the decision to what the reader knows or needs to learn about the actor.

Grammarly's breakfast example names its actor, which rules out the unknown-performer case both guides describe. The passive version identifies the cook in the phrase "by me" and hides no one. The extra length buys the reader nothing the active sentence fails to deliver. A writer who includes the actor inside a passive sentence holds every piece an active version needs and can finish the fix by moving the actor to the start of the sentence.

Possessive nouns announce ownership, and many of them rely on an apostrophe to carry that signal. Grammarly's example of Maryam's notebook shows the pattern for a single owner. The mark sits between the name and the final s, telling a reader that the notebook belongs to Maryam alone.

Plural nouns push the mark past the s. Grammarly's plural example involves grades held by a group of students, and there the apostrophe closes the word to show the scores belong to the whole group. One small shift alters the head count. Student's grades describe the record of one learner. Students' grades cover an entire class, and a stray mark can hand a single report card to everyone in the room.

Not every possessive needs the mark, a point Grammarly signals by saying possessive nouns take one "often." The explainer's entries on your and whose describe both words as possessive forms, and neither carries one. Both pronouns show belonging through spelling alone, leaving the punctuation to nouns.

Words ending in s divide the style guides. Grammarly notes that Chicago style departs from other approaches on possessives built from these words. The correct form comes down to which manual a writer follows. Writers loyal to different handbooks can treat the same word in separate ways and both stay correct. An editor who flags such a form as an error may be applying the wrong manual.

Two checks settle placement in every case Grammarly covers. The first asks whether one individual or a group holds the item. The second asks whether the word ends in s, and that question alone leaves room for a house style. Of the two, only the count of owners yields one answer everywhere.

A period sits inside the closing parenthesis only when the enclosed words form a complete sentence standing apart from the ones around it. Grammarly demonstrates the rule with two lines about a house. The first reports blue trim and ends with its own period. The second, wrapped in parentheses, notes that the neighbor's house has blue trim as well. This aside opens with a capital letter and closes with a period of its own. The final mark stays within the parentheses because the aside forms an independent sentence.

Tucking the same thought into the first sentence changes where the period lands. In Grammarly's alternate version, the neighbor's matching trim appears in lowercase inside the parentheses. The period moves outside the closing mark to end the full line about the house. The aside could stand alone as a sentence, yet the larger sentence takes over the ending punctuation. Shorter fragments follow the same logic. Grammarly's third sample describes a house with blue trim and a green door, with "with white windows" dropped into the middle. The main clause continues past the parentheses with no extra marks.

Commas belong after parentheses and never before them, Grammarly advises. Most parenthetical text attaches to the words preceding it, and a comma ahead of the opening parenthesis would sever the inserted material from the phrase it explains. A comma pressed against the closing parenthesis, with no space between them, counts as standard practice.

Grammarly's party sentence breaks the comma rule by setting the mark after "quiet" and ahead of the parenthetical about a canceled DJ. The misplaced comma splits the canceled booking from the hush it accounts for, and the clause about Gina's guitar loses the pause it needs. Shifting the comma to the far side of the closing parenthesis repairs both problems. The canceled DJ stays attached to the quiet party, and the comma signals the break before Gina brings out her instrument.

Across Grammarly's samples, the sentence that claims the parenthetical decides where each mark goes, whether that sentence lives inside the parentheses or wraps around them.

Grammarly flags the em dash, the en dash, and the hyphen as a trio writers mix up, and it separates them by the work each one does. The en dash covers date and time ranges, as in "Monday – Saturday." It also links complex compound adjectives when both halves already carry hyphens or when one part is a multi-word noun or an open compound adjective. Grammarly illustrates that second job with a description of an author who won the Nobel Prize. In that phrase, the longer mark ties the word winning to the full name of the prize and keeps the two-word award together as a single unit.

The em dash earns its place when parentheses or a pair of commas fail to deliver the tone a writer wants. Grammarly describes the mark as quick and casual. Its brisk feel suits two moves, setting off an aside and signaling an abrupt turn in mood.

Grammarly's example puts both moves on display. A sentence announces that a group fears two things, and a dash introduces the pair, spiders and senior prom. The pause before the list builds a beat of suspense, and the swerve from spiders to a dance supplies the joke. Commas could hold the same list, yet they would flatten the payoff the dash sets up.

Register governs the choice among the dash, parentheses, and commas. Parentheses and commas can carry a side remark too, so the dash becomes the pick for a sentence meant to sound lively and informal. Prose aiming for a measured voice has quieter tools on hand.

The hyphen works at the scale of a single word, joining two surnames in Grammarly's sentence about Anya Taylor-Joy walking the red carpet. The mark fuses two family names into one, with no break in rhythm and no shift in attitude. Its job is structural, and it carries none of the expressive weight Grammarly attaches to the em dash.

An em dash pries a sentence apart to make room for a digression, an en dash spans a range or a multi-word compound, and a hyphen binds two names. Swapping one for another sends a reader the wrong cue.

#5497. Why Puerto Rico, Guam and 3 other U.S. territories have no presidential electors

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Residents of U.S. territories can't vote for president, and these 10 explainers cover Puerto Rico, Guam, the Electoral College and what it would take to change that

A U.S. citizen living in San Juan can serve in the U.S. military and help choose a party's presidential nominee in a primary. That same citizen cannot cast a ballot that counts in the general election for president. The gap has nothing to do with citizenship itself. It comes from geography and from how the Constitution distributes electoral votes.

Article II of the Constitution gives presidential electors to states. The 23rd Amendment, ratified in 1961, extended electors to Washington, D.C. No provision does the same for the territories. The Electoral College, not the national popular vote, chooses the president. A place without electors therefore has no formal role in the final result.

Five inhabited territories fall into that gap: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands. These are the U.S. territories where citizens can't vote for president, and one of them adds a separate question of legal status. People born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals at birth, not citizens. They can naturalize after meeting residency requirements. Until they do, they cannot vote in federal elections, even after moving to a state.

Each territory reached its current status by a different route. Puerto Ricans became citizens under the Jones Act of 1917. Guam's residents gained citizenship through the Guam Organic Act of 1950. The U.S. Virgin Islands were transferred from Denmark in 1917, and citizenship followed by act of Congress in 1927. Residents of the Northern Mariana Islands became citizens in 1986 under the covenant that made the islands a U.S. commonwealth.

Representation in Congress is limited as well. Each territory sends one member to the House who can serve on committees and introduce bills but cannot cast a final vote on the floor. None has a senator.

The 10 slides that follow start with the five territories, one at a time. The remaining five explain the mechanisms behind the gap. They cover the Electoral College, the 23rd Amendment, nonvoting House delegates, and primaries and party conventions. The final slide explains what happens to a citizen's presidential vote after a move from a state to a territory.

Puerto Rico's residents are U.S. citizens, but they cannot cast a ballot that counts in the general election for president. The island has no presidential electors because it is a territory, not a state.

Citizenship came through the Jones Act of 1917. Spain ceded Puerto Rico to the U.S. in the Treaty of Paris, signed in 1898 at the end of the Spanish-American War. For nearly two decades after that, the island's people lived under U.S. rule without U.S. citizenship. The Jones Act extended citizenship to them by statute.

Puerto Rico is by far the largest of the five inhabited U.S. territories. The 2020 census counted about 3.28 million people there. Guam, the next largest, had about 153,800. Puerto Rico's population also exceeds that of several states, including Wyoming, Vermont and Alaska.

The island takes part in choosing presidential nominees. Puerto Rico holds contests in both the Democratic and Republican nominating processes. Voters there can help decide whose names appear on the November ballot in the states. They have no vote in that November election.

Puerto Rico has one member of Congress. Voters elect a resident commissioner to the House of Representatives for a four-year term. Other House members serve two-year terms. The resident commissioner can introduce legislation and serve on committees but cannot vote on the final passage of bills. Puerto Rico has no senators.

Local self-government is broader. Puerto Rico adopted its own constitution in 1952, and its official English name is the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. Residents elect their own governor and legislature. Those officials play no part in choosing the president.

Puerto Rico has held several referendums on its political status. Ballots have offered options such as statehood, independence and the existing commonwealth arrangement. The results do not bind the federal government. Under Article IV of the Constitution, only Congress can admit a new state. Congress has not acted on the result of any of these referendums.

Guam's voters can mark a choice for president on their general election ballot, but that choice is a non-binding straw poll. It does not count toward the Electoral College, and no electors are chosen for the island.

The poll lets residents record a presidential preference on the same ballot that elects local officials. The tally is reported publicly after the election. It has no legal effect on who wins the White House. The candidate who carries Guam receives no electoral votes.

That gap exists even though people born on Guam are U.S. citizens. Congress granted that status through the Guam Organic Act. The same law set up a civilian government for the island, which the U.S. Navy had administered before then. Residents today elect their own governor and legislature.

Guam's link to the U.S. is older than its citizenship law. Spain ceded the island to the U.S. in 1898 under the Treaty of Paris, which ended the Spanish-American War. Japan occupied Guam during World War II, and U.S. forces retook it in 1944.

The island sits in the western Pacific and had about 153,800 residents in the 2020 census. Its time zone puts it ahead of the U.S. mainland. That is the source of its long-running slogan, "Where America's day begins." Guam also hosts major U.S. military installations, including Andersen Air Force Base and Naval Base Guam.

In Congress, Guam is represented by a single nonvoting delegate in the House of Representatives. The island has no senators. Its residents have no representation in the chamber that confirms federal judges and approves treaties.

The straw poll does not change any of that. Its results show how voters on the island lean, but they carry no constitutional weight. Turning that preference into electoral votes would require Guam to become a state or the Constitution to be amended. Without either change, a Guam resident generally needs to live in a state or in Washington, D.C., to cast a presidential vote that counts.

People in the U.S. Virgin Islands are U.S. citizens, but they have no vote in the general election for president. The territory is not a state, and the Constitution gives presidential electors only to states and Washington, D.C.

The islands came under U.S. control through a purchase from Denmark. The U.S. agreed to pay $25 million in gold for what were then called the Danish West Indies. Danish voters approved the sale in a 1916 referendum.

The formal transfer took place on March 31, 1917, during World War I. The U.S. government wanted to keep the islands' harbors out of German hands. The territory still marks March 31 each year as Transfer Day.

Citizenship did not arrive with the transfer. Congress granted U.S. citizenship to most residents through a 1927 law. That status came by statute, not through the Constitution. It has no effect on how presidential electors are assigned.

The territory is made up of three main islands — St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. John — along with many smaller cays. Its capital, Charlotte Amalie, sits on St. Thomas. The 2020 census counted about 87,100 people across the islands.

The Revised Organic Act of 1954 serves as the territory's basic governing law. Residents have elected their own governor since 1970, and they also choose a local legislature. Those votes shape local government. None of them extends to the presidency.

In Congress, Virgin Islanders elect a single delegate to the House of Representatives for a two-year term. The delegate sits on committees and introduces legislation but has no vote when a bill comes up for final passage. The territory has no senators.

Presidential politics still reaches the islands earlier in the cycle. Local branches of the Democratic and Republican parties send delegates to their national conventions. That gives Virgin Islanders a role in choosing who ends up on the ballot. Once the nominees are set, that role ends.

A Virgin Islander who moves to Florida or New York can register and vote for president there. A resident who stays on St. Croix cannot, even with the same citizenship.

People born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals, not U.S. citizens. That status keeps them from voting for president anywhere, even after a move to a state, until they become citizens through naturalization.

American Samoa is the only inhabited U.S. territory where birth on its soil does not confer citizenship. Section 308 of the Immigration and Nationality Act classifies people born there as nationals, unless they qualify for citizenship through a parent. Residents of Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands are citizens. They lose the presidential vote only because of where they live. American Samoans face a second barrier tied to their legal status.

The 2020 census counted about 49,700 people in American Samoa.

Nationals owe allegiance to the U.S. and can live and work in the 50 states without a visa. They travel on U.S. passports. Those passports carry an endorsement stating that the bearer is a U.S. national and not a U.S. citizen.

The difference shows up at the ballot box. An American Samoan who moves to Hawaii or California cannot register to vote in federal elections there. A Puerto Rican who makes the same move can register and vote for president.

A national who wants full citizenship must apply for it. The application goes to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the same agency that handles naturalization for immigrants. Only after that process is complete can a former national vote for president from a state.

Courts have declined to extend birthright citizenship to the territory. In Tuaua v. United States, decided in 2015, the D.C. Circuit rejected the argument that the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause covers people born in American Samoa. In Fitisemanu v. United States, the 10th Circuit in 2021 reversed a lower court ruling that had found in favor of birthright citizenship. The Supreme Court declined to hear the Fitisemanu case in 2022.

The territory's own government opposed a court-ordered change in these cases. Its leaders argued that the decision belonged to the people of American Samoa and to Congress. They also raised concerns about protecting local customs, including the islands' communal land system.

Congress granted citizenship to the other inhabited territories through legislation. It could do the same for American Samoa with an ordinary statute, without a constitutional amendment. Citizenship alone would still not bring a presidential vote to residents living on the islands.

People in the Northern Mariana Islands became U.S. citizens in 1986 under the covenant that made the islands a U.S. commonwealth. That citizenship does not come with a presidential vote. The commonwealth has no electors.

The islands sit in the western Pacific, just north of Guam. Most residents live on three islands — Saipan, Tinian and Rota — and Saipan is the seat of government. The 2020 census counted about 47,300 people in the commonwealth. That is the smallest population of the five inhabited U.S. territories.

The path to citizenship began after World War II. Japan had governed the islands between the world wars under a League of Nations mandate. After the war, they became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a United Nations trusteeship administered by the U.S.

Instead of pursuing independence, the Northern Marianas negotiated a permanent political union with the U.S. The agreement is formally titled the Covenant to Establish a Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands in Political Union with the United States of America. Island voters approved it in a 1975 plebiscite, and Congress approved it in 1976. Citizenship took effect in 1986, when the trusteeship ended for the islands.

Commonwealth status gives the islands their own constitution, an elected governor and a local legislature. It does not change how the Constitution distributes presidential electors. Electors go to states, and the commonwealth is not one. Voters on Saipan elect their governor directly, but their presidential preferences have no path into the Electoral College.

In Congress, the islands are represented by one nonvoting delegate in the House. That seat is the newest of the territorial delegate posts. For years after citizenship arrived, the commonwealth had no member in the House at all.

The covenant also gave the commonwealth unusual local control. Under its original terms, the islands ran their own immigration system and set their own minimum wage. Congress later brought both areas under federal law. Those changes tied the islands more closely to federal rules. Neither change affected the presidential vote.

The Electoral College has no seats for U.S. territories because Article II of the Constitution assigns presidential electors only to states. Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are not states. None of them appoints electors.

Article II, Section 1 lets each state appoint electors in whatever manner its legislature directs. The number a state receives equals its combined total of senators and representatives in Congress. Territories have no senators, and their House members are not counted in the formula. The text of Article II never mentions territories at all.

Voters in the states do not elect a president directly. A ballot cast in November chooses a slate of electors. Those electors then cast the votes that decide the presidency. There are 538 electors in total, and a candidate needs a majority of them to win. A territory can count ballots for presidential candidates. Without electors, those ballots have no route into the official result.

The 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804, changed how electors vote. Before it, each elector cast two votes without specifying which was for president and which was for vice president. The amendment created separate ballots for the two offices. It left the state-based structure untouched. It also set the fallback if no candidate wins a majority. In that case the House picks the president, and each state delegation casts a single vote. Territorial representatives have no vote in that process either.

The elector system is written into the Constitution. An ordinary act of Congress cannot extend it to the territories. That change would require a constitutional amendment. Article V sets a high bar for one. Under the route used for every amendment so far, two-thirds of both the House and the Senate must approve it. Three-fourths of the states must then ratify it.

Some Puerto Rico residents have turned to the courts instead. In Igartúa v. United States, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit rejected claims that Puerto Rico residents have a right to vote for president. Courts have so far turned away other lawsuits making similar arguments.

That leaves two paths to presidential electors. A territory admitted as a state would receive electors through the existing Article II formula. For a place that remains a territory, only a constitutional amendment could provide them.

Washington, D.C. votes for president because of the 23rd Amendment, ratified in 1961. The amendment gives the district its own presidential electors, capped at the number held by the least populous state. In practice, that cap means three electoral votes.

Before 1961, the district sat outside the Electoral College for the same reason the territories do today. It is not a state. The federal government moved to Washington in 1800. From then until the amendment took effect, people living in the capital had no way to cast a vote that counted for president.

The amendment set a narrow formula. The district receives as many electors as it would have if it were a state, but never more than the smallest state. Every state's elector count equals its House seats plus its two senators. The least populous states have one House seat each, which puts them at three. That ceiling holds D.C. at three electors no matter how much its population grows.

The text also spells out how those electors work. They count as electors appointed by a state for the purpose of choosing the president and vice president. They meet in the district and follow the procedures set out in the 12th Amendment. Congress directs how the district appoints them, and it has the power to enforce the amendment through legislation.

D.C. residents first voted for president under the new rules in 1964.

The amendment is the main constitutional precedent for giving electors to a place that is not a state. It did so without granting statehood. It also gave the district no senators and no voting member of the House. A broader measure, the D.C. Voting Rights Amendment, cleared Congress in 1978. It would have treated the district like a state for congressional representation. Too few states ratified it, and it expired in 1985.

No comparable amendment exists for Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa or the Northern Mariana Islands. Giving any of them electors would require a constitutional amendment of its own. The route D.C.'s amendment took was approval by two-thirds of both chambers of Congress, followed by ratification by three-fourths of the states.

Each of the five inhabited U.S. territories elects one member of the House of Representatives. None of those members can cast a vote on the final passage of a bill, and the territories have no seats in the Senate.

Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands each send a delegate. Puerto Rico sends a resident commissioner, a title held by no other member of Congress. The resident commissioner serves a four-year term. The four territorial delegates serve two-year terms, the same length as voting House members.

Inside the chamber, these members do much of the same daily work as their voting colleagues. They sit on committees, where much of the detailed drafting and amending of legislation takes place. They can introduce bills and sign on as co-sponsors of measures written by others. They can also speak during floor debate and argue for their constituents' interests.

The limit arrives at the end of the process. When a bill reaches a final vote on the House floor, the outcome is decided by the 435 members who represent states. Territorial members can make the case for or against a measure. Their names do not appear on the final tally.

The absence of senators widens that gap. Every state has two senators, and a bill must pass the Senate before it can become law. The Senate also confirms federal judges and cabinet officials and approves treaties. Residents of the territories have no member in that chamber to speak or vote for them.

Congress also holds broad authority over the territories themselves. Article IV of the Constitution gives Congress the power to make "all needful Rules and Regulations" for U.S. territory. Laws on federal funding, local government and political status all pass through a legislature in which territorial residents have no final vote.

Washington, D.C., which is also not a state, elects a nonvoting delegate of its own under a similar arrangement.

Voters in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands help choose the Democratic and Republican presidential nominees. Both major parties award national convention delegates to the territories, even though the same voters have no say in the November general election.

The nominating contest is run by the parties, not by the Constitution. The constitutional rules on electors govern only the general election. Primaries, caucuses and conventions are party processes. Each party decides who receives delegates and how those delegates are chosen. The Democratic National Committee and the Republican National Committee have both chosen to include the territories.

The method varies by party and by territory. Puerto Rico has typically held primaries. The smaller island territories have more often selected delegates through caucuses or party meetings. The format can change from one election cycle to the next. So can the number of delegates each territory receives.

The two parties also handle delegate allocation differently. Democratic rules award pledged delegates in proportion to the vote. Candidates generally need at least 15% support to qualify for a share. Republican rules give state and territorial parties more room to set their own allocation and binding methods.

Party officials also hold delegate slots on both sides. Each Republican delegation from a state or territory includes three members of the Republican National Committee. They are the national committeeman, the national committeewoman and the state or territorial party chair. On the Democratic side, members of the Democratic National Committee from the territories serve as automatic delegates, often called superdelegates.

At the convention, territorial delegations take part in the roll call alongside the 50 states and Washington, D.C. Their votes count toward the majority a candidate needs to win the nomination.

Territorial contests occasionally draw national attention. In March 2020, former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg won the American Samoa Democratic caucus. It was his only contest victory before he left the race.

The two stages give territory residents different roles. They can help decide which candidates appear on the November ballot. They cannot then vote for any of those candidates in the general election that decides the presidency.

A U.S. citizen's right to vote for president depends on where that citizen lives, not on citizenship alone. A citizen who leaves a state and settles in Puerto Rico, Guam or another inhabited territory generally gives up a presidential ballot. A citizen who moves to a foreign country keeps one.

That contrast comes from the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, a 1986 federal law usually shortened to UOCAVA. It lets citizens living outside the U.S. vote absentee in federal elections through their last state of residence. Under that law, the territories count as part of the U.S. A person who moves from Ohio to Germany is covered. A person who moves from Ohio to the U.S. Virgin Islands is not.

UOCAVA also covers members of the uniformed services and their eligible family members who are away from their voting residence. A service member whose legal residence is in a state can keep voting there while stationed on Guam or in Puerto Rico. The deciding factor is legal residence, not physical location.

Some states go further than federal law. They allow former residents who now live in a territory to keep voting absentee in federal elections. These provisions come from state statutes, and their scope differs from state to state. A citizen weighing a move to a territory has to check the election rules of the specific state being left behind.

The vote comes back when the move runs in the other direction. A territory resident who relocates to a state can register and vote for president on the same terms as anyone else living there. A citizen born in Puerto Rico who settles in Florida or New York votes in that state's presidential contest. Birthplace plays no role in the calculation.

Federal law also caps how long a state can make newcomers wait. The 1970 amendments to the Voting Rights Act bar states from imposing a residency requirement longer than 30 days for presidential elections. The Supreme Court upheld that limit in Oregon v. Mitchell the same year.

The result is a presidential vote that can switch off and on with a change of address. Two citizens with identical legal status can hold different voting rights because one lives in Hagåtña and the other lives in Honolulu.

#5495. 20 unsolved crimes from 1892 to 1997 that still grip the American public

Free daily briefing on global business news.

From an 1892 ax killing to a 1997 Los Angeles drive-by, these 20 cases left investigators without answers and the public still guessing.

Picture a family still waiting for answers decades after a killing, years after the neighbors stopped asking and the reporters moved on. Most killings that go unsolved follow this arc. They shrink from headlines to whispers until only relatives and close friends carry the memory. A handful refuse to fade. Some crimes hold the public's imagination across generations, and people keep retelling and debating them long after the first investigators have gone. The odds of a case slipping into that silence have grown in recent years. Violent crime climbed across the country after the COVID-19 pandemic took hold, and homicides rose along with it. Police now solve a smaller share of those deaths than before.

FBI data show arrests in murder cases growing scarcer for decades. The clearance rate, the share of homicides that end with someone in custody, captures the trend. About half of U.S. murders now go without an arrest. In the 1960s, the uncleared portion sat between 30% and 40%. Some states fare worse. In New Mexico, Ohio, and Michigan, as many as 60% of homicides go unanswered. Experts caution that older clearance figures may not hold up, and that doubt explains part of the apparent decline. Guns have turned up in a growing portion of slayings over the past 40 years. Each open file means grieving survivors and a culprit who never faced a judge.

24/7 Wall St. gathered 22 notorious crimes that investigators never cracked. Its editors drew on FBI material, news reports, and regional publications. Every case had gone at least 15 years without resolution, according to the most current information available. The editors make no claim to completeness. They chose the cases that captured the most popular interest and press coverage. Not every entry involves a death. An art theft, an airline hijacking, and a prison break share the list with the killings and vanishings. The list follows chronological order and makes no attempt to rank one crime against another. This article presents 20 of the 22, keeping the same sequence from 1892 to 1997.

The 1892 bludgeoning of Andrew and Abby Borden has gripped Americans longer than any other U.S. murder, in the judgment of the list's compilers. Blows from an ax handle killed the affluent couple. The compilers consider it almost certain that Lizzie Andrew Borden, Andrew's daughter and Abby's stepdaughter, swung the handle. A housemaid may have helped her.

A court weighed the evidence against Lizzie Borden, found it circumstantial, and set her free. Her prosecutors had brought in a medical expert to match the weapon to the wounds in the victims' skulls. The jury pool excluded Fall River. Its makeup tilted toward the county's small towns, most of them agricultural. The justices barred testimony about prussic acid. Prosecutors had not disproved that the poison might have served harmless purposes.

The release left the killings without a conviction, even as the compilers treat Lizzie Borden's guilt as close to settled. A circumstantial record rests on inference, and inference alone did not persuade the court.

Lizzie Borden's community shunned her for the rest of her life, yet public fascination with the deaths never faded. Her neighbors delivered the verdict the court withheld. Attention took hold while the case unfolded and has spread into popular culture. The 2018 film "Lizzie" is the latest retelling the compilers cite. A movie arriving 126 years after the crime shows how long the unanswered question has held its audience.

Shortfall: Slide 1 runs about 231 words, below the 300-word floor. The source gives the Borden entry only a few sentences, and every approved web detail for this case is already in use. No further genuine fact is available, so the slide stops where the evidence ends.

An ax killed eight people inside one Villisca, Iowa, home on the night of June 9, 1912: a husband, a wife, and six children ages five to 12. The list's compilers count the slayings among the most horrific crimes they gathered. Children made up 75% of the dead.

Detectives chased the culprit for nearly a decade, and the long hunt led Iowa to create a state investigation bureau. One household's slaughter gave Iowans a crime-solving agency of their own. The bureau outlasted every lead those detectives pursued and became the case's most concrete legacy.

Authorities charged Lyn Kelly in the deaths. Smithsonian magazine reports that Kelly sat in on the Children's Day service at Villisca's Presbyterian church the evening the family died. The service placed him in town that night, which put him close to the scene without proving he wielded the ax. A deadlocked jury led to his acquittal, leaving prosecutors empty-handed.

Frank Jones, a Villisca businessman and state senator, fell under suspicion as well. A grand jury examined him, yet no one charged him with a part in the bloodshed. A long campaign to prove his guilt ended his political career. The senator absorbed the damage without facing trial, a reminder that the inquiry wounded people beyond the victims.

James Wilkerson claimed Jones had hired William Mansfield to kill Joe Moore. Wilkerson's account framed the attack as a paid plot aimed at one man. Payroll records placed Mansfield at work in Illinois, several hundred miles from Villisca, at the time of the murders, according to Smithsonian magazine. Mansfield went free for lack of evidence. The alibi broke the chain Wilkerson had drawn from a contract killer to the senator. Three men drew scrutiny over the years, and the case produced no conviction against any of them.

Joseph F. Crater, a 41-year-old justice of the New York Supreme Court, left a Midtown Manhattan steakhouse on the evening of Aug. 6, 1930, headed for a Broadway play, and never reappeared. Investigators never recovered his body or named a suspect. Without remains, no one could establish whether he had died, let alone how.

Crater's seat on the bench points toward a motive. The list's compilers argue that a jurist deciding cases in a major city during Prohibition would have collected enemies, and they treat that outcome as close to certain. They file the disappearance as an abduction, though no kidnapper ever surfaced. The label rests on reasoning about his position. Enemies supply a motive, but the list names no one.

Searchers chased Crater across a wide map. Their leads ran through New England, into Canada, and as far south as Orlando, Fla. None paid off. At one stage, the search team believed Crater had gone to Europe and met U.S. Sen. Robert Ferdinand Wagner, a man he had once worked alongside in law. The European theory imagined Crater traveling of his own will. It pointed away from foul play.

U.S. District Attorney Tuttle combed through Crater's records after learning he had gone missing and found nothing damaging. The review removed one obvious reason a public official might choose to vanish. Clean files offered neither a scandal to explain a flight nor a culprit to blame for a crime. Each dead end narrowed the possibilities without settling any of them.

The case seeped into everyday talk. For a stretch, "pulling a Crater" described anyone who slipped out of a social gathering without telling a soul. A judge who walked away from one evening engagement and never reached the next lent his name to the unannounced exit. The slang had a limited run. The question of where Crater went has outlived it.

A Christmas Eve fire in 1945 swept through a house in Fayetteville, West Virginia, and four of the family's nine children escaped. Searchers never recovered any trace of the other five. The lack of bodies fed speculation that someone had carried the youngsters off, and a domestic tragedy turned into a suspected kidnapping.

Officials who sifted the ashes of the Sodder house found no remains, and firefighters concluded that the heat had cremated all five. Investigators traced the blaze's origin to defective electrical wiring in George Sodder's study. George rejected the finding. He recalled that a nearby power company had inspected the wiring a short time earlier. The father's doubt set the household against the official explanation for how the flames started.

Authorities discovered that someone had severed the home's telephone line that night. Lonnie Johnson later admitted to theft and to cutting the line but denied any part in the fire. His confession accounted for the cut line, yet it shed no light on what became of the five.

George and Jennie Sodder first accepted the officials' word that their children had likely perished. Doubts took hold in the weeks and months that followed, and as rumors multiplied, the couple hired a private investigator, CC Tinsley, to chase leads on where the missing children might be. Paying for a private search signals that the parents had come to reject the firefighters' verdict and believed the five might be alive.

Both accounts rest on the same gap. The empty ashes that stirred talk of abduction also fit the cremation view, so neither side can claim them as proof. With no bodies recovered, the record cannot tell a deadly accident from a crime.

A killer murdered and dismembered Elizabeth Short, a 22-year-old aspiring actress, in Los Angeles in 1947, and investigators never caught a suspect. Newspapers shifted their focus from the killer to the victim and to how she had lived.

Coverage of Short dwelt on three subjects: her alleged loose reputation, her history of drinking while underage, and the clothes she wore. None of those topics identified a culprit or narrowed the field of suspects. Each one invited readers to judge a young woman who could no longer answer for herself. The list's editors see the same habit in many present-day cases of male violence against women, where the victim's conduct draws scrutiny ahead of the attacker's. Their comparison ties a 1947 newsroom reflex to choices journalists continue to make.

The press tagged the killing the "Black Dahlia" case, and no one has ever answered for it. The nickname attached itself to Short herself. Every later mention of the murder carried a label coined for the victim.

Reporters and authors have examined the mystery for decades, and it has fed novels, movies, documentaries, and true-crime books. All of that work never produced an arrest. The file went cold and stayed cold while the retellings multiplied. Short's story shows how a newsroom label can carry a crime through years of public interest after the evidence runs dry.

Gunfire killed Benjamin "Bugsy" Siegel in Beverly Hills on June 20, 1947. The gangster had helped build the Las Vegas Strip, and no one has ever answered for his death.

Many people believe crime boss Meyer Lansky ordered the hit over money. In their telling, Siegel sank too much of Lansky's cash into the Strip's Flamingo Hotel, and the overspending cost him his life. If that account holds, the same desert venture that secured Siegel's place in Las Vegas history also supplied the motive for his killing.

A 2014 claim from the widow of a man named Pandza put the gun in her late husband's hands. Her account arrived 67 years after the shooting, and it steers suspicion toward a figure the Lansky explanation never names.

Lansky's alleged role and the Pandza account offer rival answers to who fired and why. Neither has produced a charge, and the case remains open. Two competing explanations, with no prosecution to weigh either one, leave Siegel's death as unsettled as it stood the night he fell.

Barbara and Patricia Grimes, sisters ages 13 and 15, disappeared in 1956, and no one has ever answered for their deaths.

Their vanishing touched off a sprawling manhunt. Police fielded a flood of tips, yet none of them brought searchers to the girls. More than three weeks went by before a motorist driving past spotted the bodies in woods near Devil's Creek in Willow Springs, a community in unincorporated Cook County. A stranger's chance glimpse, and none of the calls police had logged, ended the search.

Detectives first fixed their suspicion on a local drifter. Authorities never filed formal charges against him. The earliest figure investigators pursued never faced a jury.

Reporters seized on the sisters' trip to see "Love Me Tender," the Elvis Presley film. The connection to the killings was thin. It still fed talk that the girls had run off to Memphis in hopes of meeting the singer. The rumor handed readers a famous name, something the evidence never supplied.

Public interest burned out with the speed of a viral TikTok fad, and the case went cold. Both threads ran dry. The drifter went uncharged, and the Memphis talk produced nothing. Decades on, the Grimes case stays bound to a movie star and a film title, with no killer's name beside them.
