Brothers John and Clarence Anglin and Frank Morris broke out of Alcatraz in 1962 by scrambling through the prison's ventilation ducts. The trio left behind three dummy heads arranged to convince guards the inmates lay asleep. The list's compilers call the escape elaborate, and the decoys bear out that description. Shaping three lifelike faces under the eyes of prison staff demanded patience and secrecy, a sign the scheme came together long before the night it unfolded.

The island penitentiary sits a little over a mile off San Francisco's coast, and the inmates and guards there called it "The Rock." Across nearly 30 years, its cells confined prisoners such as Al Capone and George "Machine Gun" Kelly. Cost concerns closed the facility in 1963, a year after the three men vanished, and the National Park Service now owns it. A prison that once held Capone lost three of its charges to a plot hatched inside its own walls.

Improvised tools drove the operation. The prisoners converted a vacuum cleaner motor into a drill and built a housing around it to muffle the noise. They glued raincoats together with waterproof adhesive to form a raft. On the night they fled, the three climbed onto the roof, exited through a vent, and reached the water, where they pushed off in the homemade craft. A drill from a vacuum and a boat from rain gear show how the men turned ordinary items into a getaway kit.

The raft never turned up, but the stitched life vests the men made surfaced afterward. Even so, the bureau's language stops short of declaring them dead. Dorothy Kilgallen's death certificate recorded the circumstances of her 1965 death as "undetermined," and investigators never named a suspect or closed the case. The document fixed the fact of her passing and left the central question open.

Television audiences knew Kilgallen from the game show "What's My Line?" Newspaper readers followed her too. She once circled the globe, departing New York, crossing to Germany aboard the Hindenburg, and passing through Rome, Hong Kong, Manila, Hawaii, and San Francisco on the way home. The New York Evening Journal printed her dispatches from the journey every day.

Three rival theories compete to explain how she died, and the absence of a suspect gives none of them an official edge. A claim tied to a 911 call has fed further speculation without handing investigators a name to pursue.

A reporter whose work once reached readers daily left behind an official record that ends on a single unresolved word.

The Zodiac Killer has five confirmed murders and two attempted killings to his name, all in Northern California in 1968 and 1969. Investigators have never established who he was.

He adopted the Zodiac nickname as a mask and signed it to handwritten, encrypted letters addressed to police and local media. The ciphers handed him a public platform while shielding his real name. By writing to the press as well as to detectives, he made the public an audience to the hunt. The coded messages kept him in the conversation, yet none of them gave investigators a name.

Speculation stretches his toll beyond the documented count. Some estimates credit him with as many as 37 victims, though no inquiry has confirmed a figure that high. The distance between seven established attacks and that larger tally shows how much of the Zodiac story rests on guesswork.

Independent investigators claimed on Oct. 6, 2021, that they had identified him as Gary Francis Poste, an Air Force veteran and gang leader. Poste died in 2018, three years before the group went public. He never faced the accusation in life, and no court weighed the evidence against him.

San Francisco police continue to classify the murders as open cases. Without the department's endorsement, the Poste claim stands as one team's theory. The man behind the letters remains anonymous, and the only firm identity on record is the one he invented for himself.

On Nov. 24, 1971, a hijacker known as D.B. Cooper seized a Northwest Orient Airlines flight and extorted $200,000.

A fake bomb gave Cooper his leverage. The device posed no real danger, so his hold over the people aboard depended on their belief that it might. Alongside the cash, he demanded four parachutes. He then leaped from the aircraft with the money and disappeared.

Nine years passed before any of the haul resurfaced. In 1980, a boy stumbled on a package of rotting $20 bills worth $5,800. Serial numbers on the notes matched the sum Cooper had collected. The match shows that someone had recorded those numbers before the handoff. The decay points to a bundle that had sat for a long stretch before the boy came across it. His find amounted to 290 notes, or 2.9% of the payout.

Agents never located Cooper, and the FBI calls the case an "intriguing mystery." The source reports no other recovery of the loot, which leaves more than 97% of it unaccounted for. The lone traced portion turned up decomposing in a package. Nobody had spent it. The evidence cannot settle whether Cooper lived through the jump.

The last sighting of union leader Jimmy Hoffa puts him in a Michigan restaurant parking lot in 1975, and his body has never surfaced. Investigators inherited a missing man and almost nothing else to work with.

Hoffa had no shortage of enemies. The Teamster maintained mob ties and served time for jury-tampering, mail fraud, and bribery. Bob Crane, the star of "Hogan's Heroes," died at a killer's hands inside a Scottsdale, Arizona, apartment in 1978, and no court has convicted anyone for the crime.

The Associated Press portrayed Crane as an actor known for pursuing women. The label shows how a television star's reputation followed him into the headlines about his death. Investigators settled on John Henry Carpenter as their suspect, and prosecutors brought him to trial.

Blood matching Crane's type formed the link between Carpenter and the slaying. A type match narrows the pool of possible sources without singling out one person. Many people share any given blood type. The evidence could place Carpenter among potential suspects but could not set him apart from them. DNA testing, which could have closed that gap, played no part in the prosecution at the time.

A jury acquitted Carpenter in 1994, 16 years after Crane died. The verdict freed the man prosecutors had tried and left the actor's death without a legal answer.

A killer took eight lives in Craig, Alaska, on Sept. 6, 1982, and the list's compilers call the case the worst unsolved multiple homicide in the state's history. Decades later, no one has put a name to the person responsible.

The murderer kept his composure after the slayings. He piloted the 58-foot boat into a secluded bay nearby and waved to another skipper as he departed. Even with that encounter in open water, investigators never made an arrest.

The culprit brought the craft back the following day for reasons no one has explained. He doused it with gasoline, set it on fire, and then escaped both the scene and the village.

Each move points to someone who felt no pressure to stay out of sight. A person who greets a passing captain and then returns to the vessel the next day showed a confidence the investigation never overcame.

Cyanide hidden in Tylenol bottles killed seven people across the Chicago area in 1982. Someone laced containers of the pain and fever reliever with the poison and returned them to store shelves. Chance picked the victims.

Random targeting set this case apart from murders driven by a grudge or a debt. None of the seven needed an enemy to die. An ordinary purchase of a common medicine was enough, and the danger reached any household that kept the product in a cabinet. The victims shared no link to the poisoner beyond a shopping trip. No personal motive tied any of them to whoever tampered with the bottles.

The deaths pushed the U.S. to adopt tamper-proof packaging regulations. One anonymous act of sabotage in a single metro area reshaped how medicine reaches shoppers across the country. Anyone who breaks a seal on a pharmacy purchase handles a safeguard born of the Chicago murders. Investigators have never identified the poisoner who prompted that reform.

CBC Chicago reported in January 2023 on Freedom of Information Act documents that describe DNA tests in the investigation. The records surfaced 41 years after the poisonings. Genetic analysis entered the file, yet the killer's identity still eludes detectives. A national packaging overhaul and decades of scrutiny have not produced a name.

Thieves who walked out of Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 1990 took a haul that Boston Globe reporter Stephen Kurkjian estimates could be worth $500 million or more. The men gained entry dressed as police officers. Investigators have never named them.

Kurkjian also observes that no legitimate art market could buy the stolen works. The intruders seized a fortune with no lawful path to cash. A collection valued at half a billion dollars or more could fetch nothing from an honest buyer. The distance between those two numbers sits at the center of the case.

Motive remains the puzzle. Nothing in the record explains why anyone would risk a heist for artworks no reputable dealer or collector could touch, and no answer has surfaced.

Visitors to the museum can stand before the empty frames where the paintings hung. Each vacant frame measures the loss in a way a dollar estimate cannot.

An abductor seized nine-year-old Amber Hagerman in Arlington, Texas, in 1996, and her body surfaced five days later. Police never identified the person who took and killed her.

Her death gave rise to the Amber Alert, a national warning system for child abductions that bears her first name. Her case never produced a suspect, and no one stood trial for her murder.

The Department of Justice counted 82 Amber Alert programs as of January 2023 and credited them with more than 1,127 children rescued. Each of those rescues traces back to a girl whose own killer escaped identification.

JonBenét Ramsey, a six-year-old beauty pageant contestant, lay dead in the basement of her family's Boulder, Colorado, home the day after Christmas in 1996. What took place inside the house that night still rests on guesswork.

Police mistakes damaged the scene in its first hours, in the view of the list's compilers. Supporters who arrived soon after officers wandered through the rooms, and some helped scrub the kitchen before detectives had finished gathering evidence. Whatever traces those surfaces held disappeared before anyone could bag them.

Suspicion has fallen on a range of people over the years, and no account of the crime has displaced the others. Each competing theory draws strength from the same gap. Fewer physical clues left investigators with less material to rule anyone in or out. The lost hours at the house help explain why speculation, instead of proof, still defines the case.

Four bullets struck Tupac Shakur, 25, in a 1996 drive-by shooting in Las Vegas.

Shakur, born Lesane Parish Crooks in New York City, died on the opposite side of the country from the city of his birth.

Witnesses described a hotel lobby confrontation between Shakur and Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, a Crips member, a short time before the gunfire. Their account gave investigators a named gang member and a documented clash, yet the killing remains unsolved.

Speculation about the attack draws in Marion Hugh "Suge" Knight Jr., a former rap producer and convict. Christopher "Notorious B.I.G." Wallace, a fellow rapper who died in a Los Angeles drive-by six months later, also surfaces in the conjecture.

Few cases among these 20 offer so many names. Judge Crater's disappearance produced no suspect at all, and the Zodiac Killer's identity is still disputed. Shakur's file holds a witnessed fight, a gang affiliation, and two prominent music figures, and none of those threads has closed it.

Any theory that names Wallace must also reckon with his own unsolved killing, which binds two open cases to each other.

Four gunshots from a drive-by attacker killed Christopher "Notorious B.I.G." Wallace, 24, in Los Angeles just after midnight on March 9, 1997. The rapper was walking out of an after-party for the Soul Train Awards when the gunfire erupted. His death came six months after Tupac Shakur's.

Both men were born in New York City, and both held central places in East Coast hip-hop. Wallace died on the opposite coast from the city that produced him. A shared hometown, a shared scene, and two deaths half a year apart gave speculation plenty to feed on.

Conspiracy theorists split over Wallace's role. One camp casts him as the planner behind Shakur's death, driven by a dispute. Another camp blames West Coast gang members for murdering both rappers over petty differences. Under the first account, Wallace instigated a slaying. Under the second, the same crew claimed both men.

The versions clash at their core. One makes Wallace a perpetrator, and the other makes him a target. With both deaths unsolved, nobody has proved either version.

#5494. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5493. Millionaire Walmart chair Greg Penner adds soccer club Valencia CF to his investments—he already owns NFL’s Denver Broncos and part of a baseball team

The world’s wealthiest are finding new ways to deploy their fortunes beyond luxury cars and yachts—and the latest craze is soccer. Greg Penner, the multimillionaire chairman of Walmart, just added a European league to his growing portfolio of sports investments from football to baseball.

A consortium backed by some of private equity’s top billionaires and ultra-rich investors has agreed to buy a 42% stake in Spanish soccer club Valencia CF, now valued at €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion). The deal was led by Pitchwise Holdings, whose notable investors include KKR co-founders Henry Kravis (worth $17.4 billion) and George Roberts (worth $17.7 billion). Another notable backer was Penner Sports, the family and sports investment vehicle run by Penner and his wife Carrie, the granddaughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton.

The Valencia club will also receive around €100 million (nearly $112 million) in capital injection as part of the investment.

“The club has all the building blocks needed to be a leading club in Europe in both men’s and women’s football,” Ann Rodriguez and Corey Woolfolk, general partners at Pitchwise, said in a press release. “However, we also know that the regulatory and competitive landscape of the modern game means that potential alone is not enough – it requires a clear investment strategy and focus.”

The investment comes as billionaires like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and American property magnate Stanley Kroenke have poured money into European soccer clubs as another way to put their fortunes to work. And this isn’t the first time the Walmart chairman splurged on sports—Valencia CF is only the newest addition to his global investments.

Fortune reached out to Walmart and Pitchwise for comment.

Greg and Carrie Penner have been building a sports investment portfolio for years, starting with one of the NFL’s most valuable franchises before expanding into new sports and international markets.

In 2022, the Walton-Penner Family Ownership Group (now Penner Sports Group) acquired controlling ownership of the Denver Broncos for $4.65 billion.

The Walmart chairman is now five seasons in as the NFL team’s owner and CEO—and the investment has panned out handsomely: Forbes estimates that the Broncos are now worth $9.4 billion, more than double what the Penners bought them for.

And the team seems to have rebounded competitively; after returning to the playoffs in 2024 for the first time since 2015, Denver went 14-3 in 2025, and advanced to the conference championship game. Penner has said the potential criticisms and challenges of running a competitive NFL team—on top of his executive duties—are well worth it.

“We love a challenge. We love to compete. The NFL is one of the premier places to do that,” Penner said in a 2022 interview. “And at the same time we have a chance to build a business around it, do it as a family endeavor which is a lot of fun.”

Earlier this year, the couple expanded their sports portfolio through Penner Sports Group’s investment in the Colorado Rockies.

They’re currently the largest minority owners of the MLB team, though the purchase price was never disclosed. It’s estimated that the team is currently worth $1.68 billion, according to Forbes, valuing the Penners’ stake at roughly $672 million. Multiple sources also report that the Penners “intend to take over” the Rockies from primary owners Dick and Charlie Monfort and purchase an additional 35% stake next year when MLB returns.

Penner isn’t the only ultra-rich American putting their money towards European sports leagues.

Earlier this year, Bezos joined the consortium buying around 30% of Liverpool FC. The group, led by British-Indian investor Amit Bhatia, made a provisional offer of £1.35 billion (nearly $1.8 billion) to buy a minority stake from Fenway Sports Groups (FSG)—valuing the Premier League club at around £4.5 billion (around $6 billion).

And in 2022, the CEO of holding company Eldridge Industries Todd Boehly, led a consortium that bought Chelsea F.C. for £4.25 billion—about $5.2 billion at the time. The American businessman, worth around $9.2 billion, snapped up the team from Russian business oligarch Roman Abramovich, who was forced to sell.

Stanely Kroenke, worth $29.1 billion, also bought up popular Premier League team Arsenal over the span of a decade. Starting back in 2007, Kroenke started off by acquiring a 9.9% stake in Arsenal holdings, becoming a majority owner in 2011 with 62% of shares under his name, eventually taking on full ownership in 2018. In total, it’s estimated he shelled out roughly $1 billion to buy the franchise.

#5492. Morgan Stanley is raising $2.3 billion in loans for Baldwin Insurance buyout

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The seven-year loans will help fund Michael Dell's family office and Sequence Holdings in their $7.7 billion cash deal for Baldwin

Morgan Stanley $MS has begun marketing $2.3 billion in debt that will back the purchase of Baldwin Insurance Group by Michael Dell $DELL's family office and Sequence Holdings, according to Bloomberg.

The offering breaks down into a term loan totaling $2 billion and a delayed-draw term loan of $300 million, according to Bloomberg. Both loans carry a seven-year maturity.

Pricing is under discussion at a margin of 3.5 percentage points above the benchmark, with the loans being offered at 99 cents on the dollar, according to Bloomberg.

A lender call is slated for Tuesday, with commitments to be submitted by Nov. 12, according to Bloomberg.

The financing package also features second-lien secured debt totaling $750 million that was sold to investors privately, according to Bloomberg.

Dell's family office and Sequence, a holding company with an AI focus, committed in September to purchase Baldwin, a firm that distributes insurance and provides advisory services, according to Bloomberg. The all-cash deal carries a $7.7 billion price tag and is expected to wrap up in 2027's first quarter.

The Baldwin loan is only the second leveraged loan to come to market this week, according to Bloomberg. Higher borrowing costs, along with the U.S. midterm elections, have made companies reluctant to raise money in the market, Bloomberg said. Junk-bond sales last month totaled $14.6 billion, an 18% drop from a year earlier, while leveraged loan issuance finished over 10% under the October 2025 figure.

#5491. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

#5490. Despite the tensions of war, ex-Barclays CEO Bob Diamond is long Gulf. Here’s why

“The region isn’t hiding in their bunker; they’re doing business,” Bob Diamond tells me on a call from Bahrain, where the Gateway Gulf investment conference is taking place. He is talking to Fortune against a backdrop of simmering tensions around the U.S. midterms and the possibility that the President may restart attacks on Iran.

“I don’t want to be dismissive, there is a war, there is a conflict, whatever term you want to use,” he said. “It’s real, and I’m not going to be dismissive of the impact that’s having on the UAE, on Bahrain, on Qatar. But I will tell you, if you take the time to get here and you’re on the ground, it’s business as usual. The kids are in school. People are working from the office. They’re not hiding at home. They’re doing business. They’re investing.”

The former CEO of Barclays is in Bahrain to announce that the U.K.-based advisory firm, Panmure Liberum, is opening its first regional office in the kingdom. Diamond’s investment vehicle, Atlas Merchant Capital, bought Panmure Gordon for £15.5m ($21m) in 2017. It agreed an all-share merger with Liberum in 2024.

Panmure Liberum is now one of the biggest advisors to U.K.-listed companies based on the number of clients, which total more than 250. It specializes in mid-market companies, with valuations below those served by the bulge-bracket investment banks such as Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.

Panmure’s move to Bahrain—where it will partner with the Bank of Bahrain and Kuwait—will allow it to serve the Gulf region and increase the deal-flow for the advisory firm. Activity levels in the Gulf are in sharp contrast to the number of deals announced in the U.K. In the first half of 2026, deals in the U.K. were down 13% compared with the same period a year ago, according to PwC, a consultancy.

“You have all the talent in the world in London. It’s still a very attractive place for a lot of people,” Diamond said. “The skill set of advisory is very, very deep. But there’s not a lot of deals. I think the statistics on the number of companies that have gone public or raised equity is paltry compared to what it used to be, and they’re losing out not to Frankfurt or Dublin, but to the U.S. and, more and more, to the Middle East.”

This creates an opportunity for firms keen to expand.

“It means that we can build an advisory business here in Bahrain to serve middle market and family-owned businesses, which are dying for cover,” he said. “And we can then expand that to the Gulf Cooperation Council.”

“You have all the talent in the world in London, but not a lot of deals. Companies going public or raising equity are paltry compared to what they used to be, and they’re losing out to the U.S. and more, the Middle East”

As one of the smaller kingdoms in the region, Bahrain, says it is able to offer agility and clear and simple regulatory rules to investors. At Gateway Gulf, Mastercard announced an expansion of its deal with the Bahrain-based fintech firm, Infinios, to facilitate business-to-business travel payments. Olayan Kimberly-Clark, the partnership between Saudi Arabia and the tissue paper production giant, announced that it would be expanding production at its Bahrain paper mill.

“It’s a highly regulated banking sector,” Diamond said about why the kingdom was attractive. “Great banks want great regulation. It’s also a gateway, to steal a phrase from the conference, to the GCC. So all of a sudden, Panmure, which is a U.K.-focused advisory business, is now U.K. and GCC, so we’re very happy with it.”

Diamond said that there were also opportunities for Bahrain and the rest of the Gulf to develop stablecoin payment systems, one of the fastest ways to reduce the cost of doing business. As a digital currency pegged to the dollar, it is seen as a more secure way to settle transactions.

“Tokenization is just digitizing assets,” he said. “It’s making them more efficient. All of that relies on blockchain, which is an underpinning of 24/7 instantaneous settlement, a permanent record of every transaction. So, the regulators love it, at a fraction of the cost. It is going to be the future underpinning [for finance]. It’s infrastructure.”

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Net outflows reached $1.04 billion over Friday and Monday, with BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust accounting for $405 million of Monday's

U.S.-listed Bitcoin funds saw net withdrawals of $1.04 billion across Friday and Monday, according to a tally by Bloomberg. The withdrawals followed the Oct. 29 hack of crypto exchange Binance and came as U.S. midterm elections arrived. BlackRock $BLK's iShares Bitcoin Trust made up $405 million of the money pulled on Monday, according to Bloomberg.

Binance published an initial report on Tuesday describing a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign." The company said the attackers combined fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling and endpoint compromise.

About $6.34 billion in digital assets were affected, and about $2.85 billion have been frozen or intercepted, Binance said. The company said it will absorb the financial impact rather than its users, and that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished as of Oct. 31. Binance cited the Federal Bureau of Investigation as indicating North Korea is responsible. Pyongyang has denied involvement, according to Bloomberg.

Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said the attackers worked toward the breach over months. “In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that,” Teng told CNBC. He said the attackers later pretended to be recruiters and questioned a second engineer, a process that culminated in a programming task carrying concealed malicious code.

Binance suspended withdrawals during the incident. Certain withdrawals remain temporarily restricted, according to CNBC. Binance said it is engaging independent security firms to review the incident.

Bitcoin changed hands at a bit over $77,000 on Tuesday, close to its average price across the past 100 days.

Bloomberg said the midterm elections add to the uncertainty for crypto investors. A Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could redirect focus from the market-structure legislation the industry backs toward scrutiny and probes. The Clarity Act, an industry priority, stalled in the Senate during September.

"I do not think a significant Democrat win is priced into the price of Bitcoin," said Russell Thompson, chief investment officer at Hilbert Group, according to Bloomberg.

New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5487. Hobby Lobby’s founder called wealth ‘a curse.’ His family spent millions chasing biblical artifacts

In 2021, investigative journalist Michael Blanding was reading a New York Times story about a 3,500-year-old clay tablet that federal agents had seized from the Museum of the Bible in Washington, D.C. About halfway down, he hit the detail that became his next book: the tablet, inscribed with part of the Epic of Gilgamesh, belonged to Hobby Lobby.

“I’d written about art and antiquities and theft before, and so I was really intrigued by this,” Blanding told Fortune. He asked himself, “What is this big box chain of craft stores doing with this ancient cuneiform tablet?”

The answer took him well beyond antiquities. The Gospel According to Hobby Lobby: Inside a Billionaire Family’s Quest to Craft a Christian Nation, published in July by PublicAffairs, argues that the Green family, which owns the Oklahoma City-based chain, has spent decades using the company’s profits to push its evangelical worldview into American law, education and culture. Blanding calls that effort Christian nationalism.

Few shoppers know the Greens, but many live near one of their stores. Hobby Lobby says it runs more than 1,000 stores in 48 states with about 50,000 employees, and that reach is why Blanding wrote the book.

“It’s obviously a free country; people can spend their money however they want. But when you deal with a retail company, I felt like I had a duty to expose this for people who are shopping at Hobby Lobby,” he said. “They should know what their money is being used for.”

Hobby Lobby did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. The family declined to be interviewed for the book.

The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet was one piece of a far larger collection. Starting in 2009, Hobby Lobby president Steve Green gathered tens of thousands of biblical artifacts, which Blanding says the family bought in part to “prove the historical accuracy and truth of the Bible.”

Many were bound for the Museum of the Bible, a 430,000-square-foot institution that opened in November 2017 three blocks from the U.S. Capitol. Steve Green chairs its board, and Fortune has reported that the family spent $500 million to open it.

The museum “wasn’t initially their idea,” Blanding said, but “they sort of took it over, and they became the real founders of the Museum of the Bible.” It operates as a separate nonprofit, yet he describes the line between family and museum as “always very, very porous.” In his telling, Hobby Lobby often bought artifacts and donated them to the museum, which brought the company tax benefits.

The buying drew federal scrutiny. In December 2010, Hobby Lobby agreed to buy more than 5,500 artifacts for $1.6 million despite an expert’s warning about looted Iraqi antiquities, according to the Justice Department. The company shipped the items under false labels. In 2017, the company settled, forfeited thousands of artifacts, paid $3 million, and accepted responsibility for its conduct.

The Gilgamesh tablet came next. Hobby Lobby bought it from an auction house in 2014 for about $1.67 million; agents seized it in 2019, and the company consented to its forfeiture in 2021. Prosecutors said the auction house had withheld the tablet’s false provenance from Hobby Lobby and the museum.

That summer, Iraq received about 17,000 looted artifacts from the U.S. in its largest-ever repatriation; roughly 12,000 had been held by the Museum of the Bible. A year earlier, a museum-commissioned study had found that its Dead Sea Scroll fragments were fakes.

Steve Green has said that when he began collecting, he “knew little about the world of collecting.” Blanding built on the work of what he calls a “ragtag team of biblical scholars” who spotted suspect listings online, then added documents he obtained showing how the artifacts were trafficked.

What surprised Blanding most was how the Greens use their money. “A lot of times you think of people or families having an impact through campaign contributions and electing politicians, and they actually have done very little of that,” he said.

Instead, he said, “they have spent hundreds of millions of dollars literally promoting this kind of biblical worldview and trying to impact our laws and our society to bring it more in line with what they believe is biblical truth.” He points to education, the courts, and political groups that write and promote legislation.

The most consequential court fight was the family’s own. In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in 2014 that closely held for-profit companies can be exempt from regulations that violate their owners’ religious beliefs, sparing Hobby Lobby from covering certain contraceptives. Blanding argues the ruling limited employees’ reproductive choices, and says the family has also backed anti-abortion and anti-LGBTQ causes, school prayer and teaching the Bible in schools.

The money behind it is substantial. A company-supplied biography of Steve Green put Hobby Lobby’s 2021 sales above $7.7 billion. In 2022, when Forbes valued David Green at $14 billion, the founder said all of Hobby Lobby’s voting stock had moved to a trust, Fortune reported. “Wealth can be a curse,” he said.

The Greens declined to cooperate. But because they are “really motivated to spread their story,” Blanding said, they have produced books, articles, podcasts and interviews, which he used to reconstruct their views. He added interviews with biblical scholars, former Museum of the Bible employees and experts on the religious right.

After he contacted family members, Blanding said the Greens’ lawyer told him the family would not take part, questioned his reporting methods, and asked to review the manuscript before publication. “Of course we weren’t going to do that,” he said.

He later sent six or seven pages of questions, which he says went unanswered. “I haven’t heard back from them since. And, knock on wood, I never will.”

Not every believer shares the family’s politics. “Evangelicals are not a monolith,” Blanding said, and some sources from religious backgrounds who disagree with the Greens helped his reporting.

Blanding calls the book an exposé but says he did not want “just this anti-religious or anti-corporate screed.” He wanted readers to understand the family’s motives.

“For better or for worse, they’re really sincere in their beliefs,” he said. So the book asks: “If you really do believe that, what would that motivate you to do?”

The harder question is how that conviction fits a pluralistic country. “I wanted to understand how and why they believe what they do,” he said, “and how that actually is compatible or incompatible with our democracy as a whole.”

Blanding’s comments have been edited for length and clarity.

#5486. A billionaire’s private zoo may hold the world’s rarest great ape as India becomes a top destination for trafficked primates

The villagers who first spotted the five baby orangutans in a casuarina forest in India in early September were puzzled by their reddish hair and unfamiliar faces.

The three males and two females, aged 6 to 8 months, were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700 kilometers (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India.

They’re now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been playing classical music to soothe them.

Wild orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they sustain rainforests by spreading seeds across vast areas, allowing trees to regenerate and store carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. The species is critically endangered, threatened by severe habitat loss. There are about 119,500 orangutans left in the wild, according to conservation organization World Wildlife Fund.

The global illegal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth $34 billion annually, according to a 2026 study by National University of Singapore researchers, and India is emerging as an important market. Experts say seizures reflect a fraction of a booming trade in exotic or non-native animals sold to wealthy Indian collectors.

India’s wildlife laws were mainly designed to protect native species such as elephants, rhinoceroses and tigers from being trafficked overseas. Gaps in controls on imported animals complicate efforts to trace the origins of exotic wildlife.

In 2022, two juvenile Sumatran orangutans were found in boxes at a checkpoint between the northeastern states of Assam and Mizoram. Another was rescued in Mizoram in 2023, and a young orangutan was found in an apartment near Mumbai in November 2024. At least 23 gibbons were seized at Indian airports in 2025, according to an analysis by nonprofit Wildlife Trust of India. In May 2026, Egyptian authorities seized three India-bound, sedated baby chimpanzees.

“India has become the number one destination for the live trade of primates,” said Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at the Orangutan Information Centre in Indonesia’s North Sumatra province.

Wealthy collectors who prize rare animals as “status symbols” are driving the trade in trafficked animals from Southeast Asia, a regional hub for trade in species from elsewhere, said Uttara Mendiratta, a wildlife trafficking researcher in India.

Expanding tourism has led to more direct flights to India through cities like Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, giving traffickers routes that are faster, albeit riskier, than overland border crossings.

“The profit margins are so high that they can afford to lose a few (animals) and still make a profit,” Mendiratta said.

Questions also surround legal trade. Most commercial trade in orangutans is banned, but exceptions exist for captive-bred animals. India imported 41 orangutans between 2021 and 2024, according to CITES, the global treaty regulating trade in endangered wildlife.

Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at Indonesia’s Orangutan Information Centre, questioned whether the animals were legitimately bred in captivity.

“It just shows the loopholes. And … corruption as well,” he said.

The CITES Secretariat declined to comment, saying the matter was under review.

Concerned about diseases spreading from animals to people during the COVID-19 pandemic, India allowed people to register their exotic animals in 2020 without proving their origins.

They can report births, deaths and breeding of non-native species through an online portal. But the government lacks enough staff and expertise to adequately inspect collections and identify global species. The system also leaves room for trafficked animals to be misrepresented as registered ones, Mendiratta said.

India tightened its wildlife laws in 2022, giving authorities clearer powers to seize illegally traded exotic animals and prosecute traffickers. But by then, it already had “opened the floodgates,” she said.

India’s exotic pet trade “sits at the crossroads of biodiversity loss, unbridled community demand, and organized criminal activity,” said a 2026 report by Humane World for Animals India.

India’s forest ministry didn’t respond to AP’s request for comment.

Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “active steps” to bring home the five baby orangutans found in Odisha, sending experts to verify their origins and assess their health.

Their mothers were likely killed, traumatizing infants that normally would depend on them for up to nine years.

Conservationists have successfully returned orangutans to Indonesia from Thailand, but so far only one has been repatriated from India.

When one orangutan was transferred last year to a private wildlife facility known as Vantara, run by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s family, India’s federal wildlife officials and India’s CITES authority were not informed, a federal wildlife official in New Delhi wrote in a report.

Officials concerned over the orangutan’s care at a local public zoo ordered it transferred to Vantara, which describes itself as a wildlife rescue and rehabilitation center. The orangutan was treated for a respiratory infection and pneumonia before it was returned to Indonesia on Oct. 19 after 19 months at the private facility.

India’s CITES authority didn’t respond to AP’s request for comment.

“Vantara fully supported this process and worked with the relevant authorities to facilitate his return,” the company said in a written statement.

Vantara, a 3,500-acre wildlife facility in western India, has over 150,000 animals and over 2,000 different species.

It has faced international scrutiny over its animal acquisitions. In November 2025, CITES questioned shipments to Vantara that included snow leopards from Germany, a bonobo said to have been bred in Iraq and a gorilla reportedly from Haiti. The primates are not native to those countries. CITES took no further action after questioning the snow leopard shipments.

India’s Supreme Court cleared Vantara of wildlife trafficking and animal mistreatment allegations in 2025.

In September, 27 wildlife conservation and animal welfare organizations issued a letter urging the facility to end imports of wild animals, raising concerns about endangered species and animal welfare.

The groups said they had “never encountered anything comparable to the scale and diversity” of Vantara’s imports, citing more than 60,000 animals acquired in a short period.

One controversial acquisition, according to Vantara’s 2024-25 inventory, is a Tapanuli orangutan, the world’s rarest great ape. Recognized as a distinct species only in 2017, it’s only found in a small area of Indonesia’s Sumatra island, where 716 remain in the wild.

“The Tapanuli orangutan is hovering just above extinction,” said Serhadli, whose organization is one of the few that works with the species. The one at Vantara would be the only Tapanuli orangutan in captivity.

CITES trade data shows that the animal left Indonesia in 2024 and arrived in India via the United Arab Emirates.

In its statement, Vantara said the animal was legally imported into India, though it added that the “prior chain of custody remained to be clarified with the United Arab Emirates.”

Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “seriously” reports that a Tapanuli orangutan might be outside the country. It said it couldn’t confirm the animal’s species, origins or how it got to India. An investigation would require checking permits and transfer records, along with scientific testing, the ministry said.

Milko reported from Islamabad. Associated Press journalist Edna Tarigan contributed from Jakarta, Indonesia.

#5483. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5482. Montana voters take on Citizens United with a ballot initiative to strip corporations and nonprofits of their political spending power

Sixteen years ago, the Supreme Court decided in the Citizens United case that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend money to influence elections. On Tuesday, Montana voters will decide whether their state can take that power away.

Initiative 194, also known as the Montana Plan, would strip corporations, trade associations, nonprofits, and other organizations of the legal power to spend money supporting or opposing a political candidate or ballot initiative in Montana. Backers say they’ve found a way around Citizens United, while critics argue the semantics of the ballot initiative still violate the 2010 Supreme Court ruling.

Rather than ban corporate political donations outright, I-194 would change the powers Montana grants to corporations and other entities it refers to as “artificial persons,” limiting them to only those powers that are “necessary and convenient.”

The measure would apply to entities that do business or hold property in Montana, but exempts political action committees (PACs), news and editorial content, and individuals. Organizations that violate this would forfeit the privileges Montana grants them to do business in the state, including limited liability, which protects owners from personal responsibility for business debts.

At first glance, the language of the ballot initiative looks like it contradicts what Citizens United established—that corporations can spend money on elections. But Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen Weintraub and now senior fellow at the Center for American Progress (who also devised the legal theory behind the Montana Plan), told Fortune that states have authority over what corporations can do through corporate law.

“When the state creates a corporation, it is starting from nothing and deciding what to give the corporation, and no case has ever held that they have to give local spending power to a corporation,” Moore said.

He said I-194 would no longer grant corporations and nonprofits the ability to spend money on elections, which is different from banning them from exercising an existing right.

“It’s not regulation; it’s redefinition,” Moore said.

He said he believes the measure would shut down dark money spending by preventing wealthy donors from hiding behind organizations that don’t disclose their contributors. For instance, a donor can give money to a nonprofit that then funnels it to a PAC, which would report the nonprofit as the donor rather than identifying the person. Moore said I-194 would cut off that route by preventing corporations, nonprofits, and trade associations from political giving, though individuals can still donate.

“This is not going to stop Elon Musk from writing a big fat check to some election in Montana,” Moore said. “What it will stop them from doing is laundering the money through a dark money group.”

But opponents of the ballot measure say the distinction between banning corporations from political giving and exercising their political rights is blurry. Bradley Smith, a former FEC chairman and professor at Capital University Law School, told Fortune states can’t sidestep the First Amendment by calling political spending a corporate power instead of a right.

“The Supreme Court isn’t engaged in a semantic game,” he said.

Smith said states can set rules for corporations, but they can’t make them surrender constitutional protections in exchange for the benefits of incorporation.

“The core centerpiece undoubtedly is we’re going to deny all corporations in the state the right to speak about political affairs and about political candidates, and that’s just going to fail,” he said.

Montana has tried curbing corporate influence in elections before. In 1912, Montanans passed the Corrupt Practices Act by initiative with 76% of the vote, angry at the political power of mining giant Amalgamated Copper, years after the state’s mining magnates, known as the Copper Kings, had bribed state legislators.

The law barred corporations from spending money to influence elections, but the Supreme Court struck down the restriction in American Tradition Partnership v. Bullock in 2012, ruling that it conflicted with Citizens United.

Montana also isn’t the only state trying to limit corporate influence over elections. Hawaii enacted a law similar to I-194, called Act 11, in May. It’s now facing two federal lawsuits: one from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and another from the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, which the Institute for Free Speech, an organization Smith founded, represents. The cases could help decide whether states can use corporate law to restrict political spending despite Citizens United.

Moore expects the issue to go up to the Supreme Court, whether through I-194 or the Hawaii lawsuits. If voters approve I-194, it would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, unless a court blocks it.

#5481. A Democratic Congress could curb the Iran war but not Trump’s tariffs, former ambassador says

As U.S. voters headed to the polls on Tuesday, former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam Ted Osius predicted that a Democratic-controlled Congress could curb President Donald Trump’s ability to wage war in the Middle East, but would likely struggle to unwind his tariffs.

The U.S. midterm elections could have major implications for both the Iran war and the global economy, Osius said at Fortune’s Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam on Nov. 3.

“The Iran war is extremely unpopular in the United States, and it’s one of the factors that will be decisive in this election,” said Osius, who served as ambassador to Vietnam from 2014 to 2017. “I expect that Congress would use the power of the purse to curb the president’s ability to wage war in the Middle East.”

About 65% of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling the U.S. military action in Iran, according to a Pew Research Center survey released on Oct. 8. The polling outfit noted that the war has been unpopular since it began; a March survey reported 61% disapproval of his handling of the conflict.

Most polling averages put the Democratic Party ahead of the Republican Party on the generic ballot; several independent forecasts suggest the Democrats will retake control of the House of Representatives, with control of the Senate being more uncertain.

Tariffs—Trump’s other signature foreign policy—would be harder to touch. “I don’t think we’ll suddenly go back to the status quo ante,” Osius said. “Unfortunately, it’s actually harder to unwind tariffs once you put them in place.”

A Democratic House and Senate might pressure the Trump administration into more predictable trade policy, but Osius conceded that tariff power “rests with the executive.”

Trump’s initial tariffs hit Southeast Asia harder than almost any other region in April 2025, with Vietnam in particular hit with a 46% rate, later cut to 20% in a deal, based on its large trade surplus with the U.S. Since then, Southeast Asian governments have launched negotiations with Washington to get tariffs reduced, offering to lower their trade barriers and to buy more U.S. products.

Since the Supreme Court’s Feb. 20 ruling that Trump’s tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, including his“Liberation Day” levies were unlawful, the administration has resorted to other justifications, including widespread duties imposed following allegations of forced labor and overcapacity.

Still, Osius predicted that a Democratic victory would show that Trump’s more coercive foreign policy doesn’t work. “When you sort of run a state like a mobster, it may work in the short term, but in the long term it doesn’t,” he said. “It’s much more effective, especially in this part of the world, to have predictable policies, and to show that rule of law and rules-driven trade works to everyone’s benefit.”

U.S. protectionism hasn’t dented Vietnam’s growth. The Southeast Asian country grew almost 10% in the third quarter of 2026, following growth rates of 8.2% and 8.8% in the first and second quarters of the year, respectively.

More broadly, the Asian Development Bank expects developing Southeast Asia to grow by 4.7% this year and 4.9% in 2027.

Jens Lottner, the CEO of Vietnamese bank Techcombank, explained that exports were up 30% year-on-year despite the 12.5% tariff currently on Vietnamese exports to the U.S. “If you’re a bank, you’re a proxy on the economy,” he said. “We still have a couple of very good years ahead of us.”

Amol Gupte, Asia South head at Citi, argued that global trade isn’t shrinking under Trump’s tariffs, but is instead being rerouted, often to Southeast Asia. “The aggregate amount of trade in the world is not really reducing; it’s just changing flows,” he said. “Exports from China to the U.S. have shrunk quite drastically, but China’s aggregate exports have not reduced—they’ve actually grown substantially.”

The region still sits at the center of several flashpoints. Lynn Kuok, the Lee Kuan Yew Chair in Southeast Asia Studies at the Brookings Institution, highlighted continued tensions over ownership of the South China Sea. “We see off Vietnam’s coast, for instance, a greater Chinese presence. And after a decade’s pause, China is actually starting its rebuilding of islands off the Vietnamese coast,” she said.

Kuok added that the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz has exposed a second vulnerability: the Strait of Malacca, the narrow passage between Malaysia and Indonesia through which much of Asia’s trade travels. Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore have all pledged to keep the strait open, but she warned that “a future more nationalist government might actually seek to close off the strait, or come under pressure from various powers to close off the strait.”

Kuok said members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are invoking international law as a way to defend their interests without taking sides in the rivalry between Washington and Beijing. “They’re not choosing U.S. or China; they’re choosing principles of international law,” she said.

#5480. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. #5479. A Next-Day ‘Thank You’ Can Do More for Your Career Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

Here are three situations when a next-day thank-you can make a meaningful difference.

As a business owner, I often give team members tickets to concerts, theatrical performances or sporting events. Whenever possible, I personalize these gifts. For example, if I know an employee follows a particular sports team, I may offer tickets to see that team play.

Naturally, I appreciate the initial thank you. That acknowledgment usually arrives through our in-office chat tool shortly after the employee receives my offer.

When an employee sends a follow-up text or email after attending the event, especially one that includes a photo or personal detail, it tells me something important about that person’s character.

Employees often share how exciting the final minutes of the game were or mention that the concert exceeded expectations. These details show that the gift was genuinely appreciated.

More importantly, the message demonstrates that the employee doesn’t consider these experiences to be an expected perk of employment. Instead, they recognize that someone made an effort to provide something of value.

When I don’t receive any acknowledgment after the event, I notice. While people sometimes forget or get busy, a consistent lack of expressed appreciation can create an impression of entitlement.  And entitlement is not a quality that encourages employers to invest in someone’s future career development.

Professional favors come in many forms. Your boss might invite you to sit at the company’s table at a major charity event, introduce you to an influential business contact or offer you an opportunity to attend an industry conference.

These gestures deserve more than casual acknowledgment.

Consider the invitation to a charity event. Your first responsibility is to RSVP promptly. RSVP comes from the French phrase Répondez, s’il vous plaît, meaning “Please respond.”

Yet responding to invitations isn’t something everyone does consistently. According to Greenvelope’s RSVP benchmarks, the response rate for conference and meeting invitations is approximately 66%.

Failing to respond promptly can make you appear disorganized or indifferent.

More importantly, recognize the invitation for what it represents: an opportunity to build professional relationships, demonstrate your interpersonal skills and potentially advance your career.

After attending, send a next-day thank-you message. Mention something specific you appreciated, such as an interesting conversation or a valuable introduction.

The same principle applies when a manager recommends you for a special assignment, provides career guidance or makes an introduction that expands your professional network.

Of course, you don’t need to write a formal note every time your boss buys you a cup of coffee. But meaningful favors deserve meaningful appreciation. When you thank someone immediately and follow up afterward, you have taken advantage of demonstrating gratitude twice.

Our SalesFuel research shows that 36% of B2B decision-makers will not do business with a sales professional who demonstrates poor etiquette. Even if you don’t work in sales, that finding should get your attention. Professional behavior influences how others perceive your credibility and character.

Some managers, particularly those from older generations, likely place considerable importance on traditional expressions of courtesy. Don’t miss these opportunities to show your character.

Job candidates typically have three major opportunities to impress prospective employers.

The first comes through their resumes, applications and assessment results. These materials help demonstrate whether candidates possess the skills and abilities required for the position.

The second opportunity occurs during the interview. Candidates can distinguish themselves by discussing their accomplishments, answering questions thoughtfully and communicating their career aspirations.

The third opportunity arrives after the interview ends. A well-written thank-you message sent within 24 hours can reinforce the positive impression you’ve worked hard to establish. This message shouldn’t be a generic, AI-generated paragraph that could be sent to any hiring manager.

Instead, reference something specific from your conversation. Perhaps you appreciated learning about the company’s growth plans or discussing a challenge the team hopes to solve. Briefly reaffirm your interest in the position and explain why the opportunity excites you.

In an age when AI can produce polished resumes and professional correspondence in seconds, genuine personalization matters more than ever. A thoughtful thank you demonstrates communication skills, attention to detail and an understanding of professional etiquette.

It also suggests something employers value: You recognize that another person invested time in considering your future.

A next-day thank-you doesn’t require elaborate language, expensive stationery or a lengthy message. Often, three or four sincere sentences are enough. What matters is the acknowledgment.

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort. You never know which professional relationship may influence your next promotion, assignment or career move.

Gratitude costs very little, but failing to express it can cost you opportunities. Make the next-day thank-you a habit that sets you apart.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.
