#5478. North Korea used LinkedIn, fake job interviews to trick Binance engineer in $6.3 billion hack

Binance on Tuesday disclosed that North Korean hackers used a mix of social engineering and malicious software to pull off last week’s $6.3 billion heist, the biggest in crypto history. Speaking to reporters, company executives revealed that the hackers targeted a Binance engineer on LinkedIn and arranged a series of fake job interviews in order to persuade the employee to download an “assignment” that let them invade the company’s systems.

In a related report, Binance explained, “Software Engineer B was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform by an individual posing as a Project Director. Software Engineer B had a profile on the platform that referenced his experience at Binance. The purported Project Director arranged a first-round interview with a HR representative, followed by a second-round interview with an individual claiming to be the CEO of a fictitious company.”

The report also provided additional details about the sophisticated monthslong scheme that not only involved the fake LinkedIn recruitment but also used a separate ad campaign that tricked another engineer into downloading a malicious version of a popular software package called Homebrew.

According to Binance, the engineer in question did not download the Homebrew software through the company’s regular channels, but instead clicked on an internet ad promoting a tampered version of it.

Binance says it detected the fake Homebrew download and removed it from the employee’s machine, but not before the hackers discovered critical information about the engineer’s role and others who managed the company’s wallets.

It was the combination of these exploits—the fake LinkedIn outreach and the knowledge gleaned from the tampered Homebrew download—that allowed the North Korean hackers to take over a series of Binance wallets and drain them of funds.

While many initially speculated that the hackers had used AI to break into Binance, the company’s account shows how they instead relied primarily on conventional phishing tactics. At the same time, Binance added that AI did play a role. This occurred when the hackers, after gaining control of the engineer’s laptop, used Binance’s own internal AI tools to compromise other accounts.“The attacker leveraged the compromised computer of Engineer B and used an internal AI tool to gain control over the Wallet DevOps Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C. The attacker soon discovered Wallet DevOps Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer,” stated the Binance report.

According to a Binance spokesperson, employees with non-public-facing roles are not allowed to maintain LinkedIn profiles. The spokesperson declined to explain if the engineer in question had violated that policy, or if either of the engineers would be terminated.

The phenomenon of North Korean hackers posing as recruiters has become a widespread problem across the corporate sector more broadly. In the case of Binance, the company said it flagged earlier efforts by hackers to target its employees on LinkedIn and that, in 2026, it had detected and prevented 57 North Korea–related hacking attempts.

Since the attack, which occurred over several hours on Thursday, the company has disclosed that the hackers stole around $6.3 billion, but that it was able to recover around $2.5 billion of that after two companies, Tether and Circle, moved to freeze stolen stablecoins.

In response to the hack, Binance shut down withdrawals for around 48 hours, but re-enabled them on Saturday. The company has repeatedly stated that all customer funds are safe and that it has replenished 98% of the stolen coins from reserve funds and other sources. It is in the process of acquiring the remaining 2%, which consist of lesser used currencies.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” said Binance in a statement.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5477. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5476. A 30-Year-Old Ballerina-Turned-Billionaire Says to Avoid This Common Trap While Starting Your Own Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

She is the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, unseating Taylor Swift and Lucy Guo.

As a teenager, Luana Lopes Lara studied ballet at the Bolshoi Theater School in Brazil. Competition was cutthroat; students sometimes tried to sabotage each other by hiding glass fragments in each other’s shoes. She attended technical school in the morning, then went to ballet training from the afternoon to the night.

“Since I was very little, I wanted to do big things,” Lopes Lara said in a recent episode of the podcast Confession with Ali Partovi.

That discipline laid the foundation for Lopes Lara’s later success. Now, at 30 years old, the entrepreneur is the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, unseating pop star Taylor Swift and tech billionaire Lucy Guo in December 2025 to claim the title. Lopes Lara has a net worth of $2.6 billion, according to Forbes.

She made her fortune by co-founding Kalshi, a prediction market exchange where users can buy and sell yes-or-no contracts based on real-world future events, such as elections, economic data, weather and sports. Lopes Lara is working towards a future where people can essentially bet on anything.

Kalshi is “the first federally regulated exchange in the United States dedicated exclusively to trading on the outcomes of future events,” according to its site.

Lopes Lara said on the podcast that many smart founders fall into a common trap when it comes to starting their own business: They become “obsessed with probabilities.”

“You can psych yourself out of doing anything,” she said. “I think that going for it, taking the risk, believing that things will work out, is very important.”

Lopes Lara said that if a startup’s employees are only thinking about the math of whether the company is going to work or not, it becomes a “super negative culture that overreacts to every new information you have.”

“It’s important to have a lot of optimistic people who want to build things in the company,” Lopes Lara said.

Lopes Lara created Kalshi in 2018 with her co-founder, Tarek Mansour. They both graduated from the school in 2018. Lopes Lara majored in computer science and mathematics, while Mansour majored in electrical engineering, computer science and mathematics. They met because they had classes in common, and Lopes Lara always sat at the front of the class. Mansour wanted to learn from her example, so he started sitting next to her.

Lopes Lara came up with the idea for Kalshi when she was interning at Five Rings, a New York trading firm. She noticed that people on social media were pushing the narrative that reality TV star and entrepreneur Kylie Jenner was pregnant.

“I was like, ‘I want to make a bet with you on this,’” Lopes Lara said in an interview with Bloomberg earlier this year. The only problem was that she had nowhere to place the bet.

In that moment, Lopes Lara identified an opportunity that was bigger than gossip. She found that there were millions of people with firm views about the future, but no outlet for those beliefs.

Now Kalshi, which addresses that need, is worth a reported $22 billion and growing.

#5475. Anthropic’s third-quarter results mean IPO math and history are not on its side, analysts say

Anthropic’s IPO is looking like an increasingly expensive and risky bet after the company released third-quarter financial results yesterday that showed its rate of revenue growth slowing and its expenses climbing at a faster pace compared to prior quarters.Several analysts Fortune spoke to said math and past experience are not in favor of Anthropic producing stellar returns for investors. That may explain why institutional investors are reportedly pushing the company and its IPO advisors to price Anthropic’s shares at the lower end of a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation range that the company is seeking in its public stock offering.

Even that may be too pricey, according to analysts. Any IPO valuation above about $1.41 trillion would ask Anthropic’s buyers to pay more than $40 for every dollar the company generated in revenue over the past year—a price level achieved by just 14 of the 4,110 IPOs that took place between 1980 through 2024, according to a study from Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative. What’s more, those IPOs delivered lower average returns than the broader market, Ritter said.

Against the roughly $35.3 billion in revenue Anthropic booked over the past four quarters, a valuation range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, would mean investors paying between $43 and $57 for every dollar of sales the company generated in the past 12 months.

To justify a valuation north of $1.4 trillion, Anthropic needs a path toward annual after-tax profits of at least $100 billion, Ritter told Fortune. Only a handful of companies have ever earned that much in a year, he said, including Alphabet, Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft.

In the third quarter, Anthropic’s revenue rose nearly 47% from the previous quarter, while compute and infrastructure expenses climbed about 77% to $9.9 billion. About half of that compute bill, roughly $5 billion, came from the company purchasing short-term capacity. Anthropic typically orders compute 12 to 18 months ahead, but is forced to buy more expensive short-term capacity when customer demand or research needs exceed what it has secured. The company attributed the decline in its adjusted operating margin to 15% from 19%, primarily to those short-term costs.

Tomasz Tunguz, founder and general partner of Theory Ventures, told Fortune that higher compute costs would put increasing pressure on Anthropic’s margins, although he noted that the company’s implied gross margin was still a healthy 85%. Gross margin counts only the cost of serving customers. It excludes the far larger sums Anthropic spends training models and on research, which are booked as separate operating expenses.

The pressure on adjusted operating margins arrived sooner than Tony Trzcinka, an investment grade portfolio manager at Impax Asset Management, said he expected. “The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost,” he told Fortune. He expects the company’s existing obligations and interconnected relationships to limit its ability to borrow at the kinds of low interest rates available to investment-grade companies. This means if Anthropic does need to take on debt to fund its compute capacity, that money will be expensive, further weighing on margins.

But paying more for compute can also help an AI company generate future revenue, Campbell Hutcheson, a senior researcher at Epoch AI, said. Frontier models, such as those Anthropic builds, can command premium prices and help improve the training and inference efficiency of other models, he told Fortune. Because revenue growth often depends on reaching a capability or product threshold first, as with ChatGPT and Claude Code, he said it can be rational for labs to pay a premium to get there first. Hutcheson said Anthropic continued to show “very strong growth, high gross margins” while investing heavily in AI research.

With about $131.8 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at September 30, Anthropic has resources to keep investing while it works to improve those economics. Its operations generated $6.6 billion in cash during the first nine months of the year. Ritter said those reserves, combined with IPO proceeds, would allow considerable investment. Trzcinka also views liquidity as a positive for bondholders, while watching for further spending commitments and any borrowing under the company’s revolving credit facility.

In estimating what Anthropic could be worth to shareholders, Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business, looked a decade ahead. His Oct. 28 valuation—which was produced prior to Anthropic releasing its third quarter results—assumed annual revenue reaching $1 trillion by 2036, a target operating margin of 27.5% and an estimated $100 billion in IPO proceeds. Those assumptions produced an equity value of about $1.475 trillion, which he described as at the lower end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion range.

Damodaran told Fortune that Anthropic’s third-quarter figures gave him little reason to revise his valuation, calling them “the most telegraphed 3rd quarter number of all time.” His earlier post had already discussed slowing revenue growth and continued margin volatility, he said. “If my intrinsic value changed significantly based on this news story, it would be neither intrinsic nor value, just a pricing chase.”

Ritter likewise saw no big surprises in the third quarter numbers, but his research highlights the risk of paying for exceptional growth in advance. In Ritter’s study, the 14 IPOs that commanded the kind of price-to-sales ratio that Anthropic is asking investors to swallow delivered returns averaging 15.4 percent below the broader stock market, measured from their offer prices over holding periods of up to three years, although some companies outperformed. Each company had at least $100 million in revenue over the 12 months before listing, adjusted for inflation to 2025 dollars.

Anthropic has substantial upside potential, Ritter said, but “a lot of things have to go right” for its revenue and profits to grow enough to support such a high valuation.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5474. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5473. What’s at stake as Nebraska voters decide whether to legalize online sports betting in the midterms

Nebraskans will vote on two ballot measures that can reshape the state’s gambling industry and bring mobile sports betting to bettors across the state.

Measures 440 and 441 on Nebraska’s midterm ballot would collectively legalize and regulate online sports wagering, allowing people located in the state to place bets on professional and college sporting events. The measures come at a time when sports betting has become one of the fastest-growing segments of the American gambling industry.

Since the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports wagering in 2018, sportsbooks have expanded into dozens of markets, turning professional sports into a lucrative business for gambling operators, advertisers and media companies.

And the state has much to gain from legalization—the biggest selling point being the possibility of generating additional tax revenue.

The two initiatives are designed to work together, but they address different parts of the legalization process. Initiative 440 is a proposed constitutional amendment. It would amend the state’s constitution to authorize legislation allowing people to place sports wagers through internet-based platforms operated by authorized gaming operators connected to licensed racetrack casinos.

“We know Nebraskans are already wagering on sports through illegal and offshore platforms or driving to a neighboring state where wagering is legal,” supporters of the measures wrote in the Nebraska secretary of state’s informational pamphlet. “This means millions of dollars in tax revenue leave our state every year. Initiative 440 keeps the money in Nebraska through a legal, regulated and secure marketplace that is projected to deliver more than $166 million in direct property tax relief to Nebraska homeowners, farmers, ranchers and small businesses over the next ten years.”

Initiative 441 is the accompanying statutory initiative. It would establish the legal framework for online sports wagering and authorize the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission to regulate operators and adopt rules governing the industry.

“This initiative requires that 70 percent of all wagering tax revenue goes directly to Nebraska’s Property Tax Credit Cash Fund,” the supporters wrote.

A vote in favor of only one measure would not be enough to establish legal online sports betting. Both must pass for the proposed system to take effect.

Nebraska already permits some forms of sports gambling, however. Voters approved casino gambling at licensed racetracks in 2020, and sports wagering became available at racetrack casinos in 2023. But residents have to visit a licensed facility to place their bets.

According to the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission, sportsbooks generated approximately $9.28 million in gross gaming revenue in 2025, nearly double the $4.71 million recorded in 2024. And that existing market has already contributed to property tax relief—Nebraska taxes gross gaming revenue at 20%, with 70% of the resulting gaming-tax revenue directed to its Property Tax Credit Cash Fund.

A study commissioned by the campaign estimates the proposed online market could generate more than $166 million in additional property-tax relief over the next 10 years. That would average roughly $16.6 million annually.

And the market for sports betting has never been bigger, evidenced by potential cross-border activity in Nebraska for sports wagers.

According to cybersecurity and geolocation compliance software company GeoComply, there were approximately 3.4 million attempts to access regulated sportsbook applications from Nebraska during the 2024-25 NFL regular season—which involved nearly 76,000 accounts. The company also recorded more than 326,000 geolocation checks at a single cornfield just across the border in Iowa.

“Thousands of bettors from Omaha cross the border into Iowa to place wagers this NFL season, driven by Iowa’s legal sports betting framework,” a GeoComply press release read. “This phenomenon has earned the nickname ‘The Busiest Cornfield in Iowa’ due to the sheer volume of geolocation checks observed in this rural area just over the state line.”

But the sports betting wave might not be as financially prosperous as it sounds. A September Bank of America Institute study found that one in five Americans view sports betting as an investment—with Gen Z respondent figures doubling to two in five.

The problem is that for the vast majority of bettors, gambling is a losing game. The study found that customers typically recover less than 75 cents for every dollar they send to betting platforms—and even Gen Z, the best-performing generation, falls short of breaking even.

The campaign behind the measures, Tax Relief Nebraska, attracted substantial financial backing from the gambling industry. According to campaign finance figures filed through the Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission, the committee had raised just under $17.58 million and spent $15.83 million through October. According to Fortune’s internal review of Tax Relief Nebraska’s NADC Form B-1 BQC filed on October 26, Online gambling companies FanDuel contributed over $7 million and DraftKings contributed over $9.5 million.

According to the American Gaming Association, the U.S. commercial sports betting industry generated $16.96 billion in revenue in 2025, a 22.8% increase from the previous year. Americans wagered a total of $166.94 billion through state-regulated sportsbooks, an 11% increase year over year. Sports betting also generated $3.71 billion in state and local taxes in 2025, up 32.4% from 2024.

The expansion has been driven in large part by mobile applications, which allow customers to wager on games without visiting a casino. At least 38 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico had legalized commercial sports betting in some form, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Pew Research Center’s 2025 analysis survey of nearly 10,000 U.S. adults found that 22% had bet money on sports in the previous 12 months, up from 19% in 2022. The increase was driven entirely by online wagering—10% of adults said they had placed a bet through a sportsbook app or website in the previous year, compared to 6% in 2022.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5472. My Layoff Was a Blessing in Disguise. The Business I Started on Instagram Is on Track for $168,000 This Year.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Abigail Morris followed her life-long passion into business.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with Abigail Morris, founder of Chicago-based full-service interior design studio Abigail Morris Interiors. In 2022, Morris started her interior design business on the side, building it as she continued her full-time career in corporate tech. After being laid off at the end of 2024, Morris went all-in on her business. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I’ve been doing interior design in some form or other my entire life without really realizing it. Mostly in giving unsolicited advice growing up — I always had strong opinions on colors and fabrics and things like that. But it wasn’t until much later that I realized I could pursue it as a career, which sounds silly. My family, with the best of intentions, encouraged me to go to business school and start a career that felt safe. So I worked in corporate tech for about 10 years.

Then, like many people during the pandemic, I had time to reevaluate. Am I really happy with what I’m doing? What’s next for me? I decided to follow that original passion for design. It felt like a now or never moment. So I took interior design classes at The Art Institute of Chicago. I got a certificate there, then started an interior design Instagram. I wanted people to know I was open for business. But I continued working full-time in corporate tech because I was still a little afraid to go all-in. I had a very comfortable job; I had the golden handcuffs.

Then, near the end of 2024, I got laid off. It was such a blessing in disguise — the universe setting me free to go all-in on my business. It was around that point that I also shifted focus to restoring historic residential and commercial properties. I have such a reverence and a passion for historic homes. They were just made with so much more attention to detail and craftsmanship.

My husband and I moved into our 1889 row home here in Chicago. Before I was laid off, I did a bunch of updates to our home and had it photographed. That helped me add to my portfolio on Instagram. The first few clients that reached out to me had also had historic homes and were attracted to me because I had that in my portfolio. The business snowballed from there. I get a lot of requests to work on historic homes here in the city and have started fielding some requests from further out in the Midwest and even on the West Coast. In the past couple months, I’ve gotten more requests for people who have newer builds who want that feeling of a more historic, character-rich home.

Earlier this year, I worked on the St. Elmo Hotel in Ouray, Colorado. I was connected with the owner, who also has a passion for preserving historic buildings. So he and his hospitality group had already done one project in Montrose, Colorado and were looking for a designer to work on a building that had a lot of original features. The goal was to celebrate those characteristics but also bring the design into the 21st century with more modern comforts. Because I already had experience working on a hotel on the National Register of Historic Places, they pulled me in.

Designing for historic properties requires discipline. A lot of times, when you go into a space and you’re redesigning, you’re starting from scratch and reimagining everything. But that’s not the case with historic properties. We have to think about what we can preserve. For example, in the St. Elmo Hotel, we kept as much wallpaper on the walls as we could. We didn’t remove any of the wainscoting or things like that and did a lot of repairs to bring things back to their original glory. So it’s about having an eye for editing before making any big design decisions.

During the first year in business, I was still getting my sea legs. I was still working full-time; it was really trial by fire. So my take-home pay was around $48,000 the first year. And I reinvested into the business significantly. Project photography is always a big investment. I also worked with a stylist and videographer. This past year, I’m on track for about $168,000 for the year. And my take-home pay will probably be around $100,000. The rest I’ll reinvest into the business — PR, project photography, etc. I’ve also brought on someone to help me edit social media reels because that’s a full time job in and of itself.

Next, I plan to make some more strategic hires to help me scale. Right now, I’m wearing too many hats. I don’t have enough time to do the design work and scale the business and client experience the way I want to. I do have a CPA and a bookkeeper, and I had an intern over the summer. But it would be great to have more support for procurement, technical drawings and other assistant tasks. I’m actually actively interviewing people this week.

In addition to hiring and scaling the business, one of the biggest challenges and opportunities ahead is the impact of AI. Currently, I use Claude and ChatGPT to help with some back-office tasks, like organizing the notes I take on my iPad while on a job site. But I’m seeing a lot of clients come in with designs they’ve made with AI, asking how to translate that to their rooms. On one hand, that’s great — I want people to have access to these tools. But these tools also require education. People have to understand that just because AI generates this picture, that doesn’t mean it’s structurally possible to implement. Or maybe it includes a specific chair that doesn’t exist.

In our current era, with AI and technology moving at the speed of light, I think people are really going to start to value craftsmanship. I think we’re going to have an arts and crafts renaissance. And I’m looking forward to how that plays out. The original arts and crafts revival in the U.S. was a result of the Industrial Revolution. Everybody was like, “We’re tired of having all this mass-produced, not well-made stuff.” We’re absolutely seeing that now. People crave a little bit of that imperfection in their home. They gravitate toward items that look like somebody actually made them with their hands versus in a machine across the ocean.

The world is getting wilder and wilder, and people definitely want to have respite in their home. They want that layered, cozy vibe. I’m really excited to be part of that.

#5471. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5470. AI is on the ballot. Data centers are a major political issue in the midterms. But the implications of today’s vote for AI go much further

Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition:

It’s election day in the U.S., of course, and in many places AI is on the ballot.Voters in dozens of states and local municipalities from California to Maine are deciding on measures that could impact the construction of hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of data center projects. Bloomberg has a great breakdown of the measures by type and state. Overall, there are at least 41 ballot initiatives involving data centers, according to election tracking site Ballotpedia. My native Ohio has the most pending, with 21 measures in total, including 11 that would either ban construction or force a pause in further data center developments.Among the most closely watched municipalities is Piqua, a 20,000-person city in west central Ohio, where Meta is planning to spend $1 billion to construct a data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. Meta promises the project will bring 1,000 construction jobs to the area, but local opposition is running high. Voters there will be deciding today whether to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who have supported the project. There’s also a $2 billion AWS data center project on the ballot in Sunbury, Ohio, as well as a $10 billion AWS project on the ballot in Adams County, Ohio.With a majority of Americans being more fearful than hopeful about AI, according to a recent Pew Research Center poll, many data center projects could be in trouble. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, at least 45 data center projects worth some $68 billion were disrupted due to local opposition, according to a report from Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs. These trends could spell trouble for the leading AI companies, which are increasingly compute constrained, as well as for the neocloud companies that have sprung up to provide AI compute. (For more on the risks facing the neoclouds, see my colleague Beatrice Nolan’s essay in last Thursday’s Eye on AI.)Many AI industry leaders are belatedly saying data center developers made a mistake in trying to rush many of these projects to market without doing enough to ensure political buy-in from the communities in which they are located. OpenAI has recently been trying to convince people to support data center projects by rebranding them as “compute campuses”—although it’s not clear that alone will do much.When Bea and I recently sat down with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in London, he told us, “before we bring in massive amounts of investment into a small community, I think we have to go first and let the community know what we’re planning to do. Partner with the community, invest in the community, and if the community really doesn’t want us to be there, find another community.” He said that he thought the industry now realizes this and has changed its approach. “Everybody is much more mindful about it,” he said. “I’m hoping we turn the tide on [data centers].” But this belated “hearts and minds” strategy from the AI industry and its data center partners may be too little, too late.All of this certainly heightens tensions around Anthropic’s upcoming IPO. In an updated prospectus made public on the SEC website yesterday, the company disclosed even more infrastructure and compute commitments than it had in its initial S-1 filing, with the figure now totaling some $895 billion. The company also revealed that it had to spend $5 billion in the third quarter to source short-term computing capacity to meet demand, saying that the added spending was one of the major reasons its adjusted operating margin fell to 15% from 19% in the prior quarter. Anthropic wants to lock in data center capacity on a longer-term basis, and even build out its own data centers through its new “Anthropic Direct” project, to lower some of these costs. But there’s a debate about whether the data center capacity Anthropic and its rivals such as OpenAI need will actually be available on the time scales they require, due to problems getting data centers built and connected to the grid. In fact, some think that Anthropic may be committing to buy more capacity from neoclouds than it actually needs precisely because it is assuming some portion of it won’t ever get delivered.

If the midterms result in a Democratic-controlled Congress, as seems possible, even likely if the polls prove correct, then AI policy could shift dramatically. The Democrats are far more likely to try to enact some kind of federal AI regulation. Before the election, the bipartisan Frontier Act looked like the bill that had the best odds of passing. But a new Congress will rejuggle that calculus and could open the path to other bills.Of course, any legislation that Congress does pass faces a likely veto from President Trump, who has been steadfast in his opposition to AI regulation. That means it will still require a bipartisan bill with very broad support to have any hope of garnering the two-thirds majority in both houses needed to override a veto. This probably still favors a bill that looks like the Frontier Act, but you never know.Another thing we may see in a Democratic-controlled Congress: a new wave of investigations into the leading AI companies and the safety and security protocols they’re implementing. Already Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has written to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to demand answers to questions about the risks the company disclosed in its IPO prospectus. Expect much more of this if the Democrats retake the Senate.

Another thing to watch for in the midterms will be what role, if any, AI plays in attempts at election interference, political misinformation, and manipulation. For years, experts have been concerned about deepfakes and other AI-generated content being used in this way. Increasingly, AI is being used to create political advertisements, as well as satirical social media memes, that can influence, or at least reinforce, people’s perceptions of candidates. But in most cases, it is clear that this political communication is AI-generated and the effort is aimed more at persuasion than deception. So far, in U.S. elections, true deepfakes have not proved decisive.The AI-focused publication The Transformer ran a piece in which it asked Anthropic’s Claude model how it would try to manipulate the midterm elections and it came up with an 11-page dossier on how to run an AI-powered influence campaign aimed at suppressing voter turnout. Interestingly, one tactic it did not pick up on, but which experts increasingly warn about, is poisoning the data that AI chatbots use to answer questions. This can take the form of trying to shift how an AI chatbot will answer questions about a candidate, their background and positions. But more insidiously, it can include efforts to mislead people about the mechanics of voting in their state, such as whether they can register to vote online.Also concerning are attempts to suppress the vote in certain districts with misinformation about problems at specific polling stations. And any attempts by AI-powered hackers to influence the election would present even more problems. OpenAI and Anthropic both announced that they have stood up war rooms to try to guard against bad actors using their models for political dirty tricks today. We’ll see what they report.With that, go out and vote! And here’s more AI news.Jeremy Kahnjeremy.kahn@fortune.com@jeremyakahn

Before we get to the news, just a reminder to check out the latest episode of our vodcast, Fortune AI Weekly. This week, Beatrice Nolan and I dissect Anthropic’s S-1, discuss a disturbing new lawsuit against OpenAI, and new research from Anthropic on how AI can impact professionals’ judgment. You can check out the vod here on YouTube.Also, if you want to find out what’s really happening in AI and learn more about how you can use this transformative technology to supercharge your business, join me and my colleagues for Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco. We have an amazing line up of speakers for you, including OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, AI luminaries Fei-Fei Li, currently cofounder and CEO of World Labs, and Andrew Ng, currently cofounder and CEO of LearnVector, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, LinkedIN cofounder and Greylock Partner Reid Hoffman, and many many more. The conference is taking place December 7-8. You can apply to attend here.

Anthropic’s growth slowed and costs jumped in the third quarter, updated IPO filing shows—by Beatrice NolanAnthropic’s third quarter results mean IPO math and history are not on its side, analysts say—by Wen ShaoWho pays for AI’s $2.6 trillion build-out? Look to corporate budgets—by Sheryl EstradaPalantir posts ‘highest-ever’ revenue growth rate of 96% as investors’ patience rests on a hair trigger—by Amanda Gerut

Wall Street pushes Anthropic toward a lower valuation. That’s according to a story in the Wall Street Journal, that reports institutional investors are telling Anthropic and its investment bankers that they only have appetite for an Anthropic IPO if it values that company in the range of $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, down from earlier talk of nearly $2 trillion. The push for a lower valuation comes amid a tech-stock selloff, rising interest rates, concerns about excessive AI exposure, data-center backlash, and uncertainty over returns on AI spending. Anthropic, which could begin its roadshow next week and have its stock market debut the week before Thanksgiving, reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, while also disclosing a staggering $895.4 billion in long-term compute purchase and lease commitments. Investors are watching the offering as a key test of appetite for AI stocks, with a successful Anthropic debut potentially opening the door to a wave of other IPOs early next year.OpenAI slashes funding target and valuation in latest round. The AI company has cut its latest fundraising target from $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation to about $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, as a sharp tech sell-off and mounting concerns over AI spending have dampened investor enthusiasm, the Financial Times reports. Some investors have reduced their allocations, although a UAE consortium including state-backed MGX is expected to be the largest participant, alongside firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz and SoftBank, the newspaper said. Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI has so far only managed to secure about $11 billion of the funding it is seeking.U.S. intelligence agencies say Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang targeted by Chinese spy. That’s according to a story in the New York Times that quotes unnamed sources saying that U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded that Alice Huang, an executive associated with Singapore-based data-center company Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to Beijing while maintaining a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. President Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago but chose not to act, amid concerns about disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, the stock market, and U.S.-China trade relations, the paper said. It also said intelligence agencies had chosen not to provide an official warning, called a “defensive intelligence briefing,” to Jensen Huang about Alice Huang. U.S. officials already suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese companies circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips, with investigators examining whether some Nvidia chips acquired through Megaspeed’s Southeast Asian operations were being illegally moved into China. The episode raises broader questions about the Trump administration’s approach to AI export controls, particularly as Nvidia’s Huang has successfully lobbied for looser restrictions on the company’s China business while developing a close relationship with the president.

OpenAI looks to make data centers less burdensome on power grids. As part of an effort to convince state power regulators as well as local communities to support data center projects, OpenAI said it was launching a new “Grid Protectors Program.” The initiative will seek to make its future AI data centers more flexible in their electricity consumption, reducing demand during periods of grid strain to help protect power supplies for homes and businesses. The program will begin with a planned data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where an agreement with Georgia Power provides for up to 1 gigawatt of flexible demand reduction—equivalent to the average electricity consumption of roughly 700,000 households. OpenAI says it will cover the full electricity and infrastructure costs associated with its facilities, while also working with utilities to use demand management, on-site power generation and battery storage to improve grid reliability and potentially lower costs for other customers. You can read OpenAI’s blog on the effort here.U.K. chip startup Fractile raises $774 million funding round. London-based AI chip startup Fractile has raised £577 million (about $774 million) in Series C funding, according to a filing with British business registry Companies House, trade publication Tech Funding News reports. The new funding comes just five months after Fractile raised $220 million in its Series B. The company is developing inference chips that keep data closer to processing transistors and claims its architecture can dramatically accelerate AI workloads. Anthropic has reportedly agreed to an initial $250 million chip order, with deployment expected in 2027.

AI can edit the weights of another model, no fine-tuning needed. That’s the conclusion of a research paper from a group of PhD. students at MIT’s Computer Science & AI Lab (CSAIL) that is getting a lot of attention this week.Normally, if you want to tune an AI model to perform particularly well at a specific task, you have to do some kind of additional training. Usually this is in the form of supervised fine-tuning, where the model is shown at least dozens and often thousands of examples, until it eventually excels at the task. (And remember, this is after the base model has already been trained on millions or billions of examples to perform a task such as predicting the next word in a sequence.) In other cases, models can be tuned through reinforcement learning, where they learn by trial and error to take actions that will maximize a reward that the person conducting the training specifies. Either way, the learning takes place through “gradient descent,” the process by which a model gradually adjusts the weights of its neural network in order to minimize the amount of error on a given task.But what the CSAIL team has discovered is that a large frontier model—in this case, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra—can, without any specialized training, read and interpret the weights of a small, open-weight model. Just by looking at the weights, the researchers say, Astra knows what the model was trained to do. And it can then edit these weights directly to improve the small model’s capabilities markedly—with no need to further train the small model at all. CSAL calls this method “weight space programming,” because it points the way towards being able to create neural networks that are “born” being able to excel at certain tasks, rather than having to learn these skills through training on thousands or millions of examples.The team demonstrated this potential by getting Astra to directly write the weights for a small game-playing model and found that it was better than a model that had been trained with a commonly-used reinforcement learning algorithm for 100 million steps. It also found that Astra could directly read the weights of Alibaba’s small Qwen3.5-0.8B model and diagnose the source of a defect that model has when it's doing certain mathematical functions (the model gets stuck in loops). By editing just 0.016% of the Qwen model’s weights, Astra is able to fix this looping defect and also boost the Qwen model’s score on a math benchmark from 7.9% to 48.1%.This is a big deal for three reasons: •First, it could dramatically lower the cost for enterprises that want to train or fine-tune their own models for specific tasks. •Second, it could be a big breakthrough in interpretability—our ability to understand the internal “thought” processes of large language models. It might be possible to simply ask one model to read and interpret the weights of another model and explain the model’s thinking to us in natural language. If true, this would be a lot simpler and more effective than other kinds of interpretability techniques. And that’s critical because interpretability is one of the ways we are hoping to keep AI agents under human control. •Lastly, while this interpretability finding would be a huge win for AI safety, I think the research also has potentially worrying implications for the safety of open weight AI models. It seems it would be easy for a bad actor with no technical skills to use a frontier AI model to edit out any guardrails or alignment measures that the developers of open weight models try to bake into their models. It was always true that a machine learning expert might have been able to tamper with these baked-in guardrails. But the CSAIL research would seem to open the possibility up to non-technical users too.You can read the paper here.

What do people working inside leading AI companies really think about AI’s risks? That is the premise of a new film series called “frominside.ai” in which current and former employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind provide on-camera testimonials about what they see as the dangers of the AI technology they are building or once helped to build. A few of the interviews are with former AI company employees who have emerged as prominent whistleblowers on AI safety, such as former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajilo. But more interesting are the five testimonials from current company employees who are much less well known. In particular, the testimonial of Mary Phuong, a Google DeepMind researcher who works on AI safety and alignment, has gone viral in AI circles because of how visibly emotional Phuong gets when the filmmakers ask her if she has any message she wishes to convey to her family or the people she grew up with about AI.

Phuong says that although her family sees her as a workaholic and obsessed with her career, which she says is “partly true," she then adds, tears in her eyes and her voice choked with emotion, “I want them to know that I am partly doing this for them. And for all of us.”

The film series was produced by Palisade Research, a nonprofit AI safety research organization in Berkeley, California, with clear ties to Effective Altruism and the more “doomer” wing of the AI research community. But, bearing that in mind, the testimonials are still fascinating, as a historical record if nothing else. You can disagree with those who think AI poses an existential risk, you can think they are deluded, but watching these video testimonials it is impossible to doubt the sincerity of these AI company employees.

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5469. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5468. I Took Back My Team’s Decisions During a Crisis — and Forgot to Give Them Back. Here’s How to Delegate Responsibly.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Pressure makes owners reclaim every hard call. Without an exit condition, that temporary grip becomes how the company decides.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The week a key hire quit mid-project, I took three routine calls back onto my desk “just until we stabilize.” Pricing exceptions. Vendor swaps. The weekly staffing puzzle. The crunch lasted about ten days. The habit lasted months.

I remember the quiet after more than the scramble. People stopped bringing recommendations. They brought questions. I had taught them, without meaning to, that judgment lived upstairs again.

Here’s my situation, so you know where I’m coming from. I run B:Side Capital, a mission-driven Small Business Administration (SBA) lender and certified community development financial institution (CDFI). I also teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern in restaurants, contractors, clinics and software shops: When pressure arrives, the owner becomes the decision system, and nobody writes the date when that arrangement ends.

Most owners treat a temporary grab of authority as common sense. It often is. Speed matters when consequences are coupled and information is thin. The failure is leaving the grab unnamed. Temporary control becomes institutional culture unless you define the evidence for returning decisions to their normal owners. Gallup finds that employees whose manager involved them in setting goals were nearly four times more likely to be engaged than others, yet only 30% of employees experience that basic expectation. Involvement dies first when every hard call routes back to one desk.

I used to treat the pull-up as proof I was carrying the load. Wrong lesson. Carrying the load can be necessary. Teaching the company that only you may decide is optional and expensive.

Start with a blank page and the decisions that repeat every week. Pricing exceptions. Hiring offers inside a band. Vendor changes under a dollar threshold. Schedule swaps. Customer make-goods. Write who may decide, what they may trade and when the call must move up. Goals without owners are theater. Strategy becomes real the moment someone knows, without asking, whether the call is theirs.

At BodeTree, I finally did this after another stretch where every exception landed in my inbox. The map was ugly in its simplicity. Ambition had concentrated judgment in one person, and I had been calling that leadership.

The principle fits in one line: Decision rights are part of strategy, not an org-chart afterthought.

Try the same map this week. Pick five recurring calls. Put a name next to each. If your name appears four times, you have a concentration, whether you plan to grow or not. A restaurant owner might find the same person owns menu specials, vendor credits and the Saturday floor. A SaaS founder might find discounting, enterprise renewals and production access share one login. Name the owners while the room is still listening.

Delegation is incomplete until the person receiving authority knows when and how to return a decision upward. Local actors need room to act, and they also hit threshold changes the original mandate did not anticipate. An escalation path defines the triggers, the response time and what context must travel with the issue. Skip it, and you get silent overreach or habitual upward deferral. Both train the wrong muscle.

I fought writing triggers because they felt bureaucratic. They are a boundary, not a binder. Act here. Come back when one of these conditions changes: risk crosses the band, purpose conflicts, spend exceeds the limit or two teams need the same scarce resource.

The principle: Hand someone the return path with the authority.

Say the split plainly when you delegate. “You own this up to X. Escalate when Y. Bring the context, not just the question.” A franchisee can do that for a regional manager. A clinic owner can do it for billing leads. A fabricator can do it for shift supervisors. Keep one annoyance unresolved on purpose: the issue that always climbs because nobody knows whether it belongs downstairs. That gap is the curriculum.

Crisis can justify concentrating authority. Comfort cannot. The moment you pull a decision upward, state what would let it move back down: a date, a restored capability, a risk threshold or an information flow that no longer needs your desk. Review observed capability against decisions people actually got to practice. Otherwise the exit test measures deprivation of opportunity as if it were incapacity.

I used to wait until things “felt normal” before returning calls. Feelings are a weak criterion. Normal never arrives cleanly. The temporary grip stays because returning authority requires a second act of courage: trusting judgment you recently starved.

The principle: A pull-up without an exit condition is a theory of leadership in disguise.

Test it this week. List every decision you reclaimed in the last quarter “just until we stabilize.” Write one sentence for each: what would justify giving it back, and who must explain if it stays with you. A retailer can stage a seasonal buy back to a buyer. A professional-services owner can return staffing puzzles to a lead. Ambition stays. The calendar gets a veto on permanent centralization.

Here’s where I’d start this week: Map five recurring calls to named owners, write escalation triggers beside each one and put a dated exit condition on every temporary pull-up still sitting on your desk. Say the return path out loud to whoever shares the risk with you.

The quiet after that quit still sits in my mind. People waiting for my nod was the real scoreboard. Write the exit condition when you take the call back, and judgment has somewhere to live again.

The week a key hire quit mid-project, I took three routine calls back onto my desk “just until we stabilize.” Pricing exceptions. Vendor swaps. The weekly staffing puzzle. The crunch lasted about ten days. The habit lasted months.

I remember the quiet after more than the scramble. People stopped bringing recommendations. They brought questions. I had taught them, without meaning to, that judgment lived upstairs again.

Here’s my situation, so you know where I’m coming from. I run B:Side Capital, a mission-driven Small Business Administration (SBA) lender and certified community development financial institution (CDFI). I also teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern in restaurants, contractors, clinics and software shops: When pressure arrives, the owner becomes the decision system, and nobody writes the date when that arrangement ends.

#5467. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

#5466. ‘Google Slides and PowerPoint Are Dead.’ Did AI Really Kill the Corporate Deck?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Another casualty of AI might be the PowerPoint and Google Slide presentation. Many are now using coding to create decks.

PowerPoint may soon be facing match point. People have been predicting the death of presentation software for decades, but AI strategist Peter Gostev reignited the debate last week with a LinkedIn post declaring “Google Slides & PowerPoint are dead,” according to LinkedIn News.

Why? The argument is that AI can now build interactive, web-based presentations from a simple prompt. Anthropic’s Claude Design turns a rough outline into an on-brand deck that exports as standalone HTML, as well as PowerPoint. Microsoft is fighting back by building AI editing directly into PowerPoint, and says new-user retention for the feature jumped 36%.

But some business owners are hungry for a new way to communicate. AI coach Braydon Carter says entrepreneurs at a recent mastermind asked him to teach them how he builds his presentations as websites using AI coding tools.

Not everyone is a fan. Skeptics point out that HTML decks are hard to edit without AI, and some corporate email filters block HTML attachments. E-Tabs founder Benjamin Rietti doesn’t think PowerPoint is going anywhere. What’s dying, he says, is “the old way of producing those decks”: the late nights, endless copying and pasting, and last-minute number checks.

#5465. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.
